(Soma flows... [more] than ever by men who are like the rays of light;
[the scriptural texts concerning specific rituals are distinct from the scriptural texts that establish the ultimate reality].
The general rule takes precedence.)
(Ātmārpaṇastava) Who is capable of comprehending you, O Supreme God of gods? ...
this [state] came to be.
"You are one who is to be grasped through devotion; nevertheless, I desire to know You through the path of supreme devotion.
This is a very great [desire]... or what is it that is sought? and so forth.
[He is] possessed of the parts of Your name... the thread of the realization of consciousness.
It is perceived as being merely like a dream, devoid of any agent or locus of action.

The insentient is not capable of presiding [over the world], nor is that which lacks sovereignty; therefore, O Lord of the worlds, you are the primordial one. Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Anila, Padmaja, Viṣṇu, and Īśa—they speak of these as you.

O Supreme Śiva, those who are deluded by your Māyā... [with these, everything that exists is contained within a mere fraction of your power; O Lord, you are known by the gods who have heard the Vedas... || 3 || (*)
Assuming an indescribable state of intense density within the ocean of bliss,
desiring eternal enjoyment together with the supreme Śakti Umā,
he is the maker of pure days, shining with millions of splendors beyond the paths of the universe.
You always dwell in the place of Kapardin, being served by the lords of the Gaṇas. || 4 ||
O Leader of the Universe, you are praised in manifold ways for your greatness by the Vedāntas; O Giver of Boons, you are worshipped with their respective rites by all the Brahmins and others.
You are [the goal] for those who are free from thirst for the mere fragments of pleasure found in seen and heard objects, and whose internal knots have been severed.
And on the final day, it is for the sake of dissolution by the hosts of yogis.
Some, meditating upon you, cross over the vast ocean of worldly existence;
others, according to the prescribed rites, constantly worship your lotus feet;
and still others, devoted to the duties of their caste and stage of life, uphold your command.
Having abandoned everything, I am sinking into the terrible ocean of existence.
Although I was born into this noble lineage that produced the Destroyer of Smara, and although I have tasted but droplets from the ocean of your majesty,
my heart has turned away from the worship of your feet due to the restlessness of my senses.
"Preoccupied with trivialities, I, a sinner, am wasting my days in vain.

Worship of you should be performed with flowers such as the *arka*, *droṇa*, and others; yet by that, one does not obtain the fruit of the Destroyer of Smara, nor the sovereign splendor of liberation."
O Śiva, Śiva! Even knowing this, I waste my time and, helpless in committing self-betrayal, I fall as a sinner. 8.
Or what shall I do, O Lord? For I am bound by this enemy—the wayward sense-objects—with a knot in the heart within this very body.
Together with him, I am being trampled by this bull who, though possessed of the fever of pride, is currently enjoying the joy of removing that very fever.
While the servant was running in the age of the sudden-seizing [era]. 9.
O Lord, remembering again and again the disease of the path of worldly existence, I am unable to restrain this collection of faculties that lead to evil conduct; I am sinking.
Alas! What shall I do? What is appropriate here? Having struck down [this body], I shall depart today.
I see no other remedy than the nectar of prostrating at your lotus feet. || 10 ||
Having transgressed the command of Him whose crest is the digit of the moon, wandering like a beast, now devoid of shame,
and having committed manifold long-standing offenses against the Lord, [I am cast] into the ocean of suffering.
How could I cross over without your grace? || 11 ||
You alone here are the bearer of the burden of this [world], the entire path of saṃsāra; yet, due to mere wretchedness and the fear of seeking [worldly things],
even now, at every moment, I remain with my limbs clearly manifest as a thousandfold [fragmentation].
Acting thus, this fool prays for [the state of] one who has crossed over...
|| 12 || He is able to cross over the entire world...
when, at the time of perfect tranquility, he places [his mind] upon the lotus of your feet.
O Lord, if at that time my mind were not devoid of the three defects [and] the pride of being the Destroyer of Cities, how could it be possible for me? 13.
When the body— its joints and bonds shattered by the force of vital breath— is overcome by the onset of passion, the grace of a friend’s lamentation, and the like,
one who possesses internal wisdom and worships Śiva crosses over [the ocean of existence] by means of [his] liberations.
For how could I, pierced by my enemies, offer myself to you?
(14) (... O Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, this very day I offer my own self, along with all its attendants, at the lotus-feet of you, my inner soul.
I am unable to fully describe your auspicious activities, rituals, yoga, and conduct; having reached this state, I seek refuge in you alone. 15.

I bow to that primordial light of the Guru, who manifested the self-luminous intellect, and who formerly created the Lord who fashioned the Creator of all worlds, and who [bestowed] upon him all the Vedas along with their meanings and Purāṇas.
Afflicted by saṃsāra, I now take refuge in the Lord of Pārvatī. 16.
He who, having bound all beings from Brahmā downwards with the noose of delusion— O Hara, Hara!— performs his own work as one superior to consciousness;
and he who, among these very beings, having liberated those who have taken refuge at his feet through knowledge...
I take refuge in You, who leads one to that supreme state of intense bliss. 17.
That which was meditated upon with effort by liberated yogis through their purified organs— [that] Brahmā,
the god who removes the fear of worldly existence, having himself appeared before them at the time of the departure of the vital breath, explains that saving Brahman.
I constantly serve you, O Lord of the Mountain, the teacher of the knowledge of Brahman. You,

who by some means pacify for those of supreme devotion the disease called saṃsāra with the medicine of the realization of one's own Self, even when it has been treated by others who are intoxicated [by ignorance].
O Lord of all, O Girīśa, I am afflicted by a great, long-lasting, and intense illness; I go to you for refuge, the physician of the cycle of existence. 19.
"I am your slave"—this has been eternally established by me in you, O Śiva; it is not something to be known through intellectual knowledge, yet even so, I wander about in delusion.
There is nothing else that belongs to me, nor even my own father.
Out of compassion, I must make this known to you; please accept this excellent refuge and the account of my conduct. 20.
Even by Brahmā, Upendra, and others, who for a long time sought their own welfare by propitiating him through various means in his presence, he was pleased; may I,
who am like an insect, likewise pray for the removal of [my] distress through faith in him.
O Lord of Wisdom, I place my trust solely in your compassion toward me, a wretched being.
O Protector, seeing that the entire accumulation of karma and knowledge is difficult to master,
and my heart being attached to evil and [unable] to restrain itself,
I am despondent within this great half-well of the city called saṃsāra.
Having reached this state where the long-extended [snares] have fallen away, I am now fearless.
You alone are the one who has destroyed the proliferation (*prapañca*) kindled by the birth of the world;
you are empty of the ocean of the accumulation of births.
Blessed are those who take refuge in your auspicious right face, which is free from affliction.
In this terrible existence, for a long time, by that [deed]...
|| 23 || You are alone, the Lord...; what is your destination as you roll among the coals of the afflictions? || 24 ||
Therefore, O Paśupati, [protect] me who have taken refuge in you from this birth in a terrible state and from existence that is subject to death, just as [you protected] him. 24.
O God, first [having been] impelled by devotion born of [faith],
[he] formerly beheld with his vision the Great Sages who have attained the state superior to the universe; [he saw them] as the bestowers of all power.
May she who effects the dissolution of the great knot remember [the Lord]. 25.
If Ākāśa, Śubhada, and Manuja are in the sixth and eighth houses, there is an end to suffering; that too, O Lord of Mountains... [and so forth]...
the intellect of men [is such] by means of those forms... [and so forth].
(..... through the preeminence of my mother, [I have attained] knowledge (vidyā) (..... and the *tilapāka* [penance], solely by your grace. || 27 ||
One who is ignorant of the various perfumes of the marketplace,
having reflected upon the armor, you have become... [the one who knows].

Whatever else there may be, even that is a refuge [only] when one has taken shelter at your lotus feet; by one who has thus surrendered, O Destroyer of Cities, the darkness of ignorance was dispelled by the mere glance of your ear, as if by the light of the rising sun. 29.
All my falsehoods, which have arisen before you and are prone to wicked activity, must be forgiven; my mind is to be disciplined.
But let not these afflictions, which are like a lotus in a pond of distress, ever approach you.
O Lord, it is fitting to abandon this man upon whom the entire burden has been placed. || 30 ||
O All-Knowing One, boundless ocean of compassion, possessed of perfect power, why do You not take account of me as I am drowning in an ocean of calamity—
me, who am alone, sinful by nature, and utterly wretched on every side due to my affliction?
O Śiva, if you rescue a living being, what great trouble is there in that? || 31 ||
"O Lord, please rescue this god who is utterly afflicted by disease and has no other recourse; O Protector, by whom has the path to your auspicious city not been trodden?
Alas, I take my stand upon desire, for that mode of supplication is highly venerable."
Protect him immediately out of compassion, having reflected upon the true nature of the abode!
O Lord, this wretched man has been led through such a multitude of wanderings; he is exhausted, there is no other refuge now—he must be liberated by you.

With your intellect devoid of discernment between what ought and ought not to be done, and with your limbs trembling in fear, what fruit will you reap as you watch him strike you while he bares his teeth? (33)
Having bound me with the snares of delusion, crying "Mother! Father! Son!", you have cast this child into the ocean of existence; alas, what sovereignty have you attained?
O Hero, do not bring further suffering upon him who has already been brought to such a state—may auspiciousness be yours.
Why is it that not even a trace of compassion arises from the lines of my destiny? 34.
Alas, my dear father, you have enjoyed that common treasure of happiness, which is like the practice of begging; having divided it [among us], you,
the leader and establisher of the boundaries for all the worlds, have departed.
What is fitting for you? Discerning that, apply yourself to this very Self. 35.
May you not be drawn from the ocean of the accumulation of births by the crocodile of worldly existence; may there be no birth for you anywhere at all.
For those devoted to you, the dust of your feet provides a satisfaction that cannot be attained through any other pleasures.
"... [offering] stars, O Lord... || 36 || "...
[in] the groves of *bhoruha* lotuses, at the supreme gateways, amidst the snow-giving [mountains], ...
among these, O Protector who removes the suffering of the wretched, [I offer] this single garland once again."
(…) he abandoned [them] in the River of Embers (…) || 37 ||
At the proper time, [she] was intent upon the welfare of the world;
with her vicinity rendered tender by the gentle touch of the breeze,
she causes men within to swell with pride.
Not even the gods can obstruct you, O Lord... || 38 ||
With his inner heart agitated by suppressed tears, he did not see Ghoṣa before him;
with his senses choked by abundant weeping, he did not hear [him];
and even though his exhaustion was extreme, he did not count it at that final hour.
O Kapardin, may my inner self be absorbed within your own self. || 39 ||
Behold within [him] the lotus-face smiling with water, adorned with the crescent moon,
and stealing the beauty of the blossoming buds of jasmine flowers;
this is not [the work] of the Creator.
(...... the form that transcends the world (......), the bestower of boons. || 40 ||
Whether in Prakrit or even in [Sanskrit], O knower of the musical notes...
the lotus-like face of yours... when indeed will your lotus-feet [be seen]?
Where is your [fortune]... where is your luck? Nevertheless, there remains hope.
Yet you do not bring me together with her; where is your compassion? (41)
"O monk, wander for alms in the cemetery;
you have learned all that is to be known.
For one who wishes to deceive and harms Vaikuṇṭha, Dhruva, and all living beings..."
Even in my dreams, I consider myself one who abandons the lotus feet of [the Lord]. 42.
May ashes be your ointment, and may the bones of the cremation ground be your constant ornaments; O Lord,
you who are capable of concealing [your true nature] through the realization of the essence of all the Vedas.
Even for you, who are born from the lotus of sovereign power, this is appropriate. || 43 ||
Even though there are various explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) intended for the gods who possess limited power— those common folk who are devoted to such [limited things]—
they do not apply to those whose devotion is directed toward Him who wears the moon as his crest-ornament.
How many lords of the world could possibly be imagined? || 44 ||
O Lord, having reflected upon how the strength and weakness of these blades of grass can be discerned in any way by those whose primary concern is merely the delay of Śiva’s arrival,
you have extracted the entire secret and made it manifest.
Our means of valid cognition has been established by the foremost among those beginning with Carasijabha. 45.
Whether in the Śītavana cemetery, or in the city of Viśvapāra,
or on the shore of Rajatābhra, or on the plateau of Ratnasānu,
or in the vicinity of Diśābhava— grant me the status of your servant.
O Supreme Śiva, [this is for] those who carry Your venerable sandals. 46.
O Blessed One, there is nothing whatsoever that my mind desires; whether it be happiness or suffering, let whatever is to come come to pass in this world.
[I am one] whose [senses] have been robbed of the splendor of the interior of the blossoming lotus.
May my mind always attain familiarity with this pair of feet. || 47 ||
Having repeatedly offered to base men my own state as leftover food from their meals, directed solely toward the goal of filling my belly, I now present here this offering of hymns of praise.
O Father, I have committed an offense against your lotus-like feet. 48.
May everything be auspicious; may you endure my worship.
The Great Umā has bestowed upon me the extraction of my mind.
In every way, being wretched, I offer only your lotus feet.
O Lord, having no other refuge, I go to you for shelter. 49.

O Blessed One, although this hymn of self-surrender was composed by me with a mind not entirely focused on You, nevertheless, since I have sought refuge in You even with mere words, protect me, O Treasure of Compassion, for I am wretched, miserable, and helpless. 50.
[The Hymn of Self-Dedication is completed.]
Oṃ. [The Discrimination of the Principle of Śiva]. May there be auspiciousness. Together with its commentary.

Salutations to Śiva, whose power is said by those learned in the scriptures to be complete even in a single part, who is the beloved of Nārāyaṇī and whose neck is as radiant as the sun; may he protect me from that forehead of his, matted with a mass of matted locks, which I recall when I was slightly agitated upon seeing Madana, who had drawn his bow to his ear and aimed the bewildering weapon at him while he was enraged.

I pay respectful homage to the great teachers (*mahāguru*), who are like the celestial *pārijāta* tree that destroys all other creepers of knowledge, and who are equal to all the Vedas; they have transcended the state of non-substantiality through the realization of the Śāstra, and their attainment is established without artifice.
May those virtuous ones be truly prosperous, in whose hearts all three have taken root by nature as a protection from the sorrow of this worldly existence.

O Lord, I have praised Paśupati with sixty verses that possess inner essence; enter the state of those whose tongues are silenced by my speech, so as to show compassion for me, who am the single inner self of the entire world.
I compose this uneven commentary on the path of the ancients, though another [work] exists today.
That which is partless, actionless, peaceful, irreproachable, and stainless— that wherein one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and cognizes nothing else— is [the state free from] delusion.
But where for him everything has become the Self alone, who would see whom?
That knowledge which is designated as Brahman is that in which all duality has subsided, which is pure existence, beyond the reach of words, and to be realized by the Self alone.
This is established by the consensus of the multitude of Śruti and Smṛti texts beginning with [the word] "mityā."

It is impossible to make Śiva— the one who has cast aside the entire manifold of distinctions such as agent and object, who transcends the sphere of all speech and mind, and who is devoid of qualities— the subject of praise.
Nevertheless, one should know that Māyā is indeed Prakṛti, and the Great Lord (Maheśvara) is the possessor of Māyā—
the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated,
and profoundly tranquil; he who is the formless, supreme Brahman, as enjoined with reverence in the Vedas.
All-pervading, eternally constant, true, and devoid of duality.
This is His divine form, characterized by the crescent moon as an ornament, with a throat dark as the *tamāla* tree and eyes shining from His forehead—features established by the Śrutis and Smṛtis.

It is presided over by an inexpressible Māyā that fashions the distinctions of qualities and the like; it is an inexhaustible ocean of jewels consisting of a multitude of gems of auspicious attributes such as being partless (*aṅga*) and imperishable (*avyaya*), and possessing a blue throat (*nīlakaṇṭhatva*).

He shines with various forms composed of pure *sattva*, distinguished by [the faces of] Virūpākṣa and others; His majesty and playfulness are celebrated through infinite synonyms such as Śiva, Bhava, Rudra, Maheśvara, Mahādeva, and so forth. He is the one whose manifestation is eternally present in the supreme city of Paraśiva—known as the Lunar World (*somaloaka*) which transcends all worlds up to the state of *unmanā*—and who dwells within the cave of the hearts of all people. He is the independent bestower of the fruits of all actions, [bestowing them upon] even Brahmā, Hari, and Giriśa, whose essential natures are fashioned by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of their respective functions, such as the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the entire universe.
[He is] the companion of Umā, the deity of the entire Brahmin lineage, designated by the term "Supreme Śiva" (*paramaśiva*). His very form, endowed with attributes (*saguṇa*), is that which—

by means of removing the clamor of the mouths and faces of the wicked who speak with evil intent, and by clearing away the persistence of long-standing evils resting within the hollows of hearts stained by even a slight trace of devotion to the lotus feet of the Supreme Śiva [which had been] uprooted by the curses of Gautama, Dadhīci, and others— establishes his own status as being superior to the universe and as the one to be served by the universe.

Desiring to praise [the Lord] with sixty verses composed for the purpose of establishing [His nature], [the author] recognizes that without an understanding of Him, there can be no success in composing a work concerning the majesty of the essential nature of Paramaśiva. For it is established by such scriptural and traditional texts as "He alone chooses him, by whom He is chosen; that God is not to be gained [by other means]," and "One should seek knowledge from Īśvara," that He is attainable solely through His grace. In this regard, just as Maheśvara becomes pleased through internal service toward men and women, so too does He become pleased through meditation.

Through such Smṛti passages as these, which teach that internal contemplation is an internal means (*antaraṅgopāya*), [the author] indicates in his heart that this alone is the most excellent auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
This suggests the meaning to be established by the hymn (*stotra*) beginning with the verse [starting with] *nāda*... and *śloka*.... [End of fragment].

May that Śiva—who, through even a mere fraction of his grace, [inspired] the ancient masters such as Śrīkānta, Druhiṇa, Upamanyu, Tapani, Skanda, Indra, Nandi, and others—bestow auspiciousness upon our hearts; he whose hand bears the seal of consciousness and is adorned with a lotus marked by a gentle smile.
Therefore, the Śruti declares: "Those who perceive Śiva in their hearts through [His] power of action (*sahatayā*)—to them alone comes prosperity, and not to others.

This is in accordance with Purāṇic statements such as: "One should meditate on Him who is without beginning or end, the abode of qualities such as bliss. Furthermore, according to the Śiva Purāṇa, [the Lord] is accompanied by the Blessed Lady Haimavatī, who is the form of the Lord’s power of will (*icchā-śakti*), and who, having ascended onto the lap of Sadāśiva, possesses the name "Peace" (*śānti*) and is endowed with infinite auspiciousness.

And reflecting upon the Blessed One as a treasury of virtues, even by a single utterance of his name without mental distraction, for the sake of shattering the mass of one's sins, one should speak the words: "He who is beyond the five [senses] is Śiva. One should dwell with him, converse with him, and eat together with him. That three-syllabled name which belongs to the Guru, by a single application of it, quickly destroys the sins of men.

Among the sciences, the Vedas are supreme; among the Vedas, the *Rudraikādaśinī*; therein, the five-syllabled mantra; and within that, the two syllables "Śi-va. By thus specifying [the deity] with the name "Śiva"—a name whose excellence in the power to destroy all evils is established by the Vedic scriptures, Purāṇas, and the eloquent sayings of the learned—he indicates the object of worship. [The word] "śiva" is derived from the root [śvi], which in this context signifies will (*icchā*) and effort (*yatna*); [the form is justified] because of the transposition of letters and because it belongs to the class of words beginning with *śādi*, which is an open-ended group (*ākṛtigaṇa*).

In this context, it should be understood that the form of the word is derived both from its status as a collection (*nikara*) of auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇaguṇa*) and through its formation as a derivative suffix (*pratyayānta*). For instance, regarding the first derivation, there is the statement of those learned in grammar:

"The word *siṃha* is formed from the root *hiṃs* [to injure]; *śiva* is remembered [as derived] from the root *vaś* [to desire]; and *paśyaka* and *kaśyapa* are established through the transposition of phonemes. Regarding the second, there is the statement from the *Vāyavīya*: "Alternatively, the Lord (*īśvara*), who is a single mass of infinite auspicious qualities, is called *Śiva* by the virtuous who know the true nature of the reality of the individual soul (*jīvatattva*). Thus it is said.

"He who constantly promotes the undertaking of capable men, desiring the welfare of humanity, is therefore known as the god Śiva"—such statements from the *Mahābhārata* and other texts establish that even well-known etymologies are intended here; for it is appropriate that worldly words possess multiple meanings according to the speaker's intention. Following the injunctions regarding the qualities of meditation, such as "with a serene face, adorned with beautiful necklaces and armlets," he qualifies [the Lord] by saying "pleasing to the mind" (*manojñā*), having fixed the mind upon Him step by step from the feet to the top of the head.

Following the rule for the description of qualities—that [the face] should be "tender with a serene smile" upon a forest lotus—he specifies it as "with a gentle smile. For the sake of attaining the realization of the desired greatness of Śiva, he contemplates Him in the form of the Guru, saying "of all," which means that He is the resting point of the lineage of Gurus for all those who possess the knowledge of Śiva. For it is said in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga Sūtra], introducing the Lord (Īśvara): "He is the teacher even of the ancients, being unconditioned by time. And it has also been stated:

In the Śiva Purāṇa: "He alone is the first teacher of the expansion of the scriptures for the Brahmās produced at each secondary creation (pratisarga), who exist within the limitations of time; he is the Guru of all those qualities associated with the limitations of time. He is the Lord of all, yet himself devoid of the limitations of time. He is Īśāna, the master of all sciences, the wise one who is the primordial Guru.

His disciple is Mahā-Viṣṇu, the great ocean of all knowledge. Thus it is stated in the Mantropaniṣad of the Śvetāśvatara branch: "He who in the beginning created Brahmā, and who [revealed] the Vedas..."

"He bestows [knowledge] upon him"—although this mantra does not clearly appear to be devoted to Śiva, nevertheless, it will be established that the *Mantra-upaniṣad* is entirely devoted to Śiva. Furthermore, because in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the context of the offering during the worship of Śiva, there is the application [of the mantra]: "He who [says], 'I offer myself to Brahmā,' [is] the Lord"; and: "He who formerly made me his son and bestowed knowledge upon me, by whose grace I attained this station of Prajāpati"—[referring to] Brahmā, whom the sages created first, for him...

"Maheśvara bestowed all these [scriptures] which reside within himself upon the Brahmins. From such statements in the Śiva-purāṇas, the Matsya-purāṇa, and other sources, as well as from the words of Brahmā and others, it should be understood that this [text] has Śiva as its ultimate purport (*śivaparatva*). He clarifies the aforementioned point by citing specific disciples of various great souls, beginning with "Śrīkānta": Śrīkānta and the others are well-known teachers who possessed divine knowledge (*śrivajñānin*). By the word "and others" (*ādi*), [the following are included]: the Mahābhārata, Kūrma-purāṇa, Śaiva, Saura, Skānda, Laiṅgya, Śivadharma, and so forth.

[The author] distinguishes [the feet] of Svāyambhuva, Vāyu, Vasiṣṭha, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Jaimini, and [others] by means of the mark of liberation (*mukti-cihna*). Regarding "the seal of consciousness" (*cin-mudrā*): the compound *pāṇir nalinam iva* is an upamita-samāsa (compound of comparison). One should meditate on the form of the connection between the seal of consciousness and [the feet], which has arisen...

Here, by the qualification beginning with "ending in -ktvā," the state of Śiva—His being superior to the universe, His being the object of service for the universe, and His being the object of worship—is established by means of the hymn.
It should be observed: in this way, [he] investigates the supreme knowledge which is the means of valid cognition for the purpose of establishing [the goal]... ||1||

The primordial Vidyā, whose sole purpose is the proclamation of the supreme excellence of Paraśiva, and who is the wind that fans the fire of [His] glory through the splendors of [the various] manifestations, most intensely worships Him as the soul of knowledge. Transcending the three forms, the Lord of Māyā is the lower Śiva;
and the Supreme Śiva is solely intent upon proclaiming His unsurpassed excellence. This statement is not merely a pleasant breeze, but is the defining characteristic of the Great Purāṇas.

The mention of Tapa refers to the Āditya Purāṇa as representative of the Upapurāṇas; the mention of Vyāsa refers to the Mahābhārata; and by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the authors of the Smṛtis, Kalpasūtras, and Śivāgamas—namely Manu, Yājñavalkya, Bodhāyana, Āśvalāyana, Upamanyu, Kumbhasambhava, and others—are included. Thus, these very [authors] are praised throughout all the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Smṛtis, Kalpasūtras, and Śivāgamas; and by virtue of both the natural sense of the words and these praises, they are established as being beyond doubt and not subject to any other interpretation.

The meaning is: "May the instruction on the true path—which consists of the *Atharvaśikhā* and other such forms of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), whose composition of meanings is crowded within the hearts of the Vaidikas, and which brings benefit to all people—prevail with supreme excellence in the world. By means of this hymn, everything that is about to be established will be established as being firmly rooted in the Śruti.

Furthermore, it is indicated that the refutation of the false view that the sentences of the Śruti intend some other [non-literal] meaning, and the citation of the natural force of the words (*śabdasvārasya*), will be carried out through the two [criteria] of consistency and non-contradiction with the Brahman. Now, that which the Sun...

Having raised the objection that, because of the scriptural hearing of "He is known" and so forth, one lacks the authority to praise the Supreme Brahman whose majesty is incomprehensible even to the immortals, he provides the resolution. ||2||

Therefore, enough of desiring to measure the power of the Supreme Śiva, O Immortal One, or to praise Him; abandon this wish by all means. Nevertheless, the thought that even a mere repetition of the recollection of Your name may be a vessel of merit, however difficult it may be to attain from any quarter, impels me here. This undertaking in the composition of a hymn to Śiva is not for the sake of manifesting my own intimacy or cleverness; rather, since the intellect of the dull-witted falters regarding Him whose majesty cannot be measured even by Brahmā and the other gods, such a failure is unavoidable.

It might not necessarily be an object of ridicule; therefore, if it were necessary to avoid such derision, one might act accordingly. However, for those wandering in the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) with minds distracted by various evil activities, the continuous contemplation of the name of Śiva is difficult to attain without some means. Thus, following the maxim "in every way, that which is beneficial to oneself," and in accordance with the *Smṛti* texts stating, "One should fix the mind on Śiva by whatever means possible," one should practice the contemplation of Śiva and the recitation of His name by any means whatsoever.

"That it is not a fault" is the intended meaning of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Now, having set forth the misconception of those non-Vedic people who are addicted to reviling Śiva and who cannot endure the excellence of Śiva—the subject matter to be established by this hymn—he demonstrates that their exclusion from the company of the virtuous and the fruitlessness of their ritual actions are established by the scriptures. ||3||

He clearly declares, "I alone am the Self, superior to all," and "I am to be served by the world"; yet, alas, the wicked still dispute this! Is it that they have a vice for hostility toward You? Or is it that they lack the capacity to hear the life-giving speech? [The meaning is: Why has the Veda proclaimed such things as, "Rudra is superior to all," and "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon"? The mantra reveals this very point: "They seek Rudra within themselves through supreme wisdom... [and so forth].

"By means of [his] nature, he stands... beyond the other, the supreme, the most excellent, Rudra... By means of his intellect, they act like outsiders (*tīrthyāyanti*); they wander; they consume the food of transformation through their vow. Regarding the word of the mantra, "They seize with the tongue the one who is within the mouth," this is a praise of what is not the subject at hand, as in the case of [the verse] beginning with "The winds indeed carry away. The term *kaṭākaṭaḥ* is used in the sense of going. Thus it has been explained.

[The text] beginning with *parāśa...* [describes] that which is being offered as a fault, [and] that which is swallowed by the one with the excessive tongue... this very [thing] is the water of nectar filled with flavor. Now, those who do not desire Bhava accompanied by Bhavānī—[for them], it is merely excrement... by that [statement], the intended meaning has been shown. By the second [reading], the implied meaning is... because it is itself sublated, it results in their speech being censurable. And this meaning is shown in the Mahābhārata: "Fie on them! Fie on them!"

(... "Rudra dwells in the heart through liberation from the path of evil intellect. This very meaning is demonstrated in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* after introducing it thus: "The unfortunate ones laugh at what has been practiced. There, "unfortunate" (*durbhaga*) means those born in an inauspicious field (*kukṣetra*). Having established that such a state is indeed a mixture (*saṃkara*), it is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "May one not be born in such a family [where] Śambhu is not the deity. Thus, by the statement regarding being devoid of devotion (*anurāga*)...

The very fact that [he] is to be excluded has been indicated. And this has been explained in many ways in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* and other texts; the meaning is that [his efforts] were struck down and rendered fruitless—because he was to be excluded here [in this world] and because he was averse to all Śaivas in the next. Having stated this very point, he establishes it by means of logic as well, with the words "yaduktiḥ" (as for what was said). For it is said in the *Bhāgavata*: "When the Lord, having ordained [the fate] of Karṇa and others, cast him into hell due to his lack of virtue, and while Indra was being honored, [Yama] should forcibly cut through that harsh bridge... [etc.]

"If the Lord [should hear] even our lives, He would then release them according to righteousness. The meaning of this is: when the Lord, the protector of Dharma, is being defiled by the lowest of men—who are unrestrained and have cast aside the bounds of propriety—one should quickly depart, covering one's ears so that not even the sound of a single word of defamation is heard. If one is unable to restrain them, but is able, one should forcibly break through those wicked ones intent on defamation. However, one who habitually listens to the intentional defamation of Śiva should even give up his life; and he—

The sacrifice of life [for such an offense] is indeed a religious duty (dharma), just like the sacrifice of life caused by drinking liquor and other such acts. Thus, since it is established that those who hear the disparagement of Śiva must undergo penance ending in death, there can be no penance for those who themselves delight in disparaging Śiva; they must be excluded by the virtuous in every respect. What more need be said? They are of fruitless life. And this has been clearly stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa, in the section on the rules for penance for all sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, regarding other deities:
Following the prescription of penances for general censure, there is an absence of penance for the censure of Śiva:
"For him who censures the Lord of the Universe, who is worshipped by all beings,
no expiation can be made even in hundreds of years."

Although by this method of exposition, a penance ending only in death (*maraṇānta*) is indicated for the disparagement of Śiva—since in cases concerning penances ending in death, such as the rule "no atonement is prescribed for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa," the traditionalists (*smartṛs*) are seen to employ the term "absence of atonement" (*niṣkṛtyabhāva*)—nevertheless, it should be understood that when a certain penance is prescribed for hearing a disparagement, the principle dictates that for actually performing that disparagement, the penance must be greater; thus, in this case, a penance ending in death involving extreme suffering presents itself. As for what was stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* regarding the disparagement of Śiva:

The rule for the final expiation is as follows: "One who has sought refuge in the Lord, having first performed the Cāndrāyaṇa, the Kṛcchra, and the Atikṛcchra penances, is liberated from sin. Furthermore, regarding that which is prescribed as an alternative expiation upon hearing [the scripture] during the festival of the Eightfold Form (Aṣṭamūrti): "If one is unable to punish a fool intent on reviling Śiva, he should pour water into his own ears... All this must be properly established according to the specific qualifications of those entitled [to perform the rites].

In this way, he censures those who are non-Vedic, haters of the Lord, and fools—by means of various turns of phrase from the Śruti and Smṛti, such as "For He alone makes him perform good deeds" and "This creature is ignorant and powerless"—[showing that they] do not even perceive [the truth]. ||4||

Or rather, what need is there for these wretched beasts among men? Indeed, you do not desire [such a being]. A living creature who, having destroyed its own self and everything else, acts thus—how can it be blameworthy, O Paśupati, since you yourself impel it to act in that way, being under the sway of another Śiva? He confirms the very point already stated by means of reasoning. ||5||

(... For indeed, having observed each one [of these], and having heard the teaching proclaimed in all the Vedas, O Blessed One whose crest is adorned by the crescent moon, how could these [sages] not [acknowledge] Your sovereignty, were they not [themselves] sinners? Demonstrating that those of my own ill fortune are deluded either because the true nature of Śiva is beyond determination or due to the diversity of their karma, he establishes [the point] through the maxim of the "needle in the haystack" (duravadhāraṇatva-śaṅkita-kanyāyena). ||6||

O Hari, even upon seeing you first, let the deluded Śatadhṛti (Brahmā) not recognize your presence; and O Slayer of Smara, let the hundred-fold sacrificer (Indra) likewise fail to know the state of your daughter.
What need is there for others? Even Viṣṇu, joined with the ritual of praising you, was bewildered therein.
O Master, what conversation can there be with one who is so utterly dull and wretched?

The qualification "even though he was the best" (*śreṣṭho 'pi vimūḍhaḥ*) is to be supplied (*anuṣaṅga*) to the subsequent sentences concerning Śatakratu (Indra) and Vaikuṇṭha (Viṣṇu), even though they were the ones who caused the loss of glory [to the former]. According to the *Laiṅga*, *Kūrma*, *Saura*, and other Purāṇas, it is said that in ancient times, the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*), seated upon the lotus from Nārāyaṇa’s navel, was overwhelmed by pride regarding his task of creating the world; yet, seeing Mahādeva—who had descended for the sake of bestowing grace—though he was not of the material nature (*aprākṛta*), he failed to comprehend His majesty. It was only through the instruction of Śrī Nārāyaṇa that he somehow came to understand that majesty.

It is heard in the *Talavakāra Upaniṣad* that once Indra, arrogant due to his internal sense of power and the arms of the Asuras, beheld Mahādeva in the form of a Yakṣa who had manifested for the purpose of subduing his pride and bestowing grace upon him; yet, even upon seeing him, Indra was not freed from delusion until he was instructed by Haimavatī, who was present at that time, regarding the majesty of Śiva.

This is also narrated in the *Skanda*, *Liṅga*, and *Śiva Purāṇas*. Once, Hari, while disputing with Brahmā (Kamalāsana) over preeminence, [stood] between them for the sake of awakening the truth of both.

Having perceived Śiva manifested in the form of the Great Liṅga—whose base and summit were unperceivable—and yet failing to attain the play of its majesty, he determined that its sovereignty surpassed all others, including that of Brahmā, solely through the instruction of that very one who is supremely compassionate; this is recited in the *Śaiva*, *Kaurma*, and other Purāṇas, and these three narratives have been composed here. Alternatively, the conviction regarding that majesty is obtainable only through the grace of Śiva; therefore, due to their lack thereof, that [conviction] did not arise for them—this is the intended meaning.
He says this following the mantra beginning with "nāyamātte" (he is not taken). ||7||
This [faith] is not easily obtained through the power of the teachings of the Lord of Refuge in you,
nor through an abundance of intelligence, nor by application to various treatises;
only through the grace of the Victorious One do the wise attain it.
How indeed could those of wicked intellect, being so difficult to tame, ever attain it?

Alternatively, since devotion to Śiva is of the nature of the supreme good (paraśreya), being both the cause for the cessation of all misfortunes and the cause for the attainment of all human goals, [the author] speaks with the following intention: even for those seeking trivial benefits, a divine obstacle is inevitable among the many obstacles that beset people; therefore, through that [divine] obstruction, [the obstacle to the goal] is removed.

For those devoid of a collection of merits accumulated over many births, there arises no conviction regarding the greatness of Śiva, which is necessarily associated with the attainment of various fruits. ||8||

How is it that devotion to Your glorious lotus-feet has somehow arisen? Alas! It is the destroyer of all sufferings, the sole reality for all human goals, [attained] without [effort] through hundreds of thousands of previous births.
Indeed, one does not obtain even a mere measure of what is beneficial for oneself, as it is beset by many obstacles.

The meaning is: "in some way or other," even with a desire for some slight fruit. Although, O Lord of Gods, when one acts with a specific fruit in mind, my refuge becomes insignificant—since a seeker of fruit is capable of abandoning me in its absence, and thus such activity directed toward a fruit renders [the refuge] trivial; nevertheless, even that [activity] is indeed an obstacle to that person, yet by producing a sense of extraordinary confidence through the accomplishment of the fruit, it gives rise to the aforementioned form of meaningful devotion endowed with the eight complete signs. Therefore, it is said that even this [devotion] is difficult to attain.

He says that in the absence of the fault of the Kali age—which is free from the exceptions to the curses of Dadhīci and others—there would be no arising of faith in the excellence of Śiva among them: "Those whose darkness has been dispelled by various merits accumulated through worldly existence, who are devoted to self-restraint (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and virtuous deeds, strive to know You. But those whose minds are defiled by the impurities of the Kali age and whose intellects are dull, even though they are of the same nature as Dadhīci, the son of the Mountain Lord (Śiva), and others, would fail to understand You even after making [efforts]. Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from possessiveness; purity, contentment, austerity, and self-study..."

The rules concerning the worship of Śiva as the primary deity, as well as other rites that counteract the defects of the Kali age—such as the single purification of these defects in this kind of Kali Yuga, namely, "the salutation of Mahādeva, meditation, and the gateway [of initiation]," as established by the words of Vyāsa—one who is devoted to those is the intended meaning. The curse of Dadhīci is shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Having spoken thus... regarding those haters of the Lord who were cursed, the Brāhmaṇas who had assembled there to assist Dakṣa were excluded from [the sacrifice]."

"Mahādeva Śaṅkara, who is praised by those who recite the Vedas and revered by the world, has been reviled by you. You shall all become haters of the Lord (Īśvara), speaking against the threefold Vedic speech. Indeed, censuring the divine [teachings], with minds attached to false scriptures, following improper study and conduct, and deluded by false knowledge, you will reach the terrible Kali Yuga. Afflicted by strife in that age of discord, you shall abandon the entire forest of asceticism and go once more to the hells. Even Hṛṣīkeśa, though he has taken refuge in you, will turn his face away."

In that very section concerning the proclamation of the defects of the Kali age, it is said: "The twice-born, who were formerly consumed by the curse of Dadhīci at Dakṣa’s sacrifice, will indeed take incarnations in the families of Brāhmaṇas; with their minds possessed by darkness (tamas), they will revile Mahādeva. Referring specifically to them, it is recited in the Saura Purāṇa: "In the Kali age, there will be twice-born ones devoted to the reviling of Śiva by taking refuge in Puruṣottama; Mādhava shall not be their protector. And in the Skanda Purāṇa, in the Śaṅkara-saṃhitā, within the section on the worship of Śiva, it says: "One should not look [at them]..."
At the time of the worship, having said, "O child, he has been excluded," and upon the inquiry as to who that excluded one is, it was stated:

"The lowest of Brahmins, cursed by Dadhīci for the sake of the sage Gautama, will descend in the Kali age; they are the revilers and they are the excluded. In this way, the curses of Bhṛgu and others as set forth in the Skanda Purāṇa and other texts are also to be understood. The phrase "son of Danu" means those who, being permeated by the quality of darkness (tamas), do not undertake actions that refute the defects of the Kali age.

"In the Kali age, Rudra Mahādeva is the supreme Lord of the gods; there is no other deity for men, nor is there any deity higher than Him"—since this passage sets forth the defects of the Kali age, the meaning is that [people] have been blinded by the delusion produced thereby. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that no one at all possesses such wholehearted faith in the majesty of Śiva, nor performs worship with devotion corresponding to that, nor attains the fruits appropriate thereto? Rather, [faith] belongs to the Blessed Nārāyaṇa. To this, he replies by means of an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) regarding faith in the majesty of Śiva and so forth: [the following verse].
This indicates an extreme rarity. ||10||

O Giver of Boons, in this world, the Lord who wears the forest garland (Vanamālī) alone is victorious; He alone is capable of knowing Your boundless majesty, of establishing supreme devotion toward Your feet that is eternally unshakable like the Himālaya mountains, or of attaining Your abundant grace through Your worship. Since the attainment of all other goals is already accomplished simply by receiving His grace, they are not mentioned separately.
Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana is indeed the eternal Viṣṇu himself.
For who else truly knows that Rudra as the Supreme Lord?
Indeed, there shall never be anyone equal to Arjuna in devotion to Śambhu.
Except for the son of Satyavatī, Kṛṣṇa, or the son of Devakī.

Thus, through such statements from the *Kūrma Purāṇa* and other sources, it is established that Viṣṇu possesses both a thorough knowledge of Śiva’s greatness and an excellence of devotion toward him. As for the statement in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, in the [fifth] skandha, where Brahmā addresses the gods who are praying for the pacification of the enraged Śiva: "Neither I, nor sacrifice, nor you, nor others who possess bodies, nor even the sages, know the truth regarding the measure of the power and heroism of Him who is independent of all else, whose ways are unfathomable. And as for what is said to Śiva in the eighth skandha...

The words of the deity [state]: "O Girīśa, that supreme light—which is inaccessible even to all the world-protectors, Viriñca, [Viṣṇu], and the lord of the gods in Vaikuṇṭha, and which transcends rajas, tamas, and the three qualities—is beyond the reach of others. Thus, by the logic of *akamut* (the "how much more" argument), these [passages] are intended to show that the reality of Śiva is difficult for other beings to grasp. However, there is no contradiction in [other passages] being intended to reveal the nature of Hari, as his superiority over all is established by the statement: "Just as I... and so forth.
"Since there is no other [refuge] for me than Him who has been ordained for those who perform their duties... thus from the words of Śiva in the *Sauṣaptika* [section].
Let the Lord alone be [my refuge], whose nature is not fierce; Viṣṇu is beyond recitation and immutable.
Having known Bhava as the form of all, he worships that Lord in the *liṅga*."

"What kind of joy does he not produce in him, O Bull-bannered One? From this statement by Vyāsa in the Droṇaparvan, it is established that through the grace of Śiva, he attains the highest of all states. Regarding the *liṅga* as the locus of Śiva’s manifestation, described as "the mind purifies itself for the sake of Your glory; the lineage [of devotees] goes toward Rudra, the beautiful and wondrous," it is shown by the wording of the mantra to be sixfold. The state (*pada*)...

The meaning of the verse beginning with *yad viṣṇoḥ upamaṃ dhāyi* has been clarified in the *Parāśara Purāṇa*: "Having worshipped with devotion a pure stone image of Mahāviṣṇu, beautiful and variegated, he attained the supreme state. Furthermore, in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*, in the chapter on the consecration of the Four-Armed One (*Caturbhujābhiṣeka*), it is described how, following his coronation as king (*paṭṭābhiṣeka*), Śiva granted Viṣṇu the entire abode of Vaikuṇṭha, sovereignty over the whole world, valor exceeding even his own, and other qualities difficult for others to attain. And in the *Āraṇyakaparvan*... [text fragment].
Regarding the procedure for the pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā):
From there, one should go to Suvarṇākṣa, renowned throughout the three worlds,
where in ancient times Viṣṇu propitiated Rudra for the sake of obtaining his grace.
And he obtained many excellent boons, difficult even for the gods to attain;
and it was said by the gratified destroyer of Tripura, O Bhārata:
"Moreover, O Kṛṣṇa, you shall become the most beloved in the world among all others."
"And the entire world shall become your mouth; of this there is no doubt. Thus it was established.

Furthermore, in the Droṇaparvan, in the chapter on penance (Tapodhyāya), it is elaborated that the Blessed One granted supreme valor and other qualities to Nārāyaṇa, who had propitiated him through ascetic practice for sixty thousand years on Mount Maināka. And in the Harivaṃśa, in the Pārijāta-saṃhitā: "Thus being praised, the Blessed One whose banner is the bull..."
Stretching out his right hand, he then said to Vāsudeva:
"O best of gods, may you obtain all the objects you desire."
And you are devoted to the Pārijāta; let there be no distress in your mind.
Formerly, when you performed penance taking refuge on Mount Maināka, [it was for this tree].
Then, O Kṛṣṇa, remembering my words, attain steadfastness:
you are not to be slain, you are invincible, and you are even more heroic than I.

"I said 'you shall become [so],' and since it was not done otherwise, so it came to pass"—this and other such statements should also be understood as established by the Śaiva scriptures and other authorities. Now, desiring to demonstrate the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Śiva and the qualities resulting from it in order to establish His supremacy over the universe, he first describes His true nature as free from all adjuncts. (Verse 11)

That which they call infinite, whose nature is unsurpassed existence, consciousness, and bliss; which is clear of the entire multitude of duality that has been overcome; which has arisen as the inner self (pratyak); which is to be known through the mass of Upanishadic statements whose meaning is indivisible—that light of Mahādeva is known as you, the Supreme Self. To begin with, the various Vedāntas establish the Supreme Brahman: some are grounded in the referent of the word *tat* (*padārtha*), such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and "It is neither gross nor subtle"; while others, such as "He who consists of consciousness," are grounded in the referent of the word *tvam*.

Some [great sentences] are based on the meaning of words (*padārthaniṣṭha*), while others are based on difference (*bhedaniṣṭha*) and take the form of great sentences (*mahāvākya*), such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*), and "Consciousness is Brahman" (*prajñānaṃ brahma*). Following the word *tat*, the meaning of the word *tvam* is shown by the term "the inward-facing one" (*pratyak*). When the objects of the ego-identification (*abhimāna*), such as the body and the senses, are being projected outward as "this" (*idantā*), the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) moves, as it were, in the opposite direction toward the interior; because it moves thus, the individual soul (*jīva*) is called the "extracted ego" (*niṣkṛṣṭāhaṃkāra*).

By the remaining qualifiers, that very state [of Brahman] is shown. Therein, by the qualifiers "whose nature is being, consciousness, and bliss" (*saccitsukhavapuḥ*) and "the infinite self" (*ātmānantam*), the inclusion of the five attributes—beginning with bliss—which were established as things to be combined in the Sūtra "Bliss and so forth belong to the Pradhāna" (*ānandādayaḥ pradhānasya*), is demonstrated. By the phrase "having transcended all beings" (*parābhūta-*) and so forth, the inclusion of qualities such as "not coarse" (*asthūla-*) and so on, which were determined as things to be combined in the Sūtra "The cognitions of the Imperishable" (*akṣaradhiyām*), is likewise shown. This is the distinction. And this is their combination... (Note: The ellipsis at the end of the provided text indicates that the source sentence was truncated.)

The teachers have demonstrated with great precision that [this] leads to the realization of the Brahman free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Others, however, consider it to be for the purpose of quenching thirst. By means of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—that the light is of the nature of the Self—the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) has been shown. Since the state of being free from conceptual proliferation could not be established by those means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whose intent is directed toward creation, it is stated [in the subsequent sections] by means of the latter portions.

Even for such a Brahman, because its sole essence is the favoring of the world, [the text] now describes its qualified form (*saguṇa-rūpa*), which is supreme over all and characterized by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the divisions of qualities and so forth as they are conceptually constructed.

Though you transcend all attributes, you appear as if possessed of attributes, variegated by *māyā*; adorning with Ambā your dark-throated, three-eyed form, you are renowned by the names Śiva, Bhava, and others, and thus you are victorious.
He is the controller of the worlds, including those of Hari, Hara, and the lotus-born Brahmā.

By the word "iva" (as if), he indicates that because qualities (*guṇa*) are merely imagined, they lack entry into reality. For this very reason, since the connection with name and form (*nāmarūpa*) is also understood to be imagined, there is no separate mention of it. The meaning is that [the Lord] is adorned with qualities such as omniscience and others designated as "limbs" (*aṅga*), such as knowledge and dispassion; those designated as "imperishable" (*avyaya*), such as sovereignty; those designated as "fortune" (*bhaga*), and others such as having true desires. He states the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which accounts for the qualities even in one who is essentially devoid of qualities: "by *māyā*," meaning by *māyā* consisting of ignorance, which serves as the limiting adjunct for the reflection of consciousness.

The meaning is that [the Lord] is superimposed as the substratum (*bimba*)—or rather, He is superimposed by way of being a reflection (*pratibimba*) within the limiting adjunct of *māyā*, which is distinct from *avidyā* and consists primarily of pure *sattva*.

By the term "Śiva," all the names of Śambhu well-known in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, Purāṇas, lexicons, and so forth, are understood through their association with His qualities. Alternatively, it means by the eight [names] beginning with Śiva and the eight beginning with Bhava. Although there are other names of the Blessed One such as Śambhu, Śaṅkara, and so on...
There are hundreds of names;
nevertheless, he is proclaimed as Śiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha,
the Physician of Saṃsāra, the Omniscient One, and the Supreme Self.

"This meritorious octad of names of Śiva, the Supreme Self, is a secret extracted from all the scriptures as their very essence," and so forth; for by such statements, the excellence of the eight names beginning with Śiva is established among the secret [texts], and the eight names beginning with Bhava are present in the mantras of the Āpastambas as the Self.

In the Āpastamba-sūtra, in the *Īśānabali* section of the Bodhāyana and Āśvalāyana-sūtras, in the *Śūlagavahoma* and [related] sūtras, in the ritual for the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of Mahādeva, in the rules for daily worship (*nityapūjā*), and in the rules for worship at dusk (*pradoṣapūjā*), as well as in the descriptions of the application (*viniyoga*) of oblations, libations, and offerings, its preeminence is understood through its specific characteristics; it is with this intention of preeminence that it is specifically mentioned here.

Regarding this, some do not accept a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*) beyond the *guṇamūrtis*, which serves as the cause of all things. Others, however, hold that the body is merely conditioned by *māyā*.

They consider that words such as "Supreme Brahman" (parabrahma) employed in the *Śārīrakasūtra* denote that [Brahman] which is expressible by the term "Mother. From both these perspectives, the assumption of a physical form (vigraha) of the nature described—namely, being denoted by terms such as Śiva and Bhava—belongs to the Guṇarudra included within the triad of forms (trimūrti), just like [the other two]. Consequently, one might think that the Brahman presented in the hymn is flawless in that very form. To preclude this, he specifies [Him] as "He who is Hari and Hara. This is the intention: in the *Brahmopaniṣad*, it is stated: "Now, this Person has four stations..."

The navel, the heart, the throat, and the head—therein the four-footed Brahman shines forth: as Brahmā in the waking state, as Viṣṇu in the dreaming state, as Rudra in deep sleep, and as the Fourth (*turya*) in the state beyond [the eye/sun]... [and] as Īśvara in the celestial realm (*viṣṭapa*). Thus, a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*), designated by the term "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) and consisting of all the gods, is shown to be superior to Brahmā and the others. Its very nature is such that "the gods, the sages, and the ancestors rule there"—thus its non-dependence on another lord is established; and through such statements as "The one God wanders within all beings like a bee," its status as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all is demonstrated.

And the bestowal of the fruits of all actions has been shown in the *Taittirīyopaniṣad* and elsewhere: "The letter *a* is Brahmā at the navel, the letter *u* is Viṣṇu at the heart, and the letter *m* is Rudra between the eyebrows. Thus, after describing the method of worship for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—who are denoted by the three vowels beginning with *a*—located respectively at the navel, the heart, and the space between the eyebrows, [it proceeds to describe] the Lord of All (*Sarveśvara*), who is denoted by the collective measure (*samaṣṭi-pramāṇa*) and is to be worshipped at the *dvādaśānta*, [endowed with] all sovereign powers (*sarvaiśvarya*).

Another supreme reality has been shown. In the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*, by such passages as "Salutation indeed to this one" and "He goes to this; this is indeed the form of *rajas*," and so forth, having described the division of the qualities (*guṇa*) of the darkness (*tamas*) called ignorance (*avidyā*) through the volition of another who presides over that darkness, its [emanations] have been declared: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others. Furthermore, his *rājasa* portion is he who is Brahmā, and indeed he who is... [the text continues].
"Let him dwell... that portion which is this Rudra; or else, let him dwell as the *sāttvika* portion, for all this is Viṣṇu.

By thus establishing that Brahmā and the others are distinct portions of the Supreme who presides over *tamas* and is endowed with qualities such as *rajas*, it is made clear that there exists a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*) higher than them. In the *Yogayājñavalkya*, during the description of the deities of the *praṇava* and its constituent elements (*tanmātra*), it is said: "These three syllables are held to be the three forms (*kāra*). The cause of these three is the form of the portion of Brahman, the cause of all. It is the single syllable..."

"The wise call that supreme light the Praṇava. By such statements from the Bhāgavata and other texts—beginning with "I, Brahmā, and Śarva are the three causes of the world"—which declare the Lord's words regarding those deities consisting of the *mātrās*, it is made clear that there exists another divinity of the Praṇava who is superior to the *guṇa-mūrtis* (the forms of the qualities), which are well known as the three causes. Furthermore, in the Bhāgavata, Viṣṇu Purāṇa, and other works, it is stated: "Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas are the qualities of Prakṛti; the Supreme Person, joined with them, assumes here [in this world] these [forms], as well as [the functions of] maintenance and so forth."

The designations Hari, Viriñca, and Hara [are applied] therein; indeed, by such statements as "among men, through [the qualities of] goodness and so forth, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva themselves are the primary powers of Brahman," the Supreme Brahman, which transcends the three forms, is manifested. Moreover, it is undisputed that Brahman, the cause of the world, is consciousness whose means is *māyā*.

It has been stated in the Aitareya Upaniṣad that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are indeed consciousness (caitanya) conditioned by the specific qualities (guṇaviśeṣa) of that [Supreme Being]. Furthermore, this is established without dispute in the Tāpanīya Upaniṣad and all the Purāṇas and other texts, which declare: "She is manifold, firm, and possessed of many sprouts; though she is divided by the qualities within those sprouts that are themselves divided by the qualities, she exists everywhere in the form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. Consequently, since a distinction in the substrate (upahita-bheda) is appropriate when there is a distinction in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi-bheda), [the distinction between the forms] from the Guṇamūrtis...

It is as firmly established as a diamond-encrustation that Brahman is the cause of the world, characterized by supreme *upādhi*s; and its body, which consists of Umā in union, is understood from such mantras of the *Kaivalyopaniṣad* and others as "the Lord who has Umā as His companion," "the Supreme Parameśvara," and "the Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, its designation by terms such as Śiva, Śambhu, Rudra, Īśāna, Maheśvara, and Mahādeva is determined through both the usage observed in the *Atharvaśikhā* and other texts, as well as etymological explanations (*nirvacana*). Nor should it be suspected that the possessor of attributes (*guṇin*) taught in the collection of cited Upaniṣads is Rudra; for in every instance therein—

Since Rudra is also mentioned among those manifestations (*vibhūti*)—just as Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa are—it might be argued that the word "Rudra" occurring there in the midst of the manifestations refers not to the Guṇin-Rudra (the Supreme Rudra), but to another Rudra who is a constituent part of him. However, this should not be said; for it is generally observed that the word "Rudra," when mentioned in proximity to Brahmā and Viṣṇu, appropriately refers to the Root-Rudra of dissolution (*saṃhāramūlarudra*), according to the principle that "that which is understood to be such [is so]. Now, even so, [one might object] regarding the *Kaivalya* and other mantras... always.

If it is argued that because the Supreme is beyond [form], worship is possible even through a superimposed form, and thus the existence of a described form for the Supreme is not established—[we reply: even regarding those passages intended for worship, since there is no contradiction, the restriction of the meaning as it is perceived must be accepted according to the principle of the *Devatādhikaraṇa*. Nor should one suspect a contradiction with the Śruti text "without hands or feet," for if that were so, then due to the contradiction with the Śruti concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa*), one would have to abandon even the qualities such as "desire for truth" (*satyakāma*) and the rest. This is just as it is for those who maintain [the existence of forms] while asserting [the opposite]. And as it has been said: "Just as... (as in the cited verse).

In the *Vyatihārādhikaraṇa-bhāṣya*, it is stated that when there is instruction on qualities such as truthfulness (*satyakarma*) and so forth, the Lord (*Īśvara*) is established as possessing those very qualities; thus, there is an apparent contradiction [with the present position]. The principle of resolution—that [the Lord] destroys [the effects] through the reality of *māyā*—should also be inferred here.

As for the objection that, following the commentary on the sūtra "and because of the mention of the body" (*śarīra-upanyāsācca*), the interpretation of that sūtra is improper because Brahman lacks a physical form (*vigraha*), [that is not the case]. (Note: The ellipses (... indicate portions of the original text omitted by the user.)

The commentators have presented an alternative interpretation for other mortals; however, with the intention that such a presentation of a physical form (*vigraha*) is inconsistent because it contradicts the opening statements regarding the specific Supreme Brahman in the *Muṇḍaka-śruti*, they stated elsewhere: "Even for the Supreme Lord, there may exist a form consisting of *māyā* by virtue of His will, for the sake of favoring practitioners. Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras [states] "because of the mark of equality in experience alone," indicating the equality of experience between those who have attained the ego-grasping (*ahaṃgraha*) and Brahman.

By stating this, it has been made clear that the word "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) is conventionally established for sensory pleasure dependent upon a body. Now, one might argue: "In the absence of contradiction by other means of knowledge, let the literal meaning be established from words intended for another purpose; however, here, if one were to admit a primordial fourth form of Brahman distinct from the three forms of Viriñca and the others, there would be a contradiction with another Śruti. For in the *Maitreyopaniṣad*, having introduced the Supreme Brahman as having *māyā* as its limiting adjunct, it is stated: "His foremost bodies are said to be Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu."

Since it is heard that among the various forms (*vigraha*), the triad of forms beginning with Viriñca alone possesses preeminence (*agryatva*), if there were something here even more ancient than those—namely, a form [of Brahman] subsequent to the Mūrtis—how could they possess preeminence?
For those that exist "in front" (*agre*) are called *agrya*. Therefore, it is determined that apart from the triad of forms beginning with Brahmā, there is no fourth form of the Supreme;

and it is solely by relying upon that [triad] that the usage of the elders regarding the embodied nature (*vigrahavatva*) of Brahman is established. This very point is corroborated in the account of Atri’s performance of ascetic penance (*tapascaryā*).
Regarding the words of the *Bhāgavata*: therein, having introduced the performance of penance by Atri, [it says]: "I take refuge in Him who alone is the Lord of the universe;

may He grant me offspring equal to Himself"—thus reflecting. Having stated this intention for a fruit, the Blessed One, after a long time, when the triad of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra had arrived there to grant the boon, [Atri] addressed them following the services of praise, prostration, and so forth.

"How have you come here to procreate in this mind, which is composed primarily of the element of *rajas* and is even further removed from the minds of those who possess self-restraint? Speak, and be gracious; forget this great [disturbance] here.

To this question, they offered this reply: "O Brahman, whatever resolve you have formed must indeed be so and not otherwise; for we are truly that which you meditate upon, O Brahman. By means of this presentation of their response, it is shown that there is no other formless fourth state (*turīya*) beyond the three forms beginning with Viriñci (Brahmā) which serves as the locus for the manifestation of supreme sovereignty.

If it were manifested as a distinct individual (vyaktīkṛta), it would follow that He appears there to another being in that very same form; otherwise, it would contradict the sage’s possession of true resolve (*satsaṅkalpatva*).

Furthermore, it is impossible to say here that His appearance occurs in a form assumed solely for the sake of the meditator—as in the case of the place where Gajendra was liberated—because if that were so, it would lead to the aforementioned objection regarding "one" or "both," and so forth.

Therefore, the acceptance of a physical body (*vigraha*) for the Fourth State (*turīya*) is not logical. To this, it is replied: First of all, the Fourth State is indeed perceived from the verses of the mantras such as "accompanied by Umā" (*umā-sahāya*), and so on.

It cannot be said that even that form, characterized by having Umā as its companion and so forth, is superimposed for the sake of meditation; for in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, within the same context, according to the principle of the "garland of flowers" (*hāranyāya*), there is seen a negation of old age, death, life, thirst, and other such qualities—which might generally be suspected to belong to the embodied Self—on the grounds that they are already established by the wording of the cited mantra regarding the Brahman to be meditated upon. Otherwise, a negation would not be appropriate where [the quality] was not desired to be suspected, nor indeed does [the text] admit corporeality.

Furthermore, since even qualities such as freedom from old age (*ajaratva*) are indeed superimposed [upon the Self], it is established that in this very context, desires and so forth are also contained within it; thus, the nature of these as qualities is made clear. Now, one might object: "Is it not rather the absence of old age and so forth that should be meditated upon as a favor? For by the passage beginning 'This Self is free from sin' (*eṣa ātmāpahatapāpmā*), these are stated to be the qualities of the Self. Thus, even if there is no possibility of [the Self] being subject to [old age], old age and the like do indeed exist as inherently established [in the Self]."

If it is argued that, because [the Lord] is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) as the object of worship, the old age and other attributes mentioned in the scriptures are either always to be disregarded like those of a *tīrthya* (heretic), or are merely for the purpose of praise—as in the case of the prohibitions regarding being a human, a goat, and so forth—this is not so. For, by the principle of "recognition across all Vedāntas" (*sarvavedāntapratyaya-nyāya*), it is established that Brahman possessed of a form (*savigraha*) alone is the object of worship there; and this is both appropriate and supported by the supplementary descriptions (*upabrahmaṇa*) such as: "One should meditate upon Him above [all], Śiva, who is enchanting to all, endowed with all auspicious marks, and graced with profound youth."

Because [qualities] such as being unborn (*ajātva*) are connected only as qualities of the body (*vigraha*), even if that were the case, it is possible for them to be designated as qualities of the Self (*ātman*) through that [body], and thus their designation and their recitation alongside its qualities—
as in "He is intelligent, wise, eloquent, glorious, a destroyer of enemies, mighty-armed, and so forth"— is justified. Furthermore,

since there is no possibility of [such qualities] serving as praise when they are being restated for the purpose of injunction in passages such as "In Him, one should seek what is within Him," [the objection does not hold].
Therefore, since qualities such as the body’s agelessness exist by their very nature (*svarūpataḥ*), when they are enjoined as objects of worship, one concludes that they are not superimposed;
thus, it must be accepted that the body of the substratum (*dharmin*) is also determined to be non-superimposed. This has been stated in the *Sūtasaṃhitā* regarding the Fourth [Turya]:
"Umā is embodied, pure, three-eyed, with the moon as her crest-jewel, blue-throated, supreme bliss, and fond of the joyful *tāṇḍava* dance."

"He is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva through their forms of the qualities (guṇamūrtis), yet he is devoid of all forms and is the sovereign lord of all beings; nevertheless, the eternal Vedic revelation declares that this [form] is the supreme form (parāmūrti) of these [deities]. Thus it is stated in the Parāśara Upapurāṇa.
Of that very Reality which is the supreme beyond all, the witness of everything,
there exists a supreme, pure, independent form that destroys all sin.

Beginning with "His uncommon form is Sāmba, crowned with the crescent moon," and ending with "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa meditate upon Him incessantly," it is stated that [the Brahman] who is described as "this golden person seen within the sun" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 1.6.6)— as if well-known as residing in the center of the solar disc—

is the same Brahman whose dialogue with the gods is heard in the *Talavakāra-śruti* (Jaiminīya-Upaniṣad-Brāhmaṇa) and the *Atharvaśiras*. Thus, [the identity of these two] is established, and there is no inconsistency in this.

"O Rudra, considering this one [Self] alone as unborn through various births, they praise Your southern face for the sake of protection. This mantra from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad—where the phrase "unborn" (ajāta) clarifies the beginninglessness of the Lord's manifest form by demonstrating His freedom from birth through the exclusion of all others—establishes the existence of the Blessed One’s divine form. Furthermore, the verse: "O Rudra, some wise man worships that which is unborn; protect me eternally with that southern face of Yours," likewise confirms the reality of the Lord’s divine body.

And the authority for these [four forms] is their being the object of the fourth body (*turīya-vigraha*), which is made clear here and there. Furthermore, in the *Purāṇa*, in the section concerning the description of the form of Paramaśiva, because he is established as having a corporeal form, there is no contradiction. Nor is it to be suspected that there is a different intention regarding the subject Rudra, who possesses qualities (*guṇin*); for even in those [texts] concerning the greatness of Śiva, one observes in the *Purāṇa* a description of Paraśiva’s supremacy over the three causes. Therefore, here too, [it refers to] the Fourth.

In the conceptualization of distinction (*vyatireka-kalpanā*), for the sake of [establishing] the path... having first introduced Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra in the preceding section, [it is said]: "This Lord is the Supreme Deity; He possesses a supreme body. Because of His nature as Maheśvara... [they] say... in the subsequent [section], [He is] capable, the source of all powers (*sarva-śaktīnām*).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva... the deities are powers (*śaktayaḥ*) [of Him]. [They are] for the sake of the Self (*ātman-artha*)... of the Self.

"Nirmaheshvara; some [say]... vadana... atha... kapara... others know [them as] the vital breaths... others [know them as] Agni... all the gods; their domain is that of Rudra alone. These are proclaimed to be the various manifestations of that one Rudra. Thus it is said in the Shiva Purana.

Brahmā is the initiator of creation; [Viṣṇu is] the sustainer of existence; Rudra is the destroyer. Among these two, Śiva is the one who unites them. Therefore, these three are called the triad of causes of the world. And Śiva, being the cause of the three causes, is the supreme cause—so it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. [The manifestations of the principles... among these three, the Lord (Īśvara) is the superior and the cause of all; such statements are also to be seen in the Liṅga, Saura, Pādma, Gāruḍa, Brahmāṇḍa, Śivayāmala, and other scriptures.

Because these matters will be treated extensively in various places [hereafter], and because the consensus of all [authorities] is clear, they are not written here. Therefore, since the embodied nature of the Supreme Brahman is established by numerous Śrutis and other means, the word *tanu* in the Maitrāyaṇa Śruti must be explained as referring to a "portion" (*aṃśa*)—in accordance with the natural sense of such expressions as "a portion of the King"—so as not to contradict that [embodied nature]; or else, the word *agrya* may be understood as referring to its being a "foremost" portion in relation to other forms of the Brahman-manifestation (*brahmamūrti*). Alternatively, this is because the word *agra* is well-known in the sense of "principal," as seen in grammatical rules such as *agryākhyāyāmurasaḥ*.

It should be explained that [the deities] arise from the form of Paramaśiva as the primary cause. Although, under the governing rule *chandasi* (in Vedic usage), the suffix *yat* is prescribed by the rule *agrād-yat*, and although the meaning of the root *bhū* is existence rather than birth—since one who is "born" (*jāta*) there [would not be appropriate]—nevertheless, the sense of "arising" (*bhava*) is used here because it is treated as a separate governing rule. This is seen in such passages as *namaḥ kāṭyāya ca nīpyāya ca namaḥ sūdyāya ca sarasyāya ca*, where [the names refer to the deities] merely by virtue of the presence of the Supreme Lord.
