Furthermore, because we observe suffixes denoting existence (*bhava-artha-pratyaya*), and in accordance with the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that "the coming into being of the non-existent does not occur," it follows that at the locus of birth, only an existing effect arises; thus, there is no contradiction even when [the term] *halaya* is used. Since the suffix denoting existence is seen elsewhere as well—just as in the case of *ūravyāḥ* (those born from the thighs) meaning *ūrujāḥ* (thigh-born)—and since the birth of the three forms within the body of Paramaśiva has been demonstrated in the *Śivarāghava-saṃvāda*: "The eternal God, worshipped by Brahmā, Sadāśiva, the three-eyed one, the substratum of qualities... [and so forth].

Beyond the qualities (*guṇa*), imperishable and immutable, there arose in him a desire to create. Then, beholding the three qualities residing within himself—this very triad of Vedas which is to be known as the three qualities—he separated that essence from within himself and divided it. From his right side, the Lord generated the son Brahmā; from his two [other sides], Hari; and from the region of his back, Maheśāna. Thus the Lord generated the three sons. As for that which is in the *Bhāgavata*... that too, because the form of Atri is extremely secret and difficult to behold, was somehow [attained] by Atri.

There is no contradiction [in this] regarding the manifestation through the three incarnations beginning with Soma for the sake of attaining the intended purpose; furthermore, the state of being the support (*ālambanatva*) of the form of Paramaśiva is shown in the Śiva Purāṇa by such passages as "He whose glorious body is non-material (*aprākṛta*), devoid of both the defined and the definition," and so forth, while describing His majesty. And Hari, Rudra, and likewise the gods and demons—even today—strive toward Him with fierce austerities.

Regarding the phrase "those desiring a vision": although the Supreme Being possesses a form (*vigraha*), nevertheless, because the application of terms such as "devotee of Śiva" and so forth is logically consistent when viewed through the lens of [the devotee's] perception, one might argue that the sequence of those words does not constitute a means for attaining the auspicious (*śrīkaraṇa*). If this is argued, we say no; for it is well known that in the *Atharvaśikhā* and other texts, terms such as "Mahādeva" and so forth are established as names for Brahman, which—having become blue-black (*nīlaka*)—remains in heaven with a variegated form (*mūrtiśabalita*). Thus, their application there is indeed appropriate.

And because of the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*), it must be accepted that even he who is denoted by terms such as *Śiva* is [the Supreme]. For if Umā is remembered as his companion, then in the *Śiva-purāṇas* he is depicted as having a form variegated by the three deities (*trimūrti*). Since he is established as the presiding deity over the *liṅga* and other symbols, what indeed is the nature of this third synthesis—the one who transcends the three forms (*trimūrti-atīta*) and is the Supreme Brahman—beyond the Creator (Brahmā) and the Protector (Nārāyaṇa)? It is their union.
Furthermore, what is the obstacle to that [realization]? [The Purāṇas and so forth... If it is thus, the form of Paramaśiva is such, and his names are likewise;

his form is exactly like that, and his names are those very same ones. As it is said in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*: "O Brahmin, O best of sages, the form of Rudra belongs to the Supreme One, yet it is distinct from the forms of the other [deities] by its characteristics. O lords of sages, the names of Rudra are also the designations of the three deities, due to their proximity to the Supreme Reality."
In the Śiva Purāṇa as well, after introducing the majesty of Saṃhāra-Rudra, it is said:
"This very Lord Īśa is a mass of splendor, free from affliction;
he is the creator without beginning or end, the restrainer of beings, and the all-pervading one."
Endowed with supreme sovereignty, permeated by the nature of the Supreme Lord,
he is eternally established within that power and marked by its very signs.
That name, that form, that moment of cause and effect,
that corresponding conventional usage, and the upholder of its command— [all these constitute it].

Although there is no Purāṇic statement that establishes this [nature] as its exclusive attribute, nevertheless, due to the excellence of the evidence, its exposition is found only in those Purāṇas devoted to Paramaśiva, as has been cited immediately following.
In the Śivapurāṇa: [...]
O great sage, all the Purāṇas of Maheśvara [are composed] with an uncommon form, yet by a common name.
O great sage, they declare that Śiva— the three-eyed one accompanied by Ambā— is the supreme reality;
they also declare him to be Hara among the three forms (trimūrti),
as well as his own manifestation (vaibhava) and the presiding ego (abhimāna) of that manifestation.

Thus, even such propitiation as this is directed toward his *liṅga*s and other forms located precisely in the sites of the manifestation of Paramaśiva. Because there is an equality of name, form, and so forth between Paramaśiva and Guṇirudra, and because it is clearly understood from the *Brahmaviṣṇuśiva* [Purāṇa] that [Guṇirudra] possesses no inferiority or superiority over Brahmā and Viṣṇu, Guṇirudra is specifically treated as non-different from Paramaśiva in the Purāṇas and elsewhere. Furthermore, among the Śaivas, there is an intense sense of personal devotion (*abhimāna*) toward him, as well as the designation of commonality regarding his qualities, conduct, and so forth; for this very reason, even today, some...

There is a failure to distinguish between these two. Now, regarding those forms well-known from the Purāṇas and other sources among the auspicious Śaiva forms: which are the forms of Paramaśiva and which are the forms of Guṇirudra?

Some say that the form of Ānandatāṇḍava, the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the form of Mārdhavī engaged in tāṇḍava constitute the triad of forms of Paramaśiva alone; others, however, say they belong to Guṇirudra. We do not find this view acceptable.
In the *Yogayājñavalkya*: "Having established the wind within the earth and conjoined it with the syllable *la*,
one should meditate upon Brahmā Parameṣṭhin in his four-armed form."
By retaining the breath for the duration of one ghaṭikā, one shall attain perfection;
having mounted the wind upon Varuṇa, it should be joined with the Vakaraṇa.
Remembering the gentle Nārāyaṇa— four-armed, wearing a crown,
resembling pure crystal, clad in yellow garments,
and infallible— one who wears even a single water-pot is liberated from all sins.
Or, having applied blue [pigment], provided with lines and letters.
Having recited the mantra beginning with "The three-eyed Rudra, the bestower of boons, resembling the rising sun,
his entire body smeared with ashes, most gracious... and so forth,
one should project him into the sky along with the wind, endowed with transformation (*vikāra*).
Mahādeva, whose form is the bindu, is Sadāśiva, whose nature is space.
Resembling pure crystal, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
he bears five faces, is gentle, possesses ten arms, and has three eyes.

One should maintain the mental focus for even a moment, contemplating Him who has His hands raised with all weapons, who is adorned with all ornaments, whose body is half Umā’s, who grants boons, and who is the cause of all causes— contemplating Him as He is established in meditation.

That very [deity] is described by those learned even in the Tantras as being the five-faced form of Sadāśiva of Paramaśiva; for this is established both in the *Saṃhitā* within the ritual procedure for worship known as *Yogeśvara*, and likewise in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, in the context of the severing of the fifth head of Brahmā by Nīlalohita:
"Then he beheld Girīśa situated within the circle (*maṇḍala*)."
To the eternal Mahādeva, who was seated together with the Great Goddess.

By such statements as these, [the Lord] is established as being seated on a single throne even when accompanied by Śūlin (Śiva), for his consort is also presented therein. Therefore, other forms of Paraśiva should also be understood according to the scriptures and the instructions of the teacher. However, because they are extremely secret, their detailed enumeration—which can only be accessed through the instruction of a Guru—is not displayed here.

Thus, it is established that the Lord Umāsahāya Indumauli, whose body is *māyā*, is the fourth Brahman (*brahma-turīya*) and the cause of the universe; yet he is not something transcending the three forms (*mūrtitraya*) while still possessing the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *māyā*.
That [the Lord] is also called Brahmanārāyaṇa is determined from certain scriptural statements; for instance, in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Brahmā, Dakṣa, and the others, as well as Time and all living beings—these are the manifestations (vibhūtayaḥ) of Hari, which are the causes of the creation of the world."

Viṣṇu, Manu and the others, time, and likewise all living beings— these are the manifestations of Viṣṇu, who is the instrumental cause of the world's maintenance. Rudra, Time, Antaka (the Ender), and all other living beings [are likewise his manifestations].
O Janārdana, these manifestations of yours are for the sake of the fourth dissolution.

Thus, such statements are found here and there in the *Bhāgavata*, the *Bṛhannāradīya*, and other texts, as well as at the beginning of the *Prapañcasāra*. This matter is made clear through the sequence of questions and answers concerning the three forms and Puruṣottama reclining upon Śeṣa. In the *Uttaratāpanīya*, Nṛsiṃha is designated as the Fourth (the Turīya);

whereas in the *Pūrvatāpanīya*, starting from "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Puruṣīśvara, Sarasvatī, Śrī, Gaurī, Prakṛti, and Vidyā," it concludes with: "He who is indeed all this—the Lord, the Blessed Nṛsiṃha."

By the conclusion of the passage, "All that—to you, obeisance," and because Brahmā and the others are recited among the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of Nṛsiṃha, the fact that this matter is rooted in direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) is also understood.
Thus, how can there be a determination that the Fourth (*turīya*) is Paraśiva? To this, it is replied:
"The Fourth, devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), is heard of as the foot of Vaiśvānara and the others."

In the *Uttaratāpanīya*, Hari is established as being beyond the qualities (*guṇa*); let this be the *Pūrvatāpanīya*. This is well-known from numerous other Śrutis such as the *Atharvaśikhā*: "That supreme power of mine alone is the Goddess known as Vidyā. The connection [of this] is understood through the proximity of the reading of the name "Vidyā" as established by the words of Śiva.

I shall not join [her] with the three forms of my beloved Lord Īśvara; for, according to the statement in the *Kaurma Purāṇa*, "Having joined that Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth, with Prakṛti," she is separately enumerated from the twenty-fifth who is accompanied by Prakṛti—this is what I myself accept.

Furthermore, while [the author] rejects Śambhu’s nature as Brahman conditioned by *māyā* which transcends the three forms (*trimūrti*), he is unable to deny such a status for Viṣṇu. Therefore, being intent on proclaiming the reality of all things as being contained within the three forms themselves, he even counts Kṛṣṇa’s own statement, “I am Vāsudeva among the sages,” among Viṣṇu’s manifestations (*vibhūtis*). Or rather, [he does so] because [Viṣṇu] becomes pleased by those very [manifestations]; thus, based on the beginning and conclusion—starting with "by these mantras... and ending with "...[purified]"—the intent is clearly one of praise. This is what [the author] intends.

Therefore, in the case of the *Nṛsiṃha* [incarnation], for the purpose of praising Viriñca and Nārāyaṇa, it should be interpreted as being beyond the nature of Brahman. And thus, even by means of the intent regarding the gradation [of manifestations], they are capable of establishing that the three forms are the ultimate reality. For instance, just as there are emanations (*vyūhas*) of Śiva, so too do they exist for Rudra and Viṣṇu, even in the acts of taking away, sustaining, and producing those who have not yet come into being.

[The forms] have been established. The three [forms] of Viṣṇu known as Virāṭ, Kāla-puruṣa, and [the others], and those of Rudra known as Hara, Mṛḍa, and Bhava—as well as those such as Dakṣa and Manvantaka—are intermediate authorities (*antar-adhikārin*) in matters of creation and so forth.

Furthermore, scriptural statements regarding Viṣṇu that refer to his specific forms are consistent with referring to his own triad of manifestations (*vyūha*), because even for those who differ from him, the designation of "Brahmā" and so on is appropriate due to their commonality in possessing the authority over creation and other cosmic functions.
One form is that of Bhagavatī, whose nature is knowledge, auspicious and stainless;
she is named Vāsudeva, transcending the qualities (guṇas) and perfectly partless. The second is known as Rudra, characterized by tamas, and designated as Śeṣa.
Furthermore, the supreme Vaiṣṇavī body destroys everything else.
Endowed with that third [nature], she is manifest and designated as consciousness;
that eternal Prakṛti of Viṣṇu sustains the entire world.
The fourth form of Vāsudeva is designated as Brahman;
the one called Aniruddha is of the nature of rajas, the Puruṣa who effects creation.

Thus, because we see such designations for them in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the justification for statements regarding Brahman’s supremacy over the three forms (Trimūrti) should likewise be inferred. In the *Vāyu Saṃhitā*, after introducing Brahmā with the words, "Then the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), designated as Brahman, entered this egg," it continues: "Having divided himself threefold, he proceeds throughout the three worlds;

he himself creates, devours, and protects by means of the three [qualities]. Having thus demonstrated his manifestations (vyūhas), it further states: "Sattva and rajas [are] in the state of Brahman and in the state of Time..."

[In Viṣṇu] there is only *sattva*; thus the activity of the qualities (*guṇavṛtti*) of the All-pervading Lord is threefold. This is because even in those [deities], the terms "Brahmā" and so forth are used in the verse concerning the division of the qualities among their manifestations (*vyūha*). [Objection: In that case, let it be that the statements regarding Śiva being superior to the three forms (*trimūrti*) actually refer to Bhava, Mṛḍa, and Hara, who are the manifestations (*vyūha*) of the Saṃhāra-Rudra; thus, let Śiva be intended as the Saṃhāra-Rudra himself, for he has scriptural authority as being superior to the forms constituted by the qualities (*guṇamūrti*). [Reply: No. For it is said: "The four-faced one creates the entire universe by the command of the Lord (Īśa)."

Through his three forms, he protects and, at the end, destroys. Viṣṇu protects the universe through the yoga known as Viśvayoga; he creates and devours by means of those same three forms of his own. And Haras, by his very command, takes away this entire world. The Soul of the Universe (Viśvātmā), divided into three, creates, protects, and [destroys]. Thus it is stated in the Śiva Purāṇa, in the section on the ritual of worship called Yogeśvara, where the engagement of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—each with their respective manifestations—in their individual duties is described as being under the direction of Śiva.

The transcendence of Sadāśiva from the three forms (trimūrti) is established by the fact that, in the *Yogayājñavalkya*, having introduced Brahmā and the others—who are well-known as being within their respective manifestations (*vyūha*) and veils (*āvaraṇa*)—the text describes the ritual procedure for worshiping them within the veil of Śiva;

it further establishes his transcendence by stating that Sadāśiva is superior to them, thereby demonstrating his distinction from the triad. Similarly, this is so in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*. Since [it says], "By whose grace I am Acyuta...
and so forth, how could the transcendence of Viṣṇu from the three forms not be established? For in the words spoken from the mouth of Brahmā, there is no application of the term "I" to Aniruddha.

If it is argued that [the term] "is born" (*upapadyate*) applies [to Viṣṇu], we say no; because of the presence of the conceit of ego (*ahaṅkāra-abhimānitva*), it is restricted [to others]. As stated in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*: "The ego is threefold—sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic"—and since even there the application [of the term] is possible as a partial name (*nāmaikadeśatvena*) for those very [categories], and since even if that [term] refers to the mouth [of Brahmā], the word "Person" (*puruṣa*) in the passage "And from whom the Ancient Person [arose]" can also be understood as referring to Pradyumna, it is established by the scriptural testimony that Viṣṇu is the referent of the three forms (*trimūrti*). [From] the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*...

Thus, because it is stated that the subject matter taught in the Purāṇas and other texts is none other than Brahman— the Supreme— who is the immediate cause of the world through His various powers (*śakti*), and because at the beginning of the *Bhāgavata* one hears such passages as, "Therefore, with a single mind, the Blessed Lord, the Lord of the Sātvatas, should be heard, glorified, meditated upon, and worshipped," this Blessed One is understood to be the prescriptive authority (*vidhāyaka*). Furthermore, in the verse beginning with "sattva-rajas-tamas" [1.2.23], in response to the inquiry regarding who He is:

Having first established the Blessed One as the portion (*aṃśa*) of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), who possesses the qualities of reality (*tattvaguṇa*)— and having done so by way of removing the sins that must necessarily be destroyed as previously introduced, on account of His being the source of supreme good (*śreyaskaratva*)— the sages worshipped Him, beginning with the words "as at the very beginning" (*yathāgra*). Having thus established that worship of Him has liberation-in-stages (*kramamukti*) as its fruit, and having stated that He is the subject matter of all the Vedas and so forth, [the author] demonstrated the existence of His *līlā*-form through the verse beginning with "He assumed a human form" (*jagrahe pauruṣam vapuḥ*), and [further] described Him as "the inexhaustible seed and the repository of these various incarnations."

In the *Parāśara Purāṇa*, by demonstrating that among all the Vaiṣṇava incarnations, the one who is the root of the roots (*mūla-mūla-vigraha*)—the portion of the Supreme Person (*parama-puruṣa-aṃśa*) untouched by the quality of *sattva*—is alone the supreme reality of Viṣṇu, it clarifies that after stating that the Śaiva Purāṇas (beginning with the *Maheśvara Purāṇa*) are characterized by the destruction of Śiva and intent on delusion, [it says]:

"O great sage, all the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas proclaim the supreme state of Hari through the name and form of the three deities; and two Purāṇas, the Brāhma and the [other... (the rest of the verse follows).

Since the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas conclude that Viṣṇu is indeed included within the Trimūrti, and since they clarify that he alone is the supreme reality of Viṣṇu, it is therefore logical to determine that the Fourth is none other than Paramaśiva. Alternatively, let the form of Nārāyaṇa exist even within the Fourth category; for there is no rule that there is only one single form of Brahman in the Fourth category. This is because [the presence of all forms] is well-known therein from all the Śaiva Purāṇas, as it is said by those who know the Āgamas: "They call the Goddess of Speech the one who is swallowed by Druhiṇa (Brahmā)."

This is because of the statements of authoritative teachers such as "Hari... and so forth, because Bhavānī exists even within the form [of Śiva], and because it is accepted here as well that "the body is with Ambā" (*sāmba-vapuḥ*). However, she is the manifestation in male form of Paraśakti herself, Bhavānī; for the single Śakti of the Supreme Lord appears divided at the time of her specific application, according to the scriptural teachings: "In enjoyment she is Bhavānī, among men she is Viṣṇu, in anger she is Kālī, and in battles she is Durgā. Thus, Hari is directly Umā, and she who is Hari is Śivā.

Because of the statement [in the *Smṛti*]: "You are Prakṛti, you are the male Rudra; that virility has been deposited in you. From the lotus of your navel was born the five-faced Grandfather," as stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
And because of the designation of Viṣṇu as Śiva’s Śakti in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*: "There exists no difference between us two; you are Śakti, there is no doubt. You are the moon, I am the sun;
you are the night, I am the day," and so forth, as found in the *Kūrma*, *Vāsiṣṭha*, *Laiṅgya*, *Āditya Purāṇa*, and others.

In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*, within the section describing the entry of Śiva and Nārāyaṇa into the Devadāru forest as husband and wife, it is stated: "The young woman who was by his side is Hari, born from a portion of Pārvatī," and so forth.
"You are the seed, and he is the womb; he is [the one] who [is thus addressed].
When this was said, the Universal Soul, Brahmā Viṣṇu, was questioned."
O Bhavānī, how can Maheśvara, who is devoid of the seed of "I-ness" (nirahaṃ-bīja), be the possessor of that seed? Pray, explain this subtle and unmanifest matter to me, so that I may understand it.
To those who were experts in the characteristics of the distinctions [of the Vedas],
Hari addressed a question regarding the most subtle reality.

A being greater than this is declared to be secret; it is the supreme state of Śiva, beyond the Great One, which exists among those who know the Self. It stands having divided itself by means of its own divine power.
The partless one is subtle and unmanifest, while Maheśvara is possessed of parts.

For this one who knows the method of illusion and who is like the incalculable sky, there arose from the supreme *liṅga* [the state of] being free from [dualistic] marks (*aliṅga*), which is characterized by the nature of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) and so forth, and is inherent in creation.
"In my womb... that seed, by the passage of time...

Hiraṇya... from the womb of Pā... O Prajāpati,"—by this [passage], the fact that Viṣṇu is the field (*kṣetra*) of Śiva is made manifest; thus, through the presence of both Śiva and Keśava in the Nābhi-śilā, [the deity] consists of Hari and Hara, and [is] the destroyer of sins.

Because of the evidence from the *Rvārdha* (the Ṛgvedakhilāni), such as "The jewel of the ocean of the sky... and because of the statement of Abhuyukta: "This ancient Person, the teacher of gods and demons, who exists for the sake of the protection of the caravan... this is the half [of the body] of the slayer of Andhaka; that is indeed your divinity," it is thus established that there is no contradiction in the supreme transcendence of the form of Śiva (*śivamūrti*), which is to be determined here as being subordinate to Śiva—just like Bhavānī—in relation to Nārāyaṇa, who is seated upon the fourth [state].

Two views have been presented in the *Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya*. Having reflected upon them, that which is logical therein should be accepted by the most discerning of men. In both views, it is established that the Lord Śiva, the consort of Ambikā and Lord of the universe, is the primordial source of all forms of Brahmā; just as Bhairava and others are [emanations] of Hara, and Matsya and others of the Illustrious Lord (Viṣṇu), so too are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara merely distinct manifestations of His power (*kalā*).
Even though he deceives the Lord whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon,
his preeminence over all the gods is established for that very reason.
One should determine the strength of the words uttered by the learned based on their substratum,
because the strength of all [words] is established through the power of their substratum.
And because, regarding other gods mentioned in the Vedas or in the Smṛtis,
statements asserting their equality with or superiority to Him are interpreted as being merely figurative descriptions of His qualities.
Even though it is heard that [the *agniṣṭoma*] is equal [to the *agniṣṭut*], would his ritual act— the *agnihotra*— be equal to it,
given the determination of its greater magnitude?
In ancient times, the Bhārata and all the Vedas were placed upon a scale by the gods, beginning with Brahmā; therein, the Bhārata outweighed them all.
Thus, even though the superiority of the *Bhārata* over the Vedas is recorded,
what could possibly be more powerful than all the Vedas combined?
Having entered into the dull-witted, he produced illumination in the world by means of the moon of the Mahābhārata from the great ocean of the Vedas.
Thus, when the fact that [the Purāṇas] are rooted in the Veda is determined through such statements and logical arguments,
the declarations regarding the superiority of the Mahābhārata are to be understood as mere *arthavāda* (explanatory or eulogistic passages).
Nevertheless, a delusion arises in the minds of some who are dull-witted,
or in those wicked souls who are arrogant due to their study of non-Vedic systems.
Even though Śaṅkara is the master of those things that are produced from the *sat* (Being),
let his repose in sovereignty nevertheless be found elsewhere alone.
This method has been stated as being rooted in such scriptural passages as the Atharvaśikhā;
otherwise, if those [passages] were to have a different meaning, this [method] would not be established at all.
Therefore, the purport of all the Śrutis, together with all the Upabrahmaṇas,
regarding the supreme nature of the Blessed Lord, is stated here in due order.
Having set aside all the gods, beginning with Brahmā,
and having determined that those whose power is measured by the elements and so forth are merely subordinate,
I have established you as the ultimate cause and the sovereign lord of all.
O Śiva, even that which is to be meditated upon by those established in the branches [of knowledge] is considered trivial by me.

In the *Atharvaśikhā*, following the inquiry introduced at the beginning—"What is that meditation? Who is the meditator? And what is the object of meditation?"—and after the determination of meditation and the meditator, there is a scriptural passage for the purpose of determining the object of meditation: "One should meditate upon the Lord (Īśāna), who is to be meditated upon. All this—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are all produced from Him, as are all the senses together with the elements. He is not the cause of causes; He is the Ordainer, the Meditator, and the Cause. Endowed with all sovereignty, the Lord of all, Śambhu, He dwells in the midst of space."

Thus, in passages such as "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon," "He who is Śiva alone, having abandoned all else," and so forth, the *Atharvaśiras* [Upaniṣad] reaches its conclusion. Here, because the word *Īśāna*, which denotes the Supreme Śiva through both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), possesses the capacity to signify that state by virtue of its inherent power (*tācchīlya*), it refers—through etymology—to the natural, unsurpassed sovereignty [of the Lord]. Furthermore, since it is expressed as the non-dual Supreme Śiva who is beyond the dualities of subject and object, He alone is the Supreme Śiva, possessing a sovereignty that transcends all and whose fruit is the most excellent of all.

With the intention that "he is to be meditated upon," the designation of the word *Īśāna* was made as the object of meditation (*dhyeya*). Because of the excessive nature of what has been taught, meditation is praised as being [relatively] inferior; for what else could there be for one who is ignorant, other than this power of non-retention? Having stated the preeminence of the four beginning with Brahmā within the equalized phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the form of the *Davamāṣṭi* and so forth, [the text proceeds] by means of a *dīpaka* (lamp-verse) to express their subordination to Him, in order to demonstrate the limitation of even their sovereignty.

And by [the mention of] "bhū... and so forth, their state of being born (*utpattimatva*) has been shown through the similarity of their faculties and other attributes. Starting from the words "all this" up to "by all beings," having raised the doubt that if this were the case for Paramaśiva as well, he too would have to be meditated upon in the same manner, it is said: "He is not the cause of causes; He is the Ordainer, the Meditator. The connection [of the verb] is to be supplied by changing the verbal form to "is not produced" (*na prasūyate*). Thus, the meaning is as follows: by the force of the statement regarding the birth of Brahmā and the others, that which is established as their cause—He who is of the nature of the cause of those causes—[is Paramaśiva].

Although by this [verse], which speaks of the Creator, the Originator, the Meditator, and the One who forms the initial resolve for creation— whether referring to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra as mentioned in the Mantra-Upaniṣads, or to Time and the rest—
it is understood merely that He does not originate from anything whatsoever, and not specifically that He is "Īśāna" (the Lord), nevertheless,

after pointing out the defects in those [deities] in order to establish His status as the object of meditation and thereby exclude the status of being an object of meditation from Brahmā and the others; well then, if those defects were actually present in Him...

Its status as an object of meditation (*dhyeyatva*) must also be rejected right there [in that context], in order to eliminate the doubt that has arisen at this juncture; otherwise, if one were to bypass the intermediate statement and accept that sentences such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a whisper" (*viṣṇur upāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ*) are injunctions for sacrifices, one would fail to achieve the removal of the defect of "stagnation" (*jāmitā*) caused by the immediate succession of the two *puroḍāśa* offerings mentioned in the opening. Consequently, just as with the form of the sentence in that case, an inconsistency would arise here as well. Therefore, it is concluded that the intent [of the text] lies in removing the defects previously raised against Īśāna among Brahmā and the others, by means of a method that interrupts the operation of the [preceding] sentence.

It is determined that because the cause [of the world] is already established for Brahmā and the others, the capacity to exclude them implies that Īśāna alone is the cause of Brahmā and the rest; thus, the absence of his own origin (prasūtyabhāva) is presented there. Furthermore, since the words *udgātṛ* and *dhyātṛ* used here are employed solely in their etymological sense, the particle *tu* naturally indicates the commencement of a new sentence at that point. Therefore, by this very sentence, those two [words], being devoid of any inherent gender-determination (*liṅgavyavasthā*), are understood to take on the gender of another [referent].

If [the word *kāraṇa*] were to grasp its own gender as established by a reason (*liṅga*) co-referential with itself, it would result in the neuter gender; therefore, in order to justify the heard masculine gender, there is a requirement for a masculine substantive. When there is an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) of a heard word that possesses proximity conducive to the construction of the most desired meaning, rather than the possibility of supplying another such word (*adhyāhāra*), the ellipsis of the word *Īśāna* is necessary. Thus, just as the causality of Brahmā and others is established based on the established [causality] of Śiva, [the same applies here].

It is determined that the absence of birth is presented therein. For this very reason, in the immediately following sentence, the word *kāraṇam* (the cause) is seen to be in grammatical apposition with the word *śambhu*. Furthermore, the mention of the "middle of space" (*ākāśamadhya*) as the locus for meditation refers to the world of Supreme Śiva, which is of the nature of the supreme ether. By this, it becomes known that wherever Śiva is to be meditated upon—whether in the solar disc within the heart-lotus or elsewhere—one should meditate on Śiva as being situated in the center of Kailāsa, which is the [supreme] light. O Lord of All!

Thus is the usage [of the term] as a name of Śiva. In the *Tāpanīya* usage—[namely], "Oṃkāra, the Lord of All" (*sarveśvara*)—it is established by convention that it is His name; however, this is not because it refers to the state of possessing all sovereignty (*sarvaiśvarya*), for that would result in redundancy with the preceding qualifier. Since the first member of the compound is conventional (*rūḍha*) and the second member possesses both etymological and conventional meaning (*yogarūḍhi*), the two words together indicate that state [of being the name] through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).

In the phrase "the lotuses favored by Vikiraṇa," just as the second word "lotus" [is repeated], so too is the collection of lotuses [repeated]. Consequently, Śambhu is not only [superior] because he is devoid of birth—unlike Brahmā and others—due to his nature as the self of the primordial cause (*prakṛti*) and his being unlimited; rather, he is also [superior] because he is denoted by the term "Lord of All" (*Sarveśvara*), which is not shared by any other. Thus, the statement "and he is the Lord of All" serves as a restatement of his universal sovereignty supported by reasoning. By this manner of expression, having set aside Brahmā and the others, Śiva alone is the object of meditation.

Thus it has been shown. To show respect for this very meaning, the Śruti clarifies it through explicit statement as well, beginning with "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon. Furthermore, the supplementary texts (Upabrahmaṇas) clarify the meaning of the Śruti in this way; for instance, in the Śiva Purāṇa, within the section determining the supreme excellence of Śiva, it is recited: "Because all this—beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra... (*).
It is first brought forth together with all the co-existent sense-faculties.
He who is the sustainer of causes, the meditator, the supreme cause—
who is never produced from anything else at any time—
and who is filled with all sovereignty, is himself by name Sarveśvara (the Lord of All).
Śambhu, who dwells in the midst of space, should be meditated upon by those seeking liberation as their friend.

Thus, in the first verse—the root statement beginning with "all this" (*sarvam idam*) and ending with "co-existent" (*sahabhūtaiḥ*), which demonstrates the meaning—it is established that although the phrase "they arise from Śiva" is not explicitly stated in the words, its meaning is proven by implication through a consideration of the subsequent verses. Having accepted this as established, the second verse indicates what was pointed out by the word "from whom" (*yasmāt*): namely, "the creator of creators, the meditator," showing that this much alone constitutes the connection of the action. By the third verse, [he is indicated] by name as "the Lord of All Himself" (*sarveśvaraḥ svayam*).

By proposing that the word "Sarveśvara" is a proper name (*vanāman*), and by demonstrating that this purpose—namely, that he himself is denoted by the word "Sarveśvara"—reveals his status as the Lord of All through a name that is unique and without equal, the charge of redundancy is avoided. In the *Harivaṃśa*, within a hymn of praise by Kṛṣṇa, it is recited: "I am Brahmā, and Kapila who is Ananta; all the sons of Brahmā are exceedingly heroic. From you, O God of gods, all have been born; you are the Lord of All, the causal Self, and you are to be praised. Thus it is said here.

The mention of Kapila and others is for the purpose of summarizing the internal meaning of such Vedic passages as "He who [produced] Kapila, the seer born in the beginning," and so forth; thus, the logical connection is that [the Lord] is the causal self (*kāraṇātmā*).
Since He alone reveals His nature as the cause, and because He is the causal essence of Brahmā and the others, You are the Lord of All; therefore, You are to be praised by all.

In this way, the relationship between the probans and the probandum—namely, being the cause and so forth—is made clear. Thus: "From Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Agni, Īśa, and Indra, as well as the gods and demons preceded by water and earth..."

"All have been produced from you, O Maheśvara," and so forth—such supplementary passages (*upabrahmaṇas*) from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* and other texts should also be cited. Thus, since the status of Śiva as the Lord of All has been established in the Vedas themselves by distinguishing him from all other deities such as Brahmā and the rest, the talk of another deity superior to him is merely the play of delusion on the part of the ignorant; this is the meaning. Now, [one might object]: "In the beginning Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of beings. Indra is the king of that which moves and stands."

"Indra is superior to all; Agni is the first among the deities"—thus, in the Śrutis, the sovereignty of other deities as well is heard to be unlimited. It is said [in response]: it is not possible for all to be supreme lords through alternation (*vikalpa*), because alternation is impossible regarding a real entity (*vastu*). Nor is it possible through simultaneity (*samuccaya*), because that would result in mutual lordship over one another. Nor is it possible through different cosmic cycles (*kalpabheda*), because even if the sovereignty of all were established in their own respective domains, the fault of temporal limitation (*kālataḥ pariccheda*) would arise, whereby they would not be supreme lords. Therefore, in such a case, some...

It must be admitted by all that some [Vedic passages] have their primary meaning as they appear, while others are to be interpreted differently. Among these, those passages whose meanings are well-known should not be set aside by those of impaired intellect on the grounds that they are intended for something else or are to be interpreted otherwise; rather, it is better to establish them in accordance with the *Upabrahmaṇas* (explanatory treatises). This is because human intellects lack fixed boundaries, and thus the true status of the meaning cannot be established through the elevated reasonings of such individuals. For the Veda fears the person of little learning, thinking: "May this [Veda] not [be destroyed] by me..."
"One should study the Veda every day along with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for even if the meaning of the Veda is understood by oneself, there may still be ignorance regarding it."

Since that [identity] has been determined by the sages, Kāśī was chosen by the high-souled ones for the sacrifice according to the words of Vyāsa; and likewise, it is proper to accept that the *Atharvaśikhā*—which has been cited and will be cited extensively—possesses a literal meaning (*pratītārtha*) due to its firmness as a secondary Vedic text (*upabrahmaṇa*), while other Śrutis concerning the sovereignty of different deities, being devoid of such secondary Vedic texts, possess a restricted meaning regarding their respective sovereignties so as not to contradict the immediate context. Such is the actual state of affairs. As for that which [is established] by logic...
Since he is not satisfied without an investigation into the relative strength and weakness [of the texts], he therefore establishes the superior authority of this Śruti over that [Smṛti]. ||14||
For it has been heard that absolute sovereignty exists somewhere; yet, when there is contradiction, one can only lead it to contraction by means of pure qualities and powers.
It is not through mere logic that the hosts of deities [attain this] from the mouth of the Lotus-born.
Having excluded both [extremes], may you two proclaim this existence within it.

The point is this: it is universally established that between two contradictory [authorities], that which is not otherwise accounted for (*ananyathāsiddha*) is stronger than that which is otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*). For instance, in cases such as "one cuts with the hand," when there is a contradiction with a non-otherwise-accounted inferential mark (*liṅga*), even a scriptural text (*śruti*) of that nature is admitted to be restricted. Furthermore, the other cited collection of statements—which concern the sovereignty of other deities and fall under that same category—is otherwise accounted for;

indeed, because they describe the imperishability of the senses by one desiring the fruit of the Cāturmāsya sacrifice, they can be led to have a restricted meaning. As for that which concerns Brahmā and the others...

In the middle [of this work], having raised the objection that among those [deities] there is the defect of limited sovereignty (*paricchinnaiśvaryatva*) in order to exclude them, and desiring to avoid that [objection], [the author] set out to establish the unlimited sovereignty (*aparicchinna-aiśvarya*) of Śambhu, who was pointed out as the object of meditation. However, since that [establishment] would fail to avoid the defect previously raised elsewhere if it were concerned with a limited sovereignty, and because [Śambhu] cannot tolerate limitation— given that he is the ground where the succession of all worldly movements comes to rest— it follows that [the text] intends to show that the ether (*ākāśa*), which was presented as such immediately after the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), is free from the defect of being finite (*antavat*).

In the sūtra *Ākāśas talliṅgāt*, it was determined that what is denoted by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) there is the Supreme Self. This was concluded because the statement "This is indeed the infinite" (*sa eṣo 'nantaḥ*), which is engaged in demonstrating infinity in order to avoid the aforementioned defect, is not otherwise established;

for that very reason, the mark of infinity established therein cannot be interpreted away according to the logic of the "immortality of the gods" (*tridaśāmaratva*). Thus, disregarding even the scriptural mention of a distinction among elements—which, though inherently powerful, is otherwise established by the possibility of alternative functions—because it occurs in the introductory portion, [the ether is identified as the Supreme Self]. In the sūtra *Ākāśas talliṅgāt*: "The ether [is Brahman], on account of its characteristic mark. This refers to the following passage from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (1.9): "Verily, O Gārgī, this whole world is woven, warp and woof, upon the ether. On what, then, is the ether woven, warp and woof? "O Yājñavalkya, you have led me far away with your talk of the Brahman. You should stop now. "I am about to be questioned, O Gārgī; do not question beyond the Brahman, lest your head shatter. "Let it be so, O Yājñavalkya," said Gārgī Vācaknavī. In this context, the doubt arises whether the ether mentioned here is the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) or the Supreme Self. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is the elemental ether, because it is well-known as such and because the subsequent mention of being "woven, warp and woof" is appropriate for a material element. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: The ether mentioned here is the Supreme Self. Why? Because of its characteristic mark (*talliṅgāt*). The characteristic mark of the Supreme Self is found in the passage: "On what, then, is the ether woven, warp and woof? For the ether, which is the effect, cannot be woven upon itself; rather, it must be woven upon something else. That upon which the entire universe, including the ether, is woven is the Supreme Self. Furthermore, the statement "This is indeed the infinite" serves to demonstrate the infinity of the Supreme Self, thereby precluding the interpretation of the ether as the elemental ether. Since the scriptural mention of a distinction among elements is thus sublated by this characteristic mark, the ether is the Supreme Self. This is the meaning.

If such an unerring inferential mark (*liṅga*) is capable of subverting even the direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) situated at the beginning of its own statement, then what need is there to mention that it subverts other Vedic texts intended to exalt other deities when they present the sovereignty of Śiva? Thus, having shown that the term "Śruta" alone is intended to be distinguished from the host of other deities— both great and small— furthermore, whatever quality is observed to be excluded from one place and seen in another, there is an attraction and a repulsion [of power] corresponding to that shift in position.

Or rather, it is not logical to [accept]...; thus Brahmā’s divine... the excellence of Śiva is irresistible. And so, that very unsurpassed excellence of his [is established], while the other [deities] possess inferior sovereignty... it is demonstrated therein. Therefore, its superior strength is such that, by means of the mouth of the lotus-born [Brahmā]... the sovereignty of Brahmā and the others... was presented through the mouth of another. Furthermore, the logical justification (*upapatti*) is a powerful indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyaliṅga*), whereas it is not so elsewhere regarding the ornaments of the deities.

The meaning is that [the text] "by the power and reasoning of this... and "his desire to drink... are heard as being connected to both [Śiva and the other deities], yet [it is said] "only Śruta" (*kevalaṃ śrutam*) because it intends to avoid the faults raised elsewhere, and because there is no mention of the possibility [of such a capacity] arising from anything other than Śiva. Furthermore, here, since the sovereignty of Śiva exists in the form of the scripture, [he is the one] heard in the Upaniṣad—which is primarily concerned with determining the Supreme Deity for those seeking liberation—whereas for others, [the deity is] one associated with ritual action (*karma*).

Because this [Atharvaśikhā] is preeminent among the mantras and other texts primarily concerned with illumination and so forth, its superior strength is established; furthermore, immediately after stating "the object of meditation" (*dhyeya*) and so on, the explicit mention of the conclusion—"here ends the Atharvaśikhā"—is intended to indicate that its own completion cannot be known from other scriptures for some time to come. This serves to reveal the unsurpassed wonder of Śiva as established by the fact that there is nothing further to be said hereafter, and it manifests both the nature of the text as a definitive summary of the essential truth and its character as a teaching of the supreme benefit, by enjoining meditation upon Him to the exclusion of all else.

Moreover, its superiority [is established] because in other Vedic texts, the description of the sovereignty of other deities is not manifested as a statement of factual reality (*bhūtārthavāda*). Thus, by the inclusion of the phrase "nowhere at all," these two grounds for superiority are implied. This is because it is heard in the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad: "The Lord of the universe, the Self-Sovereign."

"Agni is indeed the lowest of the gods, Viṣṇu the highest; between them lie all other deities"—thus the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa* teaches the preeminence of all the deities. Furthermore, in the *Lokākṣi-Gṛhya*, beginning with the mantra "To Agni, lord of the earth, svāhā" and ending with "To Brahmā, lord of the worlds, svāhā," after demonstrating the individual sovereignty of Agni, Soma, Vāyu, Sūrya, Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Mahāsena, Rudra, and Brahmā over the earth, stars, atmosphere, heaven, gods, spirits, waters, yakṣas, armies, and the terrestrial world respectively, [it concludes] with "To Viṣṇu, the sovereign of all..."

Furthermore, by the utterance of "svāhā," which demonstrates uncontracted universal sovereignty, the view that the repose of unsurpassed lordship belongs solely to the form of Nārāyaṇa is refuted; for the statement "the Lord of the universe" (patiṃ viśvasya), like "Indra is superior to the universe" (viśvasmād indra uttaraḥ) and so forth, is susceptible to limitation. This is because [the passage] "Agni is the lowest (or best)" and so forth is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) regarding the Agni-Viṣṇu sacrificial cake, [intended to show] "Agni is the mouth of the gods, the first of the deities; Agni is foremost among the deities; Agni indeed is the first of the deities; Agni... [and so on].

By such scriptural passages (*śruti*) as "Agni and Soma are indeed the two kings of all deities," by such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as "Fire is the foremost of deities, like the spring among flowers, and the Brāhmaṇa is the best of bipeds," and by indicative marks (*liṅga*) from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and other sources such as "headed by Agni" (*hutāśanapurogamāḥ*), as well as by Jaimini’s sūtra— which, while demonstrating the position that Agni is the deity of the *upāṃśuyāja*, intends to show Agni's preeminence— it is understood that Agni is superior; therefore, it is impossible for him to be inferior to all other deities.

In the portion stating "Agni is indeed the protector," since certain specific deities must be [specified] as the lords of the sacrifice, and because it must be stated that this [portion] is an *arthavāda* whose meaning is restricted and which serves as a basis for support, then—given its identical status (*samānayogakṣema*)—in the portion stating "Viṣṇu is supreme" as well, [the same applies]. Furthermore, regarding the purpose of grasping the [deity] for the sake of the sacrifice, [the question arises]: in the subsidiary offerings (*iṣṭi*), should the *agnyanvādhāna* rite be performed or not?

In this doubt, [the opponent argues]: "One should first offer to Agni... Having grasped the deities on the previous day, he who sacrifices on the following day [does so] by means of that [grasping]. Since the deity-grasping of the subject at hand has already been performed, one might think that it need not be done again for the sake of grasping the deities to whom one intends to sacrifice. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the sūtra states]: "One about to be initiated should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu...

Viṣṇu is the highest among the deities; having thus grasped them on both sides, he is initiated. Thus, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] is for the sake of grasping the deities to whom one intends to sacrifice.

Because of the scriptural statement that the *dīkṣā* (initiation) is for the purpose of "appropriating" (*parigraha*) Soma—as heard in the text "the initiation is for the sake of Soma"—even though its primary purpose is the Soma-sacrifice (in which Soma is not the principal element), since all deities are present in the *vaiśvadeva-graha*, the act of appropriation performed by that [initiation] incidentally accomplishes the appropriation of the deities of the subordinate parts (*aṅga*) as well. Since the purpose has thus been fulfilled, it was established [as the final view] that the [appropriation] need not be performed for those [subordinate deities]. However, if such statements as "Agni is the lowest among the gods" were taken to have a restricted meaning or were merely *arthavāda*s based on what is untrue, they could not maintain their status. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having to perform the *agnyanvādhāna* (the placing of fuel on the fires) even in the *prāyaṇīya* and other such rites.

Thus it should be stated: after the carrying forth (*viharaṇa*) of the fires, since a visible purpose is possible—namely, the maintenance of the fires in their proper sequence for the sake of providing powerful fuel—it is not logical to assume an unseen purpose, such as the acceptance by a deity, based merely on a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) that contradicts reason. In the *Soma* sacrifice, because the fire intended for the *Soma* is scattered and remains undetermined, the maintenance of the fire is already accomplished through incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Consequently, since its own function is fulfilled, the requirement for the fire-kindling (*agnyanvādhāna*) does not apply to its subsidiary *iṣṭi*s; this is established by the previously mentioned section (*adhikaraṇa*) following the twelfth [book], which concerns the purpose of maintenance.

Since it is established in that very context that "for me, the kindling of the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) does not exist," and because the cited section, by relying on a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) whose meaning was unintended, allows for the non-performance [of the rite],

and because the Mīmāṃsakas have determined in that very place that it is merely a form of debate (*vāda*) by relying on another similar supplementary statement or by accepting it as having the same purpose; and furthermore, because even if the statement regarding the "non-contempt of the fires" (*agnyavamānatva*) were accepted from both sides, it would be impossible to accept everything [if taken literally], and thus the non-contempt of the fires and so forth would be untenable.

And because the meaning [of the mantra] is not intended to be expressed [in its literal sense], and because it is clear that the *tantras* recited in the *Lokākṣigṛhya* are each employed individually in the twelve *homa* offerings which are parts of the *kṛcchra* penance—

according to the statement in the sūtra determining the extent of a *yajus*, "Or [it is] one sentence, because of the unity of purpose"— there is no single sentence formed by their combination due to their being distinct sentences. Consequently, since there is no collective intent toward a single purpose, the words ending in the dative case, such as *pṛthivyadhipataye* and so forth, which serve as qualifiers for Agni and the others, do not collectively exclude [the recipients] from Agni and the rest to establish the state of all-encompassing sovereignty in Viṣṇu.

Furthermore, due to a lack of inherent capacity—just as in the case of certain words within the *Śikhā-mantra*—there is no intention (*tātparya*) to establish the possession of universal sovereignty for some [beings] while excluding others; rather, because of the powerful contradiction with the mantra "Svāhā to Viṣṇu, the Lord of All," those mantras that admit of restriction apply only to Indra and the others who serve as world-protectors (*lokapāla*) distinct from Rudra, since Rudra is also understood to be a world-protector. Moreover, in the *Catur-purāṇa*, during the enumeration of the eight cities of the world-protectors situated upon Mount Meru, it is stated that [Rudra's city] is...

In the eastern quarter lies the auspicious and meritorious city of Śaṅkara, named Yaśovatī, which is always [the resort] of all. Therein stands the beautiful palace of Īśāna, whose body is pervaded by Rudra;

there also resides the vast abode of Gaṇeśvara together with his hosts. Because of the statement that [he] is the remainder of the enumeration of those endowed with the manifestation of the portions of Śiva along with his attendants (*gaṇa*), and because there is no room for the doubt that Viṣṇu’s sovereignty might be distinguished here as separate from Śiva, therefore, according to the *Atharvaśikhā*, it is indeed Śiva’s [sovereignty].

"The attainment of unsurpassed sovereignty" is faultless because she is stronger than all else in every respect. Let it be so; having refuted [the objection that] Puruṣottama is the one to be reached through the reality [of the syllables], let it be that the attainment of unsurpassed sovereignty belongs to him alone. For others conceive it thus: having stated at the beginning of this [text] that the three mantras of the *praṇava*—which are white in color—have the three *mūrtis* as their deities, they state that the fourth half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) consists of all phonemes and has Puruṣa as its deity.

And it has been stated that this person is indeed the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*). Because of the well-known fact that his universal form (*viśvarūpavigraha*) possesses various colors and shapes—since all colors are established as belonging to him—and because of the scriptural testimony (*śruti*) stating, "The form of this very person is like saffron, or like a white woolen cloth," and so forth; and since the opening statement (*upakrama*), being more powerful, is determined by both direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*) to refer to the Supreme Person, the concluding statements must be interpreted in accordance with that.

The terms *śiva*, and so forth—such as "the imperishable Śiva," "the infallible," and so on—must be explained in that very same manner. Furthermore, among his thousand names, there are words denoting the terms *Śambhu* and *Śiva*, such as "Īśāna," "Prabhu," and "Prāṇa. Moreover, the concluding statement, "But the Cause is to be meditated upon," is intended to determine that He is the object of meditation by way of restating what is established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); it does not, however, intend to enjoin Him as the cause of anything here.

Since the inquiry has proceeded with the question "And who is to be meditated upon?", and since His causality is heard of in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* and other texts, one might suspect that His status as the root cause is impossible; however, this is not so, because it is possible for the passage to refer to His manifestations (vibhūtis), as established by such statements as "Of the Ādityas, I am Viṣṇu. Although it may appear that this is merely a rejection of the description of His true nature—on account of the manifest weakness of other arguments and their contradiction by the subordinate [texts]—in determining the meaning of Vedic matters, which depend on resolving immediate doubts, one must rely on reasoning rather than on arguments fabricated by one's own intellect.
For the Upabrahmaṇas are more important;
they have been shown below and are heard of in the Harivaṃśa and other texts,
being capable of utterly uprooting the evil suspicions created by wrong views.
Furthermore, in the description of the manifestation of the Great Liṅga (*mahāliṅgaprādurbhāva*) within the Śaiva tradition,
her Śaiva nature has been made clear in its entirety through a detailed exposition.
"The *praṇava*, the *Śatarudrīya*, as well as the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Śikhā*—
the recitation (*japa*) of these is proclaimed as 'self-study' (*svādhyāya*) for one's son.
Thus it is stated in the *Āditya Purāṇa* in the section defining Śiva-yoga.
Just as in the case of the Śrī Rudra and other [texts], her nature as Śiva has been made manifest.

"He who is established in the Śaiva, Pārāśara, and Skanda Purāṇas as Śiva himself—described clearly even by explicit statement—having abandoned everything else, Śiva alone is the bestower of auspiciousness. He, the Lord of the presiding deities, is the one to be meditated upon; thus concludes the Ātharvaṇa Śruti."
Having abandoned everything else, Śiva alone is the bringer of auspiciousness.
"The one to be meditated upon"—thus indeed says the supreme Śruti of the Atharvaṇa;
for that auspicious Śikhā of the Atharvaṇa is the most excellent among all the Vedas.
In this matter, that [text] and other Śrutis as well have reached their conclusion.
However, it is not possible to establish that these words have any other meaning.
Although the majesty of Śiva has been introduced and set forth here and there,
nevertheless, an objection raised according to logic [would be] like a fallacious argument, in the absence of a formal treatise.
The Veda would not be pacified by the weight of secondary exegesis (*upabrahmaṇa*) for those of perverted intellect;
for in this way, the scripture, though its meaning is clear,
leads those who are obstinate and shameless into confusion regarding what is not the proper place [for such interpretation].

And how could those who seize [the property] while it is being watched, out of sheer audacity, take away that which has been produced as a supplement to the Veda along with its ritual manuals and so forth? How indeed would they not be led [to ruin]?
Therefore, for the sake of establishing their hopelessness, he utterly uproots those fallacious arguments cited by those who consider themselves wise.

By means of the words "commencement" (*upakrānti*) and "common qualities" (*sādhāraṇaguṇa*), [the opponent] intends to establish that [the subject] is Hari; however, since this is not stated, and because [the opponent] has accepted [the subject] as being understood through the causality [of the qualities], and because there is no desire for this [subject] and even a forced conclusion, who indeed would follow [this view] while remaining deluded? Even if one considers the commencement, although the *śruti* and *liṅga* are uncommon [to other deities], there is no scope here for the strength [of the commencement] regarding the Self; for in the conclusion, there are four *śruti* passages—*Īśāna*, *Śambhu*, *Śiva*, and *Sarveśvara*—which denote Śiva.

Because the import of the concluding portion (*upasaṃhāra*) is indeed more powerful than that of the introductory portion (*upakrama*), for this very reason, in a passage such as "I am indeed this space" (*ākāśo vā eṣaḥ*), the word "space" (*ākāśa*) occurring in the introduction—though it might suggest the elemental ether—is set aside by the marks (*liṅga*) of the dissolution of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and other marks such as being distinct from that [ether], immortality, and the scriptural mention of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātma-śruti*). Thus, in accordance with those [concluding marks], the introductory section—which would otherwise suggest the elemental ether—is refuted, and the passage is determined to have Brahman as its subject.

It has been established [in the *Tantravārttika*] that "space [is a substance] because of its designation as a distinct entity," etc. Here, regarding the cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Prajāpati, consisting of curd, honey, ghee, water, and so forth—since these are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *aindrāgna-sānnāyya*, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*) applies by virtue of being the first mentioned. Even though honey, water, and ghee are modifications of the *pāñcahotṛ-havis* and are heard of last, they are favored by their greater number; thus, the ritual procedure of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) applies. This is stated [by the Sūtra]: "In the case of conflicting properties..."

"In a conflict between many [authoritative sources], the nature of the majority shall prevail"—this principle, shown in the *adhikaraṇa* (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.3–4), is applicable here as well; for even by opponents, it is admitted that when there is a contradiction with subsequent qualities, the initial [indication] is weak. Thus, here too, by the force of the abundance of evidence situated in the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), one can establish the text's focus on Śiva by interpreting the initial portion (*upakrama*) otherwise. Moreover, even if one follows the initial indication, its focus on Śiva alone is proven; for this is so because of the division of letters among deities according to the mantras.

Even more so, when demonstrating the division of the worlds and so forth, after teaching the three measures (*mātrā*)—earth, intermediate space, and heaven—as the worlds, it was taught that "the fourth half-measure at its conclusion is the world of Soma. Here, the "world of Soma" does not refer to the world of the moon, because since that is included within the world of heaven (*dyuloka*), it cannot be mentioned separately. Rather, it refers to the supreme world of Śiva, as explained in the *Śivadharma-uttara* and other texts, which is otherwise known as Mahākailāsa and transcends all the worlds presided over by Umā. For this very reason...

In the chapter on the manifestation of the Great Liṅga of Śiva (*Śaivamahāliṅgaprādurbhāvādhyāya*), within the section describing the majesty of Śiva based on the meaning of the *Atharvaśikhā*, an exposition of the world of Soma (*somaloka*) is seen. It states: "Above that, beyond the world of the Unmanifest (*unmanāloka*), is the worldly world of Soma; there the Lord dwells eternally together with Umā. Since the beginning and the conclusion thus possess a single consistent meaning, the mention of the signs of other deities found in the intervening narrative—similar to how the signs of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) were interpreted otherwise [in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*]—must likewise be explained differently. Nevertheless...

In order to demonstrate the vast scope [of his own position] and to achieve the total uprooting of the opposing side, he shows that the *śruti* and *liṅga* cited by the opponent are non-conclusive due to their commonality, using the two words "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) and "quality" (*guṇa*). Indeed, the commonality of both is clear even from the primary subject [of the context]: "Except for those born blind or deaf, this is understood by everyone alike.

Nevertheless—even though there are scriptural passages such as "Puruṣa, indeed, Nārāyaṇa, desired," and "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads"—O Goddess, neither the Grandfather (Brahmā), nor Indra, nor... [is the Lord].
Furthermore, in the Purāṇas, such as "Even today they speak of Rudra’s power;

[the Creator] beheld that primordial God, the Puruṣa," and in the works of learned authors, such as "Having withdrawn the worlds, the Puruṣa lies upon them," the word *puruṣa* is seen to be used for Viṣṇu. Nevertheless, because of the necessity of its denotative power (*śakti*) residing in the general sense of the Self (*ātman-sāmānya*), given the abundance of both worldly and Vedic usage—as evidenced by lexicographical authorities (*abhidhāna-kośa*) such as "The two Puruṣas are the measure and the immeasurable"—it is logical that the term applies to that [Self] alone.

Nor can a capacity for that [meaning] be postulated even for Viṣṇu, because of the contradiction in the *Barhir-ājyādhikaraṇa*. For in that section, having raised the objection that words such as *barhis* (sacrificial grass) and *ājya* (clarified butter)—which are used by Mlecchas for mere grass and by Āryas only for consecrated grass and so forth—must have their basis in consecration (*saṃskāra*) due to the greater authority of the usage established within the scripture according to the principle of the *Yavavarāhādhikaraṇa*, [the author] refutes it by showing that the scripture’s usage does not deviate from the genus (*jāti*), and that the common practice of ordinary people is based solely on... [the genus].

Because of the deviation of [specific] linguistic formations (*saṃskāra*), one must rely on the non-deviating power of the genus (*jāti*). Since this is present in all applications and is not subject to destruction, it is established that the power [of the word] belongs exclusively to the genus; as it is stated in the *Tantravārttika*: "When even a single part of a word is observed to be based upon a genus, there is no room for postulating another cause for it, as long as one does not abandon that [genus]. Thus, when the power of the general term is established through the well-known usage among Mlecchas, the specific meaning is obtained through those means by which the conventional usage is established.

Thus, there is no assumption of a specific power (*viśeṣa-śakti*). In that case, what [is the point]? Regarding the subject at hand here, since even the general rule (*sāmānya-vyāpti*) pertains to the Āryas, there is no room for the suspicion of its weakness.

However, the constant application of other instances is otherwise pure. Right here, after the injunction of the three great deities—namely, "having Brahman as the deity," "having Viṣṇu as the deity," and "having Rudra as the deity"—there follows the injunction of the deity of the *puruṣa* (the half-measure), namely, "having Puruṣa as the deity. Because the general category of *puruṣa* is employed as the deity, [it refers] to the supreme specific deity beyond the triple form (*trimūrti*).

If it is argued that the application of the word *puruṣa*—by virtue of its placement within a context primarily consisting of injunctions regarding deities expressed by various specific terms—will, even while specifically designating the word *puruṣa*, lead it to terminate in that very [deity] in accordance with the usage of Nārāyaṇa as established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other means; we say no. For when the intended specific meaning can be reached even through a general power (*sāmānya-śakti*), it is impossible for mere proximity in a list (*prāyapāṭha*) alone to necessitate the assumption of another, more cumbersome power. Therefore, "only one [offering] is to be given."

In the scriptural injunction regarding the different options for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration)—stating that twelve should be given, twenty-four should be given, a thousand should be given, or an unlimited amount should be given—the term "unlimited" (*aparimita*) refers, according to the first section of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtras*, to that which is beyond the measure of what is prescribed by the learned. Since it is established as referring to another ritual procedure (*kalpa*) equal to or greater than one [starting from] one, and because of the principle stated in the sūtra: "Or it may be more, because of its multiple meanings due to proximity with others," even though it occurs in a list of words denoting specific numbers intended to be enjoined, it is understood through the force of the general sense of plurality (*bahutva*) alone to mean a plurality exceeding a thousand.

If it is argued: "Granted that the mere usage [of the word] might be established otherwise due to the determination of its final meaning; nevertheless, the etymological derivation (nirvacana) provided by the Paurāṇikas—that Hari is called 'Puruṣa' because he 'lies' (śayanāt) in this body known as 'puruṣa'—is not established otherwise, and thus it will postulate a specific denotative power (śakti) for the word even in its specialized sense," we reply: No. For although the word *puruṣa* possesses a general denotative power, in certain instances within the Śrutis and other texts, by the force of context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, it refers specifically to Nārāyaṇa.

Since its purpose is fulfilled by merely making known that "there is a conclusion," the etymological derivation found in the Purāṇas—which is primarily an explanatory statement (arthavāda)—is established as a qualification of a specific hymn in the *Citrādhikaraṇa*.

Consequently, because the word *puṣ* occurs in certain instances such as "one approaches with the *pṛṣṭhas*," it functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) even for the *rathantara* and other [sāmans] which are the means of achieving that [hymn].

Thus, the passage beginning with "water indeed is the *ṛc*s; their nourishment (*puṣṭi*) is Vāyu" and ending with "it turns away from their nourishment" is intended to demonstrate the grounds for applying the word *puṣṭha* to the *rathantara* and so forth, thereby fulfilling its purpose through that explanation.

Because it is established as having another purpose—namely, that it is otherwise established—it is designated as "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*). Since it is impossible to postulate a further power (*śakti*) regarding the scope of usage that can be accounted for by the powers assigned to it in lexicons, traditional texts (*smṛti*), and so forth, this is not the case. For, even though the word *puṣṭha* is established as the name of a hymn (*stotra*), there is no explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to convey a ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in the case of the *rantarāmnāya*, which is fit for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). It is for this reason that the venerable Jaimini himself, at the end of the third section of the seventh book, states: "He worships with the *puṣṭha* [verses]. Thus, the capacity [of the word] is fully accounted for therein.

In this context, regarding the inquiry as to whether the word *puṣṭha* refers to the hymn of praise (*stotra*) for Mahendra or to the *rathantara* and other [sāmans], the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by the sūtra stating that "because of the instruction of the word *puṣṭha* in connection with the ritual action," the word *puṣṭha*—due to its general similarity to the instruction—refers to the act of praising. Therefore, by asserting that the application [of the term] to the sāman is the default rule (*autsargika*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached through the argument that the word *pratiṣṭha* (in *dṛṣṭapratiṣṭha*) refers to the hymn because of the instruction regarding the designation (*abhidhāropadeśāt*) and because of the prohibition [otherwise]. Thus, by presenting the supporting arguments for its reference to the hymn and by establishing the restriction to the *rathantara* and other [sāmans], [the point is settled].

In that regard, because the secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) is made explicit there, and because all [authorities] such as the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) employ the term *lakṣaṇā* for that very case, by this [reasoning], the word "Person" (*puruṣa*) likewise refers to Vāsudeva alone. Apart from that lotus-eyed one, what other person could be the bearer of the word "Person"? Thus, both this word "Lord" (*bhagavat*) and the word "Person" (*puruṣa*) apply to the eternal Vāsudeva without any limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*).
Brahmā and the others, along with all the gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras.

Because they all possess a portion of the *puruṣa*, they are called "puruṣas"—such are the examples cited by others to demonstrate that the word *puruṣa* is not common [to all] but is restricted [to specific cases]. However, this argument is refuted by relying on the Puranic statements regarding the removal of shadows (*chāyāpahāni*), which establish its non-commonality. Since the general power of the self (*ātmasāmānyaśakti*), which is universally accepted, cannot be avoided, it follows that there can be no such thing as non-commonality [in this context]. This is analogous to the statement, "Others are indeed non-animals (*apaśavaḥ*) compared to cows and horses; cows and horses are the animals," where the term "animals" is used in a non-common way specifically for cows and horses.

Just like the statement regarding "the state of being a beast" (*paśutva*), the cited passages are appropriately intended as praises based on the fullness of human attributes such as independence; otherwise, the state of being a beast would also result in being an uncommon property [of humans] among cows and horses.
Thus it is said: "This Vāsudeva is called 'Puruṣa' by the wise."
Because it is devoid of contact with primordial nature (prakṛti), and because of its sovereignty and majesty.
"He alone is this Vāsudeva, who is called the manifest Puruṣa;
all else, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, is predominantly female (strīprāya).

This statement from the Nārasiṃha Purāṇa, along with other exclusive declarations, clearly demonstrates that [the term] refers to the activity of the male (puṃsavyāpāra). Therefore, [it does not apply to] the word "Puruṣa" [in its ordinary sense].

The capacity [of the word] is distinguished by its uncommon application and uncommon expressions regarding Viṣṇu; if that were so, then [one could cite] such scriptural passages as "We know the Puruṣa, we meditate upon the thousand-eyed Mahādeva," and "The Puruṣa who is dark-brown, the Lord, the Puruṣa, the adorable God," and so forth, after introducing [the passage] with "Śūdras are the foot-servants of the wielder of the Pināka. Of men...

Furthermore, [it is said] that "the glorious Puruṣa is to be known through wisdom and not otherwise" (Laiṅga), and in the Śiva[-purāṇa], "from his forehead was born the three-eyed one, the wielder of the trident," and so forth. Also, in the scriptures concerning Saṃhārarudra, such as "the Puruṣa, the size of a thumb, rests upon the thumb," the fact that he dwells in the foundational world at the root of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa)—a point established by the indicative mark (liṅga) of his resting upon the thumb which is the root of the microcosmic egg (piṇḍāṇḍa)—is seen in the Puruṣa who is Kālāgnirudra. And in the scriptures such as "with the Puruṣa as the oblation," the person created by him is called "Brahman" in the world.

Because it is celebrated in the *Manusmṛti* and because of its usage in reference to Brahman; and because of the etymological derivation in the *Laiṅgya Purāṇa* during the discussion on the definition of the name "Jīva," which states: "Since he lies within the city (puri), therefore he is called Puruṣa"; and because in the Vedāntas, Śiva is designated as Puruṣa by those who are engaged [in inquiry], as in the passage: "Him whom they call the one Puruṣa, who stands pervading both heaven and earth" (*Rodasī*); and because of the statement in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*: "Since he burned away (auṣat) all evils prior to all this, therefore he is Puruṣa."

Because he is defined by the name "Brahmā," he is indeed called the first embodied being and the Puruṣa by all; for in numerous Purāṇas, such as "He is the original creator of beings, Brahmā appeared in the beginning," he is taught under that name. Thus, Śiva—who possesses the characteristics of Śakti and the rest, who bears the form of Sāmba, and whose name is complete as Puruṣa—is none other than Rudra, Viṣṇu, or even Brahmā.

Thus, because the *Brahmagītās* in the *Śivendra* establish [the Lord's] uniqueness (*asādhāraṇya*), it may also be so elsewhere. Therefore, whether in a single way or in many ways, since [the Lord] is common to all through His power (*śakti*), it is not proper to determine a specific deity by means of the term "Person" (*puruṣa-śruti*). As for the one who is seen as a golden Person within the waters, and this Person who is seen in the eye—the divine, formless Person, He is higher than the highest, beyond this mass of living beings (*jīva-ghana*)... [I seek] that Person. I seek you.

If [the opponent were to argue that] the person the size of a thumb (*aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ puruṣaḥ*) is the Supreme Being because of the scriptural statements, and because He is superior even to that [thumb-sized person], because of the teaching regarding Him as being within the heart (*antastaddharmopadeśāt*), because He is logically appropriate as being internal (*antara upapatteḥ*), because of the mention of qualities such as being the Lord (*adhipatitvādi-guṇa-yoga-ukteḥ*), and because of the designation of the object of His vision (*īkṣitakarmavyapadeśāt*), then the commencement of the Sūtras for the purpose of investigating that [thumb-sized person] would be redundant.
