Even if one were to somehow justify the commencement, it would be inconsistent with the fact that [in the previous section], the subject matter was established as Brahman through various indicative marks (*liṅgaiḥ*) starting from "because of the teaching of the highest place" (*adhikopadeśāt*).

In the presence of powerful scriptural testimony, those [other arguments] are [invalidated], because they are unsuitable for that [Supreme Self]. According to the view of the opponent, action is perceived; that [Self] is supreme because of designations such as being "higher than form," "tranquil," and "immortal. Thus, the meaning of the mantra "That which is the source of these utterances is formless" is that it refers to the Person (Puruṣa).

As for the section concerning action, one meditates upon action and perceives action alone. Even though the section concerning the thumb states that the Supreme Self, the Person, is measured by the thumb—[yet the conclusion remains as stated].

Thus, although it might be possible to explain the meaning as "from that which is denoted by those [words]," nevertheless, because its commonality [with other meanings] has been established by the aforementioned principles, the venerable Bhagavatpāda has explained it simply as "from the word *Īśāna*. The author of the subsequent commentary (*Parabhāṣyakṛt*) has also explained it as "from the word denoting the Supreme Self," namely "of the past and the future" (*bhūtabhavyasya*). Furthermore, it is stated in the commentary on that subsequent commentary that the word "word" (*śabda*) is intended to refer specifically to the word *Īśāna*. Moreover, according to that view, the creation of dreams is caused by the individual soul (*jīva*).

In the section concerning the creation during the intermediate state (*sandhya-sarga*)—which proceeds for the sake of a definitive conclusion by refuting the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the agency of another—in the commentary on the sūtra "And the creator is one" (*nirmātāraṃ caikaḥ*), the statement "He who wakes among these sleeping ones, creating desires" was cited to establish the prima facie view. That too would be utterly irrelevant; for a scriptural passage that establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) cannot simultaneously be used to establish the prima facie position. [Objection: But in the Vaiśvānara section, it was argued: "It is not so, because of the word and other reasons, and because he abides within. To this, [the author] replies: "No..."

Likewise, regarding the Sūtra "One should study this [text] even if it is harsh, because of the impossibility of such a teaching being seen," it is true that the status of Vaiśvānara as the Supreme Self was determined there by the scriptural mention of "Puruṣa" in the passage, "This Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the Puruṣa. However, the intended determination there was not based on the word "Puruṣa" being unique to Brahman; for if that were the case, the doubt that Vaiśvānara might be the gastric fire—arising from the mark (liṅga) of his being established within the person—would have been rendered groundless right here [in the present context], since that mark would already have been resolved. What then?

When it was suspected that he [the Self] might be the gastric fire (jāṭhara) based on such marks as being "established within" mentioned in the words beginning with "fire" and ending with "person," it was stated that he cannot be the gastric fire because the latter cannot have the three worlds as its body; then, another reason was set forth with the words "even the person," etc., in order to refute that [gastric fire], since the word "person"—which denotes a conscious being—is heard there, and thus the intention is that the gastric fire is not unconscious. And this is like the mark of "seeing" (īkṣati) which was set forth for the purpose of refuting Pradhāna.

Indeed, because it is capable of excluding other possible alternatives even through qualities common to all conscious beings, this is entirely appropriate. For this very reason, having referred to the reason stated in the Sūtra—"and because it is not of the nature of a deity"—the status of that [Agni] as a deity consisting of the conceit of fire (*abhimāni-devatā*) is also refuted by that same [reason]. Thus, since it is ultimately impossible, only the reason "because of impossibility" is referred to, due to the uniformity of the case-ending.
Or, in the passage "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa; he reached his own deity," the word "he" refers to Prajāpati alone, or it may refer to both.

Let the scriptural mention of "Puruṣa" (the Person) be understood as merely excluding [the soul's] actual state of being [an individual]; however, in the alternative reading written by the venerable Pāda [Śaṅkara], "And they study him as having the form of a person (*puruṣavidha*)," there is not even a trace of doubt. Enough with this elaboration. Thus, because it is common to many worldly and Vedic entities, and because the existence of Śiva’s body in all castes is well-known through the distinction of the color of each conch in the form of Śrī Sadāśiva, and because such a universal-form body (*viśvarūpa-vigraha*) of his is also established in the *Padma Purāṇa* and other texts, [there is no contradiction].

Furthermore, there is hope for a definitive conclusion even from the mention of all the *varṇas* and *liṅgas*. Moreover, that form which was displayed by Vāsudeva to Pārtha among them is recognized as being Śaiva alone; for in that very passage it is proclaimed that he is the Lord (*īśvara*), stating: "He showed Pārtha his supreme, incomparable, divine (*aiśvara*) form. Having assumed that form, Kṛṣṇa described how these [enemies] had already been slain, saying: "Become merely an instrument, O Savyasācin," since the enemies were killed in the direct presence [of Arjuna] before [the vision of the form], thus describing their state as already slain.

Regarding the statement that [Kṛṣṇa] revealed his own Śiva-form to Pārtha in the *Mokṣadharma* section (*Mahābhārata*, 12.349), it is said: "By him [Śiva], your enemies were previously slain; you have merely killed them. Furthermore, [it is stated]: "Worship constantly and with self-restraint the God of gods, Umā’s consort, the Lord of the Universe, whose progeny is immeasurable. How, then, can it be claimed that Kṛṣṇa demonstrated his own Śiva-form as being identical to himself? This is because [the text] teaches that he was slain by the power and majesty of Śiva’s seed (*śivavīryaprabhāva*), and because it makes manifest the fact that he belongs to Śiva (*śaivatva*). Thus, how could Kṛṣṇa have shown his own form as Śiva?

If it is argued that [the two] do not merge because of their difference, this is not so; for in the *Laiṅgya*, Dadhīca demonstrated to the Magas the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) of Śiva through the power of yoga, and this is established here as well. Since the statement "Behold my sovereign yoga" implies that it was set in motion precisely by the power of yoga, such a conceptualization is appropriate. However, in reality, since non-difference alone is established by the Vedic standard (*vaidikamaryādā*), [it belongs] to Girirāja.

Having ascertained that this entire collection of glories— characterized by the sovereignty over the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the whole universe residing in Kṛṣṇa— was brought forth from His own mouth in the chapter beginning with "This yoga I taught to Vivasvat," and that all these glories were spoken by Kṛṣṇa with the intention of establishing His own primordial and supreme form as something already accomplished (siddhavatkṛtya), as evidenced by the force of the answer to Arjuna’s question, "Your birth was later [than His]," Arjuna says: "For the origin and dissolution of beings have been heard by me in detail from You."
"O Supreme Lord, O Puruṣottama, I desire to see Your divine, sovereign form—Your very self which is thus the reality, possessing the majesty of lotus-petal eyes and being imperishable.

Indeed, this prayer for the vision of His divine universal form (*viśvarūpa*) is the cause for the manifestation of that form. And so, since it is that very form which possesses full sovereignty, is supreme over all, and is primordial, that alone should be shown to Him; therefore, why would the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, who is compassionate toward His devotees, not manifest that very Śaiva form?
This is consistent with the statement: "Those deluded ones who disregard me, having assumed a human body, not knowing my supreme nature as the Great Lord (maheśvara) of all beings" (Gītā 9.11).

Having heard words such as "Great Lord" (*maheśvara*) in this ancient speech of Kṛṣṇa, and having further ascertained—through the collection of evidentiary factors to be presented later in the analysis of the Gītā’s meaning—that the Supreme Form of Kṛṣṇa is indeed the foundational Īśvara, Arjuna requested its manifestation, saying: "O Supreme Person, I wish to see your divine form" (Gītā 11.4).

If it is so conceived, then there is no room for objection here at all. Thus, since the form of the Cosmic Body (*viśvarūpa*) described in the *Gītā* is also perceived as Śaiva, the determination that it refers to Viṣṇu cannot be established by the aforementioned indicative mark (*liṅga*) under any circumstances. As for the scriptural passage beginning with "of this" (*etasya*) which was cited, it has been explained with supporting arguments by the venerable Bhagavatpāda in his commentary on the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* as being intended to demonstrate the various distinctions of objective latent impressions (*vāsanā*) mounted upon the instruments (*karaṇa*), which consist of the individual and collective aspects (*vyaṣṭi-samaṣṭi*) of the elements—wind, ether, taste, and earth—which are themselves divided into the divine (*ādhidevika*) and the personal (*ādhyātmika*). Therefore, [the passage does not refer to Viṣṇu].

The counter-argument raised by her is open to objection; even regarding the matter accepted by the opponent—that the Puruṣa is Nārāyaṇa—we do not see any definitive proof. In reality, at the conclusion [of the passage], that half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) of the fourth [syllable] is "all the phonemes" (*sarvavarṇā*); thus, the meditation on all phonemes is heard as being merely a quality (*guṇa*) of the half-mora, and not that it is [the deity] itself by virtue of that quality. Therefore, there is no room for the objection seeking a determination of a specific deity through that. Thus, since "being all the phonemes" has been stated, the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) alone, as qualified by *Māyā*, constitutes the beginning and the conclusion [of the text].

Therefore, since the scriptural citations (*śruti*) and indicative marks (*liṅga*) mentioned are common [to other deities], it is proper to determine the meaning through the opening statement (*upakrama*), whose sense has been ascertained, according to the maxim: "But when there is doubt, [the decision is made] from the remainder" (*sandigdhe tu... śeṣāt*). As for the suspicion that even those [terms] denote Viṣṇu—that is not so; for it is not established merely by usage, nor by the exclusion of other [possibilities], nor because their names are well-enumerated in lexicons (*kośa*). Furthermore, those names [which appear to denote others] are either used in the sense of Śiva and so forth, or they are intended to signify the universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*) [of the deity].

Regarding the opening statement "they are secondary" (*gauṇāni*), since it is stated that names are secondary by virtue of either their connection with a quality (*guṇa*) or their connection with a mark (*liṅga*), [the name Śiva] is primarily a secondary name—just like the name *paraśyena* and others—because there is no evidence for its denoting that [primary sense] given the observation that many other deities are enumerated within the midst of the thousand names.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for the names of Viṣṇu not to be included among the thousands of names of Śiva recited in the *Bhārata*, the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*, the *Āditya Purāṇa*, and so forth. [The text continues: "The names are yours... (*nāmāni tava*).

And those great [names] in the world of Govinda are indeed my own names; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. Furthermore, since it is established that during the journey to Kailāsa, through the *Śakavaca*, all the names of Viṣṇu as well as other exalted names—just like the name Himakarana (the Moon) or Ghanasāra (Camphor)—possess the nature of being names of Śiva, there can be no determination anywhere that these names refer exclusively to Viṣṇu. Moreover, having introduced Śiva, [it is stated] "all these are his names," and upon hearing this designation... [one should remember].

Otherwise, the determination of other objects would be lost; therefore, because the aforementioned words are enumerated among the names of Śiva in the lexicons (*kośa*), because of their usage in both worldly and Vedic practice, and because they are His names, it is logical that the Puruṣa—who is understood at the beginning as being denoted by the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*)—is indeed Śiva, without obstructing the summary of the established meanings. For this reason, His state of being denoted by the half-mora is established in the *Śivadharmottara*: "Alternatively, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the morae (*mātrā*) in sequence."

"He who is intent upon that [which has been] indicated [by the three mātrās] is [to be understood] by means of the half-mātrā; because he is to be reached through meditation alone, the Supreme Śiva is to be contemplated"—thus it is stated in the Vāyusaṃhitā as well.

Having demonstrated the distribution of the three Vedas among the three qualities (guṇas) and the three forms (mūrtis) of the three mātrās of the Praṇava, it further declares: "Having thus expressed the entire [reality] through these three mātrās, they cause one to realize the Self which is Śiva by means of the half-mātrā. Thus, having relied upon this opening statement, the objection is refuted. Regarding what was raised concerning the passage "the Cause is to be meditated upon," he replies:

The point is this: in the case of the *sāmidhenī* verses, where it is said that "one recites the first three times and the last three times" (*triḥ prathamām anvāha trir uttamām*), the words "first" and "last" refer—by virtue of their being the first to present themselves—to the specific *ṛc* verses such as the *pravovājīyā*, which are indicated by those positions without overstepping the property of position (*sthāna-dharma*). However, in the present case, although the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) refers to the property of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) as the first to present itself, there is no absence of its referring—by way of sequence—to the specific deity and so forth indicated by that [instrumentality]. Thus, the property of instrumentality does not here exclude the deity.

When it is established that [the text] refers solely to the state of being the cause, there is an indifference toward its counter-correlate; thus, just as in the expressions "a thousand should be given" and "an immeasurable amount should be given," the word "immeasurable" implies a plurality relative to the nearby "thousand," so too, because Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others— whose causal status has been described through proximity— are ultimately resolved within the Cause, and because no other entity besides Śiva is seen to be taught as the cause in other scriptural passages even when the three Guṇamūrtis (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra) are themselves understood from the words "Brahmā," "Viṣṇu," and "Rudra."

If it were accepted that [the cause] is established there by being included within the demonstration of its being the cause of all things and so forth in some way, then here too— since the general nature of that cause is already established by the statement regarding the birth of Brahmā and the others, and since it is possible to merely restate what has been established by the immediately preceding sentence— it would be improper to look toward other scriptural passages. Furthermore, because the specific object of meditation has already been determined in the passage "He meditates on your knowledge," this present sentence— which, along with supporting arguments, aims at a summary of that same subject— must refer to that very object of meditation.

Since it is utterly inappropriate to conceive of the word as having another deity as its referent, and since even when conceiving this very sentence as being intent upon a specific object of meditation, it is more logical to regard it as a restatement of the cause established by the immediately preceding sentence— in order to avoid contradicting the natural sense (*svārasya*) of the co-referential terms such as "Śambhu"— and because, just as in the case of the *abhyudayeṣṭi* sacrifice, a restatement of what is already established by implication (such as the quality of being a sacrificial oblation) is possible, [the deity] is understood in the form of Śiva through the power [of the context] described in the introduction to the explanation of the meaning of the cited scripture.

The cause established by the immediately preceding sentence alone is reiterated here by the word "cause" (kāraṇa), and not one established by another scriptural passage. Furthermore, even if one were to assume that some other [cause] distinct from the mere cause [of the previous sentence] is reiterated and understood as being obtained through the force of the preceding sentence, even so, there would be no stable conclusion for those of false views, because in another scriptural passage Śiva alone is declared to be the cause. With this intention, he says: ||16||

Having determined that the inert and the non-Lord (the individual soul) are not capable [of creation], and having resolved that Brahman is the source of the worlds, those who do not reflect upon it wonder: "What indeed is that? Through the vision of the Great Goddess, the thought arose: "It is You. Thus he spoke of You, by whom the state of being a horse (or the end of emergence) is the supreme Śiva. At the beginning of the *Śvetāśvatara-Upaniṣad*, the exponents of Brahman say: "What is the cause? What is Brahman? From where were we born and established? By whom do we abide in pleasure and pain?"

The settled doctrine of those who know Brahman is as follows: for some [sages], Brahman is the root cause of the world; for others, having distinguished that "Brahman is the cause" through such specific inquiries as "Which god is the cause? and so forth, they demonstrate various views, beginning with: "He alone presides over those causes which are indeed insentient and joined with time," up to: "The perishable is *pradhāna*, the immortal-perishable is *Hara*; the one God enters both the perishable and the imperishable selves; he joins the perishable and the imperishable."

The Lord sustains the manifest and the unmanifest universe; thus, by means of mantras that demonstrate the established meaning for the sake of those seeking [liberation], it is made clear that the Supreme Śiva alone—the Blessed One denoted by terms such as *Hara* and *Īśa*, who presides over the collection of intermediate causes beginning with Time—is the causal Brahman. Now, one might object: in the passage "the perishable is Pradhāna," the word *Hara* does not subsequently function to provide a specific deity-qualification for the perishable and imperishable, but rather, when there is a desire to know the meaning of the terms "perishable" (*kṣara*) and "imperishable" (*akṣara*) as heard in such scriptural passages as "this is conjoined with the perishable and the imperishable," [it is explained that] the perishable...

Following the explanation of the meaning of the word *kṣara* as "the primary" (*pradhāna*), there is a connection with the word *para* (the Supreme) as if it were the predicate in the sentence explaining the meaning of the word *akṣara*. Alternatively, one might argue that because the sentence is completed by the two words *amṛta* and *akṣara*, the word *amṛta* serves as an explanation of the word *akṣara*, and thus the sentence is complete. However, this cannot be maintained; for a compound word, whose nature is to convey a single qualified meaning through a single cognitive thrust (*ekaprasaraṇa*), would suffer a fracture of its capacity (*sāmarthyavighāta*) if it were directed toward both the subject and the predicate through separate cognitive thrusts, which would result in the impossibility of forming a compound. This is precisely why [it is not so] in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*).

In the injunction "He offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* with three parts," it is determined that the term "three parts" (*tryaṅga*), being taken as a whole, cannot possibly enjoin the number three by way of referring back to the heart and other parts which constitute the primary sacrificial oblation; rather, it is concluded that it enjoins a different part qualified by the number three. Therefore, it is said that the *sviṣṭakṛt* is sacrificed from the entirety [of the remains]; this is stated in the context of the modification (*vikṛti*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*). This is not the case here [in the present text], where it is said, "the immortal syllable."

A compound word (*samāsapada*) consisting of two words in a state of mutual relation as qualifier and qualified is logically precluded by the very definition of a compound, since such a relation is incompatible with the unity of meaning required for a compound. Furthermore, it is not appropriate for the word "Hara" to explain that [meaning], because "Hara" is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring to Śiva. Rather, it must be explained by the word "hi," which is capable of conveying the individual soul (*jīva*), following the previously mentioned Lord (*īśvara*), the controller, and the two things controlled—namely, *pradhāna* and the person (*puruṣa*). This is because one desires to know precisely the meaning of the syllables heard in the other nearby mantra. Nor is it appropriate to explain it by the word "Hara," as that term is fixed in its conventional sense upon Śiva. Indeed, it should be elucidated by the word "hi," which is competent to demonstrate the living being. Thus, the sequence is: first the Lord, the controller; then *pradhāna* and the person, the two things controlled. Finally, the individual soul is to be understood. Therefore, the meaning of the mantra is as follows: "The Lord, who is the cause of the world, is distinct from *pradhāna* and the person, and He is distinct from the individual soul. Thus, the word "Hara" is used here to denote the individual soul. Because we observe its mention within the context of the *haramantra*, and because of the supplementary explanation (*upabrahmaṇa*) in the *Brahmagītā*—"The one God rules over the perishable and the imperishable, which is the nature of the individual soul" (*kṣarākṣarātmānāv īśate deva ekaḥ*)—the word *hara* does not have its usage observed in reference to the individual soul (*jīva*). Even if one were to somehow construct a meaning based on its etymological parts (*avayavārtha*), it is impossible to abandon that established meaning due to its subsequent connection; therefore, this [objection] is an incoherent prattle. Furthermore, in the phrase "the immortal, the imperishable, Hara," there is no syntactical connection (*anvaya*) due to the absence of a relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*). Moreover, the word "immortal" (*amṛta*) is a separate term referring to Nārāyaṇa.

In the word *brahma* here, just as the term *nārāyaṇa* [is used] with a third-case ending, and just as the term *tatkṛta* is used in the sūtra "guṇavacanebhyo matupo luk" (Pāṇini 5.1.123), [the word *brahma*] has its case-ending elided by the rule "supāṃ suluk... (Pāṇini 7.1.39). It refers to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme. This is because its usage in that sense is observed in this very same scripture: "The perishable is ignorance, the immortal is knowledge; knowledge and ignorance are distinct, and he who is beyond them is another. Furthermore, the existence of that meaning is stated in another scriptural passage: "It is indeed when devoid of the individual soul that this [body] dies; the soul does not die. And those two...

An explanation of the meaning of the words "akṣara" and "śabda," which were intended to be understood, is now provided. As for the word *hara*, it is appropriate that it connects with what follows later, as its purpose is to determine the specific deity who is the Lord of the perishable (*kṣara*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*).

This is likewise seen in the *Vāyusaṃhitā* regarding the Brahman: "That which is the manifest imperishable (*akṣara*), and that which is the immortal (*amṛta*), both of these are the perishable self; yet there is one God, Hara himself, who rules over them through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true nature," and so forth. Even if "amṛtākṣaram" is taken as a compound word, it remains so.

Since the word *akṣara* is explained by the word *amṛta*, the word *hara* does not apply there [to *akṣara*]. Just as in the case of the statement "he whose sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is seventeen *aratni*s long," the primary sense of the word *yūpa* is respected, and thus even within the compound, the quality of being seventeen is predicated with respect to the *aratni*; so too here, in accordance with the primary sense of the word *hara*, the word *hara* is connected as a qualifier of a specific deity in the subsequent passage, in order to eliminate the doubt regarding whether the cause of the world is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Śiva.

(…) [The compound] *asamartha-samāsa* is not a fault, as it is understood through the worship of the reality of the sentence (or the principle of the statement). It may be argued that here the cause is not Brahmā; rather, having presented the doubt among the gods beginning with Brahmā as to which god [is the cause], the determination is made that it is Śiva alone, after first refuting the doctrine that another deity is the cause. However, by the first mantra, the doubt is first presented as to whether the entity that is the cause of the world is Brahmā or something else such as Kāla (Time), and subsequently it is determined that Brahmā alone is the cause. [As for] Time and inherent nature (svabhāva) (…) *Note: The ellipses indicate missing portions of the original text.*

"Destiny, chance, the elements, the womb, and the person—these are to be considered. But since [the self] is subject to these, the Self too is not the master over the cause of pleasure and pain"—this is because the second mantra shows the refutation of those who maintain that time and so forth are the causes; for otherwise, it would be inconsistent, as one would have to refute another alternative position, namely, the doctrine that some other deity is the cause.
Therefore, by establishing here only this much—that Brahman is the cause of the world and not time and so forth—the [status of the] cause as being a specific deity is [established].

Having determined this, the subsequent establishment of the connection with the word *hara* is stated in accordance with that; however, no deliberation is shown here as to whether the object in question is *brahma*, *kāla*, or something else, because the second alternative is not heard. For a sentence of doubt must either consist of the word *kim* alone, which is capable of presenting all possible alternatives in a general sense—such as "What tree is this?"—or it must consist of specific words referring to those particular alternatives—such as "Is this tree a mango or a jackfruit? Since the latter is the case here, there is no room for such a deliberation.

However, the presentation of only a single alternative (*ekakoṭi*) as a specific [option] is contrary to linguistic usage (*vyutpatti-viruddha*). Therefore, in order to obtain the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the word "Brahman" mentioned in proximity, the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of other alternatives is unavoidable. Otherwise, if this were a sentence expressing a doubt with one alternative predominant—like "Is it Yajñadatta?"—then subsequent deliberative sentences whose [other] alternatives are devoid of predominance, such as "From what was he born?", would result in the non-occurrence of names for people. Furthermore, in this context, the word *kiṃ* (what/which) functions exactly as in the case of "What is this standing before me, a post or a man? (*sthāṇuḥ puruṣo vā*).

Likewise, regarding the limit of the property being conceptualized (*vikalpamānadharmī*), does this [sentence] end with "Is this a post or a person? as being solely devoted to mere conceptualization? In the first case, there would be a breakdown of the recognized unity of the sentence, because one part would be a general inquiry while the other part would be a specific inquiry; furthermore, it would entail the necessity of supplying an unstated sentence that conveys the optionality of the two alternatives specifically presented. In the second case, there would be the consequence of having to conform to the reading of other instances of the word *kiṃ* (what/how) ending in properties, such as "From what [cause]... and so forth, up to the limit of the property.

If it is argued that in both cases there is no contradiction with other such statements in the specific deliberative passage, and that none of this constitutes a fault because—by the force of the subsequent necessity of refuting the doctrine of time as a causal agent—a deliberative statement regarding "Brahman as the cause" or "time as the cause" must be supplied, we say no; for that very [statement] is what is constrained by the requirement of supplying it. To explain: having first determined the meaning of the mantra immediately following it, which begins "Those who have attained the yoga of meditation saw... and so forth, [the text proceeds].

It is taught that for their sake, one should perform the meditation on the deity (*devatādhyāna*) in order to reach a definitive conclusion; however, how could this be consistent if the refutation of other alternatives within the scope of doubt were already manifest prior to that? Nor can it be said that there is no such inconsistency, because of the rule regarding the sequence between the purpose of reaching a definitive conclusion and the exclusion of other alternatives. According to the logic of the "Topic" (*adhikaraṇa*), which follows a sequential order, the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) is more powerful than the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). Therefore, following the mantras beginning with "From this [Self] are born the vital breaths," etc., the exclusion of other alternatives occurs after the meditation on the deities associated with the birth of the vital breaths and the great elements.

It must be stated that [the mantra] is "to be imagined" (*kalpya*), because otherwise there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). For the status of the theory of time and so forth as a distinct alternative (*koṭyantara*) is not established without first imagining the exclusion of those alternatives immediately after meditation. Furthermore, if the mantra beginning with "time, nature," and so on, were intended for the purpose of excluding other alternatives in the doubt regarding a specific property of the cause, then the exclusion of the "fortuitous" (*yadṛcchā*) position would be untenable; for the position that "there is no cause whatsoever" is indeed the fortuitous position. Moreover, [this would be impossible] even prior to the doubt concerning the cause.

In the absence of an agreement regarding sentience, it is impossible for that which is insentient to be a controller; therefore, the inquiry "by whom are they controlled? would be untenable. Consequently, for those who have ascertained only in a general sense that Brahman is the cause, the word *kiṃ* (what), which refers to the subject qualified by all possible alternative categories of potential causes, [is employed].

Among the causes of the world—such as the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others—who is the true deity? Since it is possible for the world to have [any of] these as its cause or even some other cause, the mere claim that "Brahmā is the cause" remains unestablished. Lest there arise the undesirable consequence of the doubt being groundless, both alternative positions must be refuted through meditation for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion; one should then determine the intended meaning. Having kept all of this in mind: [The text continues with the verse: *brahmaviṣṇvīśamūrtibhyaḥ paraṃ yacca parātparam | tasmai namo 'stu devāya kasmaicid vītikalmaṣāya ||* [Translation of the verse: Salutations to that certain God who is beyond the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, and who is higher than the highest—to Him, who is free from all taint. Having considered all this in the mind... [the text concludes].

The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) demonstrating the presentation of the subject of doubt (*saṃśayadharmin*) for the purpose of refuting time (*kāla*) and other such causes has been shown. Indeed, it is appropriate to describe the refutation of the doctrine of time and other causes in this manner; nevertheless, there remains no inquiry as to which deity is the cause, namely Brahman. Rather, the intention is to establish how the causality of this non-dual Brahman—which is devoid of all auxiliary factors—can be supported. Thus, for the sake of proving that Brahman is the cause of the world, [the text states] "without any instruments" (*na kim-upakaraṇakam*), and so forth, following their meditation.

Having raised the doubt as to what auxiliary cause accompanies Brahman in the creation of the world—since they themselves were unable to reach a definitive conclusion—their investigation concluded that the power of *māyā*, which is capable of accomplishing the impossible through His grace, is that auxiliary; for otherwise, the description of the power of *māyā* in this context would be entirely irrelevant. Thus it is said, when one assumes that the passage is intent upon investigating the nature of the auxiliary cause.
First, the term "cause" would have to be conceived as characterized by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), and reflections such as "from what were we born?

would not be tenable, if one were to assume a doubt as to whether the cause is Brahman or something other than Brahman; or if, having first accepted that Brahman is the cause, one were to assume a doubt as to whether that [cause] is Śiva or another deity, then [such reflections] would be appropriate in the form "we were born from something other than Brahman" or "we were born from Śiva or another deity."

When there is the certainty that Brahman is the cause of the entire world, its life, and so forth, and no desire to know its specific nature arises, there is no occasion for an inquiry such as "Who are they born from? among those who merely desire to know its auxiliaries. In that context, the explanation of what the auxiliary cause is and so forth involves much strained imagination; furthermore, the subsequent presentation and description of the power of *māyā* is unestablished, since the determination of the matter under investigation will come about through the grace of Ambikā, the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*), the presiding deity of the knowledge of Brahman.

With this intention, because [the text] is intent on describing the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) for those who meditate upon Her, they are said to be "conjoined with the yoga of meditation" (*dhyānayogānugata*).

For this very reason, in that mantra, since the word *śakti* is common to both [the Goddess and] ignorance (*avidyā*), the qualification "Self" (*ātman*) is used so that there might be no apprehension of the latter. Indeed, Ambikā is declared to be the Self-natured power (*ātmabhūta-śakti*) of the Moon-crested Lord; yet, due to ignorance, a difference between the two is perceived, whereas in ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), the non-difference of Śiva and Śivā is established, according to such traditional texts as: "The difference between Śiva and Śivā is like that between fire and its burning power. [This refers to] ignorance.

However, since that [power] is not its self-nature due to its being false, it is stated in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*: "The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) of the Supreme Lord is said to be pure consciousness alone; yet there exists another, insentient power of this Blessed One which is called ignorance (*avidyā*). One should not suspect that, in a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *ātman*, the word *śakti* could also refer to ignorance simply because of the word *vepa*. For in that case, it would be like the word *soma* in the mantra for the *dīrghasoma* sacrifice—"with steadfastness"—where the word *soma* refers to the vow (*vrata*) within the context of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, while the co-referential word *dīrgha* [qualifies it].

Regarding the phrase "it is produced in a form other than itself" (*svetarūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*): here, if [the term *sva*] were taken as referring to one's own [parts] or to another, then—just as in the case of the word *svena*—this particular word would be redundant as a differentiator, leading to the impossibility of a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) and thus the non-occurrence of a *karmadhāraya* compound. Furthermore, the Vārttika rule stating that "there is always a mention of the compound in the final member for *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds" applies to cases where a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) arises from the formation of compounds such as *vāktvacapriya-* or *citragavayana-*. This is not the case here, as in the example "*bṛhadrathantarasāmakāryaḥ*" (one whose ritual duties have the Bṛhat and Rathantara Sāmans).

It cannot be maintained that there is a compound of multiple words even without it being a *tatpuruṣa* [compound], because by the rule "the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) when there are many [words]" (*anekam anyapadārthe*), the status of a *bahuvrīhi* is established precisely through the inclusion of the term "many" (*aneka*), which indicates a compound of multiple words. Furthermore, even if some degree of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) were possible, its futility (*vaiyarthyam*) would remain as indelible as adamantine glue.

Moreover, since the meanings of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) and "meditation" (*dhyāna*)—which stand in a relationship of cause and effect—are the primary senses according to the method explained in the section on "The Object of Injury" (*kṣatikarmādhikaraṇa*), [it follows that they refer to] seeing and meditation.

It must be stated that cause and effect share a single object; however, this is not tenable under the view that perception has *avidyā* as its object. Now, for those who are doubting the auxiliary factors and yet understand that a determination regarding their status as auxiliaries will occur in relation to a single [object], meditation (*dhyāna*) is impossible because one cannot engage in it directed toward a knowledge in the form of a determination whose object is merely an insentient power (*jaḍa-śakti*). [This is] because [such knowledge] would have Brahman as its object... Therefore, by the grace of Ambikā, this matter has been determined for us.

With the intention that it "shall come to be," he meditated upon her in order to perceive her directly; this is the meaning of the mantra beginning with *yogānugatā*. Having performed that, the subsequent series of mantras beginning with *kāraṇāni* has as its purpose the statement that, by the power of his vision, he beheld Mahādeva, the supreme cause. Intending all of this, [the text says] "I am Mahādeva. Through the grace of Mahādeva, the thought arose, "You are [He]," for those who possess self-restraint (*yamavatām*). This refers to those who possess the limbs of yoga, beginning with restraint (*yama*).

The meaning is "of those established in yoga. Regarding the term *mahādevyāḥ*, the genitive case is used either in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) or the agent (*kartari*). Consequently, the meaning is "from seeing her" or "from her compassionate glance. Thus, the essential meaning of these mantras has been clearly set forth in summary form in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Gathering together, those high-souled sages, exponents of Brahman, deliberated upon many discourses based on self-knowledge: 'What is the root of this world? Is it indeed our own Self, or could it be some other Being who is the cause of all creatures, namely the Lord (Īśvara) himself?'"

To those who were thinking thus, relying on the practice of meditation, the Great Goddess Gaurī, daughter of the Mountain King, appeared. Beginning with these words, they beheld within that interval the Supreme Lord’s consort; they saw Śambhu, the cause of all, the Seer, the Ruler, Rudra, Brahmā, that Ancient Puruṣa. By such passages, the meaning is shown as to what is the root of this world, what is the cause, what is Brahman, and from where we have been born. Indeed, [the text says], "The Self alone is ours," by which we live.

The meaning arising from the inquiry beginning with "By whom? is established by the introduction of a person characterized as the cause of all and the Lord of all—this being proven through the capacity to refute proponents such as those who claim time, inherent nature, or other factors are the causes (as taught in the mantra beginning with "Who indeed..."), because the word "Self" (ātman) refers to the presiding controller.

The fact that doubts are centered upon Brahman has been made clear, as is evident in the *Śiva Purāṇa* where, after introducing the majesty of Ambikā, it is stated: "In ancient times, certain sages who were exponents of Brahman, their minds possessed by doubt, reflected upon things as they truly are out of a desire for liberation: 'What is the cause? From what have we been born?
By what do we live? Where is our final resting place? By whom were we brought to growth? And by whom was this eternal speaker heard amidst other pleasures?'"

The established order of the universe is inviolable; by whom was it created? Is it time, inherent nature, necessity, or chance that operates here? Or is it the elements, the source (Prakṛti), the Puruṣa, or perhaps their union? Because time and the rest are insentient, and because the Self, though sentient, is overwhelmed by pleasure and pain and lacks mastery, this matter is investigated. Following the yoga of meditation, they directly perceived the divine power, which severs the bonds and is intensely hidden by its own qualities. With those bonds severed by her, they [beheld] the Cause of all causes.

"Behold Mahādeva as the possessor of power with your divine eye—He who, together with this immeasurable power, alone presides over all causes without exception, including Time and the Self," and so forth; by such passages, this is made clear. Therefore, by the method stated, those mantras indeed have the purpose of determining that Śiva is the primordial root cause. Now, even if this is so, how is the certainty established that Śiva alone is the cause? For in other scriptural accounts of creation and similar contexts, names of other [deities] are also mentioned as being the cause.
Anticipating the objection that [the self] is seen in yoga within Brahman, he says: ||17||

In the various accounts of creation, where the Lord is mentioned within a collection of scriptural passages concerning the origin of the world, even a word that is considered appropriate as a secondary meaning is understood as referring to the [material] cause. But here, in this definitive statement, "The Lord is Hara," if that [word] is brought to its primary meaning, alas, then the discourse on definitive conclusion is destroyed! This is the sense in the contexts of creation.

By establishing the existence of a creator, the specific objects to be created, their sequence, and so forth, [the Sūtrakāra] has refuted the claim that words denoting other deities, when applied to Brahman the Creator, could have their primary meanings set aside through secondary figurative usage; likewise, he has accepted as established—on the basis of the existence of a creator and other points taught in other scriptural passages regarding the creator—the fact that words such as *prāṇa*, *ākāśa*, and *akṣara* refer to that [Brahman] in the collection of mantras cited, for the sake of [establishing] the Creator-Brahman.

In a restrictive statement (*niyamavākya*) employed as a cause for the purpose of extracting [the deity] in the form of a specific divinity, it is impossible to assume that the name "Śiva"—which is common to [other deities], whose sole function is to bring its own denotatum to mind, and which is not intended for anything else—is devoid of an inherent meaning. Thus, when the sequence of performance for the *Āgneya* and *Āgnīṣomīya* sacrifices on the full moon day is required for recollection, the very order of the mantra-texts—which have the single purpose of recalling the objects to be performed—becomes the regulator. Therefore, due to conflict with that [order], the two *Brāhmaṇa* passages, having already fulfilled their purpose through the injunction (*vidhi*), [cannot override it].

The order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is not a restrictive factor; for instance, in the *Chāndogya*, *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, and other texts, regarding the creator whose existence is generally understood from passages on creation, when there is a need to determine his specific nature, the collection of cited mantras— which proceeds to determine Śiva’s non-agency by first presenting the subject matter and appropriately considering other deities as alternative possibilities— is itself the restrictive factor, and not those [passages] which have fulfilled their purpose by establishing other objects of knowledge.

Regarding the "creation-statements" (*sṛṣṛtivākya*): in that context, even though a multitude of names for other deities is heard within the causal creation-statement, one might say "thirty-four," [but the text] says, "one should say 'twenty-six'"; having thus prohibited that [number thirty-four], the original form (*prakṛti*) is enjoined. By the principle of the relevant section (*adhikaraṇanyāya*), because that [original form] expresses thirty-four—as in the specific *ādhṛgu*-formula of the *vaiśeṣika*, "thirty-four are the steeds of the friend of the gods"—in the sentence whose purpose is merely to prohibit that, it says, "one should say 'twenty-six'."

The meaning is as follows: since there is no intent to grasp the specific number "twenty-six" as a mere restatement (anuvāda) of the *adhrigu*-formula obtained through the injunction (*codaka*), the mantra—just like the *adhrigu*-formula itself—must terminate in that very particularity provided by the mantra, rather than being restricted to the limbs (*vaṅkrīḥ*) of the goat, deer, horse, and boar as established by the logic of the section stating "twenty-six [limbs] by repetition because of their being the archetype (*prakṛti*) for the animal-sacrifice. By this, it is shown that...

That entity which others claim to be the cause of the world— designated in the *Chāndogya* and other texts by terms such as "Being" (*sat*), "Brahman," and "Self" (*ātman*), which culminate in ever-increasingly specific definitions until it is grasped by the intellect as being of conscious nature— and which in the *Mahopaniṣad* and other scriptures is denoted by the term "Nārāyaṇa," a name unique to him alone— concludes, according to the maxim "the goat [is meant] from the wording of the mantra," that Nārāyaṇa alone is the final referent. As for the words "Śiva," "Śaṅkha," and so forth, which are heard in certain passages regarding the Cause, [they signify him], just as in the common expression, "May your paths be auspicious" (*śivās te santu panthānaḥ*).

Because [the names] Śambhu, Svayambhū, Druhiṇa, and so forth are seen to be non-common [to other deities], just as the word Nārāyaṇa is non-common to Viṣṇu, so too is the word Hara non-common to Śiva, since no such [usage] is observed for him elsewhere. Thus, since a definitive conclusion cannot be reached through the logic propounded by the opponent, a determination based on the principle we have stated is appropriate, because the word Hara possesses intentional significance (tātparya). Nor should it be argued that the word Nārāyaṇa also possesses intentional significance, as its repeated occurrence is observed in certain places regarding the Cause.

In that regard, much remains to be clarified: since [the word *hara*] is not established otherwise than by its capacity to admit the postulation of another function—just like words such as "its object," "vital breath," or "ether" which apply to it—it cannot serve here to resolve a doubt concerning the specific cause among the categories of its own denotation and other deities. This is because, just as in the case of the word *puruṣa* heard in the sentence "This is a post or a man"—which follows the doubt "Is this a post or a man?"—it is impossible for the function of the word *puruṣa* to exclude anything other than its intended referent. As for what was said...

It has been stated that words such as *śiva* do not possess commonality [with other meanings] when applied to Śiva; regarding that, we ask concerning the word *śiva*: is it being said that there is no primary denotative power (*śakti*) for the word *śiva* in its unique sense of Śiva—apart from its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in common contexts such as the expression "may your paths be auspicious" (*śivās te panthānaḥ santu*)? Or, is it that even if such power exists, it lacks inherent determinative capacity because, like words such as *vyakta*, it possesses multiple meanings? It cannot be the first case, because apart from the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) stating "kalyāṇa, maṅgala, and śiva [denote auspiciousness],"...

Śiva, the trident-bearer, Maheśvara, Īśāna, the moon-crested one, Rudra, Paśupati, the trident-bearer, Śiva, Śaṅkara, Vyomakeśa, Mahādeva, the lord of the Pramathas—Śiva! [The word] *śiva* [is used] in the sense of liberation (*mokṣa*), in the auspicious (*bhadra*), and in water (*salila*). [It is used] in *śive*, *hare*, *pe* (or *pa*), *padmarāge*, *hare*, and *kīle*; [it is used] as *śivaṃ* in water. [Examples such as] "Śiva is auspicious," "Śiva is Śambhu," "Śivā is Gaurī," and "Śivā by name"—by the force of these established instructions (*anuśāsana*) which are not otherwise proven, [just as] by the force of the instruction that Viṣṇu is Nārāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇa, [there is the application of] the word *kṛṣṇa*.

Apart from the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for specific classes of beings (*varṇaviśeṣa*), [the word *viṣaya*] is prescribed for three things—substance, sin, and merit—as in the case of Viṣṇu; and since it must be admitted that its expressive power (*śakti*) toward those [three meanings] exists even in its non-common form of being eternally masculine, without the common neuter gender found in all substances (which is recorded in the Smṛti), otherwise there would result the fallacy of redundancy because, like *pathyā* and so on, it would not require a separate grammatical rule for them. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because this [word] is used through mere etymological derivation (*yoga*) alone, depending on context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth.

Just as the word *paṅkaja* (mud-born) refers to the lotus by virtue of obtaining the simultaneous favor of both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) meanings, so too the word *śiva*—by virtue of obtaining the simultaneous favor of two powers directed toward objects qualified by auspiciousness (*śubhatva*), having a blue throat (*nīlakaṇṭhatva*), and so forth—ordinarily refers to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

Since the Supreme Lord is thus understood everywhere from that word when it is not constrained by context, qualifying adjuncts, and the like, it possesses an inherent power of determination; for a single term may possess multiple powers.

It must be stated that it is nowhere observed for a word heard only once to have multiple intended meanings (*śakya*) simultaneously; furthermore, it would be improper [to claim otherwise] because two functions (*vṛtti*) cannot coexist at once. However, this is not the case in instances of *śleṣa* with a semantic split (*sabhaṅga*), because without repetition (*āvṛtti*), it is impossible to simultaneously apprehend multiple intended meanings. In instances of multiple meanings such as "bring the *saindhava*," since there is no dependence on a specific sequential split [of the word], the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is complete; thus, by means of the two apprehended powers simultaneously, as if by the eye—[the cognition arises].

Even if the recollection of two objects were possible through two simultaneous conjunctions—just as two objects are illuminated [simultaneously]—there would still be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), because each of the two independent objects would incur a separate connection with the suffix of injunction. While this might be the case elsewhere, here, due to the absence of a *sabhaṅga* (split) structure, there is no need for repetition; for in the Lord Nīlakaṇṭha, who brings welfare to the entire world, both etymological bases (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) find their final rest. Thus, since there is no possibility of two independent meanings, the consequence of a syntactical split does not arise. Simultaneously...

Because, as in a case of both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), it is impossible to restrict the meaning to one or the other through association with *saṃbhoga* (enjoyment) and so forth—given that the two powers are not contradictory and are simultaneously present—the word *śiva*, which denotes the unique form of Śiva, must be accepted as referring to the state of Śiva devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*). [As stated: "All the Dānavas and the immortals who exist are absorbed in me; I am Śiva, the source of all beings."

"By that [act], O gods, I am Śiva"—from this statement of Śiva in the *Karṇaparvan*, it is understood that the word "Śiva," which denotes him, refers to his nature as Śiva free from all limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*).

Therefore, because the word "Śiva" attains the favor of two powers (*śakti*) and thus primarily refers to his essential nature as the Unconditioned (*akāśavat*), it is rightly considered to be unique to him. By this same logic, the uniqueness of the words *Īśvara*, *Maheśvara*, and *Īśāna* when employed elsewhere is also explained. As the learned have said: "In whom the word 'Īśvara' has no other object..."

The phrase "one whose syllables correspond to reality" implies that he is none other than Maheśvara Tryambaka; furthermore, the fact that the word *Īśāna* is unique [to him] has been clarified by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa himself in the Sūtra: "But the word *Īśāna* [denotes Śiva], because of the scriptural statement. (........... As for the word *Śambhu*, one might suspect it is common to Druhiṇa (Brahmā) as well; that is indeed true, yet even so—

In passages such as "Śambhu, situated in the midst of space," since Brahman is heard of as being within the category of effects (*kāryakoṭi*), it is impossible for that [passage] to have Brahman as its purport; rather, its purport must be Śiva alone. However, this does not result in a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) based on that alone. Otherwise, in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*—in numerous places such as "At the beginning of the Kalpa, that Lord named Nārāyaṇa [became] Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds"—and in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, having introduced the subject with "Having obtained the name Padmayoni from Govinda, he is called Pitāmaha," [Brahmā is likewise described].

In the *Āśvalāyana-smṛti*, it is stated: "The Blessed One named Nārāyaṇa was the original Prajāpati. Furthermore: "From that staff was born the four-faced one whose essence is Śiva, the creator of all worlds, Brahmā, the Lord of the creators of the universe. And he, the Prajāpati whose essence is Śiva, having rested for a long time upon the waters by his own will, assumed the name 'Nārāyaṇa,' being of the nature of Śakti. Thus, even the claim of opponents—that the name Nārāyaṇa is applied to Brahmā based on the etymological derivation from the word 'nārāyaṇa' (the abode of waters)—is subject to refutation.

Therefore, the statement of others—that because Brahmā and the other deities are mentioned in similar contexts and there are words whose meanings could be suspected of referring to others, they reach the conclusion that the term *Nārāyaṇa* lacks exclusivity as long as ignorance persists—is inconsistent. Furthermore, since it has been demonstrated by the direct wording of the mantra itself that all causal statements culminate in Śiva, he says that the statement of others is inconsistent, being based merely on fallacious reasoning (*nyāyābhāsa*) that contradicts that. ||18||

O Blessed One, this mantra—which proclaims that when there is darkness, neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone remains—teaches by itself that all other words are causes [of delusion]. It renders fruitless the talk of others who are intent on anything else, for it is the ultimate secret of all [scriptures]. In this very Upaniṣad, the mantra is recorded thus: "When there was darkness, neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone existed; that is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent boon of Savitṛ, and from Him the ancient wisdom (prajñā) issued forth. And this [mantra]...

The purpose of determining that all causal statements have Śiva as their object is as follows: by means of the words "That" (*tat*) and so forth, [the text] refers to a specific time characterized by the persistence of darkness, as established in other scriptural passages such as, "In the beginning, this was indeed one, consisting of darkness alone; it was neither being nor non-being; at that time, there was only darkness," and "Prajāpati was indeed this alone in the beginning; there was neither day nor night; he moved about in this blind darkness. Thus, through this reference, [the text establishes] Śiva’s [nature].

Because they are enjoined as occurring at that specific time, the sacrifices understood from the *Āgneya*-type passages through their connection with substances such as the *puroḍāśa* cake—by virtue of the injunction for oblations made at the moment of cutting portions of those respective substances, namely "he offers [the oblation] in four turns"—result in being of the nature of *homa*. In the same way, the very Brahman denoted by terms such as "Parā" and established in the introductory statement (*pūrvavāda*) results in being of the nature of Śiva, precisely because it occurs at that time. Thus, the first half [of the verse] concludes by establishing a specific application (*upasaṃhāra*) of certain causal statements (*kāraṇavākya*) to particular objects.

The phrase "That Imperishable" (*tadakṣaram*)—found in the *Muṇḍaka* and other Upaniṣads—and the Gāyatrī mantra beginning with "That most excellent splendor of Savitṛ" (*tatsaviturvareṇyam*), which describes the state of being the inner controller (*antaryāmitva*) of the Supreme Person residing within the solar orb as an indicative mark implying His causality; and the statements "And from Him issued forth the ancient wisdom" (*prajñā ca tasmāt prasṛtā purāṇī*), "He thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'" (*tadaikṣata bahu syāṃ prajāyeya*), "He willed" (*sa īkṣata sṛjai*), "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'" (*sa aikṣata bahu syāṃ prajāyeyeti*), and "Brahman is built up through austerity" (*tapasā cīyate brahma*)—all these describe the Creator’s contemplation of the multitude of objects to be created at the time prior to the first creation.

For those who maintain that the causal statements heard in the *Chāndogya* and other Upaniṣads refer to the act of "reflecting" upon the object to be created—expressed by words such as "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*)—if one were to grasp that reflection by means of any one of those specific terms, the conclusion would be restricted solely to those scriptural passages containing that particular term. Therefore, by using the word "wisdom" (*prajñā*), which is common to all [causal texts], this entire mantra results in a conclusion that encompasses the specific means for that [reflection]. Thus, it serves to determine the specific subject matter of all the causal statements within our entire collection of mantras. Consequently, it is contrary to any determination of a specific subject matter that is not directly indicated by the evidence presented.

The meaning is that this is the rambling of a fool and is not to be accepted. As for what has been stated by others—that this mantra itself leads to *tamas*, the cause—this is because it restates a specific time of attainment (*prāpti*) through the phrase "when" (*yadā*).

Furthermore, attainment is established by the statement of the *Subāla Upaniṣad*: "The unmanifest dissolves into the imperishable; the imperishable dissolves into *tamas*; *tamas* becomes one with the supreme Divinity. And in that same [Upaniṣad], beginning with "whose body is...", following the sequence of the unmanifest and the imperishable, it says: "This Self is free from evil... the one God, Nārāyaṇa."

Because another Śruti passage—serving as a *pūrvapakṣa* (prior argument) for the text beginning with "From Nārāyaṇa..."—indicates that the darkness (*tamas*) presided over by Nārāyaṇa leads [to rebirth], the word *Śiva* occurring in the mantra of that [passage] as a restatement must, in accordance with that [other Śruti], refer to Nārāyaṇa himself as the presiding deity of that darkness. Even if one were to rely on the other Śruti passage beginning with "This was one" (*idam ekaṃ āsa*) as the *pūrvapakṣa*, since that too concludes with a specific [deity] established by a more powerful statement, there is no difference [in the conclusion]. And thus, even by the passage beginning with "the Imperishable" (*akṣaram*), [the same result follows].

This is merely an instruction on a specific mode of Nārāyaṇa himself. In this regard, just as in the case of the statement "the Viśvajit sacrifice has the *pṛṣṭha* [chant] for all [days]," where—due to compliance with the meaning of the word "all" (*sarva*), which refers to many objects that are to be enjoined—one assumes that the passage aims at restating the *pṛṣṭha* chants of the six-day period (*ṣāḍahika*) by abandoning the original *pṛṣṭhas* consisting of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans]; likewise, because the passage "When there was darkness... (*yadā tamaḥ*) has the purport of enjoining Śiva, one must abandon the *saubala*-type passages that appear to have other subjects, since various contradictory particulars are heard in other scriptural texts (*śruti*).

Although it could be argued that [the text] is merely intent upon restating the meaning already established by the *Maitrāyaṇīya* Śruti and other sources—which are not concluded anywhere else—it is shown that, even according to the opponent's own view, the mantra itself would incur a twofold nature (duality), thereby indicating the maxim of "losing the root through greed for the branches" (*mūlahāninyāya*) due to their desire for expansion. ||19||

If [it is argued that] the word "Auspicious" (*śiva*) is merely mentioned here in the mantra to restrict the Self to a form already known from other prior statements (*purovāda*), then consider this: O Enemy of Smara, what indeed could this Mantra accomplish for you at that time, since it merely restates a time beginning with "when," while failing to establish your own existence? The meaning is this: it is true that "When darkness...

is a restatement (*anuvāda*), but the statement of Saubala alone is not the *purovāda*, because there is no distinction [in the status of the mantra], as other sources are also heard that provide the object being restated. Nor is the passage beginning with "nor that [darkness]" a restatement.

Because, through the application of its function at that time, there is the cognition of something to be enjoined; and in this context, what is to be enjoined is neither "neither day nor night"—since the absence of such distinction has already been established by the preceding arguments—nor the "absence of the phenomenal world consisting of being and non-being," since those two are already obtained from the preceding statements. [The mantra says: "The sky is the head of that pervasive one, space is the navel of the Supreme Lord; from the region of his thighs came the Vaiśyas, and from his feet the Śūdra, O wielder of the Pināka."

With the intention that its status as being devoted to Śiva—supported by the *Liṅga-purāṇa* and other texts, as well as by internal corroboration—cannot be set aside, [the author] says: "The [references to other deities] are for the purpose of providing an explanation.

Let this be what is intended by the mantra. Granted that there may be an application of even mantras dedicated to other deities in the worship of another deity due to the force of a scriptural injunction (*vidhi*), yet, according to the principle of the section on Mantras (*Mantrādhikaraṇa*), since the application of a mantra occurs through the medium of conveying the meaning of the sentence, if the word situated in the mantra lacks its primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) toward the deity [intended by the injunction], [the secondary function must prevail].

According to the principle of the *aindryadhikaraṇa*, since the deity to be worshipped is indicated even by another mode of expression (*vṛttyantara*), the qualifying words associated with it— just as "greenness" applies to the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and so forth because it is possible for those meanings to apply there— serve to manifest the qualities and other attributes of that deity. Thus, in the mantra "Soma flows on,

the progenitor of thoughts," although the quality of being the progenitor of Indra and others is impossible in the case of the Soma-plant itself, there is still the denotation of this non-inherent attribute as a qualifier of that which is inherently present.

The manifestation of the form qualified by the specific [words] heard in the mantra is that which effects the [ritual] performance; thus, the statement of a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) for them is not excessive, because it is established in the ninth book (*navamika*) that they are employed for other purposes. Since it is established in the ninth book that [mantras] serve the purpose of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), just as the mention of a fruit in the passage "May we go from good to better" is for the sake of generating intense reverence, so too here—by means of mentioning a collection of qualities (*guṇajāta*) that are not inherent in the act itself—the [mantra] is fulfilled by reaching its conclusion therein. This is known to those well-versed in Mīmāṃsā. Therefore, in this case...

Even though the *Puruṣasūkta* is restricted by the Vedas and other authorities to Śiva alone, for the sake of accounting for other applications seen in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, some mode of propounding Nārāyaṇa—just like the mode of propounding Dhanada and others—must be postulated even through human intellect in the absence of Purāṇas and similar texts; thus, that [mode] is restricted within the Purāṇas and Āgamas which primarily deal with his worship, its ancillaries, and the resulting fruits. Indeed, such supplementary elaborations (*upabrahmaṇa*) are seen to be otherwise established.

Even for those mantras whose specific meanings are not [explicitly] stated, there are likewise explanatory supplements (*upabrahmaṇas*) in the Purāṇas and Āgamas, such as: "They created Soma for the sake of nourishment; from Soma, Soma was strengthened. Dharā, Vahni, Sūrya, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra), the Lord of Śacī (Indra), Viṣṇu, the glorious Nārāyaṇa—the entire world consists of Soma. Therefore, these [mantras] are not capable of subverting the fact that the Śrutis and other authorities establish Śiva as the supreme object. Nor is there any contradiction in a single mantra conveying multiple meanings, since a single [entity]...

Just as a mantra may have multiple applications due to the convergence of two authoritative means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for its application, so too must it possess a multiplicity of referents (*anekārtha-paratva*), which is inferred because those applications would otherwise be inexplicable. Since this is accepted by all on the strength of the evidence, and since even in common worldly usage one and the same word is observed to convey multiple meanings through different applications—and thus there is no contradiction with the nature of reality—it may be argued that this is indeed the case.

If it is asked how this hymn—which aims to establish multiple deities through different ritual applications (*prayoga*), and which teaches that "there is no other path for going" and so forth—can be understood as either establishing the reality of this entire collection of majestic entities in their true nature, or as merely illuminating matters such as prosperity even when those entities are already present in reality; the answer is as follows: regarding mantras employed by an agent, where there is no natural fitness (*svārasya*) with respect to a deity due to the presence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other means of denotation, [the mantra's power resides] in the collection of specific qualifiers heard therein.

In fact, the general rule (*utsarga*) is that [a mantra] conveys its own meaning, because it is favored by the direct hearing of the words (*abhidhānaśruti*), and because there is no reason to override this; furthermore, all Tantric authorities who advocate for the superiority of specific deities cite as evidence for the superiority of a particular deity those mantras containing the characteristic marks (*liṅga*) of that deity which are employed in various other contexts. However, where there is a certainty—based on another means of knowledge—that the specific qualifiers of the subject matter are contradicted regarding the natural sense of the words, there the general rule is abandoned, as in the case of the measure (*māna*).

The factual state of affairs is this: in some cases, their syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with another [predicate] occurs only when they are presented by a different verbal function (*vṛtti*), as they are in reality intended to be conveyed there; however, in other cases, where they are unfit for such connection, they constitute a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the meaning of the *kṛtya*-suffixes and so forth. Consequently, in the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*), whether one follows the general rule (*utsarga*) here, or whether—out of fear of its sublation—one disregards another Śruti passage, in either case, it is Paramaśiva alone who, in accordance with the actual nature of things, conveys this collection of majesties. This is because his name is recited here in the Śruti, and because this very [text], the *Atharvaśiras*, is the Upaniṣad of that [Lord].

In the Kaivalya-vṛtti and other texts, no other [path] exists for reaching [the goal]; or rather, as [stated]: "Like a hide covering the sky, theirs is eternal peace, not that of others. And because of the determination in various passages that there is no other path to liberation (*mukti*) and that these alone are the means to liberation; by this application (*viniyoga*) and corroboration (*upabrahmaṇa*), the attempt by others to establish that the hymn (*sūkta*) has Viṣṇu as its subject is refuted—even though the word *puruṣa* is common to many [entities], in the Āruṇaka [Upaniṣad], however, [it refers to... *(Note: The provided text contains ellipses indicating missing portions; the translation reflects the extant Sanskrit fragments.)*

Since it was previously stated that [the term] refers to Nārāyaṇa, who is presented by the *liṅga* in the form of a tortoise, and since the status of being a "Puruṣa" belongs to the Tatpuruṣa [form of Śiva], the author first explains the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "Puruṣa" therein— because the subsequent text reads, "The Puruṣa, having become one with a thousand activities, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet, arose"—

and because this establishes that the word "Puruṣa" in the mantra beginning with "sahasraśīrṣā" refers to Nārāyaṇa by virtue of having that same ground for its application; and because he is heard of here at the beginning of the Sūtra and so forth, [he is] Mahādeva.

Or [one might object]: "One should worship the Great Person (mahāpuruṣa)"—since the word *mahāpuruṣa* has its specific application understood from the ritual manuals (*kalpasūtra*), and because it is recited in the mantra "I know this one" (*vedāham etam*); and since the mark of being the Lord of Lakṣmī is presented in the verse "Lakṣmī and Hrī are your two wives"; and since there are specific passages in the Purāṇas and other texts—characterized by the marks of reclining upon the ocean and having the color of lightning, such as "The sages enter into Him who is within the ocean; from the Puruṣa come the lightnings"—which are intent on describing the form of Nārāyaṇa, [the text] refers to that very form in the passage concerning the waters (*ambhasya*).

By virtue of its syntactic unity with the immediately preceding Anuvāka— which, through the statement established in the *Tadanuvāka* ("Born from the waters, Hiraṇyagarbha," etc.), consisting of eight verses beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbha existed in the beginning" and employed in the Smṛtis for the propitiation of Him and the offering of oblations along with the Sūkta "Pāre," is proven to have Nārāyaṇa as its ultimate referent—

and by virtue of its syntactic unity with that [preceding] Anuvāka which is engaged in describing the greatness of the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa) who is its own subject matter, the attributes such as "having a thousand heads" and so forth, which are understood in reference to Nārāyaṇa in the Nārāyaṇa-Anuvāka, [are established].

In the Subālopaniṣad, after declaring that everything has Nārāyaṇa as its self through such passages as "The eye and the object of sight are Nārāyaṇa," and because of the recognition of the mantra "Puruṣa alone is all this" recited at the conclusion [of the section], and because Āpastamba and others designate the hymn by that name— stating that "the sacrificer worships with the Puruṣasūkta"— it is clear that this [Upaniṣad] has Nārāyaṇa as its ultimate referent; thus, what has been stated by the opponent regarding the whole of it is correct.

Because it appears like a mere line in the expanse of the sky, who indeed would rise up in the Dāruṇaka forest as a man out of madness? Thus, by demonstrating that the unprecedented being attains the state of a "man" (puruṣa), one concludes that the word *puruṣa* found in the mantra beginning with "thousand-headed" (*sahasraśīrṣā*) possesses a specific basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) as understood from the immediately following statement. Otherwise, if it were denoted by the word "man" even previously through that same basis for application, there would arise a contradiction with the statement, "Having become a man, I offer myself. Therefore, according to the very method stated by the opponent, he is indeed named "Man."

"He is as if complete, characterized by truth and other virtues; he bears the form of Śambhu, and there is no other—neither Rudra, nor Viṣṇu, nor Brahmā," according to the statement in the Skanda Purāṇa. Since the word *puruṣa* has "completeness" (*pūrṇatva*) as its primary etymological ground (*pravṛtti-nimitta*), it is unique to Śiva. Therefore, wherever there is a lapse in ritual action or a failure in sacrifice, one should meditate upon the *Puruṣa* and recite the *Puruṣasūkta*. This is because, as stated in the *Dhūla-sūtra*, "He is known as *Puruṣa* because of his completeness," referring to the word *parapuruṣa* found in the *Puruṣasūkta* and that which it expounds.

This is because [the term] is determined to have that as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Furthermore, immediately after the statement "All this is indeed Rudra," the Śruti says "Puruṣa alone is all this";

and in order to dispel the suspicion of contradiction with this mantra, the Śruti "Puruṣa is indeed Rudra" explains it as having Rudra as its referent. Thus, it is easily established that this is a Śruti passage concerning Paramaśiva. Moreover, there is no grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) anywhere that the word *mahāpuruṣa* is a name for Nārāyaṇa; its usage merely occurs in the Gautama-smṛti within the Kṛcchra mantras.

Regarding the term *mahāpuruṣāya*, since it is established that even through yoga (etymological derivation) it is possible [to denote Śiva]—because He is the primary object of designation (*abhidhānatva*)—even if that were the case, one would have to say *puruṣaṃ mahāntam* (the great person).

However, because only these two words are heard here, once the establishment of the meaning of the individual components (*avayavārtha*) is secured, it is difficult to avoid the application elsewhere of a sentence whose component meanings are conveyed by a word based on both yoga and conventional usage (*yogarūḍhi*). For those who argue for the *yogarūḍhi* status of words such as *paṅkaja* (lotus), if one were to state a consequence that applies the same logic elsewhere, they would be reduced to silence; thus, [the opponent's position] falls away.

Because it would result in the impossibility of [establishing] a sequence, and because among the eight names of Śiva beginning with Bhava, the word *mahiṣī* (the Great One) is recited as a name distinct from the *ādhāra* (support) in the Bodhāyana Sūtra; and since it is worshipped by the gods eternally, and because in the *Sāmba Purāṇa* the word *mahat* is etymologically defined as a name for Him—specifically through the reading "the Great Person" (*puruṣaṃ mahāntam*) in the context of the worship where it says "He is remembered as Mahādeva because He is great" (*yat surair nityaṃ mahāṃś caiva... maheti pūjāyāṃ mahādeva iti smṛtaḥ*)—therefore, [it refers to] Śiva.
Its "otherness" (paratva) is indeed perceived from the *Sūkta* beginning with "The noose of the waters," where it says: "Whom the sages call within the ocean, even more than the person of lightning.

Or, it may be the Liṅga-form (*liṅgamūrti*) consisting of the aforementioned signs, or the great flame (*mahājvālā*). Within the middle of this Liṅga, there is the beautiful form of the Moon-crested Lord (*Candraśekhara*) in the path of the sky;

likewise, within the Liṅga, there is Brahmā in the form of a swan (*haṃsa*), and Viṣṇu in the form of a boar (*varāha*). Furthermore, at the base of the Liṅga, Brahmā stands facing downward with his palms joined in reverence (*añjali*).
