On the left is Viṣṇu, mighty-armed and likewise with palms joined in reverence; in the center, one should meditate upon the Aghora-liṅga situated in the waters of the great ocean at the time of dusk, and thereby attain union with Śiva. When the three worlds have become a single ocean, Brahmā is of the nature of Nārāyaṇa.
The serpent, having swallowed the three worlds, lies upon his bed.
O God, while being meditated upon by the yogis in Janasthāna as the lotus-born one,
the Soul of the Universe then descended, entered the body of the wielder of the discus,
and having become one with Viṣṇu, lay down upon the bed of Yoga.
Brahmā has the luster of a lotus, and Rudra resembles the fire of universal dissolution.
Beholding that man, who shone like a lotus— the form of the Supreme Self,
resembling a mass of molten gold, with a blue throat and three eyes,
his face gracious and serene— they bowed down, their curiosity aroused.

From the observation of such Purāṇas and the eight mantras beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbha," as well as the mantra "He who rules over this... and "The two-footed and the four-footed," which cites the mark (*liṅga*) of being the Lord of Animals (*paśupati*)—as established in another Śruti passage stating "These indeed are the animals, both two-footed and four-footed"—and because the term "Hiraṇyagarbha" is common to both Śiva and Prajāpati, his exclusive identity with Nārāyaṇa is not established; therefore, by virtue of syntactic unity with that [passage], [the mantra] "Hrīśca te lakṣmīśca... [is interpreted accordingly].

Since there is the cognition of the mark of being the husband of *Hṛllekhā* (the goddess of the heart) through the word "husband" (*pati*) in the passage "by the wife" (*patnyā*), and because it is impossible to establish that the *Uttaranārāyaṇa* refers to Nārāyaṇa based on the mark of being the husband of Lakṣmī, [the opponent's position] cannot be maintained even as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) with that [passage]. Furthermore, because at the end of the section beginning with "On the far shore of the waters" (*ambhasya pāre*) one hears: "We know the Puruṣa, we meditate upon the thousand-eyed Mahādeva;
may that Indra impel us," and because in the middle [of that same section] it says: "Neither above nor across, for this god faces all directions," [the deity in question is Mahādeva].

Because of the recognition of the mantras recited as the head of the *Nāman-mantra-upaniṣad*, beginning with "He whose eyes are on all sides and whose faces are on all sides," and because the word "Prajāpati" in the passage "the boon of Prajāpati within the womb" is applicable through its etymological derivation—as it is seen in the *Laiṅga-purāṇa* among the names of Śiva: "He from whom all creatures are protected as if by sport is remembered as Prajāpati; and among the gods he is the great god, therefore he is remembered as Mahādeva"—it follows that Śiva alone is appropriate [as the referent], since there is gold (*hiraṇya*) within his womb.

Because he was born from the Golden Embryo (*hiraṇyagarbha*), he is therefore called *Hiraṇyagarbha* in this Purāṇa; for such is the etymological derivation provided in that very same text. Furthermore, because he is enumerated among the twelve [forms] beginning with Śiva and Śaṅkara in the *Bodhāyana-sūtra*, and because the word *hiraṇyagarbha* is appropriately applied there in the verse "In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose" (*hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre*), [the mantra] "In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose" is employed in the second operation during the ritual of pouring the foundational libation (*āghāra*) in the Vāyavya [section], following the sequence of the *samārādhana*.

Furthermore, because there is no contradiction in its application and because it forms a single syntactical unit with that [preceding text], the mantra *hrīśca te* is applied by some to Gaurī—the presiding deity of Soma—in the *grahayajña* for the sake of progeny, as stated in the *Smṛtis* and other works; since no other application is observed and because it is heard first, the word *lakṣmī* [is used] in the *Vāyusaṃhitā* in connection with the *Hṛllekhā* [mantra] and the [deity] Bhuvanā... beginning from "of the Lord, the possessor of the form of Māheśvara... and so forth, in reference to her.

The supreme Śakti Māheśvarī, who is the bestower of boons, is mounted upon the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). Mahālakṣmī [... by those two she captivates the mind. Regarding the Śrutā [goddess], who is a manifestation of the supreme Śakti in the form of Maheśvara’s power and whose play consists of a portion of that supreme power, because of her being established as prior, there is the statement: “Śrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives.

Or, according to the reading in the *Āneyapāṭha*, because of the conformity with the scriptural mention of Hṛllekhā within the same context, and because of the observation of the usage of the word *śrī* specifically for Umā in the *Āyuṣyasūkta*—where it says, “Śrī, Lakṣmī, Aupalambikā, Gā, and so forth”—[it refers to her].

Since there is no room for suspicion of a reversal [of meaning] due to the observation of the application of *kamalā* and *umā* in the *Hṛllekhā* mantra upon its recitation, and because the *Liṅga Purāṇa*—in the hymn to Śiva composed by Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa—contains the two readings "namo 'stu lakṣmīpataye" and "śrīpate hrīpate namaḥ," which, when combined, support the secondary scriptural authority (*upabrahmaṇa*) of the statement "hrīś ca te lakṣmīś ca patnyau" (Hrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives), it is understood that this refers to Umāpati; furthermore, in the Ardhanārīśvara form, the phrase "pārśve" (at the side) refers to Śarvarī, as stated in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara: "This is Indirā."

Regarding the form [of Śiva], because of its intrinsic nature, I shall describe the true form of the Destroyer of Tripura, who is the embodiment of Time (Kāla), whose form as Time consists of the stars—by whom, O best of sages, the sky was swallowed by him who desires the welfare of the world; wherein are Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and a portion of Kṛttikā; the zodiac sign of Aries (Meṣa), the domain of Mars (Kuja), and the head of him whose form is Time—and so forth, up to the portion of Proṣṭhapadā (Uttarabhādrapadā), Revatī, and the second [portion] which is the abode of Jupiter (Jīva), while the two feet are Pisces (Mīna)—according to this collection of statements from the Vāmana Purāṇa.

Since the form of the Lord has been established as being of the nature of Time (*kāla*), and because [the *Uttaranārāyaṇa*] is prescribed in its entirety as a constituent mantra of the *Śrīrudra*, the *Uttaranārāyaṇa* is determined to have Śiva as its referent; furthermore, by virtue of syntactic unity with that [text], it is easily demonstrated that it likewise refers to Him alone. Even while conforming to the recognition of word-meanings from other scriptural passages, it is more appropriate that it refers to Śiva due to the abundance of such evidence. Thus, in the passage "with the Puruṣa, [that is] Nārāyaṇa, the sacrificer worships," this...

According to the *Śaunaka-smṛti*, which states, "Nārāyaṇa is remembered as the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the *Puruṣasūkta*," one should first recite "by Puruṣa" (*puruṣeṇa*) to indicate the deity; subsequently, one should recite "by Nārāyaṇa" (*nārāyaṇena*) three times to indicate the seer. This is appropriate because it is justified to designate it by its well-known name, just as one speaks of the "Aghamarṣaṇa [hymn]. Furthermore, this is confirmed by the *Vādhūla-sūtra*, which explains that by worshipping the altar (*citim*) presented through the *Puruṣasūkta* seen by Nārāyaṇa, one becomes a "Puruṣa" (a perfected being) in this very birth.

Even by the designation "Nārāyaṇa," his being the primary subject [of the hymn] is not established; on the contrary, since the aforementioned statement from the *Kalpasūtra* establishes that Nārāyaṇa is a seer (*ṛṣi*), and because of the distinction between the object and the agent expressed in the phrase "I know this" (*vedāhametam*)—where the word "I" refers to him—the principle stated in the Sūtra [JS 1.1.25] leads to the natural understanding of a clear distinction [between the seer and the deity] regarding the subject matter of the hymn. Therefore, since the status of Nārāyaṇa as the primary subject cannot be established by the arguments put forward by others, and since the status of Śiva as the primary subject is very well-established by those same arguments according to our own method, [Śiva is the deity].
It must be accepted that the Puruṣasūkta is solely intended to establish the greatness of Śiva. ||24||

Furthermore, the *Atharvaśiras* proclaims your universal selfhood (*sarvātmatva*), your being worshipped by the gods, and—by teaching that even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others are your own manifestations (*vibhūti*)—it clarifies, through its etymological derivation (*nirukti*), that even they ultimately dissolve into you; thus it reveals your supreme glory over Śumbha. In the first section of this Upaniṣad, beginning with "The gods indeed went to the heavenly world, and there they questioned Rudra," when the gods asked him, "Who are you?", he replied to them: "I alone existed in the beginning..."

(... "I exist and I shall exist, and there is no one else whatsoever distinct from me"—by such words of Śiva, ending with "the Veda which is mine [is] all the gods" (...), the fact that Śiva is the self of all (*sarvātmatva*) has been established. Immediately thereafter, the gods did not see Rudra (...). "With upraised arms those gods approach Rudra; praising him with upraised arms..."—thus his being worshipped by the gods and his being praised have been shown. And then, in the second section, he who...

Beginning with "O Rudra... and "O Vṛtra...", and continuing from "He who is Viṣṇu and he who is Maheśvara," [the text] establishes that Brahmā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Indra, and the other great elements (*mahābhūta*) are His manifestations (*vibhūti*). Furthermore, in the fourth section, His supreme nature (*parabhāva*) was clarified through various means, including the absence of names; and in the fifth section, it is established precisely through His worship.

Having stated "liberation" (*mokṣa*), the method of worshipping [the Lord] through the *Pāśupata-yoga* was shown. Thus, when considered from beginning to end, the meaning is that the *Atharvaśiras* causes Vāmadeva to perceive this [Lord] as the scripture (*śāstra*). As for the mass of words uttered here by others regarding the *Atharvaśiras*, the meaning is that it clarifies: "He alone is superior to all. As for what has been prattled here by others—that because Rudra is mentioned in the *Atharvaśiras* he is not the Lord of all, and thus his status as the Lord of All is not established, unlike that of Vāmadeva—[this is incorrect].

Because that [omnipresence] is established through the teaching of the scripture, one might raise the doubt: "Since the omnipresence of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is indeed well-known, how can it belong to you? To eliminate this doubt, and to establish the statement of omnipresence from the perspective of the Supreme Self by means of His entry into oneself, his own words are employed: "He who is within the innermost. This refers to the statement of omnipresence from the perspective of the Supreme Self—having entered into oneself—in order to dispel the doubt: "Since the omnipresence of the Supreme Self is indeed well-known, how can it belong to you? In that context, the word "I" (*aham*) [is used].

Since that [subject] has been introduced as culminating in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), its meaning is this: that Supreme Self entered from within—as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*)—the host of individual souls (*jīva-varga*), which are more internal than the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and which are more internal than the directions, including the entire collection of things existing in all directions. Nor should it be argued that this sentence is intended merely to state the aforementioned fact—that Rudra alone enters by being the inner controller of all—and that the preceding sentence also intends merely to state his universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*) through his own essential nature; for if that were the case, [the subsequent text]...

It cannot be argued that [the passage] "I enter by falling into the midst of Rudra's speech" results from a formal application (prayoga), nor can it be said that because the particle *iti* indicates the completion of Rudra's speech in the phrase "There is nothing else whatsoever distinct from me," the passage beginning with "He who is within the sun" (*so 'ntarāditye*) must be understood as Śruti alone; for after the words "he entered" (*saṃprāviśat*), there follows the continuation of Rudra's speech beginning with "I am eternal and non-eternal" (*so 'haṃ nityānityaḥ*), and thus its completion is not established. Otherwise, the Śiva-speech context would be interrupted in the middle by a Śruti passage.

Regarding the interruption [of the sentence], it is because there would be the contingency of having to supply the words "he said" (*so 'bravīt*) later on. However, as for the reason—namely, that [the Self] is "within" (*antara*) from within (*antarāt*)—this is understood as meaning "omnipresence" (*sārvātmya*) by way of the mode of the Supreme Self's entry, or as the cause. This is established even in the sense of "mode" (*prakāra*) and so forth; whereas if it were taken to mean "conclusion," its connection would be with the conclusion of the entire statement of Śiva. For, according to the maxim "preference is given to a connected construction over a supplied one, and to a proximate connection over a remote one," and because it avoids the postulation of further attributes (*dharmakalpanā*), as for that which... [text ends].

Regarding the scriptural statement in the second section, "He who is Rudra is indeed the Blessed Lord" (*yo vai rudraḥ sa bhagavān*), that too is intended to convey the universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*) of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) alone, for it is in agreement with Rudra’s own statement, "I alone existed first," and thus shares the same purport. Furthermore, the etymological explanations (*nirvacana*) of the names beginning with *Oṃkāra* and ending with Mahādeva found in the third and fourth sections concern the *Praṇava*; yet even though they ultimately refer to the Supreme Reality denoted by the *Praṇava*, according to the method already stated, they are directed toward the Inner Controller. And as for the fact that in the fifth section the worship of Rudra is presented as a means to liberation (*mokṣopāya*), [it is likewise intended for the Inner Controller].

That injunction as well, by the logic already stated, is intended for the meditation on Him who dwells within [the sun]; for it has been established in the *Adhikaraṇa* concerning the *Madhu-vidyā* that the meditation on the sun—which is the object of enjoyment for the Vasus and others—has as its actual object the Inner Controller (*antar-yāmin*) of that thing, since such a vision is possible. Since this is likewise appropriate here, the one taught in the *Madhu-upaniṣad* is indeed Nārāyaṇa, the Inner Controller, according to the *Saubāla* Śruti: "This one, the inner Self of all beings, free from sin, divine, the one God, is Nārāyaṇa. He is your inner Self, mine, and those of others.

"Residing within the body, he is the witness of all; he cannot be grasped by anyone anywhere"—from this Smṛti, as well as from such Vedic passages as "He who is within the sun," and because other Śrutis are observed stating "Nārāyaṇa is to be seen with the eye" and "Nārāyaṇa is to be heard," and because [otherwise] there would be the inconsistency of [the Lord] possessing multiple universal selves (sārvātmya), for whom...

For whatever belongs to whom, by that very thing he [attains] it... "One should bring the universe under the control of one's own self through meditation"—it is precisely here that the word *praveśa* (entry) must be understood as entry by means of the intellect (*buddhi-anupraveśa*). [The text] "He entered by means of *samādhi*" is to be construed as a scriptural statement intended to establish the teaching of his identity with all things (*sarvātmya*) from the perspective of the scriptures. Therefore, this scripture also is in every way devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa. For this very reason, "He who is Rudra, he is..."

Since the term "Bhagavat" is used as a unique designation for Him in passages such as "Bhagavad-," he, wishing to refute that [notion], first demonstrates his own [misplaced] pride by showing the meaning and the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of such passages as "He who is within the sun" (*antarāditye*). 25.
In this [instance], your hidden intention has been realized by the words you have spoken; for it is consistent with those words joined to the Supreme Śiva,
which would otherwise be impossible for that [intention] which finds no correspondence in its own proper place.
The folly of the wicked matures in the form of wisdom.

This is the meaning: from "I satisfy life with life, truth with truth, and dharma with dharma" up to "with my own splendor"—this being the end of Śiva’s speech, it is clear that the subsequent portion beginning with "the gods did not see Rudra" is the Vedic statement (*śrutivākya*). In that context, the word *iti* serves to indicate the conclusion of Śiva’s speech, while the phrase "they did not see" establishes the fact of their non-perception.

And since that demonstration of disappearance was required, the passage from "He entered within the sun" up to "and he entered [everything]" cannot—without excessive strain—be connected to His own abode;

for without that very [disappearance], nothing else distinct from Me could exist, as is clear from such statements as "I am He, the eternal and the non-eternal," which refer to His own nature. Moreover, He is able to fulfill what is required there by abandoning His gross form visible to the gods and manifesting thereafter His supreme, all-pervading, most secret, and perfectly full form.

Because it is logical that [the word] "entered" (*prāviśat*) serves to demonstrate its disappearance (*antardhāna*), and because of the mutual expectancy (*anyonyākāṅkṣā*) between the terms, a connection is appropriate even when there is an intervention, since expectancy is stronger than proximity (*sannidhāna*). This is stated in the *Vārttika*: "Whichever word has a semantic connection with another, even if it is distant, that connection occurs; for those words that are semantically incapable, mere contiguity is no cause," and from Jaimini’s sūtra: "Proximity is not a mandate. Furthermore, there is no disagreement among opponents regarding the superiority of a remote connection over ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).

Even though [the mantra] beginning with "He who is within the sun" (*antarāditya*) is recited in the midst of Śiva’s words, its placement is seen to be at the very end of those Vedic passages, for it is observed in such Vedic texts as: "This very one indeed I have sung unto; therefore, thou art my only one," thus said Kauṣītaki to his son; and "Thou art the sunbeam; turn back; many shall be born of thee;
otherwise I shall not live, lest I should eat [him]," and "Desire has become my well," and so forth—within the midst of certain statements spoken by a person.

The phrase "even by the Śruti" and so forth implies that, due to mutual expectancy (*anyonyākāṅkṣā*), there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) at the end [of the passage] as a single Vedic sentence; and this very connection of the sentence has been determined through corroboration (*upabrahmaṇa*). For it is recited thus in the *Sūtasamhitā*:
"In former times, all the gods, Viṣṇu and the others, having come together, [inquired about] the cause..."
Having reflected upon the world, O Brahmins, their minds were filled with doubt.
They arrived at the world of Rudra, which is exceedingly blissful and pure;
in their midst was Mahādeva Hara, the destroyer of worldly existence.
O twice-born ones, Rudra himself appeared out of supreme compassion;
seeing him, whom they had never seen before, the gods, led by Viṣṇu, [were struck with wonder].
Having prostrated, Mahādeva asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am the Blessed Rudra, the Lord and Master of all creatures (*paśu*),
omniscient, the eternal essence of all principles (*tattva*)."
I alone was the cause of the world, the primordial Lord.

"I exist and I shall exist; there is no one other than me. The entire world, including all moving and unmoving things, is fashioned by the power of my Māyā"—beginning with these words, the Lord Rudra entered his full form. Then the gods, led by Viṣṇu, did not see Rudra. Thus, in the Liṅga Purāṇa as well, having introduced Śiva, the gods, being deluded, asked him: "Who are you?"
The Blessed Lord Rudra said: "I alone am the ancient one;
I was the first god, and I continue to exist, O best of beings."
And I shall exist in this world; there is no one else besides me. I am eternal, O sinless one; I am Brahman, I am Brahmaṇaspati.
Having begun with these words, [the Lord said: "By means of Dharma, I satisfy all through Dharma.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Rudra vanished on that very spot.
Then the gods... [and so forth]. In those three chapters, the entire *Atharvaśiras* is shown to be devoted to Śiva; however, due to fear of prolixity, the detailed account is not set forth here.

(..... Although it is recited in the *Saṃhitā* and the *Ādityapurāṇa*, it should be regarded as a mere supplementary narrative (*upabrahmaṇa*). Having thus demonstrated his own preferred method of genealogical succession (*anvaya*), he proceeds to refute the position stated by others. ||26||

In this context, when asked by Varada (Indra), you were questioned by the gods regarding your own form; that which was stated by you alone—what is the purpose of this composition of the text? Or is it the prattle of those who claim, "The Inner Controller is [the object]," or "He spoke himself"? To whom do such words enter the hearts, even if they are not ignorant? It is appropriate [to say] that in the narrative of Prahlāda, the statement of Indra beginning with "Know me alone" refers to Brahman from the perspective of the *śāstra* (scriptural vision). In that regard, [the text says]: "Choose for yourself a boon, whatever is beneficial for a human being... and so forth. Thus.

Regarding the question [of what the subject matter actually is]: since that which is the actual object of the inquiry lacks the status of being the object concerning Indra, it is appropriate that even the declaration of Vāmadeva’s universal identity—“I was Manu, I was the Sun,” and so forth—is directed toward Brahman by virtue of the perspective of the scriptures (*śāstradṛṣṭi*). This is because in that case, there is no such interrogative statement at all. However, in this instance, when the gods ask, “Who are you?”—a question regarding a form unique to Śiva—the Śiva-statement that serves as the answer, beginning with “I alone existed first,” would, if it were intended to signify the universal identity of another [deity], be inconsistent.

Since that would result in a discrepancy between the question and the answer, there is no room here for the application of that logic. By the force of such scriptural statements as "All this is indeed Rudra" and "Rudra is indeed all this," which are supported by the *Śruti* and *Kalpasūtras*, it is determined—on the basis of the authority of the *Śruti* passage "All this is indeed Brahman"—that the Brahman realized as the Self of all is none other than Śiva. Therefore, even if the teaching of the universal selfhood of many [deities] appears contradictory, it is [resolved] either through the perspective of the scripture (*śāstradṛṣṭyā*) in the *Subāla-Upaniṣad* or elsewhere.

It must be understood as "instruction" (*upadeśa*), because otherwise the fault of violating the Vedic context would arise; for if that instruction were to be interpreted in that very way, then the conclusion in the *Mantropaniṣad* and other texts—following immediately after "The eye and the object of sight are Nārāyaṇa," etc.—with the mantra "Puruṣa alone is all this," which is accepted as referring to Śiva, becomes even more appropriate. Furthermore, since the word "I" (*ahaṃ*) culminates in Śiva himself as the speaker, there is no presence of any other [referent] brought about by the word. Therefore, he...

By this [argument], even those of base views (*kudṛṣṭi*) would be able to say: "The non-apprehension of that [Self] is untenable; the word 'that' (*tat*) refers to the very same thing as the word 'I' (*aham*). For if one accepts that wherever the word 'I' is used in its primary sense, there the use of the word 'that' for that very same thing is logically consistent, then in passages such as "He who is within the sun" (*so'ntarāditye*), since it is possible that the speaker intends Śiva himself, there would be no room for any objection against that position.

Furthermore, even in the opponent's view, in the Śaiva statement beginning with "He who is within the sun," the word 'that' (*saḥ*) must refer back to the same entity brought to mind by the word 'I'. Thus, regarding that sentence...

It is appropriate that [the Gītā] is intent upon establishing Śiva alone as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of all; for in passages such as "Seek refuge in Him alone" and "Prostrate yourself before me today," since it is impossible even to suspect that the use of the word *tat* (He) with respect to one's own self is untenable— given the acceptance that the words *tat* and *aham* (I) terminate in the very same Self without a perception of them as distinct inner selves— and given that the hearers do not understand the word *aham* to refer to anyone other than the speaker, [the Lord says] "He" with respect to us.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for [the text] to convey anything other than that [Śiva], one cannot even suspect that it might somehow convey something else due to a doubt imagined by a false view (kudṛṣṭi), on the grounds that such a thing might reside in the intellect of that person.

This is because no such doubt or indicative statement is perceived, and thus the postulation of such a faulty doubt is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). Moreover, since Śiva alone is the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all, the interpretation of the sentence’s meaning—that another entity is taught to be his inner controller—is utterly improper. This is the essential conclusion of the purport. ||27||
If it is asked, "From where is his status as the inner controller of all known? he says in response:
"That you alone are the inner controller has indeed been established by the Upaniṣads, which are intent on revealing the Lord as the presiding authority over everything without exception."
And by the Manu-sages, who taught that his body was the very embodiment of bliss for the eyes of Bhagavān Anumāna, as he dwelt within the orb of the Lord of Light.

Indeed, mantras devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet as the foundation of all things are heard in the *Mantropaniṣad*: "He who alone presides over every drink, in whom [all] this exists, and so forth. Thus that Lord, the Blessed One, the venerable one, the source-nature, presides alone;
he alone presides over this entire universe, and he who ordains all qualities. Having known Śiva—who is like the supreme essence within clarified butter—as the subtle one... [he is the goal].

"Among all beings, [he is] firm. This god, the architect of the universe, the Great Self, is ever seated within the hearts of people. The god who is in fire, who is in the waters, who has entered the entire world; he who is in the herbs, who is in the trees—to that god, salutation after salutation. And so forth, including the *Rudra Upaniṣad* with its five sections beginning with "Salutation to Bhava," and the passage beginning with "Salutation to him who is in the water and on the island," all of which are intent upon establishing the presence of Śiva in all things. Furthermore, in the *Mahopaniṣad*: "The Rudra who is in the fire..."

"He who is in the waters, he who is in the plants, Rudra who has entered all beings"—these and other such passages [establish this]. Furthermore, it is universally accepted that the person residing within the sun, as taught in such scriptural texts as "This golden person who is seen within the sun," is indeed the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), because the *Brahma-sūtra* states, "And because of the designation of difference, He is another. Moreover, in the *Mahopaniṣad*, within that very context beginning with "The sun, indeed, is this orb" and continuing with "All is indeed Rudra," up to "Obeisance to the golden-armed one," [He is described].

The mantra is: "Obeisance, obeisance to the golden-hued one, the lord of gold, the husband of Ambikā, the husband of Umā. In the Rudra Upaniṣad, after introducing [the deity] with the words, "He who is copper-colored, ruddy," there is the mantra: "He who glides along, blue-necked, deep red. Among the mantras for the worship of the Sun as a subsidiary part of the Kṛcchra penance, [it says]: "Obeisance, obeisance to Rudra, the Lord of Creatures, the Great God, Tryambaka, the sole sovereign, Hari, Śarva, Īśāna, Ugra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the glowing one, the one with matted hair; obeisance, obeisance to Sūrya, the Āditya; obeisance, obeisance."

The mantras beginning with "Salutations, salutations to the blue-necked one, to the white-throated one; salutations to the moon-browed one, to the one clothed in animal skin" teach a form characterized by having Umā as a companion, a blue neck, and so forth. Nor should one suspect a break in the context of the Savitṛ-maṇḍala-vidyā in the Mahopaniṣad starting from the passage "All this is indeed Rudra," because there is no interrupting factor such as the intervention of a collection of unrelated words, given that [the subject] is the one residing within the sun.

Because it is capable of forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the *Kūrmapurāṇa*’s *Sūryahṛdaya*—which is intent on providing the specific forms required for the meditation (*upāsanā*) upon the Golden Person (*hiraṇmayapuruṣa*)—it says:
"Salutations to you, the glowing one, to Sūrya whose form is Brahman;
you alone are the supreme Brahman, as well as water, light, and immortality."
O Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, you are the syllable Om, Śarva, Rudra, and the eternal;
you are the Puruṣa, the Great Being, and the Great Fire—I bow down to you, O Kapardin.
You alone are the universe, that which has been born in manifold ways and that which is yet to be born;
salutations to Rudra, who is one's own self—I have come to you for refuge.
Salutations to you, O Pracetas; salutations to you, the most bountiful giver. Salutations, salutations to you, O Rudra; I have come to you for refuge.
Salutations to you, the golden-armed one; salutations to you, the lord of gold.
Salutations to you, the husband of Ambikā; salutations to you, the husband of Umā.

Thus, because the three *anuvākas* beginning with "All this is indeed Rudra" (*iti sarvo vai rudraḥ*)—in conjunction with the single syntactical unity of the *anuvāka* beginning with "The glowing Sūrya, Āditya" (*ghṛṇiḥ sūrya ādityaḥ*)—clearly demonstrate their purpose of providing the form required for the knowledge within the inner sun (*antarāditye*), one should not suspect that they refer to Viṣṇu on the grounds of the use of the word "Hari" in mantras used as parts of the *Kṛcchra* penance. This is because such a view would contradict numerous preceding and subsequent scriptural texts and indicative marks (*liṅga*). Furthermore, according to the observation of the lexicon (*kośa*) which states, "Yama, Anila, Indra, Candra, Arka, Viṣṇu, Siṃha, Aśva, Śuci, and Vājī [are synonyms]," [the term 'Arka'] refers to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) precisely by virtue of being a name of Āditya.

Because [the application of the term] is appropriate: "This Rudra is Mahādeva, Kapardin, and Ghṛṇī; he is Hari, the Lord Āditya Sūrya, Nīlagrīva, and Trilocana. (In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "...he is the thousand-rayed one, [worshipped] by the Sāmaga, Adhvaryu, and Hotṛ priests. Furthermore, in the words of Dadhīci addressed to Dakṣa—which establish that Paramaśiva resides within the solar orb—the use of the word *hari* is explained in exactly the same way. Also, in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "That golden person who is within the sun..."

If it is argued that, beginning with the passage "As the golden lotus... (*yathā kapyāsaṃ puṇya...*) and proceeding with the mention of "lotus-eyed" (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*), this refers to his Vaiṣṇava form, we say no. First, having eyes equal to a lotus is not an exclusive attribute of his; for that is well-known in both worldly usage and the Veda.

Moreover, even though it is common [to others], the word *puṇḍarīkākṣa* is established as an exclusive designation for Viṣṇu through its etymological and conventional meaning (*yogarūḍhi*). Nor is it [the case] for him...

It can be said that the scriptural passage beginning with "yathā" (as... [establishes this]; for even in a sentence whose primary intent is the conventional meaning of its constituent words, there is a restriction on usage. Even so, when considering the meaning of the *Puruṣasūkta*, if it is argued that the mention of "two eyes" is intended to signify the form of Tryambaka (Śiva), we reply: no. According to the principle of the section concerning the *uddeśya* (the subject under description), the specific quality residing in the subject is not intended to be emphasized. Furthermore, since the eyes are closed (*mukulita*), it is precisely those two eyes that possess the resemblance to blooming lotuses; thus, even if that [resemblance] is intended, there is no contradiction.

The *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* also culminates in the very form of Śiva as determined by the *Mahopaniṣad* and the mantras of the *Rudrādhyāya*; thus, there is no contradiction. For this very reason, the conclusion of even the three scriptural citations quoted in the *Vāyusaṃhitā* is shown to have Śiva as its subject:
"He who is Rudra, the Great One—unto Him [is] the Supreme Person, the Great."
"The Lord with golden arms, the Lord of gold, the Sovereign;
the Lord of Ambikā, the Ruler, the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose vehicle is the bull"—
beginning thus and ending with "the one with golden hair, lotus-eyed, ruddy, the Savior, he who moves as this god, blue-necked and golden"— in this very manner.

When it is stated at the conclusion of the procedure for the propitiation of Viṣṇu in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*—beginning with "He should always be meditated upon as residing in the center of the solar disc" (*dhyeyaḥ sadā savitṛmaṇḍalamadhyavartī*) and so forth—that refers merely to the fact that the solar disc, like the heart and other centers, is the locus for the worship of all deities, and thus the worship of Him (Viṣṇu) must be performed there at the end of His own ritual; for in the *Purāṇas* and *Āgamas*, we observe the prescription of the worship of deities such as Durgā and Gaṇapati by their respective worshippers at the time of the *sandhyā* and at the conclusion of their rituals. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. In this way...

The meaning is that the Upaniṣadic mantras establish that Śiva is the inner controller of all by demonstrating Him as the substratum of everything and by teaching His form as the Śaiva inner controller. Now, an objection may be raised: "He is the inner self of all beings"—thus the inner controllership of Nārāyaṇa is heard in scripture. True, such a scriptural statement exists; however, even here, what remains is the fact that the supreme Śaiva body presiding within the solar orb exercises internal control—this is the unrestricted conclusion. Therefore...

Just as in the case of Kṛṣṇa, the designation of him as the slayer of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa and others is appropriate as the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of Vedic words; otherwise, there would be no systematic consistency (*vyavasthā*) regarding the diverse deeds of the Lord of Ramā performed during his various incarnations, because they are also celebrated elsewhere. Furthermore, the deeds of other incarnations and the actions accomplished by the Supreme Primordial Person (*ādipuruṣottama*), such as the birth of Gaṅgā and others, are indeed proclaimed in the sections praising Kṛṣṇa within the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, through the perspective of their non-difference from him. Therefore, in accordance with powerful evidence, it is Śiva alone [who is the Supreme].

In the determination that Śiva alone is the inner controller of all, it must be accepted that the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* and other such texts also culminate in Him. However, some say that because the Jābāla Śruti uses the expression "these indeed are the names of the Immortal" (*etāni hi vā amṛtasya nāmadheyāni*), and since the word "Immortal" (*amṛta*)—which requires no further justification—is naturally understood to refer to Śiva, it is therefore evident that the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* has Śiva as its subject. For this reason as well, he states that it is clear that Śiva alone is the inner controller of all. ||28||

"O Blessed One, the great elements, the sun, the moon, and the self—this entire reality is indeed known as your body. O Hara, by this much, has your status as the presiding controller not been established? Otherwise, delusion would needlessly make these fools talkative. For the eight forms, beginning with earth, of the Enemy of Tripura are well-known in the Śaiva, Liṅga, and other Purāṇas, as well as in the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa. It is described there that these bodies have attained the state of being governed by the Lord who dwells within."

Therefore, by means of that uniformity of form, they would establish Śambhu’s unimpeded state as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of all things through his eightfold form (*mūrty-aṣṭaka*). All entities, including earth, water, and the rest, are described as being his body; however, only the eight forms beginning with earth are well-known as the forms of the Lord of Girijā. These very eight are [the basis for] him. Therefore, for the inner ruler of all conscious and unconscious beings, the manifestation of the body consisting of the eight elements beginning with earth is proclaimed.
It is said that [the Lord] exists within the eight forms of the enemies of desire;
he is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) as described in the *Brāhmaṇas*,
his entire body being present because even the modifications of the elements are contained within him.
The Lord dwells in the heart-lotus of all beings.
(... All beings are these machines created by Māyā; Māyā is the instrument for the recollection of what has been done [by the Self], belonging to the inner controller (antaryāmin) of Māyā. O!
Regarding these, it is not at all appropriate to speak of "nirukti" (etymological derivation) or "niyati" (destiny), because of the failure to grasp that [reality].
And for this very reason, [there is no such application] regarding time, yoga, Śiva, or Māyā.
Even the doubt that "no comprehensive collection has been made here" is dispelled by the fact that the Self is the eighth form of Śiva, the Supreme Soul.
"Therefore, Śiva is the auspicious essence of all forms, both pervasive and otherwise"—
thus [it was said] by Samīra to the sages of the six lineages in the Śaiva [tradition].
The class of living beings has been described in its entirety; thus, when the class consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious is grasped in its totality, the eighth form is declared.
What object indeed remains in the world that is yet to be grasped? For is it not [already] presided over by earth, water, fire, wind, ether, the sun, and the moon?
Thus, according to the words of the Liṅga Purāṇa, the sacrificer was established in the place of the Self.

Therefore, according to the logic of the goat-sacrifice and similar cases, because [the general rule] is withdrawn from the *cityā* and other instances, the word "Self" (*ātman*), although heard in the Śaiva scriptures, is restricted to a specific [meaning]. This is not correct;
for the universe consists of the pervasive and other forms, and therefore it is of the nature of Śiva.
Because such things as these would otherwise be impossible, those [scriptures] cannot have any other purpose.
Just as the branches of a tree flourish by watering its root,
so too does the world flourish through the worship of Śiva.
Likewise, it brings about benefit for all and bestows grace upon everyone.
And they know that the granting of safety to all beings is the worship of Śiva.
If the suppression of any embodied being whatsoever is carried out, that is undoubtedly an offense committed against the Eight-formed Lord; of this there is no doubt.
Thus,
because in the immediately preceding passage it was stated without distinction that all embodied beings indeed possess the form of the Blessed One, [to claim otherwise] would be a contradiction.
A general rule that is unclear may be restricted by a specific one;
however, since this [present rule] is clear, its restriction is therefore not appropriate.
As for the mention of those initiated in the section on the common self in the *Liṅga-purāṇa*,
that is intended in some instances merely to demonstrate the excellence of their benefit to the world.
O you who were born from the lotus-born [Brahmā],
you have been consecrated by the earth, water, fire, wind, ether, the sun, and the moon— by the deity who possesses all forms.
Thus, having introduced the subject there, the benefit to all the worlds brought about by each of the forms has been demonstrated in detail.
Thus, established otherwise than that, the mention of those initiated therein does not preclude the status of being a form of the Pināka-wielder for other selves.

Just as the sequential order of certain modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) serves the purpose of providing a single rule for the archetype (*prakṛti*), and does not cause one to understand a different fire-altar (*agni*); and just as there is the mention of a path already attained among the various branches of knowledge (*vidyā*).
For the sake of praise or for the sake of meditation, one should not turn away from others.
In the Laiṅgya [Purāṇa] as well, at the conclusion of the description of the grace bestowed upon all people,
it is summarized in general terms even within the mention of those who have been initiated.
"The Self is his eighth form, residing within the bodies of all beings"—
according to such statements found in the path set forth by the Śaiva Purāṇas.
Thus, he whose form is the universe is proclaimed as the eight-formed (aṣṭamūrti),
because he presides over the universe divided into eight parts.
If it is thus intended that everything consists of both the sentient and the insentient—
The universe is contained within the eight forms of Maheśa.
At that time, however, the number eight is not a defining characteristic of the forms of Śiva;
rather, it is to be restated through non-separation (avayukti), just like the [number] eight among the twelve potsherds of Vaiśvānara.
Just as in that case, among the twelve potsherds, only eight [are specifically mentioned].
They are recited without logical connection, with the intention of expressing various types of praise.
When the worlds have been thus praised as having become the embodied forms of the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva),
it is understood that eight [of them] are specifically reiterated for the purpose of praise.
Alternatively, it is conceived that within the innumerable forms, there is here a description of eight [forms],
consisting of the prescription of different names and their modes of worship;
this occurs in the *Śaiva* and other Purāṇas in the delineation of the group of eight forms (*mūrty-aṣṭaka*).
This is because the names of all eight forms have been taught according to their specific distinctions.

For it is observed that in the case of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*) and others, when there are long and short [periods], the mention of the *sautya* days is for the purpose of completing the [sequence] by means of those [shorter ones].
Alternatively, it may be conceived that within those same eleven [senses], just as there are seven vital breaths (prāṇas) in some cases,
certain forms are grasped through meditation.
"...those who meditate upon and bow down to Rudra,
to them the Lord of eight bodies grants the supreme state"—
thus it is said by the authors of the Purāṇas regarding those eight specific forms.
Through the worship of the Viśvamūrti [image] and the chanting of the names of the gods—
or else, even when permission is granted for the sixth meal as prescribed in the Vājasaneyi Śākhā— ...

(... as seen in the *Ṣaṣṭikāgni* [and other texts], in the enumeration of the five fires, and likewise in the eight forms (*mūrti*s), for the sake of the excellence of the remaining [forms] by someone...

even the renown of the Lord as "Eight-formed" (*Aṣṭamūrti*) is appropriate, since he is the seer (...). Even though [the sacrifice] was accomplished in a hundred days, because of the predominance of the gentle [days], it is celebrated as the "Twelve-day" (*Dvādaśāha*) sacrifice. In every way, however, the state of being a form (*mūrtitva*) belongs to the All-pervading One through his internal presence; indeed, it is due to his entry into those eight."

This is appropriate within the systems of the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*) found in the Purāṇas and Āgamas, because we observe the recognition of the meaning of the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa*. In the *Āditya-purāṇa* and other scriptures cited in the *Śrutikoṣa*, there are millions of instances such as: "Salutation to Him whose form is the earth, who is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) within the earth. It is not proper to subvert this clear recognition. Therefore, the Lord Paramaśiva alone is the inner controller of all. As for that which you call "your inner self" and "my [inner self]," [it is He].
And so forth; these are words of praise.

In that *Mahābhārata*, following the question—"O Brahmin, are there many Puruṣas, or is there only one?"—the supreme view is presented: "O King, descendant of the Kuru lineage, those who investigate Sāṃkhya and Yoga do not accept a single Puruṣa. Having thus introduced this, [it continues]: "Just as a single source is said for many Puruṣas, so shall I describe that universal Puruṣa."

By the verse beginning with "guṇādhikam," [the author] states his own thesis following the declaration: "I shall explain how the entire universe stands as the womb of that one Supreme Person alone. This follows the scriptural vision in the passage, "That very person within is the time-limit" (*sa vā eṣa puruṣo 'ntara-samayaḥ*), which shows that just as earth is the single source for all grains of sand and remains present in the form of every body, so too the one Supreme Person exists as the womb of the whole universe. Thus, it is devoted to the doctrine of non-duality (*aikātmya*). It is not... [the other view].

It is intended to enjoin [Viṣṇu] as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of someone, for otherwise it would result in the fault of being irrelevant (*apṛṣṭa*). As for the statement in the *Karṇaparvan*: "O Bhava, you are the self (*ātman*) of the Lord of immeasurable splendor," there the word *ātman* refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*), because that is its natural sense in that very context, as seen in the *Mokṣadharma*: "Therefore, O Bhava, I do not worship Rudra before my own self (*ātman*)," where the word *ātman* stands for Kṛṣṇa’s own essential nature. [Furthermore: "By means of Māyā, through the differentiation of qualities, [I create] Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha."

For the *Skanda Purāṇa* states: "Having created them, Hara entered into them as their inner controller (*antaryāmin*). Furthermore, since it is possible for Paramaśiva alone to persist even within the forms of the Guṇas—which, like individual souls (*jīvas*), are His own parts subject to His control—it is determined that He alone is the inner controller of all. Consequently, because the word "Self" (*ātman*) here cannot refer to the inner controller [in the sense of a subordinate deity], and because the fact that Śiva alone is the inner controller of all is thus established, it remains impossible to imagine that passages such as "He who is within the sun" refer to anyone else. Thus: "He who is indeed Rudra... [and so forth].

The assumption that passages such as these refer to Nārāyaṇa is refuted by the opponents; likewise, their assumption that the etymologies of names such as Rudra, Īśāna, Maheśvara, and Mahādeva refer to him is contradicted by common usage, and their assumption that the injunctions for the worship of Rudra are intended for him—following the logic of the Madhu-vidyā—is also rejected. This is because the word *bhagavat* is seen to be used extensively in the Purāṇas and elsewhere for anyone who is merely worthy of honor, and thus its connection with [Nārāyaṇa] alone is not established. As for the claim that the etymologies of the names Rudra, Īśāna, Maheśvara, and so forth, actually refer to the Praṇava...

This is because the etymologies (*nirvacana*) intended to establish the independence of the creation, preservation, and destruction of the universe cannot properly have the *praṇava* as their subject. How, then, can they share the same subject matter as the names of Rudra and others? In that regard, it is due to the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) between the name and the named; for instance, among the etymological names such as *Oṃkāra* and *Praṇava*. As it is stated in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*: "Either this *praṇava* is Śiva, or Śiva is remembered as the *praṇava*; for nowhere does an absolute distinction exist between the signified and the signifier."

Therefore, those who have reached the further shore of the scriptures declare the God to be the single syllable (ekākṣara), and the wise, considering the identity of the signified and the signifier. Thus, it is established that even the Atharvaśiras sets forth the supreme excellence of Śiva alone. ||29||
Having established Śiva— the blue-throated one, who moves with the daughter of the best of mountains, the three-eyed one, whose half-body is joined with [Pārvatī] in the cave of the mountain—
along with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, as a single source of splendor;
The scripture concerning liberation proclaims all this of you:
being in a secluded place, seated comfortably, pure, with body, neck, and head held erect,
one who belongs to another stage of life (an ascetic), having restrained all the senses, and having bowed with devotion to one's own guru.
Having meditated upon the stainless and pure lotus of the heart, in its center [one perceives] that which is luminous and free from sorrow—
inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite in form, auspicious, tranquil, immortal, and the source of Brahman.
Then [he beheld] the one, all-pervading Lord, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, whose form is wondrous consciousness-bliss;
the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated [Lord].
The Sage goes to the source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness.
He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Indra; he is the Imperishable, the supreme syllable. He alone is Viṣṇu, he is Prāṇa, he is Time, he is Fire, he is the Moon.
"He alone is everything—that which is real, that which is to be, and that which is eternal;
having known him, one does not transcend death; there is no other path to liberation.

Thus it is stated in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad. In the section concerning the method of meditating upon the "small space" (dahara) within Śiva, it is traditionally taught that this entire world, together with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, is his own manifestation (vibhūti). Therefore, [it is established that] Śiva...

The meaning is: "the manifestation of absolute pre-eminence. Now, an objection may be raised: since in passages such as "That is Brahman" (*sa brahma*), it is appropriate for the word *tat* (That) to refer to the Source of Beings (*bhūtayoni*) mentioned in proximity as the object to be attained, it follows that the scriptures establish that Brahman and the others are merely its manifestations (*vibhūti*), and not manifestations of the Object of Worship (*upāsya*). If this is argued, we say no. For even though the word *bhūtayoni* is etymological (*yaugika*), it refers to Śiva alone because of his proximity; and according to the principle of "that [is what one becomes] by meditating on that" (*tatkratu-nyāya*), it is logical that attainment occurs precisely through meditation upon Him. Furthermore, there is no reason to assume that the term applies to anyone other than Śiva.

If it is argued that "knowing what" means "that knowledge," and thus this is a presentation of liberation through knowledge—this is not so; for in the doctrine of Saguna Brahman, liberation is established as resulting from knowledge alone. If it is further argued that in the doctrine of Nirviśeṣa Brahman, liberation is not possible through knowledge of the Saguna [Brahman], and therefore, because the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "knowing that, one transcends death" must necessarily refer to the Nirviśeṣa, it follows that the preceding words must also refer to it—this too is not so. For in such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sa deva somyedamagra āsīt*), the term *tejas* (heat/light) and so forth...

Even though the words "tat" (That) heard in sentences such as "sṛjati" (He creates) function with reference to the qualified [Brahman], the word "tat" heard in the sentence "tattvamasi" (That thou art) cannot be so applied. Since it is illogical for that very word "tat"—which must be understood through its primary sense—to undergo a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on an inconsistency elsewhere, it is improper to apply it figuratively to the river Kāverī, which is merely a place to be reached. Thus, it refers to Paramaśiva, who is superior among those possessing qualities (*saguṇa*) by virtue of His form characterized by being accompanied by Umā and other attributes.

Through meditation, the practitioner attains that very Paramaśiva, the cause of the entire universe which is devoid of darkness and lack of control; for all beings, beginning with Brahmā, are His manifestations. And by knowing Him—who is the single essence of extracted consciousness—as one's own inner self (*pratyagātman*), one attains liberation. Such is the meaning of the Śruti, and this very meaning of the Śruti is demonstrated in the sixth chapter of the Mānava Purāṇa, wherein the methodology of the Kaivalyopaniṣad itself is followed. For there, the sage Aśvalāyana [speaks] directly.

Devoted to truth, having approached the Blessed Lord of the World, he presented the inquiry of Āśvalāyana beginning with "O Supreme Lord," and therein, through the medium of Parameṣṭhin’s reply, he demonstrated in detail the method of meditating upon Śiva, beginning with "inconceivable, unmanifest, and of infinite forms. Having meditated in this manner, the sage [beheld] Him, the direct witness, beyond darkness.
Through the knowledge of their own self, they go to that primordial source of all beings,
the ancient enemy of Tripura, who is this eternal Śiva with Ambā, described as the object of meditation.

He remains as if divided in the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others. Beginning with "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva," and ending with "Having known Him there, one transcends death; but by means of the inner Self alone, and not through any other knowledge, is there another path to liberation," the meaning we have stated is clearly demonstrated. Likewise, the meaning of this Śruti has been established in the *Brahmagītā*. Therefore, [regarding] Brahmā and the others...

It is not correct [to claim] that one should merely attain the state of being a manifestation (*vibhūti*) but not worship that manifestation; for, by virtue of its consistency with the cited *Kaivalya-śruti*, the three sections of the *Taittirīya Mahopaniṣad* beginning with "smaller than the smallest" (*araṇo 'raṇīyān*)— after uprooting the suspicion that they might have another purpose by means of the detailed exposition of Nārāyaṇa’s majesty described in the middle section— are established as having the injunction for the meditation on the *dahara* (the small space) according to the Śaiva school as their primary purport.
Thereafter, he meditates upon his supreme excellence. ||30||
Thus, this great Upaniṣad, which was previously described to you in brief as the Dahara-vidyā, now establishes it through further particulars;
may it abide within your heart as the inner essence of the Enemy of Mura for the sake of constant meditation.
I am the most powerful darkness for those of ruined intellect who have fallen into this [heretical] mantra.

Thus, first of all, this doubt arises here: that the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka is not devoted to the worship of Śiva. For, after describing the majesty of Nārāyaṇa with the words "The thousand-headed God," and so forth, and then demonstrating the specific configuration of the lotus of the heart—the locus of His worship—with the words "Resembling the interior of a lotus bud," and so forth, it concludes by stating that the Supreme Self is established within the crest of that [lotus]. By this presentation of Him within that small lotus...

Because Nārāyaṇa is the presiding deity of the meditation, for that very reason he is not enumerated among the manifestations (*vibhūti*) to be meditated upon, as Brahmā and others are in the *Kaivalyopaniṣad*. Now, one might object: "Is there not an injunction for meditation in our own *Anuvāka*? For it says, 'That which is within it—that is to be meditated upon'. [We reply: That passage merely provides the specific qualities required by the meditation enjoined in that *Anuvāka*; therein, the word—whether the term *yat* or the term *gagana*—which serves to designate the deity to be meditated upon...

If it is argued that because the two mantras "devānām yaḥ" and "vedāvaḥ" culminate in the specific designations *Rudra* and *Maheśvara* respectively, there is a contradiction with the connection to Śiva as established by the original injunction regarding his manifestation (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), and therefore it is not appropriate for Nārāyaṇa to be connected here as the object of worship— let there be no such connection; however, precisely here, on the strength of the description of the multitude of Nārāyaṇa’s qualities,
one may postulate an injunction for his worship according to the principle of the *Saṃbhūty-adhikaraṇa*, [as indicated] by the passage beginning with "padmakośapratīkāśam."

It cannot be argued that, because of the contact with the lotus-heart (*puṇḍarīka*) prescribed in the preceding section (*anuvāka*), this [section] must be understood as being intended for the injunction of qualities required by that [lotus]; for the context of the meditation on Śiva remains uninterrupted by the intervening words "the lotus-bud" (*padmakośam*) and so forth— words which, like the *nivit* verses, are unrelated to the context and merely serve to proclaim the multitude of attributes of Nārāyaṇa— just as the *upavyāna* (wearing of the sacred thread across the shoulder), though separated by the *nivit* verses, is still an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses.

Because it is impossible for [the qualities] to be connected as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to the worship of Śiva, and because the small ether (*dahara*), unlike the ladle (*juhū*) and other implements which have an invariable connection with the sacrifice (*kratu*), lacks an invariable connection with the Śaiva Dahara-vidyā— such that, even in the absence of a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), their connection to it could occur through the heart by means of the sentence-evidence (*vākya-pramāṇa*), just as the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood connects to the sacrifice through the ladle— it would follow that mantras such as "piercing the bright [eye]," "piercing the heart," and so forth, would also [be connected] through the heart.

Because it would result in the undesirable consequence of contradicting the established *adhikaraṇa* (sutra-section) regarding the difference in meaning due to the application of [the mantra] as a subordinate part of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*) for purposes such as piercing (*vedha*), it is therefore logical that even though the preceding section (*anuvāka*) is devoted to the injunction for the worship of Śiva, the passage beginning with "padmakośa" should be construed with a different form of worship, one inferred from the capacity of the nearby description of the multitude of Nārāyaṇa’s qualities. Alternatively, according to the method stated by others, even the preceding section is devoted solely to the injunction for the worship of Nārāyaṇa; they indeed declare its meaning to be such. First of all, the mantra "yo devānām... is not devoted to Śiva. In that regard:

The passage beginning with "yo devānām" cannot be taken as referring to Nārāyaṇa, because the restatement (anuvāda) regarding Hiraṇyagarbha as the cause must be understood as having Nārāyaṇa as its object in accordance with the preceding statement (purovāda), "From Nārāyaṇa Brahmā was born," and it must be assumed that the word "Rudra" is somehow applied there [to Nārāyaṇa] as well. Nor does the mantra "yadvedāva... apply; for its meaning is as follows: according to the Smṛti, "O Sage, the Vedas, which begin with the Praṇava, are established within the Praṇava," the syllable called Oṃkāra—which is established at the beginning and end of the Vedas as their source of origin and dissolution—is indeed the letter 'A'.

Because of the scriptural revelation "all speech," that which is the supreme denotable object—attained through the nature of the letter *a* (which is the source of all speech) by means of its own inherent form—is Maheśvara. This is because the word "supreme" (*para*) is employed in such expressions as "this is beyond the supreme" (*idaṃ parastāt paraḥ*) to denote that which is the ultimate referent. Thus, he is the one denoted by the letter *a*, which is the source of the entire web of words; he is the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) of the worlds. And so, since he is denoted by the preeminent letter *a* as the source of the entire web of words, it is logical that he possesses the excellence of all sentences; this is established by relying on such reasoning regarding the denotable object of the letter *a*.

Since this mantra, which is intent on establishing [the Lord] as the sovereign of all, is seen to be expressive of Viṣṇu through the syllable *a*, it ultimately results in establishing Nārāyaṇa as the supreme object. Therefore, because the preceding and following mantras—though they may appear to have other meanings—are devoted to Nārāyaṇa, the intermediate section concerning meditation is determined to have that very same subject matter. Furthermore, the subsequent collection of mantras beginning with "The thousand-headed God" clearly has that as its subject; and that is not for the purpose of determining a specific identity apart from the well-known supremacy of the Whole.

However, this is for the purpose of clarifying the specific object of worship in the *dahara-vidyā* under discussion. That reality—which has been described in various contexts as the cause of the world, the inner ruler of the world, the goal to be attained, and the object of worship for those seeking liberation—is made recognizable through the words heard in those respective contexts, such as "the Supreme Brahman," "the Supreme Reality," "the Supreme Light," "the Supreme Imperishable," "Śiva," and "Śaṃsa.

This is because all such statements have, by the authority of the sentence (*vākya-pramāṇa*), the purpose of enjoining that everything is Nārāyaṇa; for the sentence is more powerful than the context (*prakaraṇa*). Thus...

Since there is also a connection with the present *dahara-vidyā* for the purpose of determining which among all other sciences (*paravidyā*) is to be worshipped, the subsequent section beginning with "like the interior of a lotus" (*padmakośam*) prescribes its qualities;

furthermore, by demonstrating that other deities are but manifestations (*vibhūti*) of Nārāyaṇa, it proclaims His supreme excellence. Thus, both of these sections (*anuvāka*) are devoted to Nārāyaṇa. Therefore, the claim that the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka* is intended for the worship of Śiva in every respect is refuted; for in the first section, there is indeed an injunction for the worship of Nārāyaṇa.

The underlying intention here is that [the author], keeping in mind the uprooting of the pride of others, is establishing the *dahara-vidyā* for you. First of all, the mantra "yo devānām" is not devoted to Nārāyaṇa;

for in the *Atharvaśikhā*, Śiva is established as the cause of Brahman, and since there is no statement anywhere to the contrary, it is impossible to assume that the word "rudra" in that [mantra] has a non-primary meaning. For one who possesses such pride, even the suspicion that the mantra beginning with "yo devānām" might be a restatement (*anuvāda*) is unworthy of arising; for this very mantra [refers to] Sadāśiva.

Because [the passage] culminates in establishing that Brahman is the cause. For it is not possible—even with a thousand repetitions of the word "yat" (which)—to assume the status of a restatement (*anuvādakatva*) for Nārāyaṇa regarding the fact that Brahman is the cause, as long as the meaning being perceived has not already been established [elsewhere]. If you argue that this is established in another Śruti, we say no. Oh, what a display of misplaced ingenuity from your honor!
For when the statement asserting Śiva’s status as the cause of Brahman requires its antecedent corroborative text (*purovāda*), [it refers to] Nārāyaṇa’s status as that cause—[not Śiva’s].

He introduces the scriptural authority: "Indeed, it is not fitting to object that because there is no preceding statement (*purovāda*) even when the word *yat* is attached to the sentence concerning the *Āgneya* sacrifice, its status as an injunction cannot be asserted; for the sentence concerning the *Saurya* sacrifice and others does exist. If it is argued that there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) because the term *rudra* is accepted as having a secondary figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) in reference to Nārāyaṇa, we say no.

For if any word such as *agni* were to have a figurative meaning in some sense, one could find some means of proof (*pramāṇa*) to establish that, which would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even sentences such as "that which belongs to Agni" (*yad āgneya*) would lose their injunctive character.

Furthermore, because of the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), if the application of the term *Rudra* to Nārāyaṇa through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) were established, then—since there would be no lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*)—the status of passages such as "Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa" as a prior statement (*purovāda*) would not be established. If its status as a prior statement were established, and that were established, then by following that prior statement, the term [Rudra] would not have a secondary indication for him (Nārāyaṇa). Therefore, since attainment [of the meaning] is impossible, the fact of being preceded by the word "that" (*yat*) and so forth does not constitute an indicative mark of a restatement (*anuvāda*); thus, it is not proper to assume the character of a restatement on the strength of that. However, if both [terms refer to] gold...

If the status of being the cause of the womb were not possible [for both], then it would be necessary to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for one or the other of the two specific scriptural terms, *rudra* and *nārāyaṇa*. One might even suspect that, in order to favor the connection with the word "who" (*yaḥ*), figurative indication is applied specifically to the word *rudra* in the passage "He who [is] of the gods," in accordance with the scripture stating "From Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā is born. We shall demonstrate, however, that the causality of both exists according to different cycles of creation (*kalpa*). Furthermore, even within a single cycle, their causality exists through the relationship of mother and father.

Since the status of Nārāyaṇa as the power (śakti) of Śiva is established, this mantra is in every respect devoted to Śiva alone; and its meaning is as follows: "The great seer" (maharṣi) is the great observer, who is omniscient (sarvajña), all-knowing (sarvavit), and the manifestation of pure, unerring intellect regarding all objects. Thus, he is enriched by the realization of all objects as established in the Śrutis and Smṛtis.

He is superior to the entire universe consisting of the conscious and unconscious (cid-acid-ātmaka) manifold (prapañca). Because he is the controller of the entire class of bound souls (paśu) and fetters (pāśa), he is Rudra, [the protector] of the liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra.

The Lord, the impeller of the gods, first beheld Hiraṇyagarbha at the beginning of the kalpa, arising from Himself by His own volition. With a glance of command—filled with compassion and expert in bestowing the creation of the entire universe—He looked upon him. May that Lord [grant] to us a pure and supreme remembrance, characterized by compassion for those who have reached the state of being lost, which, as is well known from the Śruti, brings about the complete liberation from all knots through the attainment of such remembrance regarding His own domain.

"Let him join [the sacrifice] well. For it is thus explained in the *Laiṅgya*: "From the Unmanifest arose Sthāṇu Śiva, the supreme cause, the seer endowed with the cause and effect of all that exists, the Lord who transcends the universe.

He beheld Brahmā first, as the foremost god among gods, being born from his lotus-face; and by his command, he looked upon him. Having been seen by Rudra, the Lord of Gods created the entire world. And in the *Kaurma*: "O Hiraṇyagarbha, inner self of the world, the ancient Puruṣa was indeed born from you; being born, he was [sustained] by you."

"Being appointed according to the injunction, he created everything in its entirety. By this [verse], having accepted that this mantra has Śiva as its ultimate referent, [the author] refutes the alternative interpretation of non-Vedic followers:

namely, that the Great Sage—who, through the power of yoga, is capable of directly perceiving the multitude of the three periods of time—[observes that] Hiraṇyagarbha was born from Nārāyaṇa even before the manifestation of Rudra.

Because it is seen that the reading of this mantra in the *Śvetāśvatara* is "He generated Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning," [the author] has directly perceived through the power of yoga that [the Lord] brought about [Hiraṇyagarbha] in the state of being born, like one who seizes an elephant by the throat. And thus, in accordance with this, it is also clear that the subsequent mantra, "That than which there is nothing higher," refers to Śiva. For this very reason, there is the traditional teaching of Āśvalāyana:
"There is nothing higher than Him, nor anything other than the Supreme Self;
there is nothing greater and nothing subtler—salutations to that Self-existent One."
Salutation to that great Śiva, whose nature consists of subtle syllables, by whom this entire world is filled, and who is remembered as having forms composed of māyā.

Thus, the conjecture that the mantra "That which is, and that which is in the Vedas" (Yaccāsti yacca vedānteṣu) refers to Nārāyaṇa is also untenable; for according to the opponent's view, words are qualities of the five elements, and even in that system, it is impossible for them to stand in a relationship of mutual material cause and effect.

If one intends to express that [the letter 'a'] is the material cause (*prakṛti*), it would have to be stated as "that which is beyond its own material cause"; furthermore, since it is merged within its material cause, the expression "that which is beyond it" would be semantically incoherent. Even if both [meanings] could somehow be applied, there is no evidence for the letter 'a' being the material cause of the *praṇava*. [Objection: But surely we establish that the letter 'a' is the material cause of all speech based on the Vedic scripture stating, "The letter 'a' is indeed all speech," and from that very fact, its status as the material cause of the *praṇava* is also proven.

Nor should one suspect the opposite—that the entire Veda is pierced by the syllable *oṃ*—merely because of the scriptural statement; for, just as [the letter *a*] follows the *praṇava*, its following the letter *a* is not observed, and thus that [statement] is assumed to be intended as praise. If this is argued, we say no.

Regarding the statement in the Śruti, "having made the measures the primordial measure" (*mātrāḥ prakṛtimātrāḥ kṛtvā*), by contemplating how each subsequent element—the *a*, *u*, and *m*—is the locus of dissolution for each preceding one, it is clearly demonstrated that the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) alone is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of the three measures. Since dissolution is impossible into that which is not the primordial nature, and since the Śruti passage "the letter *a* is indeed all speech" can be understood as a mere eulogy—just like the statement "Agni is all the deities"—it follows that [the half-measure is the source]. As stated in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa: "O Brahman, from the Supreme Lord Brahmā, whose self was composed in meditation..."

Having introduced the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) in the form of *nāda* with the words "From the space of the heart, *nāda* arose," and then explicitly stating its status as the source of the *praṇava* with the words "From that, the *oṃkāra* emerged," it follows that even when the meaning of this mantra is interpreted according to the system of others, the conclusion is reached that Maheśvara is the referent of that which is expressed by the half-mora. Furthermore, it has been clearly established in the investigation of the *Atharvaśikhā* that Śiva alone is the referent of the half-mora; for even if the letter 'A' is the source of the *praṇava*, the letter 'A' is [described] as "the one who does not move within the lotus-seats of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa."

Thus, because the authors of the *Kośa* have taught that the letter *a* has multiple meanings, the designation of Maheśvara as the referent of the letter *a* does not conclude exclusively with Viṣṇu; however, it was stated here that this is not an injunction that Maheśvara is the referent of the letter *a* as the first constituent of the *praṇava*. If it is argued that since the letter *u* takes the form of the first constituent of the *praṇava*, by including that which is designated by the letter *a* in that form, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [Maheśvara] is included among those things generally denoted by the letter *u* alone—if that were the case:

Since the Śrutis—such as the *Adhamaśikha*, *Uttaratāpanīya*, and others—as well as the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Āgamas, establish that Brahman is the primary meaning (*vācya*) of this [term], it follows that Brahman alone must be understood here. Furthermore, according to the method stated in the Sūtra, "And like the cup, because there is no distinction," one must determine the intended purport (*aidaṃparya*) of these mantras through their application, supporting arguments, and so forth, following the principle of the *ajā* mantra in its various interpretations; otherwise, the definitive establishment of the meaning would not be achieved, for it is indeed possible to apply this mantra to other meanings by means of a different method.

In these [mantras]—"agnimīle purohitam," "yonaḥ samudre bandhuḥ," and "samānaṃ param"—the letters *a*, *o*, and *m* are well-known as the beginning, middle, and end of the Vedas. The vowel (*svara*) proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda is the letter *a*; that same [vowel] is established at its end in the word "samānaṃ param," where it is the penultimate letter, and since there is no other vowel following it, it is the final vowel. Of that [vowel], which is dissolved into its source (*prakṛti*), the source is Viṣṇu, for the scripture states: "Vāsudeva is the supreme source."

And because of such Smṛti texts as "You are Prakṛti, O Rudra, [I am] Puruṣa," there is no absolute difference between the denoted and the denoter for one who is merged in Him—that is, for one who has attained non-difference through the relationship of denoted and denoter—as stated by Vāyu: "In some cases, no difference whatsoever exists between the denoted and the denoter. Regarding that which is "higher than Him"—referring to Viṣṇu, who is the primordial form (prakṛti-rūpa) denoted by the syllable *Oṃ* (*akāra*), whose state of being most venerable is established by His presence at the beginning and end of the Vedas—the term "Rudra" is used in the sense of being his primary manifestation, as established by statements such as "You are Prakṛti, O Rudra, [I am] Puruṣa. Consequently, in passages such as "of those intent on beholding Him," the word "para" (the higher) refers to Him.

Because the word is employed with reference to the primary [meaning], even in a linguistic usage directed toward that [primary meaning] as its object, the one to be conveyed is predominant in relation to the word; thus, since the application of the term is justified solely by its denoting the primary [meaning], it is improper to postulate a separate denotable object. Therefore, [the texts say]: "He is Maheśvara, He is Rudra, the Great Lord."

Alternatively, because this mantra belongs to the Yajurveda, the Veda is the Yajurveda; the vowel *i* recited at its beginning in the phrase *iṣe tvā* is the very same that is established at its end in the phrase *aiśvaryaṃ patati*. Its source is Lakṣmī, for in the Kūrma Purāṇa, after beginning with "the goddess Śrī became [the source]," it continues, "the immutable primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛtiḥ avyayā*)."

In that [context], because the vowel *i*—which is joined to it through the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*)—is the name of Lakṣmī, it has attained a state of length; that which follows it (the sixth case used for the fifth) is the vowel *u*, which is the Supreme Lord (*maheśvara*). That which is signified by it is Śiva, the Lord of All. Therefore, since the determination of meaning cannot be established through independent imagination, one must present the context and so forth to ascertain the intended purport (*edamparya*), and this context is found in works such as the *Śivarāghavasambhava*.

In the performance of the Śaiva rite consisting of the application of ashes to the limbs and the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), [the procedure] begins with the mantra "nāṇor aṇīyān" (smaller than the smallest), which is marked by the name of Śiva: "dhātuḥ prasādānmahimānam īśam" (by the grace of the Creator, [I seek refuge in] the Lord, the Great One).
