From the mantra recited in the middle, "yo devānām," it is determined that the subject is Śiva; and in the passage "yaḥ paraḥ sa maheśvaraḥ," because of the predominance of the dative case in the word *maheśvara*, it is ascertained that the purport lies in enjoining the nature of Śiva—the very referent of the term—as being identical with that which was previously restated (anūdita). Therefore, it is concluded that it is appropriate to construe the portion of the restatement—which can be construed in many ways—in accordance with the element to be enjoined (*vidheya*), just as in the rule: "If both fires have gone out, or if one has been carried away by a forest fire, the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) is his expiation."

In this context, although it is established by the *havirādyadhikaraṇa* principle that the mention of two fires (*agnidvitva*) is not intended to be significant—since even the following of a single fire constitutes a cause for re-establishment (*punarādheya*) and is thus understood as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*)—nevertheless, because the re-establishment (*punarādheya*), which is the enjoined act of similar form (*sarūpa*) for the purpose of re-consecration (*ādhāna*) known from another scriptural passage, cannot produce only a single fire, the intention to signify two fires in the restatement portion is maintained in accordance with that requirement, as discussed in the *punarādheyam odanavat* section.

Since it is established by the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so") that in a context where the meaning of the restatement (*anuvādya*) is already understood through its actual state, it is appropriate to describe the restated meaning in accordance with the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), this mantra in every respect refers solely to the majesty of Śiva. Even that syllable which they call the first sound at the beginning of the Veda—due to the relationship between the inexpressible and the expresser—which is to be known solely through the Veda according to its true nature, and which is established in the Vedānta; that very same [syllable] is merged in the *prakṛta* (the subject under discussion), which is considered the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).
The supreme beyond that primordial nature (prakṛti) is Maheśvara; for it is heard in the Vāyusaṃhitā that "the activity of both primordial nature and the person (puruṣa) is dependent upon Him."

In accordance with the *Upabrahmaṇas*, that which was proclaimed at the beginning of the Vedas as the *praṇava*—the sound *oṃ*—is, by way of figurative identification (*abhedopacāra*) between the signifier and the signified, and by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), none other than that very non-differentiated Brahman which is signified by it and is established in the Vedānta because it is the object to be propounded by the portion of the Vedas known as Vedānta. Furthermore, for the *puruṣa* who is attached to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—known as ignorance—by virtue of being its reflection, and who, together with that *prakṛti*, is the controller, He is the primary one, the Lord of the *pradhāna* and the *kṣetrajñas*, and the Master of the *guṇas*.

Since this is well-known from such scriptural passages, it must be accepted that he who is designated by the term Maheśvara is indeed Śrī Sadāśiva himself, and not some other deity. Thus, when the section beginning with "smaller than the small" has been determined to concern Śiva through an examination of its opening, conclusion, and internal references, the Dahara-vidyā enjoined therein must have Śiva as its presiding deity; consequently, there is no room for the connection of any other deity as the object of meditation. Furthermore, because of the recognition of the multitude of qualities traditionally recited in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad, it is concluded that this [Dahara-vidyā] has that same [Śiva] as its sole subject matter.

For thus, first of all, the identity of the locus of worship is clear; likewise, the form of the object of worship is established there by the passage beginning with "accompanied by Umā" (umāsahāyam), and it is described here in the very same way by the mantra "Ṛtaṃ Satyam. This is because the words *trilocanaḥ* (three-eyed) and *mā sahāyaḥ* (with me as companion) have meanings identical to the terms *virūpākṣa* (the odd-eyed one) and *kṛṣṇapiṅgala* (dark-brown). [Furthermore, he is] half-mooned, half-naked, possessing bones, and wearing a garland of lotus petals.

One should pay homage to Mahādeva, because the *Kūrma Purāṇa* prescribes his application in the ritual of saluting Śiva through the statement: "I salute the person who possesses half the marks of a man, who is dark-brown (kṛṣṇapiṅgala)," explaining the term *kṛṣṇapiṅgala* as referring to Umā and Śabala; and because of the Vedic texts concerning Virūpākṣa and Viśvarūpa. One should also pay homage to Īśvara with the mantra: "Ṛtam, Satyam. This is established by the injunction for its application in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*.

In the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*, beginning with "Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for the water from the feet of Mahādeva," and concluding with the instruction that one should cause [the disciple] to consume [it] with the mantra "Ṛtaṃ satyam," this mantra is determined to have Śiva as its referent; furthermore, it is logical that the explanation provided therein should correspond exactly to what is heard in the text. As for that certain person—who has not even caught the scent of the derivation of word-meanings, who is confused by his own fabricated concoctions of Vedic and Smṛti passages following his own sour curds, and who has thrown all Vedic boundaries into disorder—[his view is rejected].

One who proclaims his own descent from Marut—a source of derision for all people—while remaining fixed in his vow, might conclude that the meaning of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is simply "one whose semen flows upwards. This statement of the mantra’s purport is laughable even to children; it would render fruitless even the speaker who is intent on refuting [the true meaning], and thus it is to be disregarded. In the phrase "ūrdhvaretas," however, the expression refers to the state of having *kuśa*-grass as semen, characterized by an upward-flaming nature.

Nor should it be argued that, although this mantra is primarily concerned with the majesty of Śiva, it serves as an authoritative source for the meditation on the "small space" (dahara-upāsanā) by providing the form of the object of worship therein; for in that context, the syntactical connection must necessarily occur in accordance with the requirement of supplying the form of the object of worship that is needed. As stated in the Dhyāna chapter of the *Yogayājñavalkya*:
"Alternatively, one should know the Supreme Self, whose body is supreme bliss, the Person who is dark and tawny, through the instruction of the Guru."

"O Gārgī, through practice they behold [Brahman] in the lotus of the heart within the ether in the city of Brahman; indeed, you too should do likewise. Because it has been shown in this very manner, the word "also" (api), used in the sense of a conjunction, indicates that this is likewise supported by other specific means of recognition, such as the particular location of the heart-lotus and so forth. Now, one might object: "In that case, how is the inclusion of the supreme mantras of Nārāyaṇa in the middle [of the text] appropriate? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For the sake of meditation (anudhyāna). This is the intended meaning: it is not, according to the view of others, that these mantras aim at determining the object of worship for all the higher vidyās.

By means of the words beginning with "The thousand-headed God" (*sahasraśīrṣaṃ devam*), Nārāyaṇa is referred to using accusative case endings; since he "lives depending upon" (*upajīvati*) them twice, their status as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) naturally conveys the intent of establishing his being the sustainer of the universe. To abandon this natural understanding and instead assume that the accusatives function as nominatives, and further to construct a syntactical unity based on the principle that every subordinate element must culminate in its own injunction (*pratyuddeśyaṃ vidhiparyavasāna*), is improper. Thus, according to the method of the opponent, [the status of] passages such as "All indeed are Rudra" (*sarvā vai rudra*)... [is undermined].

Since it is difficult to deny that the intent of all words such as "all persons" (*sarvapuruṣa*)—which denote clearly distinct entities free from obstacles such as contradictory case-endings or the co-occurrence of verbs requiring them—is to determine that the entire range of objects of worship in higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), including those in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the Puruṣasūkta, the Sad-vidyā, and the Vyāhṛti-vidyā, is essentially Rudra through the recognition of their identity; and since in the *Atharvaśikhā*, the question "Who is to be meditated upon? (*kaśca dhyeyaḥ*) is raised without the introduction of any specific meditation (*vidyāviśeṣa*), [the answer] refers to the object of meditation in all higher knowledges.

Furthermore, because the determination that Śiva is the object of meditation is explicit, and because it would otherwise be necessary to resort to strained interpretations for the mantras beginning with "The thousand-headed god," there is no room for the suspicion that they might have a contrary meaning; nor does this section aim to determine the object of worship in the present Dahara-vidyā, since the determination of the deity as Śiva—designated by the terms Rudra and Maheśvara—is already established by the two immediately preceding mantras, and the mantra "Ṛtaṃ satyam" (Truth and Reality) has already provided the appropriate form for Him; nor [does it refer to] "the virile powers, of which Brahmā is the eldest."

Just as in the case of mantras such as "saṃbhūtāni," it is not possible to assume that they have as their ultimate purpose a meditation on Nārāyaṇa—which is distinct from the glorification of qualities—because if one were to assume that this passage is devoted to an independent meditation on Nārāyaṇa that is not an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the current Dahara-vidyā, it would result in the logical fault of having to extract it from the context, since it would fail to connect with this very section that continues until the conclusion of the immediately following Anuvāka. Furthermore, since such an extraction is improper when the connection within the context itself is possible, it is also incorrect to maintain that the meditation on Nārāyaṇa is an auxiliary to the Dahara-vidyā in the sense of being a remote means of assistance (*ārādupakāraka*), like the Prayāja sacrifices are to the Āgneya and other offerings.

By means of the passages beginning with "resembling the interior of a lotus bud," "in its center there is a great fire," and "in its center there is a flame of fire"—as well as through the power of praising the qualities of the great flame of fire shining within the hollow of the heart-lotus—the meditations on that [flame], which are obtained through such praise, are established as being conducive to the worship of Śiva by virtue of residing within the great flame of fire shining in the hollow of the heart-lotus; therefore, it is improper to assume that they are merely indirect auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*).
This is stated in the *Śrīnandikeśvaragītā* within the *Kūrma Purāṇa*.
Having meditated upon the supreme lotus previously described within the heart,
one should then visualize oneself as the agent therein, possessing a radiance equal to fire.
In the center, one should contemplate the twenty-fifth principle, the Supreme Self, in the form of a flame of fire; and in the middle of that, the supreme ether.
The reality awakened by the syllable Oṃ is eternal, auspicious, and immutable;
it is unmanifest, merged within primordial nature (prakṛti), higher than the highest, and unsurpassed.

"One should constantly meditate upon Maheśvara, who is beyond darkness, whose reality is supreme, who has the Self as His support, who is stainless, eternal, and of one form"— thus, first, in His own place within the heart-lotus, He is described in the root scripture (mūla-śruti) as being in the center of that [lotus] in the form of fire, characterized by agency and other attributes.

This is because [the text] clarifies the specific mode of worship: the worship of Śiva—who is described as "that which is beyond" (paraḥ sa maheśvaraḥ) within Nārāyaṇa; who is taught to reside in the center of that flame by the words "of that flame" and so forth; who is described therein by the passage beginning with "the thousand-headed deity" and so forth; who is the twenty-fifth principle identified there as the crest of fire; who is of the nature of the sheath of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*), being exclusively focused on the consciousness extracted from within that ego (*ahaṃkāra*) which is itself of the nature of the sheath of consciousness (*vijñānamaya-kośa*). Thus, it is the worship of Śiva.

In that very same section on Dharma, having begun with "At the junctions of time (sandhyās), one should meditate upon the Lord of sacrifice through the specific fire," and having prescribed the meditation on Viṣṇu within the heart-lotus with the words "Having placed [Him] named Viṣṇu, the source of the universe, in the abode of the heart-lotus," it is further observed that the method of worshipping Śiva as being internal to Him is established by the passage beginning with "Within Him [is] the Lord of all beings, whose form is Brahman," and ending with "one should meditate upon Śambhu, the Ancient Puruṣa; he is liberated from bondage. Therefore, just as in the Antaryāmin-vidyā (the Knowledge of the Inner Sun) as well...

"This sun indeed shines as this orb; therein are those *ṛc*s," and so forth—this mention of the Person presiding over the orb is solely for the purpose of enjoining the meditation upon the Supreme Lord as being within that [orb]. Likewise, the mention of Nārāyaṇa in the *Dahara-vidyā* is for the same purpose; thus there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Others, however, following the identification with the *Kaivalya-śruti* which states "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva," and so on, maintain that the passage beginning "In the middle of that crest the Supreme Self is established" refers to that which was previously taught as the object of meditation.

Thinking that Maheśvara alone is supreme, they consider the method of meditation described in the middle section (*madhyamānuvāka*)—following the glorification of Nārāyaṇa’s qualities—to be as follows: first the heart-lotus, then the great fire (*mahāgni*) within it, then its crest (*śikhā*), and finally Paramaśiva, who was previously enjoined as the object of worship. Thus, since passages such as "He is Brahmā, he is Śiva" are established as being intent on teaching the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of Paramaśiva, the enumeration of Nārāyaṇa among these manifestations—as seen in the *Kaivalya-śruti*—refers to him as the supreme Self for the sake of the practitioner.

Because the sequence is observed, they say that one should first contemplate one's own self as Nārāyaṇa, and then meditate upon Him—not as residing within the center of the flame of the Vaiśvānara fire in one's own heart-lotus—but rather [as the Self] itself, because by the power of that [contemplation], He becomes clearly manifest as its subordinate. This method is also approved by the Paurāṇikas; for it is thus corroborated in the Sūta-saṃhitā: "Or else, I am Hari himself, the omniscient Supreme Person, the Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet."
Having meditated thus: "Viśva is Nārāyaṇa, the God, the Imperishable,
the Supreme Lord," [one should place Him] again within the lotus of one's own heart, the temple of the Supreme Lord, which has been opened by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Endowed with the petals of the eight sovereign powers and joined with the filaments of knowledge.
When the great bulb of the wind of knowledge has been awakened by the syllable Om (praṇava),
there blazes the great fire with universal flames, facing in all directions.
One should meditate upon the Lord Vaiśvānara, whose source is the Jagatī meter, who has the crest-lock as his body,
and who heats his own body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
In that place, the sacrificial fire blazed like a lamp in a windless spot,
radiant as a streak of lightning amidst dark rain clouds.
One should contemplate its form as having a yellow luster, like the awn of wild rice (*nīvāra*).
In the center of the crest of that fire is the supreme cause—
the Supreme Self, bliss, the supreme ether, the Lord.
He is the Cosmic Order, the Truth, the Supreme Brahman, the one with Ambā, the medicine for the disease of worldly existence.
[He saw] Maheśvara, whose semen is drawn up, who has diverse eyes and universal forms,
the blue-throated one who beholds his own Self and destroys all sins—
meditated upon by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, yet himself devoid of being an object of meditation.

"Thus, with great reverence, the yogi should meditate upon the Lord of the lords of yogis. Now, whether it is intended by the Śruti that Nārāyaṇa is included among the ranks of worshippers, or whether it is intended that Śiva is to be meditated upon within the heart of that very worshipper as being even more internal—under either interpretation, the superiority of Paramaśiva over Brahmā and the others who have been taught [as objects of meditation] as his own manifestations or as the manifestations of Nārāyaṇa is established; thus, his absolute supremacy is beyond dispute. But [it may be objected]: "In this very context, it says 'Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman'..."

How can Nārāyaṇa—who has been taught by explicit statement (*kaṇṭhoktyā*) as being the Supreme Brahman—be said to have the status of a subordinate to another? This is not a fault. For the phrase "nārāyaṇaparam" (that which is beyond Nārāyaṇa) functions as a single compound; thus, the meaning is that the Reality (*tattvam*) is the Brahman who is superior to Nārāyaṇa, while Nārāyaṇa is the one who is beyond [him], i.e., other than him. This interpretation is justified precisely because the mantra aims to establish the intended relationship of primary and subordinate between Śiva—the Supreme Brahman designated as the object of worship in the words "ṛtam satyam param brahma"—and Nārāyaṇa.

Regarding this, it has been stated by others that because the *Mahopaniṣad*—in its corresponding section—shows the recitation with a word-break (*padaviccheda*) such that Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman, one must follow that precedent here as well. Even though the term is a compound, since the word "Nārāyaṇa" consists of separate words, one must assume the elision (*luk*) of the nominative case-ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* etc. Furthermore, even when it is a compound, it is more appropriate for it to be a coordinate construction (*samānādhikaraṇa*), following the logic of the "chief of the Niṣādas" (*niṣādasthapati*). Thus: "I alone am the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate reality, the Grandfather; I alone am the supreme light."

Furthermore, the claim that this mantra is intended to establish Nārāyaṇa alone as the Supreme Brahman—based on the observation of the *Laiṅgyopabrahmaṇa* stating "I am the all-pervading Supreme Self"—is incorrect. This is because, although this mantra is indeed recited in the *Mahopaniṣad*, it is not found in other [recensions] transmitted through the traditional lineage. Even if it were present there, one could justify the reading in the *Mahopaniṣad* by assuming that the fifth case ending was replaced by the nominative according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* in accordance with the reading of the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*.

Because it is impossible for the accentuation of the *prakaraṇa* (the specific grammatical context) and so forth to be subverted; because a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*) is also untenable due to its contradiction with the paribhāṣā concerning semantic competency (*samartha*); and because, contrary to the definition of a determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*), a genitive-tatpuruṣa compound conforming to that [interpretation] is more appropriate. Furthermore, since a "taddhita-ending compound" (*tapara-samāsa*) is observed in the rule *tataḥ kālasya*, by applying a similar analysis through the division of the yoga-rule (*yoga-vibhāga*)—"the fifth case [is compounded] in that manner"—the formation of a genitive compound here is established.

In this mantra, because it is improper for the two masculine words *madhyama* and *para* to be qualifiers of the light of reality (*tatvajyotiḥ*), and because of the scriptural statement of Nārāyaṇa—such as "I alone am the supreme Brahman"—which was recited during the dispute between Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa regarding their mutual superiority prior to the manifestation of the Great Liṅga, [we conclude that] Śiva, who appeared immediately thereafter to quell that dispute and stood in the midst of the manifested Great Liṅga, is the one referred to: "We behold Mahādeva; let all fear be abandoned."

"You two were previously born from my limbs, O mighty ones; let me be divided threefold under the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Bhava—the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), who is flawless and the abode of all qualities for protection. Because the truth of the matter is established by such statements as "O Viṣṇu, you delude the world," which are presented in that very context; and because, according to the statement in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* concerning Nārāyaṇa—"He is the supreme, immediately following [in rank] among all powers of Brahman"—his status as being subordinate to Brahman is indeed [established].

Furthermore, because [the text] has been refined by [Sudarśanācārya], even when adopting the meaning stated by others, since it is impossible for both "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman" and "Ṛta, Satya, the Supreme Brahman" to be taught as the state of supremacy, one of them must necessarily be interpreted otherwise. According to the principle of the *aṅga-guṇa-virodha* (conflict between the primary and the subordinate), that very quality—the teaching of the supremacy of Nārāyaṇa—must be interpreted otherwise in the manner taught by Sudarśanācārya in the verse: "Brahman is said to be he; He is the Supreme and the Ultimate Reality. By the force of this, the introductory statements (*upakrama*) and so forth are also established [in favor of Nārāyaṇa].

Furthermore, because it is illogical to render the meaning confused, and because of the principle established in the *adhikaraṇa* "In case of conflict between the quality of a subsidiary and the purpose [of the principal], [the former] is for the sake of that [latter]," it was determined that in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and the *somayāga*, which depend on the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of the one-day (*ekāha*) sacrifices and so forth, since one or the other is impossible, when the priority of the time [of performance] obtained from the scriptural injunctions such as "if by an *iṣṭi*" must necessarily be abandoned, it is more appropriate to favor the principal; thus, the abandonment applies to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* alone. Therefore, there is not even a scent of contradiction in the point already established. In fact, however, regarding the passage beginning with "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman," etc., [it is as follows].

Even though this [text] is intent on establishing Nārāyaṇa as the non-figurative Brahman, it will be demonstrated more thoroughly below how his status as subordinate to Śiva is nonetheless consistent. ||31||
The summits of the Vedas, headed by the auspicious Bṛhadāraṇyaka,
as well as others who are knowers of the qualities of Your Lordship, have proclaimed the power of the Heart; they have also [proclaimed] the entire rule for the withdrawal of all [attributes].
They know that their hearts belong to you alone; so what is the use of these foolish words?

The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti, beginning with the Harividya meditation on the Supreme Lord as the object of worship—"That which is the space within the heart, in that He is hidden"—describes His unique and extraordinary power:

"He is the ruler of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of all; may He not make us greater by good deeds, nor smaller by evil deeds; He is the Lord of all, He is the overlord of beings, He is the protector of beings, He is the bridge and the support so that these worlds do not fall into confusion. Thus it speaks.

The Chāndogya Śruti also begins with, "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace, the small space within it," and then, by proclaiming its qualities—stating, "This is the Self, free from sin, without old age, death, sorrow, doubt, or distress, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true"—it teaches that those who meditate upon it attain such results as:
"Those who depart from here having discovered this Self and these true desires, for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds. And so forth.
And having thus proclaimed its greatness by extolling its great fruits, [the text] then proceeds with the Mahopaniṣad itself;

following the method of the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka, it describes Nārāyaṇa—who is to be meditated upon as identical with the worshiper—through such passages as "The God with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, the source of all happiness," and so forth.
It further describes his heart-lotus and the flame of the Vaiśvānara fire therein, stating that within that very flame resides the Puruṣa, the Supreme Self, who is the essence of the heart.

By demonstrating that Śiva resides in the center of that [space] through such passages as "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva," and by proclaiming that others are His manifestations (vibhūti), he illuminated His majesty.

Although, in the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, the passage beginning with "In the middle of that crest" (*tasyāḥ śikhāyā madhye*) is held to refer to Nārāyaṇa, and since this Upaniṣad—by virtue of recognizing that same subject in the passage beginning with "In the middle of that crest" (*tasyai śikhāyai madhye*)—is intended for the worship of Nārāyaṇa, it may in some contexts serve as a subordinate element to ritual action; [nevertheless...]

Just as a deity who is to be worshipped is the primary object of worship within a ritual action, and just as the heart-lotus— which is to be meditated upon as a subordinate element in the meditation on the *dahara*—

is to be meditated upon as the primary object for the sake of specific fruits taught in the Pātañjala Śāstra, so too, in the Śaiva meditation on the *dahara*, Nārāyaṇa— who is to be worshipped as a subordinate element— is obtained as the primary object of worship by virtue of this [textual authority]. Nevertheless, according to the position favored by the *Sūtasamhitā* and other texts, which holds that "in the middle of that crest" (*tasyāḥ śikhāyā madhye*) refers to Śiva, [the following applies].

In the same way, this Upaniṣad also culminates solely in the worship of Śiva. Other scriptural passages (śruti) should likewise be understood according to their respective contexts. It might be argued that in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, within the section concerning the Nirviśeṣa (the Attributeless), attributes such as "mastery" (*vaśitva*) and so forth are enumerated for the purpose of praising that very [Brahman]; however, there is no occasion whatsoever for Śiva—the object of worship in the *dahara-vidyā* mentioned in the *Kaivalya-śākhā* and other texts—to appear there. Although the *Chāndogya* contains injunctions for worship, nevertheless, there is nothing therein to indicate that it is the worship of Śiva.

No such authority is found. Nor can the identity [of the object of meditation] be established on the grounds that the meditations taught in the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad* are identical; for in the *Ātmaprabodha Upaniṣad*, beginning with "Now, this city of Brahman is this lotus" and ending with "meditating, one who is freed from grief and delusion does not perish," the worship of Viṣṇu within that lotus is also enjoined. Consequently, it is impossible to restrict [the identity] to that alone. As for the collection of mantras from the *Mahopaniṣad* that was cited, since there is no prior mention of Śiva—just as in the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka*—it is not [applicable].

It can be stated that the text is devoted to the worship of Him (Nārāyaṇa), because from the opening statement, "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed," through the introduction of Nārāyaṇa, it is perceived that the work is indeed devoted to His worship. Nor can it be argued that, due to the recognition of the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka* style, the text is devoted to the worship of Śiva;

for such a claim would contradict the opening statement, "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed," and the recognition of that style is internal [to the text], just as in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* there is the instruction: "One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha."

Having raised the objection that—since the Udgītha-vidyā in the Vājasaneyaka, which concerns a part of the Udgītha-chant (the *bhakti*) according to the introductory context (*upakrama*), renders irrelevant the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning the performer of the entire Udgītha-chant found in other recensions—it might be argued that due to this recognition of the *prakriyā*, the text must instead be devoted to the meditation on Nārāyaṇa, as that is the position favored by the opponent—he says: "Of the qualities" (*guṇānām*). This is the intended meaning: [The text continues: "Because the qualities [of the individual soul] are subordinate to the primary subject, and because the recognition of the *prakriyā* establishes that the meditation is indeed upon the Supreme Self. This is the underlying intention.

Although the teaching of "mastery" (*vaśitva*) in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* occurs within the context of the section concerning the attributeless (*nirguṇa*), it cannot refer to an attributeless mastery and so forth. This is because it must be understood that its ultimate purpose lies in praise, achieved solely by extolling the qualities of the ether (*ākāśa*) as characterized by specific attributes. Since it is recognized that the extolling of the qualities belongs specifically to Śiva—who resides within the cavity of the heart and is designated by such terms as *Īśāna*, *Sarveśvara*, and *Bhūtādhipati*—the scriptural mention of qualities such as mastery pertains exclusively to Śiva. Thus...

In the *Chāndogya*, following the reasoning established in the *Daharādhikaraṇa* regarding the passage "The small [space] within this," the term "ether" (*ākāśa*)—which refers to Brahman—is used to introduce the Brahman that is to be meditated upon. Having stated, "That which is within it is what must be sought," and so forth, the text itself raises the objection, "What is there that must be sought? and so on. Then, by the subsequent sentence, "All desires are contained within it," those qualities such as "having true desires" (*satyakāma*) and others are taught as existing within that [Brahman]. Consequently, there is an inclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) of these qualities along with qualities such as "mastery" (*vaśitva*) mentioned in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*.

Furthermore, because it is accepted by all, the scriptural passage in the *Mahopaniṣad* beginning with "The thousand-headed God" (*sahasraśīrṣaṃ devam*) is intended to establish a specific mode of worship of Śiva; this is because it recognizes the method of the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka*. As for the objection raised that there is a contradiction with the opening statement (*upakrama*), we ask: does this contradiction arise because worship of Nārāyaṇa is enjoined in the opening, or because the injunction for his worship is inferred from the description of his manifestations (*vibhūti*), or else [because of something] in the opening?

The contradiction [raised] is that because [Nārāyaṇa] is described as being pre-eminent over all, it is improper to conceive of Him as entering into the sphere of meditation as a subordinate element to another. This is not the first [contradiction], because in the *Mahopaniṣad* there is no hearing of an injunction for meditation at all. Nor is it the second, because through the recognition of the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, the meditation on Śiva is obtained precisely as being within Nārāyaṇa;

and since Nārāyaṇa himself enters into the category of objects of meditation, there is no contradiction with the introductory passage even by virtue of that recognition, making due regard for it appropriate. As for the *Chāndogya*:

Although, at the outset of the passage "That which is within it is to be sought," there is the appearance that the meditation concerns only qualities such as *satyakāmatva* (having true desires), nevertheless—due to the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the *Chāndogya* text and because we must accept a meditation on the substrate (*guṇin*) with its qualities as subordinate—it is possible for the syllable *oṃ*, which is a part of the *udgītha*, to enter into the meditation on the performer of the *udgītha* through the vision of *prāṇa* as a qualification, even when the *udgītha-vidyā* of the *Chāndogya* is recognized in the *Vājasaneyaka*. However, [the text continues]: "Now, this very one... [and so forth].

The meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the vision of it as such, as established in the *Chāndogya* Upaniṣad in passages such as "The principal vital breath meditated upon that [Om] as the *udgītha*," would be contradicted; thus, a distinction [between the two meditations] is appropriate.

Now, let the third alternative be accepted: that there should be a combination (*upasaṃhāra*) of the two statements, "That which is within this [Om] is to be sought" and "That which is within it is to be meditated upon," on the basis of the principle that "the pronouns *tyad* and so forth are always used in the neuter gender when combined with a non-neuter word."

If it is argued that this is not so—because by applying the grammatical rule *cāsyānyatarasyām*, one may conceive of [the term "ether"] as referring to both ether and the class of qualities residing therein, thereby allowing for the description of the injunction to meditate upon both; and because the demonstration of Nārāyaṇa’s supreme excellence in passages such as "Nārāyaṇa alone existed" cannot tolerate being subordinated to another—[we reply: no, for in passages such as "Nārāyaṇa alone existed," [Nārāyaṇa] is subordinate to Śiva.

Since this will be explained more precisely later on precisely because it conforms to logical reasoning (*kalpanā*), by this [argument] the opponent’s misconception—that the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka* alone, in accordance with the *Mahopaniṣad*, is intended solely for the meditation (*upāsanā*) on Nārāyaṇa—is seized by the throat. For if that were the case, then just as the Chāndogya scripture would have to be interpreted in accordance with the Taittirīya scripture regarding a single meditation, the latter scripture would consequently result in being intended only for the meditation on mere qualities (*guṇa-mātra*). This is because the scriptural passages cited from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and elsewhere serve to describe the additional qualities associated with the Dahara-vidyā.
It is well said that these [scriptures] proclaim the unsurpassed power of Śiva. ||32||
Furthermore,
O All-pervading Lord, even the Māṇḍūkya Śruti, its meaning elucidated by other scriptural passages of identical purport, ordains for you the sovereignty over all.
Likewise, in the *Īśāna-mantra-smaraṇa-narudra-upaniṣad*,
the mantras are extensively set forth, as are many others even more clearly revealed.

This is the purification of the subject (*viṣaya-śuddhi*). Regarding the divine (*adhidevata*) and the internal (*ādhyātma*), there are three forms each for the Self, which is itself without distinction, differentiated by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

According to the Śruti, Vaiśvānara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Īśa are the forms with respect to the divine; Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña are the forms with respect to the internal. Among these, Vaiśva and Vaiśvānara are associated with the presiding deities (*abhimānin*) of the gross bodies through their individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*) aspects, while Taijasa and Hiraṇyagarbha are declared [to preside] over the subtle [bodies].
The *prājña* and *īśvara* are conditioned by the two states of *avidyā* and *māyā*.
The *viśva* exists in the waking state; in the dream state, the *jīva* becomes the *taijasa*.
Because it is the witness of mere *avidyā*, it becomes the *prājña* in deep sleep (*saṃprasāda*).
Here, the Lord Vaiśvānara is called the Sovereign Person (Rāṭpuruṣa),
whose entire body is the three worlds with all their moving and non-moving beings;
he is Hiraṇyagarbha, the nourisher of the worlds through his subtle vision.

He who takes delight in presiding over the *māyā* that shines forth from pure *sattva*— that which the knowers of the Veda declare to be subtle and like the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the means [of liberation].
This Lord, however, is the Blessed One, beautiful with half his body as Ambikā;
some maintain that here [in this context], the distinction between the limiting adjuncts of Māyā and Vidyā is merely conceptual.

They say that through ignorance the Lord assumes the state of a living soul (*jīva*), appearing as the reflected universe; all this is clearly stated in the scriptures for those who possess the training therein. Therefore, we have not cited the verses from the *Mūla* (the *Māṇḍūkya-kārikā*) here. In that context, for the sake of ease of understanding, the *Māṇḍūkya-śruti*—after defining the two quarters with the words "The waking state" (*jāgaritasthāna*) and so forth—describes the four-quartered Self (*catuṣpād ātmā*) by means of the passage beginning with "This very Self is four-quartered" (*so'yamātmā catuṣpāt*). Among these, Viśva and Vaiśvānara correspond to Taijasa and Hiraṇyagarbha respectively. (Note: The text identifies Viśva/Vaiśvānara with Taijasa/Hiraṇyagarbha for the purpose of pedagogical clarity, following the sequence of the *Māṇḍūkya-śruti*.)

In the context of defining the third quarter (pāda), it is stated: "The state of deep sleep is the stage where consciousness has become a single mass; he is indeed composed of bliss (*ānandamaya*), an enjoyer of bliss, whose face is the mind—the Prājña is the third quarter. At that point, [the text] establishes his sovereignty over all by declaring:

"He is the Lord of all, He is the All-knowing, He is the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmī*), He is the Fire; for He is the origin and the dissolution of all beings. Now, although the status of being the Lord of all and so forth is inherently impossible for the Prājña, the teaching of those attributes [is intended] to express the identity of the Prājña with Brahman as conditioned by *māyā*.

[The opponent might argue: "Even so, since the possibility of its being another deity exists, this scriptural passage cannot be restricted to referring to the Lord (Īśvara). To dispel such a weak doubt, [the author] says: "having the same meaning" (*samānārtha*). In the *Uttaratāpanīya*, following the very method of the *Māṇḍūkya*—in the section defining the four-footed Self with the words "That Self is four-footed," etc.—it is stated: "The Wise One is the Lord; He is the third foot," and so on, beginning with "He is the Lord of all."

The meaning is as follows: in the investigation of the third quarter (*pāda*), having stated the identity of the wise one with the Lord (*īśvara*), since [the Lord] is traditionally taught as the "Lord of all" (*sarveśvara*) and so forth, it is inferred that the *Māṇḍūkya-śruti* also has that same intent for the sake of that unity.

Regarding the mantra "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" and so on, this is the *Īśāna-mantra*, the *Rudra-upaniṣad*, and the *Śatarudrīya*. According to the usage in the *Caraṇavyūha*: "There are one hundred and one Yajurvedic branches; among them, the *Rudra-upaniṣad* is traditionally taught," the twenty-one mantras beginning with "Namo hiraṇyabāhave" recited therein indeed belong to Śiva.

By means of introducing the sovereignty over each [direction] beginning with the East, he clarifies the universal sovereignty; the other mantras are those recited in the *Yudhyasūkta*, the *Śivasamkalpa*, and so forth. ||33||
Innumerable mantras, composed of boundless prostrations, manifest some ineffable majesty that cannot be attained by others;
they themselves fall at the feet of even the *śūdras* and other such classes, [bestowing] auspiciousness.
Fools do not acknowledge the burden in a salutation, but the wise do.

In all four Vedas, mantras addressed to Candraśekhara are generally seen. [They are] adorned with salutations (*namaskāra*), whether repeated, mentioned once, or recited at the beginning and end; thus it is clear that they are innumerable. However, the mantras of other deities renowned in the scriptures do not possess such a quality, even when a salutation is occasionally joined to them. And so, by the abundance of salutations—which serve as a sign of the excellence of his own domain and are not shared by other deities—[he is distinguished].

It is clear that the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, *Atharvaveda*, the *Śatarudrīya*, the *Devavrata*, and other such texts proclaim the greatness of Śiva as something unique and unparalleled. As for what others have prattled there—that prostration (*namaskāra*) is not an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of excellence regarding its own object, because one is seen in the world to offer prostration even out of fear toward someone capable of harming oneself, and because in the Veda too we find prostrations prompted by both motives, such as "Salutation to you! Do not harm me"—in this context, however, there is an abundance of such [prostrations].

Thinking that [the objection] might arise because of the abundance of fear, he says "himself" (*svayam*) in order to refute it. This is the intended meaning: if, here, due to the preponderance of fear, one were to offer salutations (*namas*) to the gods who are limited by their respective ends—[thinking] "I am entering the state of Brahman, which is not common to others"—this is because we see in the *Kaṭhavallīs* that "the great fear, the thunderbolt," and because in the Sūtra "on account of trembling" (*kampanāt*), that [Brahman] is indicated by such a sign. Furthermore, even out of fear, a salutation does not imply superiority; for in the Śruti: "In this world, who indeed is there that is not subject to Rudra? Thus, "Salutations to you."
Let it be so; let him not harm me. Even though this act of salutation (*namaskāra*) arises from fear, its excellence as an object of that salutation is established.

This is because the Brāhmaṇa commentary on the mantra "Homage to you for your heat and your flame" (*namaste harase śociṣe*), which is identical in form to the salutation heard in the mantra "Homage to you for your heat and your flame," states: "Having paid homage, they treat one with greater respect. This is because it declares that [the act of salutation] is not abandoned when prompted by the general excellence of its own object. Furthermore, in mantras such as "All is indeed Rudra," etc., [this principle applies].

In those [texts] that are free from the marks of fear and are composed solely for the purpose of establishing the meaning of Śiva’s names and so forth, the prostrations being performed are motivated exclusively by reverence for the subject matter;

thus, it can be argued that there is no other possible explanation (anyathāsiddhi) for them here. And it is said in the *Laiṅgya*: "The sages who perceive reality declare that everything is indeed Rudra;

they offer salutations along with reverence to the Supreme Lord. Therefore, others, such as the *Tvaritarudra* and so on, which are generally adorned with garlands of prostrations, proceed without restraint.

Thus, it is as firm as adamantine cement that [the scriptures] reveal nothing other than the unsurpassed majesty of Śiva. Therefore, the prattle of those who have entered the wicked path hated by both the world and the Vedas—claiming that the salutation of others is performed solely to conceal one's own lowliness by prostrating at the feet of outcastes and the like, and not out of a sense of their excellence—is not something that touches the hearts of the wise. ||34||
Furthermore:
Alas! [I bow] to the sole object of worship for all those worthy of homage, and by my word, even to the progenitor of Viṣṇu and the other gods in heaven.
O Giver of Boons, I consider those who speak of you to be proclaiming your majesty;
they hold even the Lord of the Mountains and the Lord of the Gaṇas in high esteem.
To him to whom obeisance is due, [the text] shows that you, O Śiva, are the object of all salutations, while Niyata-jīma is [merely] a subordinate.

Since being the object of a salutation intended for oneself is common to all [beings], it necessarily follows that this [text] aims at [Shiva] being the object of all salutations, because it is incapable of establishing the unique nature of Shiva through that [commonality]. Nor can its purport be merely that He is the object of a multitude of salutations; for while the mantras of the Rudrādhyāya and other such texts constitute a multitude of salutations, they are capable of establishing His unique nature, as the fact that Shiva is the object of all salutations is established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It should not be argued that [the mantra] lacks praise because it does not conform to those [other mantras], for there is no word here that conveys a profusion of salutations to Śiva exceeding those offered to other deities; nor does it result in the fault of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) to assume such an intention for the word *namaḥ* alone. This is because the status of being the object of all salutations is established either by the power of the word *namaḥ* to denote a genus (*jāti*), or by the force of determining the appropriate syntactic connection based on the general linguistic rule (*sāmānyavyutpatti*) that "this is mine" and so forth. Thus, the attainment [of the desired fruit] is logically justified.

Even though [the identity of] that [being] as Śiva is not understood from another Vedic text (*śrutyantara*), since it is possible for the meaning to be established by implication—namely, that in the mantra "yo brahmāṇam... there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Supreme Lord, excluding only His role as the teacher—and because the portion "viśvaṃ narmīya vai namaḥ" in the mantra dedicated to propounding the qualities of the Supreme Lord associated with the *dahara-vidyā* is appropriately intended to signify all obeisances and the specific qualities connected thereto, the existence of a prior statement (*purovāda*) is also possible; thus, for whom... [text ends].
Passages such as these may also be cited here as examples. Likewise, the mantra "imā rudrāya sthiradhanvine giraḥ" demonstrates that Śiva is the object to be propounded by the entire mass of words.

Subsequently, in the *Rudrasūkta* (RV 2.33), because the word "giraḥ" clearly refers to [the hymns] dedicated to Śiva, and because the term "īśvara" is used in the sense of "lord," the word "mā" [in the verse] refers to all words brought into proximity through perception and other means. Although salutations such as "namo brahmaṇe namo brāhmaṇebhyaḥ" are also found which do not have [Śiva] as their object, [the principle remains the same].

Nevertheless, just as those who sing this upon the lute are designated as "singing this upon its strings," so too the Supreme Lord’s designation as the object of all salutations and as that which is expounded by the entire web of words— though He exists within the circle of the *vikrama* [steps]— is intended to express His universal nature (*sārvātmya*).
Thus, one should understand that phrases such as "to whom [I bow]" reveal His supreme state by manifesting His identity with all things.
Certain Vedic verses, having taken recourse to the form of Rudra within Śiva, the supreme cause, were [revealed] by the Brāhmaṇas who are most proficient in the Vedas.
O best of Brahmins,
some of these statements conclude with the Sun-form, while others, O foremost of sages, do so with other forms.

Thus, by means of the very door of the designation of forms, Mahādeva is the one to be propitiated, as seen in the statement of the Skanda Purāṇa: "Mahādeva stands in all forms. By the power of the mantra, "Today I offer praise to Rudra, the skillful, the dweller in the house; may he grant me desired wealth," it is conceived that even praises and prostrations—which appear to have other objects—ultimately terminate in Śiva, the Inner Controller.

Furthermore, because there must necessarily be a conceptual resolution of such [mantras] as "Obeisance to the dogs and to the lords of dogs" by concluding with that [Lord], some teachers maintain that the mantra beginning with "To whom obeisance" intends [Him] as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all. Likewise, the mantra "Soma flows" (*somaḥ pavate*) impels one toward the Lord who is the progenitor even of the gods such as Mahāviṣṇu;

for by the instruction "He was born from Viṣṇu," there is a manifestation of superiority over the aforementioned meanings such as "He was born from Agni," and thus the word *Viṣṇu* refers to the Protector of the Universe (*jagatpālaka*).

Since the capacity to produce His incarnations exists even in Daśaratha and others due to their devotion to Mahāviṣṇu, that [status] does not constitute His excellence because He is also the producer of fire and other elements. This is evident from the mantra in the *Āyuṣyasūkta*: "He who was alone in the beginning, who spread this world downwards and upwards, the protector of the universe; unto Him, the Supreme Person, they go"—a verse intended to establish Śiva as the cause, protector, and destroyer of the world, where the phrase "from whom the protector of the world arose" is used to manifest His sovereign power to sustain the universe.

Furthermore, because it is necessarily the case that the supreme state belongs to the form of Mahāviṣṇu who has *sattva* as His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), [the text says]: "The progenitor of heaven, earth, fire, the sun, and even of the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra), is indeed Mahāviṣṇu, the Lord (*īśvara*) through Soma. And since there is a corroborative statement (*upabrahmaṇa*) in the Rudrasaṃhitā, [it follows that] this mantra is not merely concerned with Pavamāna. True, it is so; nevertheless, because the causality of Agni and the others is actually established therein, and because of the twofold connection and the corroborative statement, [there is] the connection with Umā and the rest.

And this has been established almost entirely in the investigation of the meaning of the *Puruṣasūkta*. This being so, there is no contradiction with the traditional exegesis (*nirukta*) resulting from the denial that the word "Soma" occurring in the mantra is *sakhaṇḍa* (composite); for since the word also possesses a secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*) directed toward [Śiva] for the sake of its ritual application (*viniyoga*), its study as a constituent word is justified by virtue of having Him as its referent. Furthermore, because He is called "Soma" by people together with Umā—as in the phrase "Śambhu-Soma"—and because He is directly the progenitor (*janaka*) of Him [Viṣṇu], and because His status as Śiva is necessary according to the etymological derivation (*yoga*) shown in the Purāṇic statements regarding Viṣṇu as well... [omitted].

The Rudrādhyāya and other hymns dedicated to the deity Rudra, when performed extensively by disciples, attendants, and others with various offerings, lead one to attain the second state, that of the Gaṇapati; having attained the third state, one likewise enters [into him]. Knowing fear through the yoga of the ascetic, and becoming a non-transmigrating being, one rejoices together with him—thus, by means of such Śruti and Smṛti texts, liberation is understood as having this nature. In this way, there is indeed only one Rudra, not...

The mantras beginning with "When [the sun] is in the second solstice" (*dvitīyāyanasthe*) and so forth—which are devoted to Śiva and others—should be supplied here. As for the explanation that in a particular ritual (*karmaviśeṣa*) there is only one Rudra as the deity and not many, that is incorrect; for in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, even without reference to ritual, it is heard: "There is only one Rudra, no second stands beside him; he who rules these worlds by his powers" (*ya imāṃl lokān īśata īśanībhiḥ*). Therefore, the statement "there is only one Rudra" has the same meaning as "one only, without a second" (*ekamevādvitīyam*). ||35||

Thus, there are indeed certain illustrative passages from both the Vedānta portion and the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) of the Veda, as well as those of the Lord of Vow-holders (*vratīpati*) in this world. Furthermore, in that regard, the Purāṇas, the scriptures of Śiva, the *Mahābhārata* and others, are the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [All this] is supported by innumerable, extensive branches of tradition and is to be understood through extremely subtle series of logical arguments. Having extracted the essential power here in many ways, the Purāṇas—like the discus of Viṣṇu—are sufficient to move even Mount Kailāsa, which is as firm as Kapardin (Śiva).
In the Śrī Śiva Purāṇa, it is stated:

"While the sages of the six lineages were listening to one another, a very great dispute arose as to 'this is supreme' and 'this is not'; because the Supreme is difficult to define, no one there emerged victorious."

Having begun with "The Determination," and having described how those sages, while disputing among themselves, approached the assembly of Brahmā, saying: "O Blessed One, we are enveloped by a great darkness;

distressed and bewildered, we do not perceive that which is supreme here," and so forth—thus raising a general question regarding the Supreme Deity who is the cause of all—they were then addressed by Brahmā. Beginning with "Thus questioned," and having stood up and meditated for a very long time, uttering the word "Rudra," his entire body drenched with bliss, he spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Because all this, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra, is Brahman.

By the statement of Brahmā beginning with, "He was first born together with all the vows and the senses," and so forth, it is established through a detailed exposition— that which possesses the fullness of essence, which is common to all, and which aims at extracting the essential nature from the manifold glories scattered across numerous branches that transcend the reach of speech and mind— that Śiva alone is the supreme deity.

These virtuous ones have been taught this region— which is the instruction of the supreme Brahmā, a compendium of the essential meaning of the ocean of all sacred scriptures— and their [wisdom] does not decline.
Even in another birth, may there be devotion to Maheśa as the supreme deity.
Likewise, in the Pādma [Purāṇa] it is said:
"O high-souled Sūta, all the Śāstras, all the Purāṇas without exception, and the Dharmaśāstras have been heard by us; [therefore, grant us] omniscience."
A certain very great doubt dwells within our hearts, because of which we are as if afflicted; you ought to sever that doubt for us.
Who is the supreme and most exalted deity, and how indeed is he propitiated?
What would be the fruit when he is worshipped? Tell us this truly.

Having thus presented a question from the sages— who, unable to determine for themselves whether the various expositions of the preeminence of different deities found in passages throughout the Vedas and many Purāṇas were intended to convey the ultimate truth or were composed merely to conform to the understanding of their listeners—
[the author says]: "In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history."
The dialogue between Viṣṇu and Sanatkumāra, which destroys all sins.
In former times, the venerable Sanatkumāra, who distinguishes between the higher and the lower, asked this very same question of the immutable Viṣṇu.
Having heard the words of that sage, listen without distraction to what Viṣṇu, the supreme among the wise and highly blessed, has said.
Having thus set forth the Sūta’s reply, [he said]:
"Śiva alone is the supreme; though heard of as twofold and manifold, he is sung of in the Vedas and Purāṇas, along with their limbs and sub-limbs."
By such words of Viṣṇu, which establish the supreme excellence of Śiva— (as stated: "Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata—
these are the five systems of knowledge, and the one to be known is Maheśvara alone."
By such statements as these, he establishes the manner in which those scriptures culminate in Śiva, as well as the purpose for the engagement with the various systems of the scriptures.
"The Lord of Pārvatī is the Great Self, possessing all forms yet devoid of form;
there is nothing higher than that Sadāśiva, who is both knowledge and the object of knowledge."

With these and other words, having thus lamented while establishing his own defeat, he says: "Those who do not hear my words as I cry out so loudly—the best of sages—will have the fires of hell kindled for their sake. By this description of the transgression incurred by disregarding the instruction, this matter is further reinforced; and in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa* as well, it is stated: "In ancient times, on the peak of Mount Meru, the great ṛṣis, having bowed to the divine Lord of Gods, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha), began with the question: 'What is that one imperishable reality? Then, through the illusory power (*māyā*) of Maheśvara..."

"Deluded by the origin of the world, not knowing my own true nature as Śambhu, he spoke thus to the Lord of the Ṛṣis," and so forth. Having heard this instruction regarding his own supreme state from Brahmā, and having introduced the demonstration of his own supreme state by Nārāyaṇa, who is the soul of sacrifice and who could not tolerate it, [the Lord said]: "Thus we two dispute, each desiring victory over the other through our respective praises."
Today those two gods departed from there; indeed, the four Vedas remained there, having observed the god Brahmā and being established as the very soul of sacrifice.
One with an agitated heart should declare the true nature of the Supreme Lord. The *Ṛgveda*:
That in which all things abide, from which everything proceeds, and which they call the supreme reality—that is the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*), the God. The *Yajurveda*.
He who is not attained even by all sacrifices and by [all] ascetic penances—he whom they call the Lord, the God, he is the one from whom even the God has not been uplifted. The Sāmaveda.
That by which this wheel is made to revolve throughout the vast expanse of space—
that reality which is realized through yoga is Mahādeva, that Śaṅkara. (Atharvaveda) The Lord of Gods, whom the sages perceive as the Supreme while striving with discipline.
That god, the blessed Bhava, is Maheśa, Puruṣa, and Rudra.
Having heard this auspicious account called the Brahmavedya, the Blessed One, the Soul of the Universe, laughed; and Yajña, too, was utterly bewildered.
How does that Supreme Brahman, who is free from all attachments,
take delight with his wife and his exceedingly proud attendants?
When this had been said, the eternal Lord, whose essence is the syllable Om,
appearing in embodied form though he is formless, spoke these words to the Grandfather.
The Praṇava:
For this Blessed One never delights with a wife who is distinct from his own self;
such indeed is Maheśvara, even though he is Rudra.
O Goddess, this is that Blessed Lord Īśa, the eternal self-luminous one; he is said to be the serpent Sukiśiva, who is the very embodiment of his own bliss.

By means of the instruction on the *praṇava* of the Vedas, even that [instruction] was disregarded by Brahmā as he remained [in his state]; thereafter, following the severing of his fifth head by Rudra, who had manifested at that time for the purpose of universal dissolution (*saṃhāra*), the supreme nature of that [Brahmā] was made clear through the instruction of Paramaśiva himself, who appeared within the solar disc. And in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, after the meaning of that [instruction] has been stated in its entirety and the excellence of Śiva has been established in many ways through detailed description, [this occurs] at the conclusion of the *Vyāsagītā*.
Thus has this lowest of men among you been instructed by me;
and for the sake of propitiating Maheśvara, the eternal yoga of knowledge [has also been taught].
Endowed with this method, one should practice the yoga of knowledge;
he beholds Mahādeva, and no other even in hundreds of kalpas.
He who establishes the dharma of others—that knowledge is the supreme lordly (pārameśvara) knowledge.
Such a person is considered superior to this [yogi] in the world; he is regarded as the highest yogi.
As for that person who, though capable of establishing it, does not do so because he is deluded—
"Even though he is engaged in yoga, he is devoted to the Blessed One for the sake of [attaining] liberation";
thus it is made clear by the injunction establishing the excellence of Śiva. And likewise in the Āditya Purāṇa, in the section analyzing the duties of the castes and stages of life:
"Śiva, who is the inner controller of the universe and whose face is kissed by Viśveśvara..."
One should not say that Brahmā and the others are equal to Śiva, nor that Pārvatī is equal to his powers;
yet one may say that Śambhu is equal to the gods, such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Whoever is possessed by darkness should never touch him;
one should speak of the Blessed Lord, the Consort of Umā, as being superior to all.

By such statements as these, [the superiority of Śiva] is made known through the prohibition of assertions regarding His equality with others, and by the injunction to establish His state as the sole object of devotion. Furthermore, His pre-eminence is proclaimed in the Skanda Purāṇa:

"Those of small intellect who remember me as equal to Brahmā and the other gods, or as equal to Lakṣmī and the other Śaktis, or who remember their Guru as equal to ordinary men—their sins are destroyed by keeping vigil in worship on Śivarātri. Thus, by prescribing an expiation for the remembrance of equality with other deities, His superiority is established. In this same manner, [His superiority is affirmed] throughout all the Purāṇas concerning Him who is conditioned by Māyā.

The preeminence of Paramaśiva, the fourth state (turiya) of the Supreme Brahman, has been established and should be reflected upon by the learned; for even one who knows the truth is free from the suspicion of any [contrary] statement regarding the essential conclusion. This is because any occasional perception of inferiority relative to Brahmā (Aḍruhiṇa) or Nārāyaṇa refers specifically to the domain of the manifestations (vibhūti) of the Destroyer Rudra and his particular incarnations, such as Nīlalohita and others. Indeed, in the Vārāha, Bhāgavata, Vaiṣṇava, Gāruḍa, and other Purāṇas, the claims that Viṣṇu or even the Creator (Vidhātṛ) are the sole agents of destruction are merely partial and do not apply to him directly or in his entirety.
And these [qualities] are from the fourth chapter of the Śiva [Purāṇa]; we shall explain this in detail immediately below.

(39) Even the primordial Goddess Bhāratī herself proclaims your power, O Lord, which is more manifest than that of the terrifying [deities], the foremost among the powerful. We hear, O Lord, that even Mukunda—who was solely intent on worshipping your lotus feet—is devoted to Brahmā, Acyuta, and Hara; for in many places in the Mahābhārata, Nārāyaṇa is described as being devoted to the worship of Śiva.

This has been established and illustrated in the *Namaślokavivaraṇa*. All of that was done for the sake of favoring the world by demonstrating that Śiva—through his various forms as other supreme Brahman manifestations—is both his own object of worship and the source of himself, thereby manifesting his status as the one to be worshipped by all; and by means of specific incarnations among gods and humans, as well as through the eternal nature of the [scriptural] tradition, Śiva-worship is practiced for the sake of attaining various respective fruits. This was for the purpose of establishing that Paraśiva is superior to the universe and is the one to be worshipped by the universe.

It must be stated that [the text] culminates [in this way], because we see other purposes for the Great Sage’s extensive effort in composing that work. In the *Laiṅgya*: "All the gods are permeated by Viṣṇu; all the Gaṇas are permeated by Viṣṇu. Indeed, no other state of existence equal to Viṣṇu is ordained. Thus the Vedas constantly sing; there is no doubt in this. That very Lord, the God, is intent upon the worship of your Liṅga. O Lord, how did the God become so exclusively devoted to your complete [Liṅga]? [This was said] to the Grandfather (Brahmā), who had thus questioned him.
You, Nārāyaṇa, Śakra himself the lord of the gods,
and the sages, having always worshipped the Liṅga according to the prescribed rites,
have attained their own state of Śiva; therefore, they worship it.

Thus, [the claim] that "by Śiva’s word—whether by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, or anyone else—the maintenance of one's own station is achieved by abandoning the worship of the Liṅga," and so forth, is contradicted by various passages in the Śiva Purāṇa and elsewhere. Furthermore, since Nārāyaṇa is a distinct form of the Supreme Brahman and his sovereignty is to be accomplished through ritual action (*karma*), it is impossible for his worship of Śiva to be for the sake of maintaining his own station; therefore, [such statements] are merely *arthavāda* (explanatory or eulogistic praise). [And as it is said: "By means of incarnations, through the worship of You, [He attains] Your fame..."

"‘I shall accomplish [this]’—for it is established in the *Vārāha-purāṇa* that Viṣṇu granted a boon to Rudra. (... Furthermore, regarding the statement of others that the worship of the Supreme is accomplished otherwise by means of incarnations such as Kṛṣṇa for the sake of protecting those who have been granted [the boon], [Viṣṇu] then beheld himself, unmanifest and of infinite forms, at the left side of the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), praising him with many words beginning with ‘O Śaṅkha-...’"

Regarding the statement "the first [form] with hand placed upon the disc," since even Viṣṇu’s primordial form demonstrated its devotion to the worship of Śiva at the time of manifesting Śiva during Kṛṣṇa’s ascetic penance, it is logical that this refers to Viṣṇu’s worship of Śiva for the purpose of proclaiming his actual, superior excellence—even the words of Vārāha support this. Furthermore, it is improper to claim otherwise, as there is the possibility of alternative explanations (anyathāsiddhi), such as the mention of the granting of the Pāśupata boon by Varadarāja, which follows the logic to be explained later. Therefore, [the opponent's view] is intended merely to delude those of a tamasic nature.

Because the mere empty prattle that "it is the worship of Śiva" is contrary to all means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and thus unworthy of refutation, [the Lord said] to Mārkaṇḍeya, who had asked the question: "Having observed Kṛṣṇa's perpetual worship of the Śiva-liṅga, tell me, which deity is being propitiated by you through these auspicious rites? He who is to be worshipped by those with self-restraint and meditated upon by yogis—[is it he?
[The Lord replied: "Everything spoken by you is indeed the truth; there is no doubt."

Nevertheless, by the words "I worship the eternal Lord Īśāna," and so forth, up to "Thus they do not see that [Lord], being deluded by my *māyā*," and concluding with "Therefore, making known my own lineage, I worship Him"—these words of Kṛṣṇa as recited in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*—are intended to demonstrate Śiva’s status as the supreme over the universe, on the grounds that his own worship of Śiva is the very foundation of his own [divine] nature. As it is said in the *Mokṣadharma*: "If I were not to worship that Lord Śiva, the granter of boons..."
"No one should worship themselves"—this is the conviction of my mind;
for the world has made man its authority and follows his lead.
"O delighter of the Pāṇḍavas, whatever boon there may be for me," having thus reflected in my mind, I formerly [approached] the Lord of the Universe.

This is because it is established through the words, "I have worshipped myself by means of my own self for the sake of a son," that the purpose of this [statement] is to demonstrate Śiva’s status as the object of worship for all, by means of such discernment; and furthermore, because in the Droṇaparvan, regarding Aśvatthāman, it is said: "The birth, deeds, austerity, yoga, and resolve of both you and me are abundant; by these two [means], the Lord has been worshipped by you in the linga, and in an image (arcā) in age after age. Thus, it is from the worship of the linga alone [that the result follows].

While the living beings were being afflicted by various conditions individually, Yudhiṣṭhira asked the Grandfather (Bhīṣma), who was expounding the excellence of Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna through the words of Bādarāyaṇa:

"Tell me that by which one may cross over difficulties, both in this world and the next. To him who had thus asked for the means of crossing over hardships, [the Grandfather replied: "Those who here, with devotion, take refuge in Nārāyaṇa Hari—whoever they may be—cross over all difficulties; of this I have no doubt. (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the specific duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*), but the translation reflects the available portion.)

Following the demonstration that [the worship of] Brahmā, Śakra, and the sacrificial rites are means for crossing over difficult obstacles— beginning with the passage "contemplation by the mind" (*manodhivicāraṇā*) and so forth— it is stated: "Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śambhu,
as well as Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds,
praise the Great Lord, the God of gods, with various hymns."
"Those who constantly worship Him transcend all misfortune.
Thus, by the words of Bhīṣma in the Śāntiparvan, it is shown that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Kaśyapa, and the hosts of gods worship Him;
and by Upamanyu’s words to Indra, it is shown that Śiva is the one to be propitiated by Viṣṇu and the others.
Furthermore, because his unsurpassed excellence is clearly manifested therein, it is understood from the *Mahābhārata* that Śiva is the root of all, and consequently the object of worship for all.

This is established by the fact that he is the one worshipped by Nārāyaṇa—who is distinguished by the supreme greatness described in many passages [of the epic] such as (*...*); thus his status as the root and his being the object of worship for all are discerned. Likewise: "This blessed Lord Īśa is the imperishable source of all principles; he is the ordainer of all principles, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa."
(... From his right side he created Brahmā, whose origin is [inexplicable] (...);
likewise, from his left side, he created the Lord Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting the world;
and when the end of the age had arrived, he then created the Lord Rudra.
Through such an extensive array of instructional statements, [it is taught that]: "Īśāna is the other agent; Puruṣa is the cause;
Śiva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śaśin, Sūrya, Cīkro, and the gods with their lineages—these are created at the beginning by Him, just as this world was once composed of darkness."

"Then the entire world was unborn, for there was Maheśvara alone"—by such statements from the Śāntiparvan, it is seen that Śiva’s status as the root of the entire phenomenal expansion (prapañca), including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, is established even by direct declaration (kaṇṭhataḥ). Therefore, since statements in the Gītā and other texts regarding Kṛṣṇa being the cause of all and so forth are impossible when applied to his manifest form (tan-mūrti), they must be understood as referring to his root-form (mūla-mūrti) through their implied meaning (ārthikatayā). This is because those statements require a final point of rest (paryavasāna-sāpekṣāṇām).

The conclusion—that everything ultimately culminates in the form of Śiva, who is the root of all things such as the "First" (Ādi) and whose existence is established even in partial references—will be easily reconciled as it is further elaborated upon hereafter.

Thus, the entire Bhārata rests without contradiction solely on the exaltation of Śiva. As for those passages that appear to express a drawing of the mind toward humility [toward others], they all concern specific manifestations of Viṣṇu and Viriñca (Brahmā), who are themselves subordinate to Him. For instance, wherever in the Bhārata or in any Purāṇa there may be an apparent superiority of Viṣṇu or Brahmā over Rudra...

In all such cases, the evil one (Pāpman) is understood as that very Rudra; he is made known as a specific manifestation of his power through the employment of qualifiers that distinguish him from the Supreme Śiva—such as being the cause of dissolution due to the limiting adjunct of the quality of tamas (*tamaḥ-guṇopādhika*), being born from the wrath of Hari, or being produced from the forehead of Viriñca.

This applies wherever such distinguishing qualifiers are not employed, as in the *Mahābhārata* passages: "Brahmā, the preceptor of the Asuras, Sthāṇu, Manu, and the Parameṣṭhin," and "Brahmā, Sthāṇu, Manu, Dakṣa," and so forth.

And in the enumeration of the names of Prajāpati, as well as in the account of Sunda and Upasunda, [it is said]: "There Viṣṇu, Mahādeva, and Agni together with Vāyu... ending with "...all these sages were worshipping the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).

Following that description of the state of being of all the deities, such as Viṣṇu and others, and of the sages who were worshipping the Grandfather, [it continues]: "Indra and the Lord Sthāṇu, having abandoned their fortitude, remained [there]. And thus: "The four-faced one and Sthāṇu, Mahādeva, are in your city."

Furthermore, just as in the account of the creation of the four faces of Rudra upon seeing Tilottamā, or in the narrative of his origin from Death (Mṛtyu), where it is stated that "Hara is the pillar of the world" (*jagat-sthāṇu*),

and even in passages such as "Indeed, by you [Brahmā], I was not appointed as the protector of creatures...," the term *Viṣṇu* is appropriately employed; therefore, by that very fact, [the application of the term] toward himself is specific...

"It is proclaimed that the Lord who wields the trident remained with his entire self [withdrawn] within, established in [his own] nature until the end; thus, from that time forward, this God did not procreate auspicious offspring. He remained as one whose vital seed was drawn up, fixed like a pillar (*sthāṇu*), until the submersion of the earth. And in the *Āditya Purāṇa*: "From that time forward, the Soul of the Universe did not procreate auspicious offspring; because he remained motionless like a pillar (*sthāṇu*), he is therefore remembered as *Sthāṇu*. [This occurred] after [the birth of] Brahmā, who was born from his body..."

Having introduced a partial incarnation of Śiva upon the earth, the *Mahābhārata*, in the *Bhīṣmaparvan*, establishes the supreme nature of the word *sthāṇu*. In that section, after stating the presence of the worshipful Śiva on Mount Maināka—saying, "There, the eternal Lord of Beings, having created all the worlds, was worshipped by thousands of beings according to his vow"—it further states, in a passage enumerating the worshippers: "Where Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Yama, and Sthāṇu as the fifth, worship the Supreme during the course of a thousand yugas."

In the subsequent verse, by including him among the worshippers of Śiva within the context of the duties of kings, [the author] further clarifies this: "The Lord, whose excellent weapon is the trident, having meditated for a long time, made one the sole sovereign of that particular class. He made the thousand-eyed god the lord of the deities, and he also made Yama, the son of Vivasvat, the master of the ancestors. Passing over the others, he appointed the great-souled Mahādeva, the eternal and large-eyed Īśāna, as the protector and lord even of the Rudras. This is also evident from his inclusion among the regulations of Śiva.

Furthermore, because it is clearly demonstrated that the form designated as Sthāṇu is a distinct incarnation-form separate from the primary form of Paramaśiva, the term Viśālākṣa in the *Rājadharmavacana* refers to Sthāṇu himself. In that very same work, after introducing the account of Brahmā’s penance, it says, "Then the Lord Stambha," and previously, "Bahurūpa, Viśālākṣa, Śiva, Sthāṇu, and Umāpati. Since these terms are used for him there, immediately thereafter it says, "That god is the self of all beings."
Mahādeva is eternal;
he is the imperishable abode of countless thousands of Rudras.
Having perceived the decline of the lifespan of the Yugas, the Blessed Lord Śiva [acted].
"He summarized the *Śāstrī* falling [upon him], which was of great significance and composed by Abrahmaṇa;
that which is called the *Vaiśālākṣa* is now being expounded to Indra.

Because of this mention of the name *Vaiśālākṣa* in the *Nītiśāstra* composed by him (Indra), where even the name of such a specific portion is not mentioned, there [the authorship] belongs either to the non-creator Viṣṇu or...

Since it is impossible for there to be any superiority over Paramaśiva, and because even opponents must necessarily admit that when they accept him as transcending the three forms (trimūrti), the descriptions of Rudra’s "touchstone" (nikaṣa) and manifestations refer specifically to the Saṃhāra-Rudra and his incarnations; furthermore, since a relative inferiority is observed in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas— this being understood from such statements in the Parāśara Purāṇa and others as "This [inferiority] of Rudra is merely due to the manifestation (vibhūti) of this Hara"— and not even from statements regarding the birth of Śiva, Viṣṇu, or Viriñca.
One should suspect an indication of inferiority.
From the crooked mouth of Candra-vat, at the end of the kalpa,
I shall become a son born of your wrath, bearing a terrible form and holding a trident in my hand.
He who is without beginning or end, endowed with divine power, consciousness, and so forth;
he under whose control are all knowledges, including the *tāraka* [mantra] and others without exception;

he who is possessed of the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest; and who is not artificial, but has arisen from the forehead of Brahmā as his son for the sake of creation—such is [the Lord], according to the words of the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the *Rājadharma*, and other scriptures.

Since it is stated that his incarnations occur by his own will for the sake of favoring the worlds, the sense is that, despite any apparent contradictions in every respect, the Mahābhārata ultimately rests upon the exaltation of Śiva alone.
