Salutations to Paramaśiva, the most excellent of all. ||37||

The composition of Vālmīki clearly confirms your supreme devotion to Brahmā, Acyuta, and Hara; for from that time forward, O Lord, when the King of the Raghus was desirous of performing a sacrifice, you were manifested through the expression of his inner state at the *Bhavamīdhya* [sacrifice]. Furthermore, in the *Yuddhakāṇḍa* of the *Rāmāyaṇa*, within the *Ādityahṛdaya*, it is shown that Śiva possesses the nature of Brahmā, Acyuta, and Hara: "Salutations to the Sun, the Lord of Brahmā, Acyuta, and Hara, who possesses the splendor of the sun, who is radiant, the devourer of all, and whose form is fierce. Thus, the lordship of Śiva over Brahmā, Acyuta, and Hara is demonstrated.

Because the *kārikā* "maṇḍalābhimāninyā" is incompatible with [Śiva] being a member of that lineage, and because of the force of the qualification "raudrāya vapuṣe," that [mantra] culminates in Śiva who resides within it;
furthermore, because it is understood from the entire hymn—beginning with "This is Brahmā and Viṣṇu, Śiva, Skanda, and Prajāpati"—that its purport is directed toward him.

Moreover, in the *Uttara-rāmāyaṇa*, at the time of deliberating on the specific sacrifice to be performed prior to the commencement of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), it is stated: "Having propitiated Viṣṇu by means of the horse-sacrifice, Indra (Śatakratu) crossed beyond the sin of Brahmin-slaughter."

When Lakṣmaṇa praised the Aśvamedha sacrifice, Rāmacandra—acknowledging its praiseworthiness and personally recounting the legend of Ilā to demonstrate how it pleases Śiva—spoke these words within that very narrative: "I see no other medicine than the Bull-bannered Lord; there is no sacrifice superior to the Aśvamedha, and it is dear to the Great-souled One. By indicating through this speech that Śiva alone is to be propitiated, he spoke thus in private.

Immediately after the consultation with the ministers, he summoned Vasiṣṭha and the others and announced his intention. Having heard this from Rāma, those twice-born sages paid homage to the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) and constantly honored the Aśvamedha sacrifice solely as being connected to Śiva. Thinking, "Though the Aśvamedha is praiseworthy, Rāmacandra seeks to propitiate Śiva through the renunciation [of the kingdom] via the horse-sacrifice," Rāma, being supremely righteous, protected the kingdom; and as stated specifically in the passage beginning with "He honored all the Brāhmaṇas and the Lord," he indeed worshipped all the Brāhmaṇas and the Supreme Lord.

"By means of sacrifice, [one worships] Śaṅkara, the destroyer of sacrifice, through the Aśvamedha"—by this statement from the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the lotus-eyed Rāma was then consecrated in his kingdom. O best of sages, while protecting the entire earth, he worshipped Śaṅkara, the Lord of the God of Gods, with the Aśvamedha sacrifice; thus, the fact that Śiva is to be propitiated is explicitly stated in the *Āditya Purāṇa*. Likewise, in the *Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa*, it is said: "Having performed his ablutions, that king shone together with Lakṣmaṇa like a second Śiva."

Having performed his consecration, the King of Mountains—by means of similes such as "like Rudra" and "like the Lord Viṣṇu"—the excellence of Śiva was made manifest even by the Primordial Poet. Furthermore, in the *Vāsiṣṭha-Rāmāyaṇa*, through passages such as "The lotus-eyed God, and not the three-eyed God," and so forth, the supremacy of this very [Lord] has been clearly revealed. How could one approach [Him] as an object of worship? One should worship the Consciousness.

Because of the conventional usage [of the terms] "Śiva" (.... "jyā" (.... "raṃ" Śiva (.... and "Paraśiva," and because of the well-known [status of] the Unmanī state (......... as being like the Imperishable (akṣara), and because [He] resides upon the Śiva-pīṭha (.........), and because of the demonstration that the entire world (.... up to the end of Unmanā (unmanānta) is situated within His feet (tapada) (.........), and because in the Bālakāṇḍa there is an equality (sama) of Śiva and Nārāyaṇa (.........), [it is said]: "My [state] is free from enmity (nirerviṣṇa) (..........); O Nārāyaṇa (.......... [and so forth].

As for the objection regarding the [apparent] inferiority [of Viṣṇu]: in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, it is established that Śiva bestowed upon him a prowess superior to his own; therefore, because this is not otherwise accounted for by Śiva’s pride in protecting the boon he himself had granted, it does not serve to demonstrate the superiority of Viṣṇu—thus there is no contradiction. ||38||

O Blessed One, the renowned saviors of us [beings], such as Śiva and others, as well as Patañjali and other authors of philosophical systems of celebrated intellect, though they open various paths toward other objects, nevertheless acknowledge You as superior to the entire universe. Thus, at the conclusion of the *Dharmaśāstra*, Manu describes [the Lord] as the ruler of all,
subtler even than the subtlest, golden-hued, attainable in deep sleep, the Supreme Person who destroys ignorance, and endowed with attributes such as being the inner controller of all.

Having taught the Supreme Self (Paramātman), [the author] states: "Some call this very one Agni, others the Maruts, some Prajāpati, some Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman. Having thus demonstrated the manifold Vedic usage therein, he clarified his own position—that Śiva alone is the Supreme Self—by showing that He pervades all beings with His five forms and perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay, thereby demonstrating His universal pervasiveness through the fivefold liberation (muktipañcaka).

For indeed, the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*, having introduced Śiva as residing within the orb of the sun, teaches his pervasion of all that exists through his five forms by means of such passages as, "That person is fivefold, by whom all this is woven together. Although it is heard there in a general sense as "fivefold," nevertheless, since the five forms beginning with Sadyojāta were previously established there, it is understood that those very same forms are presented here for the purpose of teaching pervasion. For this very reason, the five forms are mentioned in the *Liṅga Purāṇa* and other texts.

The five supreme [forms] known as the Five Brahmans belong to Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is the refuge of all worlds. Thus, having established his fivefold form beginning with Sadyojāta, which consists of the Five Brahmans, O Omniscient One, that [form] is to be understood as his own lower manifestation. Generally, in the sequence beginning with Īśāna, their [correspondences are] with the individual soul (kṣetrajña), primordial matter (pradhāna), the Great Principle (mahat), ego (ahaṅkāra), mind (manas), ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, and the five elements, subtle elements, and their respective products.

By demonstrating that the five elements are essentially non-existent (*yābhūta*), and specifically by establishing that [Nārāyaṇa] pervades all [beings], it is shown—starting from the introduction to the *Dharmaśāstra* of others—that he is the source from which Saṃbhū and Bhūmi arose; and by concluding with the praise of Nārāyaṇa as "the one who is the support of all," etc., the fact that Nārāyaṇa is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all is established through the phrase "the ruler of all."

Regarding the passage beginning with "enameka" (He is one), [it is shown that] His state as the inner ruler of all (*sarvāntaryāmitva*) is established without mutual contradiction within each respective portion of the Vedas by means of various designations such as "atyādi" and other words; furthermore, through the verse "eṣa sarvāṇi" and others presided over by Himself, His pervasion of all things (*sarvavyāpitva*) is demonstrated. Thus, there is no room for doubt concerning the initial statement (*upakrama*), since it serves to establish the excellence of Śiva alone by defining the limits of His sovereignty.

In determining the meaning of the opening passage of the *Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad*, it will be most skillfully uprooted [by us]. That which possesses the state of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all, and whose designation as "Self" is attained through terms such as "rays" and so forth applied to individual parts of the body, and which possesses pervasion over all beings through the elements such as ether (*viyat*) that constitute its own form—that is determined to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is a point of agreement even for our opponents. Such being the case, it is possible for them to maintain that Śiva alone is thus determined.

Because it was established below that he alone is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of all, and because in portions of the Veda such as "Agni is ancient, [born] from the mind of Manu; Rudra indeed is this Agni; these two are his bodies—the one terrible, the other auspicious"—the usage of the word "Agni" for him is observed. What fruit is there in worshipping these other immortals in the sacrifice? If Rudra is not worshipped by you in this sacrifice, what is the point? Those Brahmins who know the Vedas know two bodies of that god: one is terrible and the other is auspicious; and they are indeed those two.

Furthermore, by means of supplementary texts such as the *Vāyusaṃhitā* and the *Mahābhārata*, beginning with the words "A hundredfold," and by the determination that the Śruti passages—such as "We [invoke] Rudra, the king of the sacrifice, the Hotṛ priest, the true sacrificer of the two luminaries; for Agni is indeed Rudra"—have Śiva as their ultimate purport, it is established. Moreover, the *Kūrma Purāṇa* states: "The Veda has placed you, O Rudra, as the fire;
I seek refuge in you alone, Rudra, the Lord. Likewise: "Agni is Mahādeva, and likewise the god Maheśvara; he is the single-syllabled Tryambaka, the universal-formed Śiva."

Likewise, because in the *Ānuśāsanika* [Parvan] it is established that Śiva is designated by the word "Agni" in the portions of the Vedas; because in the mantra "Abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ," and in the *Atharvaśiras*, following the etymological definition of the name "Īśāna," Śiva is designated by the word "Indra"; and because he is designated by the word "Prajāpati" in the passage "Prajāpati moves within the womb," and through the intended meaning of the statement "Brahmā brought forth Brahmā; may Śiva be my Brahmā"; and because of [the passage] beginning with "From Rudra... [it is so].

Thus, because the term "Rudra" is applied to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—as seen in the *Mārutasūkta* ("Among the Maruts, who is the most virtuous?"), in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka-śruti* ("Those who are Rudras are indeed the vital breaths; those who are the vital breaths are of that [Rudra's] nature"), and in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*—the intention is that they are presided over by Rudra. Consequently, Rudra is determined to be their name by virtue of his being their inner controller (*antaryāmin*).

And because the pervasion of all beings by means of the forms beginning with Vidhi is [taught] in that very same [text], the *Aṣṭamūrti*, and because of the determination (*nirdhāraṇa*) therein of the one who is ignorant (*ajña*)... likewise, the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*) also, in the chapter on *dhāraṇā* in the *Yogayājñavalkya*, has prescribed the meditation (*dhyāna*) upon the deities beginning with Brahmā and ending with Sadāśiva in various locations. This is what is meant here: "In this world, Gāyatrī is the supreme among the knowers of Brahman."

Having withdrawn their respective forms as effects—beginning with Brahmā—into themselves, [the author] describes the Supreme Lord as the one to whom they are joined; thus, by demonstrating that each preceding deity among Brahmā and the others is an effect of the subsequent one, he introduces Sadāśiva. He then reveals his supreme state as the primordial cause of that [Sadāśiva], who is of the nature of Śakti.
Āśvalāyana also, at the commencement of his Dharmaśāstra, having introduced the root cause and its presiding deity, Śiva, with the words "In the beginning, all this was this [alone]," and so forth...

Having established that *tamas*, which is of the nature of the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*), undergoes agitation (*saṃkṣobha*)—a state oriented toward activity obtained through proximity to Śiva—and having begun with the statement that "that agitated power was embraced by Śiva," the seventh chapter proceeds to describe the division of the qualities (*guṇa-vibhāga*), the creation of Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, the four-faced Brahmā, and so forth: "Desiring to create, Śiva himself sat alone at the beginning. Having seen the subtle form of Māyā consisting of the qualities (*guṇa-mayī*), he cast it aside. Then, having created Viṣṇu, who is of the nature of that [Māyā], as the protector of the gods... Thus [ends the description] of Viṣṇu.

Having spoken thus once, he then described the manner in which the *yajñopavīta* originates; at the time of distributing the presiding deities for its specific parts, it is said: "The two worlds, the three Vedas, the three gods, the three fires, Śiva the creator, and the three castes—these rest upon the three threads. Those who take refuge in its knots are joined with the Self alone; neither the knot nor the non-knot is conjoined with anything else here, for by the command of Śiva, Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, [presides over] the three gods."

By describing the taking of refuge in the portion of the sacred thread (*upavīta*) through the command of Śiva, and by stating in the *Kalpasūtra*—after introducing Śiva—"All these indeed are His names; all armies and all elevations [belong to Him]," Bodhāyana demonstrated His status as the Lord of All (*sarveśvaratva*). Furthermore, in the ritual for the worship of Śiva, because he places Brahmā and Viṣṇu within His retinue (*āvaraṇa*), and because in the rituals for the worship of other deities Śiva is not mentioned among the attendant deities (*āvaraṇadevatā*), he indicated His supreme excellence. Kātyāyana also...
"Rudra indeed is all this"—thus [the scripture] illuminates his supreme nature (*parabhāva*) by virtue of his being the self of all. Among the authors of the scriptures, Patañjali states:

"Īśvara is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, its fruition (*vipāka*), or latent dispositions (*āśaya*). His indicator is the scripture; therein the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed. He is the teacher even of the ancients, because he is not limited by time. His designator is the *praṇava*; the repetition of that and meditation upon its meaning [constitute yoga] directed toward the Supreme. And the *praṇavas* do not constitute bondage."

For him, there is neither the fruit of dharma nor karma, nor is there the state of being material, nor indeed is there bondage consisting of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). There is no disease, nor hatred for Śambhu, whose splendor is tranquility;

nor is there any dogmatic attachment for him toward either the auspicious or the inauspicious. The Blessed One, the Infinite, has been described as a specific kind of conjunction. In the world, [he stands] through excellence, by means of knowledge...
by the state of being... established in... skillful... born of those who are... (Note: The ellipses indicate portions of the source text that were illegible or missing in the provided image.)

[This is] the extensive exposition of Brahman... that which is [expressed by] the *praṇava* at the beginning... for those who abide in the [state of] dissolution and are joined with [the practice of] cutting [off worldly bonds], he is the teacher of Varuṇa.

He is the Lord of all, devoid of limitation by time; he is Śiva, the supreme mind, whose designator is the *praṇava*. It is remembered that the *praṇava* is the highest [signifier] of words such as "Śiva" and "Rudra. Whatever perfection is attained through the meditation upon and the recitation (*japa*) of Śambhu—who is signified by the *praṇava*—that indeed becomes the supreme [perfection]; of this there is no doubt.

The aphorisms (*sūtra*) were composed in accordance with the meaning of such statements found in the seventh chapter of the *Vāyusaṃhitā-uttarabhāga*, and they establish that Śiva alone possesses the supreme state (*parabhāva*). For this very reason—and precisely because of their agreement with that [text]—the author of the *Kaumudī* determined that the aphorisms have that [text] as their source. In that regard, concerning the aphorism "The seed of the omniscient one is unsurpassed," he sought the specific understanding of its designations and so forth from the *Āmata*; and at the occasion of explaining the *vairyāsika* state, he stated: "The designation is Śiva, Rudra, Maheśvara, and so forth; by the word 'and so forth' [is meant] the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the ten..."

By stating "those who are included," he clarified that the subject matter of the Sūtras is Śiva. Those who employ terms such as Bhava, Śiva, Sthāṇu, and Īśvara to refer to the Supreme Self (Paramātman) as they conceive it, have revealed the supreme state of the Parameśvara himself as their own intended object. Likewise, those who follow the doctrine of the sage Bharata [state]:
"At the end of a Kalpa, Maheśvara, having burnt the worlds, created Viṣṇu and Brahmā by his mind alone."

The phrase "by his own will," and so forth, is used in the chapters on the origin of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and other such contexts; this is cited as an example. However, in many *āgamas*, the supreme excellence of Śiva is established quite clearly. ||39||

The author of the *Nibandhana* on the Sūtras, while elucidating the meaning of the Upaniṣads, has also made clear the intent of those who reflect upon the fact that you are devoted to Śiva: "O Lord, he [the person] measured by the thumb, having disregarded other systems, perceived you through the *Īśāna-śruti* as the 'Svara' (the Sound/Self), according to the teaching of Varada. This has already been stated above: when the author of the *Brahma-sūtras* establishes the meaning that [the Self] is known from the Word alone (*śabdād eva pramitaḥ*), the person within the thumb is the Supreme Self by virtue of the denotative *śruti* "Īśāna Śambhu," which is independent of any other reasoning.

This matter has been settled: it is agreed even by others that the Supreme Nature (*parabhāva*) of Umāpati—He who is designated by the term "Lord" (*īśāna*)—is what resides in the heart of the author of the Sūtras. This is because [the term] cannot be applied to other deities through either etymological derivation (*yoga*) or figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as there is no such instruction for them;

and because, in their case, the application of the word would not constitute a direct scriptural designation (*śruti*). Thus, through the Purāṇas, the Mahābhārata, the Rāmāyaṇa, and the various scriptures, the Supreme Nature of Śiva has been established.

Now, considering that the word *brahman*— which is accepted as being beyond all speech— is designated as *oṃ tatsat*, and that in the *Gītā* it is treated as a name [of the Lord] in the passage "in Brahman" (*brahmaṇi*), and furthermore, since its status as a name of Śiva is revealed in the scriptures through usage, etymological definitions, and traditional instructions— as in "that which is *bra* (the supreme), *tat* (that), and *sat* (existent)— O Ocean of Bliss for the Daughter of the Mountain!"— its state as the Supreme is established.

Because these [qualities] constitute his essential nature, and because he brings about the cessation of suffering through the authority of the scriptures, it is clearly understood, O Lord, that you alone are the supreme deity here.

Regarding the etymology of the term *brahman*, in the *Atharvaśiras* Upaniṣad, during the discussion on the etymological definitions (*nirvacana*) of the names of Śiva, it is asked: "Why is he called the Supreme Brahman? [The answer is: "Because he is the head of all, and because everything is Brahman. Furthermore, in the *Laiṅgya Purāṇa* and the *Āditya Purāṇa*, as well as in the commentary on the *Atharvaśiras*, it is stated: "Because he is vast (*bṛhan*), therefore he is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman (*paramabrahman*). Thus it is employed.

In the Ādiparvan, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa describes Yudhiṣṭhira as the great tree consisting of dharma, Arjuna as its trunk, Bhīmasena as its branches, the two sons of Mādrī as its abundant flowers and fruit, and Kṛṣṇa along with Brahman and the Brāhmaṇas as its root. For it is well known that the victory of the Pāṇḍavas resulted from the assistance of Kṛṣṇa and the grace of the Brāhmaṇas; thus, among those who were the means of their victory—namely Kṛṣṇa and the Brāhmaṇas—he likewise designates them as the root.

(…) Likewise, it is appropriate to understand the meaning of the word *brahman* as being of that very nature, for the sake of its uniformity [with other terms]. Thus, their victory was achieved solely through the protection of Mahādeva’s splendor; this is clear from the *Sauptika-parvan*. Furthermore, in the *Śānti-parvan*, after introducing Śiva, there is Kṛṣṇa’s speech to Arjuna regarding those previously slain by him: "O enemy, you have killed them for the sake of fulfilling your vow. And in the *Aśvamedhika-parvan*, after introducing Śiva, [Kṛṣṇa says]: "(…) We are all his devotees, and he is ours."

"He is pleased; by his grace we have obtained the kingdom, O joy of the Kauravas. "O Great King, who could even in thought overcome that army, which was repelled by the great archers and strikers led by Droṇa and Karṇa, except for the great archer Maheśvara of many forms, the god? And it is by his very grace that our enemies have been slain. This is from Bhīmasena’s speech to Yudhiṣṭhira. In the *Pādmapurāṇa*, it is said: "There, Kṛṣṇa, a portion of Viṣṇu, stands as this master of illusion; he will show [us] the means."

Furthermore, from the words of Śrī Mahādeva addressed to Pārtha—"And that position is to be disregarded by me"—it is determined, both by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) and by propriety, that he alone is the referent of the word "Brahman.

Since it is well known that "where there is Dharma, there is victory," and thus Dharma is the root of victory, the Veda—the referent of the word "Brahman" which serves as a means to victory in some way through the mediation of that [Dharma]—exists; yet, because one observes here the construction of a metaphorical whole (*sāvayava-rūpaka*) consisting of conscious parts, [the verse states]: "Duryodhana is a great tree made of wrath..."

The neck and shoulders are its trunk, Duḥśāsana its branches, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra the king its root—by these alone is its completion shown. Furthermore, since the word *brahman* necessarily refers to a conscious being and cannot refer to sound, [it is established] by the Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "Om, that, sat... which constitutes its feet.

"May Śiva [be] Sadāśiva, Oṃ! We know Tatpuruṣa; Puruṣa is indeed Rudra, the Great Being (*sanmahaḥ*). These and other such specific names for the Supreme are employed in the *Skānda-purāṇa* and elsewhere through the word "Tatpuruṣa" and so forth.

Because these are the names of Śiva, the scriptural injunctions regarding them are to be observed. Thus, by means of the usage of well-known supreme names applied to Śiva, His state as the Supreme (*parabhāva*) is established. Now...

He establishes that those [names] renowned as names of Śiva possess unsurpassed sovereignty, [perception], [will], and power up to the limit of strength. "Whom other than you could we call the Supreme Lord of All, Paramaśiva? Indeed, you are the one to be denoted by the scriptural words beginning with Īśāna; yet, because these scriptures are merely designations (*samākhyā*), the minds of even the wise do not fall into the dark cave of delusion, like the vision of the Purva-mīmāṃsā. For the terms *Īśāna*, *Īśa*, and *Īśvara* may, through mere etymological connection (*yogamātra*), apply to others as well.

Because these [terms] are applied through both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) as being unique to Śiva, and because their etymological meaning is clearly manifest—since the Blessed One is the primordial Lord of great lords, the bestower of joy, and the source of delight—therefore the virtuous and learned, who understand the meaning of all scriptures, call You "Īśvara," the Lord. This is seen from such statements in the *Harivaṃśa* and other texts. Thus, for these terms when applied to Śiva, the etymological meaning (*yoga*) emerges within its own proper object just like conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Furthermore, the words *pati* and so forth, when applied elsewhere, are not different from those used here.

While in various other instances, the word conveys the sovereignty of a specific deity through the constraints of the sentence (*vākya-maryādā*) by depending on its co-occurrence with words denoting that particular deity, here, when applied to Śiva, it brings Śiva to mind by itself through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) without depending on co-occurrence with other words. Thus, by the force of the Vedic injunction (*śruti-vidhi*), it establishes the meaning of the component parts—sovereignty—within Him. Therefore, all means of proof for application (*viniyojaka-pramāṇa*) conclude, by the power of numerous scriptural texts (*śruti*) and conventional usage, that the ultimate rest of supreme sovereignty lies in Śiva alone.

The meaning is that [the authority of the name] is established. As for what has been stated by others—who are satisfied merely by hearing a fragment of the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka*—namely, that "the name (*samākhyā*) is an etymological designation" and that "words such as *Īśāna* are indeed names and are weaker than [the other means of proof] based on statements such as 'the Lord of the universe' (*patiṃ viśvasya*)"; with the intention of refuting that, he says: "The name. This is the underlying thought: the relative strength or weakness of the means of proof, beginning with direct statement (*śruti*) and ending with name (*samākhyā*), is determined by the specific degree of proximity or remoteness regarding the determination of their respective objects of cognition. When an object has been determined by a means of proof more rapidly [than another], [the latter cannot override it].

Because [the application of words] proceeds through different levels of delimitation; and because even by the Mīmāṃsakas, the relative strength and weakness between direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*)—and likewise between direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*)—is established precisely on the basis of their being more or less swift in reaching their object. Thus, when words such as *Īśāna* and others are employed with reference to Śiva, they are established as remote (*viprakṛṣṭatā*) in the sense that they depend upon the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with other words to convey His sovereignty. How, then, can their relative strength and weakness be determined by mere technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) alone?

A reversal would occur even for those who speak according to the *Smṛti* regarding the etymological (*yaugika*) power of words. For [Patañjali] himself said: "In a word joined with a suffix, the agent is expressed; however, when joined with a primary suffix (*kṛt*), the agent is not always expressed. This is seen from such statements of his. In a case where there is an etymological word, there is the presentation of only the two meanings—the qualifier and the qualified—through its two constituent parts, as in the sentences "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) and "He buys [the cow] with the red one" (*aruṇayā krīṇāti*), where the accusative and instrumental case-endings [respectively] express the object and the instrument.

If the nature of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) were indeed like that [of the previous cases], then the sixth means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which consists of conventional designation (*samākhyā*), would not be reckoned as a valid authority regarding the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*). However, this is not so; for even in the case of etymological words where the meaning is expressed by the root or other components, it applies to their general category.

Thus, although words such as *āgneya* are etymological, because the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) exists there to express the divinity (*devatātva*) of Agni and others, their status as deities is accepted through those very words due to the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding them. And here, in words such as *īśvara*, the sovereignty of Śiva—

According to their own doctrinal system, even for the component of *prakṛti*, there is only the status of being directly denoted (*vācya*); thus, for them, there is no room for the status of being a "name" (*samākhyā*) even in that portion. For us, however, based on the explanation in the *Vivaraṇa* according to the method stated above—derived from the etymology "that which is both equal (*samā*) and a designation (*ākhyā*)"—a "name" (*samākhyā*) is a common designation (*saṃjñāsāmānya*) that serves as the cause for a relationship when it is recognized elsewhere in relation to what has been understood. For example, the commonality of the name *Ādhvaryava* serves as the cause for the mutual relationship between mantras such as "May Agni lead the sacrifice... and the *Atimuktihoma* offerings; thus, there is no [contradiction] here.

How could there be any room for objection regarding this designation? Indeed, although words such as *Īśāna* and others denote the sovereignty residing in Śiva and his purity, we do not observe their usage in scriptures—such as "the wise one offers the *sthālīpāka* to Īśāna" or "Īśvara is the third foot"—with the intent of propounding the sovereignty residing in Śiva. This is because in those instances, they are employed solely for the purpose of providing a specific attribute to the deity within another word that is the object of an injunction (*vidheya*). [Therefore, the Lord] is the one who has become the Lord (*pati*) of all that exists, based on the intended meaning of the sentence which is possible [in this context].

If it is argued that superiority is not established from statements such as "He existed," because the purport belongs only to a sentence that has a specific purpose (*tātparya-vākya*), we say no; for these [statements] are never seen to be used in isolation without being incorporated into a sentence with another subject matter, and such independent usage is impossible. Even though there can be no purport to independently establish the sovereignty residing in Śiva, this is just like the case of [the sentences] "One offers the cake on eight potsherds to Agni" (*āgneyam aṣṭākapālaṃ nirvapati*) and so forth, where Agni and the others are established as deities [only within the context of a larger ritual injunction].
"A person the size of a thumb resides in the middle of the self; he is the Lord of what has been and what is to be. O Arjuna, the Ruler of all beings dwells in the region of the heart.

Since these and other such passages from the Śruti and Smṛti refer to the well-known region of the heart and are intent upon enjoining the abiding of the Supreme Śiva—qualified by all His attributes—within that very place, there is no restriction on the primary purport of the injunction regarding His sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), which is the meaning of the verbal root *īś* (to rule), as He is the one who enters therein. For even when a primary purport is possible, [the text] does not intend an injunction [of sovereignty] merely as a qualification of another thing to be enjoined.

It is by virtue of *tātparya* (intentional meaning), and not through independence (*svātantrya*). For if it were otherwise, even in the case of two established injunctions (*utpanna-śiṣṭa*)—such as those from independent injunctions regarding the *kḷpti* [of mantras] and so forth, or the expiation known as *balya-śaṅkā*—there would result a reversal of the relative strength (*balābala*) between them. Therefore, since the scriptures such as *Īśāna* and others, when free from restrictive factors like qualifying words (*upapada*), establish Śiva’s unsurpassed sovereignty (*atiśaya-aiśvarya*) with the firmness of "adamantine glue" (*vajralepa*), there is no consequence that the scriptural mention of the word *Indra* would likewise establish the supreme sovereignty of the thousand-eyed one.

Because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of establishing that [the Lord] through a single scriptural statement (*śruti*) which contradicts numerous authoritative scriptures (*śrutipramāṇa*) and other proofs that establish [His] transcendence, lack of subjection to karma, antagonism [to evil], and so forth; and because here, such contradictory means of knowledge (*virodhipramāṇa*) likewise find no scope. [In the] mantra [and] in the *Taittirīyopaniṣad*, the term is applied to Śiva, as is seen in Purāṇic statements such as "He is the Lord of the universe" and "He is superior to the universe," where [His] uniqueness is established.

Having censured [the opponent] and having [established] the yoga, [one observes] his extremely clear conceptualization which, failing to grasp all aspects, does not even serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the subject at hand regarding the term "beyond the universe" (*viśvādhika*). Just as the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) was formerly applied [to that], so too is the term "beyond the universe.

O deluded one, when that [term] is clearly delimited—having been understood by the entire world—it causes extreme pain to the ears of those who are well-disposed. Thus, through an investigation into the power of the constituent parts of words such as "Īśāna," the supreme nature [of the Lord is established].
It has been established. Now, by means of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), he determines that the form of Supreme Śiva is [the one to be worshipped], as it is the locus [of all].

If sovereignty were not free from limitation anywhere, O Lord, may Your exhaustion cease, O Blessed One! For in every aeon (*kalpa*), the various Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are constrained by You; ever-new [beings] bear Your command. And in this regard, in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*:

Thus, millions upon thousands of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) of Īśāna are to be known, existing in the intermediate and upper regions because the *pradhāna* is all-pervading. Therein, the four-faced [Brahmās], the Brāhmaṇas, the Haris, and the Haras were created by the *pradhāna* for the sake of the presence of Śambhu above the seven worlds. According to the *Āditya Purāṇa*, there are thousands of millions of such cosmic eggs, extending horizontally and upwards.

"The Brahmās, Haris, and Rudras are stationed here and there by the command of Mahādeva, the trident-bearing God of gods. Thus, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the dissolution of the triad of Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Īśāna occurs into Prakṛti. Furthermore, in the *Parāśara Smṛti*, it is stated: "The one Lord, Īśa, is Time (Kāla), whose memory does not fail. And: "In every Kalpa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara dissolve along with their Lord. This refers to the eternal nature of dissolution and origination, as well as the proximity of dissolution to origination, in accordance with the Śruti, Smṛti, and traditional practice.

The meaning is that they become perceived. In the *Vāsiṣṭha-rāmāyaṇa*, it is said: "O Sage, we are not capable of describing the destructions of the worlds (*saṃsāra-balayah*), the millions of Rudras who have been swallowed, or the Viṣṇus who have been devoured. And in the *Skanda-purāṇa*: "The Pitāmahas (Brahmās) called Time are innumerable, the Haris (Viṣṇus) are also innumerable, yet Maheśvara is only one. The Brahmās, O best of the learned, are innumerable; the Viṣṇus and Rudras are innumerable, as are the Vāsudevas and so forth. Thus, there are innumerable dissolutions.

In the northwest corner, although Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are equal in their dissolution (*laya*), it is stated that each subsequent one remains for a longer duration; as for your statement that "Brahmā lasts for one day of Viṣṇu, and likewise Viṣṇu for one day of Rudra," and the passage beginning "He who eternally protects this world of moving and unmoving beings... this Puruṣa, Vāsudeva, the eternal," that refers solely to the eternity of Viṣṇu’s essential nature (*svarūpa*), since his body (*vigraha*)—being composed of *māyā*—cannot be eternal. Furthermore, the demonstration of [his] eternity [refers to the Lord].

Since the word *bhakta* (devotee) refers here to the mere reality (*vastumātra*)—due to its identity with the Self (*ātmaikya*) and because the category of insentient things (*jaḍavarga*) is illusory—it is appropriate [to use this term]. For this reason, up until the passage "having known even these as the Lord, one is called wise," there is an exposition of attributes (*guṇa*). Immediately following that is the teaching: "In this world, all beings, both moving and stationary, exist eternally for my benefit; except for me alone, the unmanifest space. Thus, in the doctrine of Saguna Brahman, the eightfold form is established on the basis of accepting the eternal manifestations and other qualities of Maheśvara and others.

However, because this would contradict the natural sense of the mantra-vedānta passage beginning with "He is indeed unborn," this statement of the Sūtra must be taken in a figurative sense. There is no contradiction whatsoever; for while the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are limited by space and time, and thus possess only a manifestation of excellence in sovereignty, [the Supreme] exists as the fourth state (*turya*) beyond them.

Even in His own essential nature, because He is subordinate to Śiva in the form of His power (*śakti*), the manifestation of unsurpassed sovereignty belongs exclusively to the form of Śiva by process of elimination. Therefore, this has been taught with certainty.

Even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others are the causes of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the worlds; they have received the power of restraint and favor from Śiva’s energies. But Śiva, in turn, is not the object of restraint or favor for anyone. Therefore, it is well-established that [Śiva] is like one whose sovereignty is unsurpassed. ||44||

Furthermore, having observed sentences with contradictory meanings, for those whose minds are deluded, a definitive conclusion is properly reached through the consensus of many; otherwise, the Vedic path would perish, as the cause of Brahman [would be lost], since even a mere trace of the tradition would show that Brahman is not the cause. Therefore, because of the abundance of authorities and the preeminence of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, this meaning is demonstrated so that it may be determined through reasoning: "Enough with other measures! O Lord of all courses, your supremacy can be clearly declared by this much alone. Where else?
When the collection of Āgamas spreads the excellence of Śiva’s vision, they manifested for that purpose the Purāṇas and other texts;

and the Atharvaśikhā and other Upaniṣads, as well as the Mantras and Arthavādas in the Karmakāṇḍa, are likewise devoted to the supreme excellence of Śiva—this is clear from the explanations of the preceding and following verses in this very work. And the learned have said: "The Mantras are the boons of the gods, yet your true nature alone [is the goal] for those within the divine assembly."

Their power has been demonstrated. It is not possible to comprehend the extent of you, who have acquired renown through the description of your own essential nature and qualities; likewise, it is clear that the *Śiva Purāṇa* and other texts devoted to the excellence of Śiva are more numerous in terms of the number of verses than the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* and others. This abundance of the number of *Purāṇas* is also shown in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "In the eighteen *Purāṇas*, the Lord Viṣṇu [is present] in four, Brahmā in two, and likewise Ravi (the Sun); in the remaining ones, the Lord Śiva [is present]. Thus it is said.

The abundance of Upapurāṇas, Śiva-Āgamas, and so forth is already evident to the learned. By the phrase "explaining their meaning," [the author] indicates—based on Vyāsa’s statement that he "himself knew the meaning of the Vedas"—that these texts are not open to doubt under the name of the Śruti which is devoted to the exaltation of Śiva; rather, they possess the character of being established as otherwise unaccountable. Furthermore, this implies the superior authority of the Purāṇas and similar works over the Smṛtis of Sāṅkhya and others, and the superior authority of Manu’s and other Smṛtis over those [latter], characterized by their conformity with direct Vedic revelation. ||45||

Thus, having first proclaimed the strength of the various [scriptures] that focus on the excellence of Śiva—such as the Śrutis and Purāṇas—the determination of Śiva’s supreme status has been established. Now, the weakness of those [other scriptures] asserted by opponents and the strength of the Śrutis and Purāṇas focused on the excellence of the Supreme Refuge will be demonstrated. Regarding this, some, based on certain Śrutis, imagine a reversal of strength and weakness; yet, although other deities besides Nārāyaṇa are also mentioned by various Śrutis...

The supreme nature of Nārāyaṇa has been established by Vedic statements whose meanings are directed toward Him; therefore, it is proper to maintain the meaning in accordance with those very [statements]. Thus, through their own words—such as *agnim īḷe*, *pra... hitāya*, *devam ṛtvijam*, *staumy agnim*, *nātha tejo havīmi*, *abhi tvā śrīranonuma*, and so forth—it is shown that He is the Worthy One (*arhan*) who bears the arrows, and that "He who is indeed Rudra... and so on, ending with "the gods with uplifted arms [praise] Thy greatness," [confirm] that He is the Worthy One who bears [all things].

One might argue that [the Rudrādhyāya] is intended as praise because of the internal statements such as "He who wields the bow and arrows," "I praise him indeed, not for myself," and so forth; and because it is determined to be praise through its connection with the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of salutation, as well as the indicative marks of praying for the attainment of the desired and the cessation of the undesired. Furthermore, even those passages that convey Śiva’s status as the cause of the universe—such as "But the Cause is to be meditated upon"—do not establish Him as the cause of creation and dissolution, and thus they refer to meditation (*upāsanā*).

Because it is determined to have another purpose by virtue of its specific character, and because there is no ascertainment of any other purpose for the *Puruṣasūkta* and similar texts which are intent upon propounding the supreme nature of Nārāyaṇa; for the *Puruṣasūkta* indeed propounds that Nārāyaṇa, the Puruṣa, is the cause of all and the Lord of all, and it is not understood—either through an indicative mark (*liṅga*) or through syntactical connection (*vākya*)—to be intent on the praise of any other deity. Furthermore, since it lacks words such as "ha vai" which indicate the status of a restatement (*anuvāda*), its nature as a mere restatement is not established; on the contrary, it is said: "This very thing has been declared by the Ṛg-verse: 'As great as this... (RV 10.90.3).

The *Mahiman* [section] of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, by virtue of being a witness to the essential meaning of that Upaniṣad through the recitation of its hymns and mantras, and because it is determined to be a treatise establishing the majesty of Nārāyaṇa; likewise, the mantra "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim" (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.15)—which sets forth the statement of all the Vedas as a thesis to be proven—reaches its ultimate conclusion by demonstrating, "That is the supreme state of Viṣṇu" (Kaṭha Up. 1.3.9), [and thus one] attains the Supreme through the knowledge of Brahman.

The statement of the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*—“Brahman is bliss, from which words turn back along with the mind, not having attained it”—shows that Brahman, who is to be known by those seeking liberation as "truth, knowledge, infinite," is in essence Nārāyaṇa, denoted by the term "bliss.

Furthermore, the fact that the *Subāla Upaniṣad* and others establish Nārāyaṇa’s status as the cause of the world, situated within the context of the creation and dissolution of the universe, is also determined to be non-different [from this]. [The opponent] refutes this [claim]: "In the Śrutis, the supreme state is revealed through words whose meaning is not other [than Him]; [it belongs] to Śrī..."

The Lord of the Goddess alone, and not others, is the one who bestows the fruits [of practice]; therefore, it is by Him alone that the purpose is achieved or that stability is maintained. Thus, the claim that the *Mantropaniṣad* and other texts merely "make the fool talkative" regarding the *Mṛtyuñjaya* [mantra] is in vain. Whether through the worship of the non-dual Supreme Deity as having attributes (*saguṇa*) or as being without attributes (*nirguṇa*) according to the scriptures, or as a means for attaining the Brahman devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca-brahman*) by way of such scriptural passages, in every respect, all scriptural mentions of His lordship over all, His causality, and so forth, are entirely subordinate to Him. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the doctrines of non-duality (*advaita*) regarding their respective objects of action.

Since a division of supporting strength and weakness is possible within a context established by the words of certain Vedic passages that admit no other alternative, [this applies] when one desires to adorn the state of Brahman—both with its limbs (*sāṅga*) and its qualities (*saguṇa*). This is evident in the case of the examples beginning with "Niṣada" or in the awakening [passages]. For instance, it is clear that the *Mantropaniṣad*—beginning with "What is the cause? Brahman? and so forth—is engaged in the definitive determination of the reality of Paramaśiva alone, the Lord who possesses the context [of the entire scripture].

As for the removal of [the notion that] sacrifice is the [means], since that [text] is engaged with that very [subject]— namely, the direct realization of Paramaśiva, who has been established therein as the supreme cause and so forth— which is the means to liberation, it is possible to suspect that the Upaniṣad reaches its full conclusion in that very place; for even here, although [the text] proceeds primarily with Brahman, among the various instruments [of knowledge], injunctions such as *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) are observed.

It is universally accepted that even for these [passages], the final purport (*tātparya*) culminates in Brahman; nor does it follow that because there is a prayer and so forth with the mantra beginning "When you have gone away, O Rudra... (*yāte rudra...*), this would lead one to understand that the entire section—whose primary focus is the description of the Supreme Brahman as determined by an examination of the *upakrama* (opening statement) and other criteria—is subordinate to mere praise, for there is no reason (*āpādaka*) for such a conclusion. Otherwise, there would be an absence of a single context (*prakaraṇa*) whose subject is the Great Person, established through the recognition of the meaning of words consistent with the proximity (*sannidhi*).

Due to the presence of signs such as the specific mantras heard in the *rānuvāka*, salutations (*namaskāra*), and prayers for desired objects, the *Puruṣasūkta* is also understood to be entirely devoted to praise; otherwise, there would result the collapse of the conviction that the *Puruṣasūkta* has no other object than the Lord. Similarly, the *Atharvaśiras* is determined to be devoted to stating the true nature of reality, because it proceeds as an instruction on His nature in response to the gods' question regarding the essential nature of Paramaśiva. As for the passage beginning with "He who is Rudra," it [serves] through the instruction of Śiva to the gods...

Since the hymn occurs after the realization of the universal self (sārvātmya), it cannot be maintained that even the portion concerning the instruction on the true nature (*yāthātmyopadeśa*) preceding it is intended as praise. For even that which appears to be mere praise is actually an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the instruction, having proceeded by taking as its basis the universal self understood through that instruction. The same applies to the *Śatarudriya*, the *Rudrasūkta*, and so forth; wherever the intent of a mantra is determined to be praise—whether through indicative marks (*laiṅgika*) or direct denotation (*vācaka*)—it is precisely there [that this principle holds].

It does not remain fixed by that alone; for if it were [fixed] merely by being contained within a single hymn (*sūkta*), then other mantras would also necessarily result in being intent upon praise. As for the claim that the frequent occurrence of the form of salutation (*namaskāra*) in Śiva-mantras is a mark (*liṅga*) of praise—that is a mark only for praise in general, but rather [it is a mark] for the excellence of the object of praise, as has been established below. And thus, by the mark of the abundance of salutations—which is unique and not shared with others—the preeminence of Śiva is established through the salutation.

Since [the deity] is established as having the form of universal sovereignty and so forth—which constitute the literal meaning of the words—it is proven that when "supremacy" must necessarily be postulated on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is illogical to abandon the supremacy that constitutes the literal meaning of the words and postulate supremacy in some other manner. Just as in the case of the mantra group beginning with *hiraṇyastūpa ābhuvat senānīḥ*, even though there is the presence of an indicative mark of praise for universal sovereignty and so forth, their abandonment is not appropriate; likewise, [this applies] to Śiva and the other deities regarding the crest-lock (*śikhā*).

It has been stated that the method of worship (*upāsanā-vidhi*) is supplementary to the demonstration of gradations [of excellence] through the relationship of cause and effect; that too has been addressed. Even among those [passages] establishing the superiority [of Śiva], such as the *Saucālīya* mantra (*"saucālīye śrutimantre...")*, the method of worship is equally accepted by others as well. Furthermore, in the *Atharvaśikhā* (*"atharvaśikhā...")*, the vision of Śiva (*darśana*) is seen here at the end [of the passage].

The description of [the Lord] as the cause of all would not be possible; for it is determined that his praise is like a statement possessing a specific referent. Indeed, he is not praised merely by way of his form alone, such that the learned [would understand him thus]. As for the *Puruṣasūkta* and other such [texts] which are declared to have no other purpose, since the *Puruṣasūkta* has been established as being devoted to Śiva, following that, the *Ṛgveda* itself [is likewise] non-dual in its intent. Having presented the created [beings], Brahmā...

Even if one accepts the presiding presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the *Bṛhaṇī* [power] as established in the *Sahasraśīrṣā Puruṣa*, because that [power] functions within the *Atharvaśikhā*, [it is stated] at the end [of that text] in the section defining the names of Mahādeva: "Mahādeva is all-pervasive. Furthermore, in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*, it is said: "All the gods [are pervaded]. In the *Vāyusaṃhitā*: "The Blessed One, because of the existence of *bhaga* (fortune/attributes), because of his stainlessness... [is the Lord]; whatever belongs to the Lord, all that [is pervaded] by the entry of Viṣṇu. Thus, Śiva presides by pervading everything from the principle of Śiva down to the earth, as well as bodies and jars and so forth.

Since there is seen an etymological derivation [of Viṣṇu] as being a name of Śiva in the passage "Therefore Viṣṇu-Rudra... and so forth, the identity with Nārāyaṇa is not established. Even if such identity were granted, by the arguments previously shown, the word *paratara* (the Supreme) in the *Mantra-upaniṣad*—which refers to Brahman as the cause of the universe—is not subject to other interpretations; furthermore, because it cannot be reconciled with other Smṛtis that follow that [Upaniṣad], there is no room for the opponents' hope therein. By this, the citation of the scriptural text "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" is also refuted, since that [text] speaks of "the supreme state of one who knows Brahman. What is that? It is the One.

In this sentence, which is intent upon defining the essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman in response to the inquiry "What is Brahman?", the mention of words such as "truth" (*satya*) and so forth—being in the nominative case and neuter gender—is impossible for them to denote Viṣṇu; for according to grammatical instruction, only the masculine form is taught to denote Him, as in "Ananta is [Viṣṇu], the serpent, and the ocean," and "the infinite [is] the sky and Nirati. Furthermore, in the immediately following sentence, "That which is hidden in the cave of the Veda," the word must be in the accusative case, because the act of knowing mentioned therein requires an object.

It must be stated that [the passage] begins with the word "Truth" (satya). Since the phrase "hidden in that very cave" is in close proximity, and because it is a statement about Brahman intended to present the ritual action, the "Truth" passage cannot abandon its status as a presentation of the definition of the seeker's desire in accordance with that [proximate statement]. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Therefore, since a distinction between the strength and weakness of the Śruti texts according to the method proposed by others is untenable, it is established—by the arguments we have set forth—that the Śruti texts concerning Śiva alone possess superior authority. 46.

Having refuted the division of strength and weakness as postulated by our opponents, we shall now refute the formless [doctrine] that takes the shape of the conceptualization of the division of the Purāṇas into *sāttvika* and so forth.

Thus, the opponents imagine: in certain *kalpas*, Brahmā awakens with his *sattva* predominant; in some, he is swallowed by *tamas*; and in others, he is not. And those *kalpas* are born from the respective nature of each one of those causes; they are designated by the great sages with names such as *sāttvika* and the rest. Among them, regarding the *mantra-kalpas*:
The *Sāttvata* and other Purāṇas are indeed composed even within the *Sāttvika* [kalpa]; for that very reason, the classification of the Purāṇas as *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and so forth is established.

Regarding their relative strength (*balābala*) and their suitability according to the qualities of the speaker (*vaktraguṇocita*), they maintain that the statement of the Purāṇas themselves is the root authority, for therein it is stated:
"The *Sāttvika* and others... Thus, having shown the fourfold nature of the *kalpas*—such as the *Rājasa* and so on—in whichever *kalpa* [a Purāṇa is situated]...

Regarding that which was previously declared by Brahmā to the Brahmins in ancient times, its majesty is described according to its own nature; having stated that those various Purāṇas were created by Brahmā, [it continues]: "In these [Purāṇas], the majesty of Agni is proclaimed among the Tāmasa ones; in the Rājasa ones, the majesty of Viṣṇu is known and fully narrated in the Karṇa [Parvan]; and in the Sāttvika kalpas, the majesty of Hari is predominant."
"In these [works], those who have achieved perfection through yoga will go to the supreme goal"—herein lies the division of the *kalpas* into *rājasa* and so forth.

This division occurs in those respective *kalpas* precisely because of the predominance of those specific qualities (*guṇa*) of Brahmā. Furthermore, regarding the Purāṇas composed by him in those various *kalpas*, which proclaim the mutual superiority or inferiority of various deities and contain contradictory statements—[this division serves] for the sake of establishing their validity and, in order to fully discern what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted among them.

This is because it serves a purpose by indicating the relative strength or weakness of the qualities of the speaker; whereas a classification of [Purāṇas] as *rājasa* and so forth would be purposeless by way of another method. Furthermore, since those classifications result in establishing the presence of speaker-qualities or defects conducive to determining whether a work is authoritative (*pramāṇa*) or non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*), and since the classification of the Kalpas as *rājasa* and so forth, the enumeration of their supplements, and the description of how they were spoken by Brahmā within those Kalpas collectively indicate the relative strength or weakness according to the qualities of the speaker, what then [remains] regarding the lineages of deities?

If one specifically desires to know by which Guṇa Brahmā spoke [these], it is said to be the Māhātmya of Agni-Śiva and so forth; and because they were composed through the realization of the principles of Tamas as defined in the Nirukta, the Śaiva Purāṇas are proclaimed to be *tāmasa*. However, would not this very statement itself be sufficient to establish their lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*)? For the majority is more powerful (*balīyastva*), and there is a necessity for Brahmā’s [authority]... [omitted].

If some Purāṇas were composed by him in that state [of ignorance] and were thus characterized as *tāmasa*, would this very statement itself not also be *tāmasa*? It is replied: No; that [statement] is set aside because it contradicts other statements. However, since there is a mutual contradiction among the Purāṇas such that they lack the capacity to definitively determine the meaning of the entire corpus, and when the question arises as to which ones should be accepted and which ones belong to whom, this statement—which concerns the distinction based on the characteristics of having *sattva* and so forth as their source—is intended to resolve that requirement. Thus it is said: "This is the highest [truth]."

The strength of the majority [of authorities] prevails over that [single instance], because there is no sublation (*apavāda*) of the statement cited. Indeed, for the Māddhāyaṇa school, through the Śruti beginning with "yo ha khalu vā vāsyā," the various specific deities established as possessing those respective qualities are presented by the textual compositions (*prabandha*) which have those very qualities as their basis.

Because the inherent validity (*svataḥ-siddha-prāmāṇya*) is thus stabilized by means of such capacity, there is not even the slightest suspicion of being rooted in darkness (*tamas*), which is a cause of invalidity. In this regard, the *Mātsya* [Purāṇa] has been cited.
Having established that [the Purāṇas] everywhere aim at demonstrating authority despite their mutual contradictions,

and because of those contradictions, [one must effect] the distinction between the Devatās and Paramaśiva-Saṃhārarudra; since the Purāṇas are not authoritative [in their current state], he says— intending the welfare of others like that of a son through his own [scriptural] means alone— that one should ordain [the rites] for those who possess superior knowledge.

The statement that [the Matsya Purāṇa] declares the non-authoritativeness of the Purāṇas due to differences in their respective *kalpas*—by means of such words as "the greatness" (*mahima*)—only serves to make me, O Paśupati, garrulous in an improper place. This is the intended meaning: the collection of cited statements is intended to establish the authority of all Purāṇas without contradiction by demonstrating that they have as their subject matter the appearances of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra at the end of various distinct *kalpas*, thereby making evident their mutual superiority; it is certainly not intended to bring about the non-authoritativeness of some of them.

For instance, just as the designations "summer," "winter," and so forth are applied based on the excellence of qualities such as the arrival of heat or the arrival of cold due to the predominance of heat, rain, and so on at those respective times; and just as men are designated as "sāttvika" and so on based solely on the predominance of the quality of *sattva* and the like within those individuals— so too, by the verse beginning with "the *sāttvika* [kalpas]," the *sāttvika* and other portions of the *kalpas* arise from the excellence of *sattva* and the rest through the power of the command of Paramaśiva during those *kalpas*, and not from the particular [nature] of the Brahmā residing in each respective *kalpa*.

It has also been stated that because of the excellence of its qualities (*guṇotkarṣa*), the absence of such a statement by Karṇa, and out of consideration for the purpose (*prayojana*), the intention of a division (*vibhāgābhiprāya*) is thus inferred. Furthermore, in response to the question, "O Sūta, tell me in due order the number of Purāṇas, the specific *dāna-dharma*, and [the *dharma*] according to the sequence," the answer is that the detailed exposition of the rules for giving for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*) pertains to all Purāṇas. Dharma is the tree of the Purāṇas; that is the essence. It is the medical science (*cikitsita*). These four are established by authoritative command (*ājñāsiddhi*).

The recollection that [the Purāṇas] are to be accepted as authoritative based solely on the Purāṇas themselves—such as the statement "they are to be inferred by means of reasons"—is disregarded because it is uncontradicted and accepted by great assemblies (*mahājana*). Furthermore, it is impossible for some to maintain that certain Purāṇas are rooted in delusion, while others have as their sole purpose the instruction of those who are ignorant of the path of the Vedas. For in the view of our opponents, since the majority of the primary content of the Śaiva Purāṇas is contradicted, their lack of authority is unavoidable in every respect. This is so even when considering the classification of the *kalpas* into *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* according to the method we have described.

By establishing the authority of all Vedic scriptures as a general rule, and by demonstrating the validity of the *Sammita* and *Nikhila* Purāṇas, [the goal] will be reached right there; for it is stated in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) of those [texts] that "having attained yoga in them, they shall go to the Supreme. Furthermore, having introduced the *Kaubera* and *Anvika* Kalpas, it says: "Having obtained knowledge through infinite penance, and having worshipped me within those very [Kalpas], the yogins attain that supreme state. Also, because practices such as the performance of austerity are purposeful and superior, and because [the goal] is most excellent... and not otherwise. Nor is it...

At whatever time [this] was proclaimed here, that [is] the sorrow [of those who say]: "The Purāṇas were composed by Brahmā in various Kalpas, being intent on the rules for proclaiming the mutual superiority and inferiority of the gods. Having cited the Purāṇas—which in those Kalpas were composed by Brahmā and were intent on proclaiming the mutual superiority and inferiority of the gods—the author states that they are intent upon the rules for describing their respective [qualities], and that the particle *eva* (only/exclusively) would indeed be the defining characteristic of what is to be accepted (*upādeya*), according to the statement of the learned: "An eva-particle occurs where there is the exclusion of others (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the affirmation of the subject itself (*svarūpa-sattva*); it is the defining characteristic of what is to be accepted. Thus, the text intends to establish that while the Purāṇas may differ in their specific sectarian emphases regarding the deities, they are fundamentally authoritative as they describe the essential nature and rules pertaining to each.

Even though that [account] follows the proper sequence, nevertheless, because there is no engagement with the description of the greatness of the *Kalpa* in its essential form, and because a specific deity is perceived therein, and furthermore,

in accordance with the immediate connection [of the text] stating "the greatness of Agni Śiva," the description of the rains and so forth refers to the period when rain and other phenomena have increased during that time.

The description of the various Kalpas, such as the adornment of trees with flowers, fruits, and sprouts, is like a description of their respective greatness. However, the subsequent section concerning the "non-rite" (avidhi) ultimately culminates in the very same "rite" (vidhi), because it consists of a description of the greatness of the deities appropriate for the predominance of those respective times. Thus, the matter set forth in the immediately following verse would be inconsistent with the view of the opponent; therefore, even for the sake of logical consistency, the classification into *sāttvika* and so forth must be accepted according to the method we have stated. Now, [one might object]:...

If it is argued that— just as the classification of Purāṇas into *sāttvika* and so forth is understood from the natural force (*svārasya*) of the subject matter (*vidheyārtha*) of the immediately preceding verse for the purpose of establishing their authority (*prāmāṇya*)— likewise, from the natural force of the object being restated (*anuvādyārtha*), it is also understood that this classification serves to distinguish between those that are authoritative and those that are not; even if this were the case, when a contradiction exists, it is proper to determine the meaning solely according to the natural force of the subject matter (*vidheyārtha*), and not to allow the non-subject matter (*avidheya*) to follow the natural force of the restatement (*anuvādyasvārasya*).

Because [the soul] is all-pervading and powerful, for this very reason, in the context of the application of the *jātakarman*, *iṣṭi*, and other scriptural passages, although there is an understanding that the person exists for the same duration as the body due to the natural force of the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the occasion (*nimitta*) consisting of death, it is nonetheless established as a final conclusion (*siddhāntita*) that the person’s persistence beyond the body—established by the force of the injunctions (*vidhi*) regarding rites such as the water-libation (*udaka*), the *kāpāya* garment, the *jātakarman*, and the *iṣṭi*—must necessarily exist; thus, its birth and death are figuratively attributed to it through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the body. [This is stated by] the Blessed One...

However, in the section concerning the reliance on the activities of the Lord’s incarnations (*daiśvaracaravyāpāśraya*), it is stated that, in reality, the Purāṇas were composed by Brahmā in various specific kalpas.

At the time of the commencement of the Vedas at the beginning of creation during the Kṛta-yuga, this body of Purāṇas—divided according to distinctions such as the *sarga* (creation) and extending to a hundred crores of verses—was revealed simultaneously.

Of that very [original] composition, a summary was made consisting of one crore of verses by eighteen sages, beginning with Brahmā, who divided it into eighteen parts. Therefore, it is of that very [work]...
Furthermore, at the end of the Dvāpara age, a similar abridgment was made. It is stated that the *Purāṇa* alone was first remembered by Brahmā as the foremost of all scriptures;

subsequently, from his mouths, its [expansion] was indeed one hundred crores in extent. Beginning with this, and because its meaning has been established here through an abridgment of equal proportion, it is thus presented in the *Brāhmaṇa*. And those [sages], in the beginning, [composed] the *Purāṇa* containing the *Dharma-saṃhitā*; that was composed in eighteen varieties.

By the phrase "through the differentiation of millions" and so forth, the statement that [the number] is small is intended merely as a teaching regarding specific distinctions and is not intended as a definitive formulation; therefore, according to the Pāṇinian sūtra (*prādayaḥ upasargāḥ*), even if there were a division of [phonemes] such as *pra* and so on, it would still serve the purpose desired by the opponent.

But for the ascetic observer of vows, [the Purāṇas] were not composed by another creator; rather, their meaning was established long ago. At that time, having received them from the Supreme Lord along with the Vedas, he set them forth.

And he who was the nine-gated [organ] sent forth [the teachings] from the collection of the Purāṇa sections. To him, at the beginning of his birth, the Vedas were given for the sake of fulfillment and bliss, according to the vision of the supplementary texts (*upabrahmaṇa*). From this Great Being, whose manifestation is the universe, arose the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda.

According to the Śruti, "The Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, and so forth," the Kavi—the direct wielder of the trident—is the original author of these eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) which consist of distinct sentences. Furthermore, based on the corroborating texts (*upabrahmaṇa*) such as, "Having meditated for a long time, that Blessed One, Mahādeva Maheśvara, whose excellent weapon is the trident, created all the scriptures," and ending with, "These are the sciences (*vidyā*) proclaimed by Śaṅkara, endowed with the meaning of words," the statement regarding the duties of kings (*rājadharma*) [is established]. (Note: The ellipsis (... indicates a portion of the source text where the specific application of the *rājadharmavacana* to the *vidyā* is omitted.)

They say that this is also because the supreme Lord is established as the creator of the worlds; however, in that view, there is no room whatsoever for the [Vedic] sacrifices (*kratavaḥ*). That which was well-stated—namely, that the *kalpas* are characterized by the predominance of specific qualities (*guṇotkarṣa*), such as the *sāttvika* and the undivided [pure] *sāttvika*, and so forth—is incorrect. For the verse beginning with "In which *kalpa*" (*yasmin kalpe*) is intended to describe the greatness of the deities active in the various *kalpa*-divisions that arise from the predominance of those respective qualities, and thus does not contradict the truth.

It is indeed proper to understand [the scripture] as being intended to demonstrate non-contradiction, just like the Puranic verse beginning, "The various forms of the Linga are seen in succession; those very same ones appear likewise at the beginnings of the Yugas and other periods.

Having thus demonstrated the absence of contradiction, [the author] proceeds to show—by way of the natural capacity of things—that the excellence of the qualities mentioned in the scriptures regarding specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) during times of the predominance of *sattva* and the other *guṇas* is appropriate;
and he also shows that for certain other deities, there exists a particular limiting adjunct which causes the variation in their mental states across different Kalpas. This is [the case] with Agni...

The passage beginning with "the majesty of Śiva" (śivasya māhātmyam) and so forth is not stated according to the manner of others—namely, that a Purāṇa was spoken by Brahmā possessing certain qualities—in response to a desire to know which deity is supreme. Rather, in order to state its specific distinction, the word "kalpa" is employed in the phrase "in the Sāttvika kalpas," etc.; since the words "Sāttvika" and so on refer to the *kalpas* and not to the Purāṇas themselves, it is established that in those specific *kalpas*, the majesty of Hari is greater. This is because the superiority of his majesty is self-evident and is what is being propounded; thus, it is declared in this direct statement.

Because it is impossible to assume the connection of a verb heard in a preceding sentence (*pūrvavākya*) [to subsequent ones], and because in the initial sentences verbs such as "is proclaimed" (*prakīrtyate*) and "is known" (*viduḥ*)— rather than "is spoken" (*gadyate*)— are heard, in the *tāmasa* cycle the sequence proceeds by way of the excellence of the fires within the fire-god (*agnyantaryāmin*), and so forth. Furthermore, if these sentences are somehow considered part of a subsequent section (*aparavākya*) in the *sāttvika* cycles, then since the majesty of Hari is greater in those cycles, the establishment of Hari’s preeminence occurs through the [repetition] of the words of the [initial] sentences.

Having determined that the purpose [of these texts] is to establish the specific arrangements of particular kalpas, the various greatnesses of the deities are recorded as being innumerable. Furthermore, they have been described by the sages who contemplate time in the Purāṇas as consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. In Sāttvika kalpas, the majesty of Hari is predominant; in Tāmasa kalpas, that of Maheśa; and in Rājasa kalpas, that of Prajāpati. In some instances Brahmā is praised, in others Rudra, and in others Viṣṇu.
By this, there is no increase or decrease whatsoever in those [numbers] on the part of the great seers,
with respect to the various accounts of events at the end of the respective kalpas.
"A wise man is not deluded regarding those various exalted [states] therein.

Furthermore, because the *Vāyusaṃhitā* clearly establishes the superiority and inferiority of Brahmā and the others according to the distinction of the Kalpas, and because the arrangement of all the Purāṇas—including those that appear contradictory—is established by the very words of the *Matsya-purāṇa* cited by our opponents, it is therefore not proper for certain others to harbor a misconception regarding the lack of authority of some Purāṇas. Moreover, as for them...

Even if the Śaiva Purāṇas and other such texts were intended to convey the doctrines of others, it would only be established that they were composed by Brahman under the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the quality of darkness (tamas) and so forth; yet, for some, their authority [remains]. "O Lord of the World, for him [Brahman], knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and virtue—this fourfold set—is innate."

Thus, because the Smṛti records that Brahmā possesses unimpeded power of knowledge, he is beyond even *tamas*, which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for his composition of the Purāṇas; for it is only that *tamas* which serves as the limiting adjunct for his role as the destroyer [of the world] that can obstruct the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Furthermore, since one who does not corrupt the knowledge rooted in the application [of means] cannot render that application invalid, if Brahmā were like us and his knowledge of reality were obstructed by *tamas*, then certain parts of the Purāṇas composed by him would be non-authoritative (*aprāmāṇya*).

In that case, since the suspicion of the same [lack of authority] would be unavoidable even regarding the cited statements from the *Matsya Purāṇa*, how could any determination of meaning be established by them?

As for the claim that their general authority remains intact because no subverting statement (*apavādaka-vacana*) is seen, that too is incorrect. For it is said: "On one hand, there are the Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas in their entirety; on the other hand, this supreme [text] excels even those. For those desiring proficiency in Dharma and those desiring proficiency in knowledge, there is no other supreme means except for this single Purāṇa."

Since one hears such disparaging remarks against specific Purāṇas recited in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* and others which establish the superiority of those very same texts, even the argument that their authority is stabilized by the "power of the subject matter" (*vastusāmarthya*)—characterized as appropriateness (*aucitya*)—is also untenable. For in deceitful works like the *Bhārata*, although there is the description of the conduct of Asuras and others, Vyāsa is established as being *sāttvika*; thus, because the quality of the speaker conforms to the qualities of the subject matter, the claim of appropriateness is unproven. Furthermore, it would not follow that something is subject to degradation merely by being *tāmasa*. Nor does [the mere presence of *tāmasa* elements] entail inferiority.

It should be stated that, according to this sequence, what is intended by "propriety" (*aucitya*) is that it is appropriate for one describing [the Lord] to possess the quality of *tamas*. This is because the Lord Rudra, in assuming *tamas* for the purpose of destroying the world, possesses the *vibhāva* (determinant cause) that serves as the reason for his excellence; as will be demonstrated in the section concerning the establishment of the equilibrium of the *guṇa*-forms, where it is said, "As it is in reality, so it is [for them]. Furthermore, the Vaiṣṇava, Nāradīya, Gāruḍa, Bhāgavata, and Vārāha Purāṇas are *sāttvika*, while the Brahmāṇḍa, Brahmakaivarta, Mārkaṇḍeya, Bhaviṣyat, and Vāmana Purāṇas are [also *sāttvika*].

[The texts] belonging to the *Rājasa* category—namely the *Laiṅga*, *Śāva*, *Āgneya*, *Skānda*, [and so forth]—are not to be accepted, according to the statement of certain moderns; thus, even their division into *Sāttvika* and so on, which contradicts the intention of their own countrymen, has been rejected. Since that [division] pertains to subjects such as the number of faces [of the deity] and the like, and since we have no objection to its referring to deities associated with specific *Guṇas*, it remains [valid] within what is considered *Sāttvika*.

In the *Garuḍa*, the *Śivarahasya*, the *Padma*, and many other Purāṇas such as the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava, the preeminence of Śiva is established; furthermore, since it is impossible to fulfill the wicked desires of men through this [work] alone, and because it was taught by Parāśara—who had attained the knowledge of the supreme reality of the deities through the boon of Pulastya—regarding the general inquiry into the subject matter of the cause of the universe, [it is stated] in the sequence of the reply that "this world, including all things moving and unmoving, has arisen from Viṣṇu," and so forth. Thus, [the truth] has been revealed.

(... [The objection that] "it might not produce confusion of intellect—unlike other Purāṇas which take the form of a dialogue between Mahāviṣṇu and a specific deity—is refuted by the principle that the intended meaning of the questioner must be accepted as primary, since it is impossible to interpret it otherwise and because it would otherwise be rendered unestablished. Furthermore, the claim made by others that the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* is superior to all other Purāṇas has been set aside as being too trivial to refute.
