For even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, despite possessing powers of knowledge superior to those of Parāśara, did not [perceive] the supreme Brahman, which is without beginning or end.

The Ṛṣis do not know the Vedas; only the Lord Āditya, the lord of lights, knows them—such statements establish that [the Purāṇas] have as their object [the Supreme], yet no instances are seen where Parāśara establishes the supreme status of Śiva here and there in the Śaiva Purāṇas. Nor are there found in the Vāyusaṃhitā and other texts introductory narratives (avatārāṇi) consisting of a sequence of answers that determine, in response to a general inquiry regarding the Supreme Reality, that Śiva alone is the Supreme Reality. However, this much is the distinction.

In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, it can be argued that even though the question was general, the teacher—who already knew the heart of his disciple, who had previously been a student—gave an answer concerning specific details favorable to him in order to increase that disciple’s pre-existing devotion. However, in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*, the answer proceeded from questions posed by many sages who were disputing with one another; thus, it cannot be interpreted in the same way. Therefore, by the principles we have set forth here and there, such a distinction between the relative strength (*balābala*) of the Purāṇas is not tenable.

It is established that the Śiva Purāṇas alone are more authoritative. By this, the boastful talk of fools regarding the authority of the Śivādvaita-mata—derived from the hands of their teachers—is refuted; for in the Śiva Purāṇas, which stand at the pinnacle of authority, they are praised in many ways, and in some instances, their status as authoritative is explicitly established. Furthermore, this is supported by the statement in the Mahābhārata: "O best of sages, these are the systems of knowledge: Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata; indeed, these are known by name according to the traditional rule."

Just as the Pāśupata Āgamas are recognized as being distinct systems from the Vedic tradition—similar to Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and others—their authority has been refuted in the final quarter (antima-pāda) of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā along with Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Pāñcarātra. Likewise, in the Kūrma Purāṇa, it is stated that Keśava, impelled by Śiva, composed such delusive scriptures: "Kāpāla, Lākula, Śākta, Bhairava, Pūrvamīmāṃsā, Paścimamīmāṃsā, Pāñcarātra, and Pāśupata."

Likewise, others—[those who follow] the *Śaiva*, the *Nirgranthas* (Jainas), those who know the *Pāñcarātra*, [the followers of] the *Kāpālikas*, the *Pāśupatas*, and other such heretics (*pāṣaṇḍas*)—eat his sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*). For him, there is no fruit after death [from such acts]. In that Kali age, those of perverse conduct, the *Pāśupatas*, and likewise the *Pāñcarātrikas*, will become [false] Brahmins.

And [regarding] them, their status as delusive scriptures (*mohaśāstra*) has been revealed by the *Krānti* and other [Tantras]. Therefore, how can their authority (*prāmāṇya*) be consistent? It is said: the Pāśupata tradition is indeed twofold—Vedic (*śrauta*) and non-Vedic (*aśrauta*). For it was previously stated by me: "The Pāśupata vow... most secret, subtle, the essence of the Vedas, for the sake of liberation," beginning thus, up to:
"This Pāśupata yoga is to be practiced by those seeking liberation; for it is constantly covered in ash by those free from desire"—so says the Śruti. By that [vow], it is eternal.

The Śrauta-pā[...], the Tantara[...], and other scriptures indeed intended for the delusion of the world—those which contradict the teachings of the Vedas—were spoken by me alone. The Vāma, Pāśupata, Soma, Lākula, and Bhairava [traditions] are not to be practiced; they are declared to be outside the Veda (vedabāhya), while the other is [the Śrauta]. This is because Śiva has shown that the non-Śrauta Pāśupata is not the means to liberation. And in the Vāyusaṃhitā, even the Śaiva Āgama is divided into two: the Śrauta and the Astra. It is clearly stated that the Śrauta division consists of the essence of the Śruti.

Because it has been established as such. And thus, those statements that express censure regarding entry into the Pāśupata scriptures refer to those who are qualified [for Vedic rites] but have entered non-Vedic scriptures, like the Vedas themselves;

for this is consistent with the meaning of the statement: "This should not be practiced, as it is outside the Veda, and so is the other. Furthermore, the statement from the *Mahābhārata* that was cited also refers to the non-Vedic Pāśupata.

It does not concern the supreme Vedic observances known as Pāśupata, Śāmbhava, and so forth—which are taught in the *Atharvaśira-upaniṣad*, the *Kālāgnirudra-upaniṣad*, and others—as its primary purport.

Since there is no difference between one who has entered [this path] and the Vedic way, the refutation of the authority of the Pāśupatas found in the passage beginning with "and because the Lord is ignorant" (*patyurasāmañjasyāt*) refers specifically to the non-Vedic Pāśupatas; for it is indeed the doctrine of God as a mere efficient cause that is refuted therein, and that doctrine is well-known precisely in that [non-Vedic] context, but not in the Vedic Pāśupata. In the *Vāyusaṃhitā*, within the summary of the meaning of the Vedic Pāśupata, it is stated: "From Śiva-tattva arise everything from Śakti down to Earth; by that one [tattva],..."

Just as a jar and the like are pervaded by clay, so too is this established; for since it is demonstrated that [everything] has existence (*bhāva*) as its material cause (*upādāna*), there is the designation of "existence" (*bhāvatva*) for all things, just as bracelets, crowns, and other ornaments are designated as "golden" because they have gold as their material cause. This is well-known among those proficient in the Śaiva scriptures.

Therefore, because it constitutes the essential extraction of the secret meaning of the Vedānta—having bestowed the Purāṇas, the science of logic (*tarka-śāstra*), prosody, poetics, grammar, the Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, and indeed the duties of the disciples...

Because the *Varāhapurāṇa* and other texts praise that gift by stating, "He shall become the king of kings over the earth with its two-fold continents," [the author] establishes the matter through these two [verses]. ||47||

Those who know the scriptures perceive that the purity of mind which brings about the fortune of enjoying great wealth in this world is the fruit of worshipping Maheśvara; may all those [fruits], including the station of Brahmā, Indra, and others in the hereafter, remain in your divine state, where one sports with the innate Gaṇas. Now, regarding the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), since there is no possibility of increase or decrease as there is in worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), he establishes its distinction from other forms of worship by demonstrating that the propitiation of Śiva is the internal means (*antaraṅgopāya*) therein. That which is supreme is Brahman, the imperishable and auspicious remainder.

And that which is sung in the *Śruti* for the assembly—that too is the fruit of your worship. Indeed, knowledge regarding Śiva, the pure Self, arises here through the means [of devotion]; by your grace alone does some fortunate person attain it. In this regard: "I take refuge in that Maheśvara, who brings about the destruction of evil and bestows the fruit of liberation; he who ordained Brahmā and [created] these [beings]. "I, seeking liberation, truly take refuge in that God of gods, the light of the self-awakening intellect."

"A certain fearful person might leap [into the fire] thinking, 'I am unborn'... "I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation indeed to Sadyojāta! In every birth, do not transcend me; favor me, salutation to Bhavodbhava! Thus, in the Śrutis, regarding devotion to Śiva... then they said to the Brahmins in the winter season: "Tell us, by what recitation does one attain immortality? Yājñavalkya replied: "By the Śatarudrīya. These indeed are the [mantras] of immortality here.

These are His names. By these, indeed, one becomes immortal; thus it is said in the Jābāla Śruti. "You alone are the Lord of all worlds regarding bondage and liberation. Thus it is stated in the eighth book of the Bhāgavata. "The wise worship Him, the Guru who removes the distress of those who have sought refuge. Thus in the fourth book of the Bhāgavata, concerning Him who has approached [the devotee]. "Whose blameless conduct [is that] of the Great Sage... [The text continues with: "...which is served by the crowns of the great sages, those whose minds are intent on the goal of Brahman. Thus in the fourth book, concerning Him who has approached. "Whose blameless conduct [is that] of the Great Sage... [The text concludes with: "...of the Great Sage."

They declare that [the Lord] desires to drink away the veil of ignorance (*avidyā-paṭala*). Thus, in the third *skandha*, it is established that even the favoring of His deeds—such as the swallowing of the *kālakūṭa* poison at Puruṣottama—is a cause of liberation.

Likewise, in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas*, it is observed that the worship of Viṣṇu and the chanting of His names are also established as causes for that [liberation]. Consequently, by the maxim "there is an option because the fruits are distinct," an option (*vikalpa*) is obtained. Nevertheless, regarding liberation in the form of the cessation of ignorance, knowledge (*vidyā*) alone is the direct means.

Since it has been determined through both scripture (*śruti*) and logic (*nyāya*) that liberation belongs to no one other than her, the authorities (*pramāṇa*) for other [means] being its instruments must be explained as intending them to be indirect means. In this regard, the worship of Śiva is the cause therein by way of *vidyā*; for the Jābāla Upaniṣad and others state: "When the life-breaths of a living being are departing, Rudra explains the liberating Brahman," thus [liberation comes] from Śiva, who has been propitiated by the meditation of the liberated.

Because it establishes the attainment of the knowledge of the meaning of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) whose form is the *praṇava*—the savior from *saṃsāra*—and because the verse of the mantra, "May that God unite us with auspicious mindfulness" (*sa no devaḥ śubhayā smṛtyā saṃyunaktv iti*), shows that the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) which effects liberation is obtainable through His grace; for here, by the word "mindfulness" (*smṛti*), it is precisely the liberating direct realization that is intended, since its usage in that sense is seen in another Vedic scripture: "By the breaking of mindfulness, there is the complete loosening of all knots. (*smṛtipratibhedāt sarvagranthīnāṃ vipramokṣaḥ*).

Because it arises from the knowledge produced by the words of one who awakens [the sleeper] from a forgotten dream, and because its object is something already attained, it does not require an act of salutation—as in the case of "I shall teach you"—since the application of the term "smṛti" (recollection) there is justified by its definition. Furthermore, although the worship of Viṣṇu is a means to knowledge, it is not conducive to liberation through the gateway of [direct] impulsion, as stated in the mantra-text of the *Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad*: "Having mounted the syllable Oṃ as a chariot and having made Viṣṇu the charioteer, one seeks the station of the world of Brahman; for Rudra, he is not beyond that."

Through devotion to the syllable *Oṃ*, there is grace from Viṣṇu; one who is intent on his worship shall obtain the grace of Rudra. Then, through that [worship], one attains knowledge, bliss, non-duality, and the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, from the statement addressed to Viṣṇu in the sequence: "Without taking refuge in you, the world [cannot exist]; the yogi shall not come to me," and by such words as, "Whomsoever I favor, I shall gradually take away this wealth; therefore, they abandon wealth," and "In this state, there is suffering... and so forth.

And because it teaches, for the sake of generating detachment in Viṣṇu-prasāda, the general application of engaging in the means of knowledge that lead to liberation. (.... [The text] begins with "sāda" (....), "paryaṅka" (....), "nyā" (.....), and "kāma" (.....); thus the great scripture, which brings benefit to those such as Kuṇḍa and others, proceeds. Thus, the syllable *ukāra* is shown for women, Śūdras, and so forth, in the tenth book (*daśamaskandha*) of the *Bhāgavata*.

(…) would be [the case]. Where the *vaiṣṇava* sacrament (*saṃskāra*) for women, *śūdras*, and slaves is prescribed, one should likewise observe the specific determination of eligibility for the Tantras in the *Sūtasaṃhitā* and other such texts. As for that which is stated in the [*Viṣṇudharma-uttara*] and the *Laiṅga*: “By you, O Śāṇḍilya, my worship was performed solely by means of intoxication; yet I was not pleased by that, for I am dear to you. Even though it was performed by you through a wrong path, O Śāṇḍilya, my worship was [accepted] because of you. From this [it follows...]

"(... you shall go"—this was a statement of censure by the Blessed One toward Śāṇḍilya, who had entered the *pāñcarātra* initiation. Having obtained the supreme good (*paraṃ śreyaḥ*) within the four Vedas, Śāṇḍilya [went] to this [path] because he heard [the teachings] from this [teacher]. Since he possessed the qualification for the Vedic path, the intention is that he abandoned it to enter elsewhere out of propriety; it is not intended as a denial of its authority. For who is there—not bound by the strength of sin—who is not devoted to the conduct of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramācāra*) without [the authority of] the Śruti?

"Those [penances] are prescribed in the Śruti. This has been made clear in that very same place; therefore, enough of this digression. By this, the claim that the Pāñcarātra is the most authoritative among the Āgamas is refuted by the aforementioned method.

For it is established that the Śaiva Āgamas alone—being compendiums of the essential meaning of the scriptures and entirely free from the stain of even the slightest suspicion of defect—are more powerful than all other Āgamas. Furthermore, as has been described by others, because the Śiva Purāṇas constitute the very essence of the Yajñas, they establish the absolute superiority of the Śiva Purāṇas over the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Āgamas. Thus, by them... [the conclusion follows].

Since [the Lord] abides as the cause of all and the inner controller of all, other scriptural passages (śruti) and the like that appear to exalt another deity must be interpreted in accordance with this fact. Thus, it is established that there is no room for the objection of a reversal of meaning here. This may be so; let it be that everything [is explained] in accordance with the more powerful śruti and other authorities, even if it concerns merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda) such as "All that, O Indra, is under your control."

This refers to the shifting [of the meaning] to "belonging to you" (*tāvakatvena*). He explains the manner in which one must effect this shifting—how it is that the supreme sovereignty of Nārāyaṇa, consisting of his independent agency over the creation and dissolution of all worlds and his status as the inner controller of all, which is established in the *Subāla Upaniṣad* and other scriptures, as well as in the *Gītā*, the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, and so forth, specifically within the contexts of the accounts of creation and the like, must be interpreted otherwise. ||48||

The Vedic scriptures teach that Your sovereignty—comprising all three [of the Trimūrti]—is supreme even in Your incarnations, because they are one through being Your portions (*aṃśa*). O Blessed One, some who do not understand this much that has been declared by the sages sink into the various darknesses of delusion due to their childishness. This is the meaning: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva do not differ from Śrī Śambhu, the Lord of all, because they are His portions, just as the incarnations of Hari [do not differ from Him]. This being so, when the incarnations such as Kṛṣṇa are glorified, the qualities of Mahāviṣṇu are likewise glorified as belonging to them.

In this way, the qualities of Śiva—such as being the creator of all, the inner ruler of all, and the lord of the cities—are proclaimed in his portions (tadaṃśeṣu), as well as the lords of the Akathas. Furthermore, the eloquent sayings of Kṛṣṇa recited in the beginning of the Bhagavadgītā, such as: "O son of Kuntī, at the end of a kalpa all beings go to my own nature; at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth again," and so on, are not applicable to him [Viṣṇu] in that very form, because he is subject to change (tadhañcana). Therefore, these eloquent sayings—which concern the Lord who is the singular foundation of the root of the world—must be accepted even by others. And thus:

When it is firmly established that the root of the world consists of powerful forms of pride, let the repose of their being be sought in the very form of Śambhu. This being so, O Sat [Arjuna], that divine and sovereign knowledge has been understood by you exactly as it is. Hṛṣīkeśa himself, the eternal one, is pleased with you. Go, go to your own place; you ought not to cause delay. Worship Śiva with supreme devotion—thus did the Blessed Bādarāyaṇa impart the divine knowledge of the Bhagavadgītā. And that which he...
"Nārāyaṇa also [is] Hari, the son of [Viṣṇu]; out of compassion for those ignorant of [the truth], he bestowed this supreme [teaching].

Thus, at the conclusion of the *Īśvaragītā*, he describes the *Bhagavadgītā* as being composed of the grasping of its meaning; and in the *Bhagavadgītā*, the Blessed One reveals his own fundamental form, showing the auspicious form that is the soul of the universe. Furthermore: "Those whose wisdom has been carried away by those desires resort to other deities; their fruit is indeed finite."

"...becomes the protector of those with little intelligence; people sit around [him] in reverence... Having heard the entire *Gītā-śāstra* accompanied by such words, Arjuna remained there, saying to his teacher at the conclusion of the scripture, "I shall act so as to remove my doubt. Even though he was devoted to Śiva-bhakti for as long as he lived, having offered the daily worship and oblations intended for Śaṅkara to the Lord during the midst of the Bhārata war, he followed him to Kailāsa and remained by Śiva’s side.

Behold, all of this is consistent with the royal [status], given that the collection of greatnesses—such as being the cause of the universe and so forth—as described in the *Gītā*, [is established] when [Kṛṣṇa] is determined to be the Supreme Lord (*īśvara*). His status as the knowledge of the Lord consists in his taking up the meaning of the *Īśvara-gītā*. With the intention that his true nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), he describes himself as the cause of the universe and so forth; and when requested to reveal that form, Kṛṣṇa reveals his Śiva-form. Furthermore, from the perspective of perceiving a real distinction (*vāstava-bheda*), Kṛṣṇa declares, "I am the source of all," and so forth, [attributing] the causality of the universe and other such qualities to Śiva alone.

Since it is faultless as being his own, by determining that intention, there is the ascertainment of Śiva’s supreme excellence; and because Arjuna possesses a firm yoga of devotion toward Him for as long as he lives and a certainty regarding their non-difference, he offers the materials for Śiva’s worship to Vāsudeva with the very thought that He is Śiva.

Thus, the consistency of [Arjuna] not seeing [Kṛṣṇa’s] face even when it was near his hands—due to his own state—is perfectly clear. Therefore, in this way, when it is certain that the supreme state described in the Gītā culminates in Śiva:

By this same reasoning, it should be understood that even the supreme state described in the Subālopaniṣad, the Nārāyaṇānuvāka, and other Śrutis culminates in Śiva; and this has been determined by the venerable Parāśara himself in the Vaiṣṇava Śrutis, Purāṇas, and so forth, regarding how the propounding of the supreme state—such as being the cause of the universe—finds its finality in Śiva: "O best of men, that excellence which is seen in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas belongs to Viṣṇu in his essential nature (tattvātmanā), not in his own individual form (svarūpeṇa)."
"Īśāna, accompanied by Ambā, is the cause of all things and is characterized by truth and other such qualities;
neither Viṣṇu, nor Viriñci, nor Rudra, nor any other person [is so].
Thus say the Śrutis, the Purāṇas, and the Bhārata and other texts, O best of beings."
"Indeed, they speak [of Him] while always holding Śiva together with Ambā in their hearts.

Thus, one should observe the scriptural statements in the *Sūta-saṃhitā* and other texts regarding these very matters. Furthermore, the description in the *Subālopaniṣad* concerning Nārāyaṇa’s role as the agent of the great creation and so forth—though it culminates in that [Nārāyaṇa], according to the manner explained by others—it establishes that Śiva exists during the interval between the time of the beginning of creation and its conclusion.

By the Śvetāśvatara [Upaniṣad] stating "yadātamaḥ" (when there was darkness), which establishes that [the world] existed at that time, even the sages—having already seen this path of easily maintaining non-contradiction as being thus approved by them—[rejected] the displays of knowledge consisting of imagining it otherwise; this is also an indication for the [interpretation of] the Vedic passages in the verse beginning with "tad eva".

Thus, in every instance, regarding Nārāyaṇa, who has been described as the cause of the world and so forth—by means of the passage beginning with "In the beginning there was only Nārāyaṇa; there was no Brahmā, no Īśāna," etc.—the text establishes through the exclusion of all others such as Brahmā and Īśāna that it is Nārāyaṇa alone [who exists] at the beginning of creation, and then teaches the emergence of the manifold world consisting of the elements, the senses, and so on. Furthermore, [it says]: "Then Nārāyaṇa, desiring to bring forth other beings, meditated with his mind; while he was absorbed in meditation..."
From his forehead, sweat flowed; from that water, a golden egg (*hiraṇmaya-aṇḍa*) consisting of fire came into being. [Then it is said: "From it, the four-faced Brahmā was born," and so forth.

Furthermore, by the passage beginning, "That Nārāyaṇa, desiring something else, meditated with his mind; while he was absorbed in meditation, a three-eyed, trident-bearing person was born from his forehead," and so on, there is no possibility of the description of Brahmā and Śiva as creators ending in [the supremacy of] Śiva alone. Nor can it be argued that there is no contradiction here because the mention of Śiva’s creation refers specifically to the *saṃhāra-rudra* (the Rudra of dissolution).
It cannot be argued that the description of Nārāyaṇa’s role as the creator culminates in Paramaśiva; for that would contradict the *Upabrahmaṇa* (the supplementary Purāṇic texts). For instance:

"In the beginning, there was the primordial being, unknown, without characteristics, inactive, indefinable, as if asleep on all sides. Then the self-existent Lord, the unmanifest, who dispels darkness, appeared, manifesting this world through the activity of the great elements and so forth. He who is beyond the senses, ungraspable, subtle, yet manifest and eternal..."

The final [form] consists of all beings, and he himself manifested as that very being. Desiring to create various progeny, he meditated and first emitted water from the half of his body; into that water he cast his seed. That became an egg of gold, possessing a radiance equal to the thousand-rayed sun. Within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds. Water is called *nārāḥ*, for water is indeed the offspring of *nara*; since that was his place of movement (*ayana*), he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.

This statement from the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] is rooted in the Śruti. Here, the very method of the Upaniṣad cited as an illustration introduces the one designated by the terms "Nārāyaṇa" and "Svayaṃbhū," indicated by the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) about to be performed;

having first briefly shown the creation of the elements and the senses through the statement that He possesses the creative power (*vīrya*) transformed into the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth, it subsequently describes the contemplation on the manner of creation and the like, the emission of water from His own body, the emission of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) therein, and the emission of Brahmā within it, showing the demonstration of the production of the specific [gross elements] from His four faces.
Because the state of being the root-of-roots is evident.

Now, one might object: since the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the name Nārāyaṇa occurs in this very context, it must apply only to Brahmā—given his proximity here and because his constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*) are established by being born from an egg within the waters—and not to the Self-born Creator (*svayambhū*). Thus, it would be improper to claim that this passage is rooted in the cited Upaniṣadic texts. Furthermore, it cannot be argued that proximity (*sannidhi*) is weaker than context (*prakaraṇa*), and therefore the application of the term belongs to the subject of the context—the Creator himself—because his residence in the midst of those waters is established by the force of the description of the creation of the great flood of water, which makes the etymological meaning of the parts applicable there as well. To this, we reply: it is not so, because of its [the etymology’s] presence here...

Since the quality of being the primary cause will be established by the principal [text] itself, there is no observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) or the like [to suggest otherwise]. For, regarding the statement of the great seers concerning the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire collection of beings—a discourse on the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) initiated in response to a question about dissolution for the purpose of defining it with the words "From that, this... and so forth—it is logical that the etymological derivation of the name Nārāyaṇa, which occurs in proximity to that [statement], applies specifically to Brahman. This is because even in the Purāṇas, [the same logic applies]. *Note: The ellipses (... indicate missing portions of the original manuscript.*

Because that name is well-known [in that context], and because there is no fixed rule [to the contrary], there is no proximity of Brahman here. Furthermore, in the verse "From him were born the waters and the sons," since the word *nara* refers to the creator of those waters, it is more appropriate for the etymology (*nirvacana*) to apply to him due to his proximity;

it does not refer to the unmanifest, eternal cause consisting of both being and non-being which depends on Brahman. This is clear from the subsequent verse: "That person, emitted by Him, is celebrated as 'Brahmā' in the world."

Furthermore, since the qualification of the named object (*saṃjñin*) in the rule prescribing that name would otherwise be rendered redundant if this were merely a prescription of names for the objects of creation, there might arise the suspicion that—due to proximity—the second name also refers to those same objects.
To prevent such a doubt, [the qualification is necessary], just as in the case of the term *saṃjñiviśeṣaṇa*. For if both names had the same object, their purpose could not be established.
However, at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), everything is composed of the darkness of ignorance (*tamaḥ*).
Like a cataka bird fast asleep, it was unperceived and showed no sign of life.
Then the self-existent, unmanifest source of meritorious deeds,
dispelling the darkness, appeared manifesting this entire universe.
Beyond the senses, superior to the manifest,
the eternal inner controller known as Nārāyaṇa— he himself appeared.
Desiring to create various kinds of beings, he first emitted water from his own body;
into that water, he cast his seed.

That very egg, consisting of the nature of gold, became the world; therein Brahmā was born. Since the word *Nārāyaṇa* is used unambiguously for the very act of creation in the words of Manu (which are of identical meaning), and since it is certain that the various statements of Manu—which show a single form for many meanings—are rooted in the *Mahopaniṣad*, it follows by necessity that the etymological definition (*nirvacana*) of the word *Nārāyaṇa* must also pertain to the specific context of the usage of that word within that [Upaniṣad]. And thus, from that, the Self-born...

By the words "the Blessed One," etc., it is established through the force of the statement that "He first emitted water alone and then cast His seed into it" that the etymology of the word *Nārāyaṇa*—referring to the activity and cessation of the Lord's dwelling in those waters—is already well-known as the denotation of the term *Nārāyaṇa*. This leads to the conclusion that the purpose of the teaching is to establish [the Lord] as the Creator. For if the conclusion were elsewhere, then by necessity the term *Nārāyaṇa* would also have to conclude there [in that other sense], which would result in a contradiction with the context.

Thus, in accordance with the *Upabrahmaṇa*, it must be admitted that even in the cited *Niṣad*, the demonstration of the quality of being the creator (*sraṣṭṛtva*) culminates in Nārāyaṇa alone. This is because we see the words of Śiva addressed to Nārāyaṇa in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "And at the end of the kalpa, I, assuming a terrible form and bearing a trident in my hand, shall become your son, O dear one, born of your wrath. Furthermore, in accordance with that, in the passage "From his forehead [appeared] the three-eyed, trident-bearing [one]," it is necessary that the referent of the word "his" (*tasya*) must necessarily culminate in Nārāyaṇa.

[Objection: "Even if this is so, nevertheless, since in a certain intermediate creation (*avāntara-sarga*) it is possible for the four-faced Brahmā alone—and even for Nārāyaṇa—to be the cause, the cited Upaniṣadic passage finds its fulfillment by referring to him;

thus, there is no contradiction with Paramaśiva being the root cause. [Reply: No, because this [passage] is seen to teach that the creation of the elements and so forth occurred from Nārāyaṇa, and therefore it refers to a creation at the beginning of a Great Kalpa (*mahā-kalpa*) and so forth, as indicated by the phrase "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed," which excludes all others.

Furthermore, because the conceptualization of the *rasa* [of the narrative] for the purpose of establishing its persistence at the time of the beginning of creation is inconsistent, one might object: "Is it not the case that since there is an injunction to recite all narratives during the *pāriplava*, this [passage]—which occurs when those weary from hearing the remainder of the meaning [of the Veda] are addressed with two narratives—is restricted to the exclusion of Brahmā, Īśāna, and others mentioned in the supplementary portion of the sentence 'Neither Brahmā nor Īśāna,' etc., and thus has no other purpose? If you say this, we reply: No.

Because it is impossible for a statement heard for the first time to be restricted by its [subsequent] meaning, [the word "first"] cannot be restricted here in the passage, "This indeed is the first of sacrifices," to mean either the primacy of the Jyotiṣṭoma over all other sacrifices, or the primacy of the Jyotiṣṭoma as the enjoined element. This is because such restriction is refuted by the definition [of "first"], in accordance with the supplementary portion of the text which mentions only the *stoma* and the sacrifice in general, stating: "Whosoever approaches another sacrifice or ritual with this [Jyotiṣṭoma], he causes it to fail. Thus, there is no room for restriction.

Regarding the injunction "they should recite the *pāriplava*," which follows the rule "all narratives [are to be told] during the *pāriplava*": if one were to argue that this subsequent injunction is redundant, it must be understood as intended to restrict the scope by means of the specific details heard in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*). This restriction is necessitated by the force of the repeated injunction (*punarvidhi*) which acts as a delimiter; it is not based merely on the mention of specific items in the supplementary passage. In this case, however, although the exclusion of Brahmā and the others is already established by the exclusion of everything else, its explicit re-mention is justified by the fact that it serves a specific purpose. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

[This refers to] the capacity for bringing about contraction. Therefore, having raised the objection that the method of introducing a contradiction between your [proposed] properties—which is intended to demonstrate the state of abiding at the time of the great creation and so forth through the exclusion of all others by means of the passage beginning "There was indeed one" (*eko ha vai*)—does not ultimately apply to anything other than Nārāyaṇa and thus is not universally applicable, [the author] now explains that very method of such application. 49.
In the beginning, you alone, without a companion, arose from yourself to subdue even the lotus-seated Puruṣa, the Destroyer of the world;

yet that which was declared by the great Upaniṣads—that he is the Lord of Lakṣmī—does not find its ultimate fulfillment in you. It is true that the presentation here of Nārāyaṇa as the Creator proceeds with reference to his specific form (svarūpa), but it does not culminate in the embodiment of Supreme Śiva; does it not?

Since the Mīmāṃsakas have established that the verbal root *tviṣ* denotes the second modification (*vikāra*) known as "existence" (*sattā*), which is included within the state of origination, and because we observe such usages as "Lohita was born from Rohitā," "Vāsuki was born," and "his son became Bhava," the statement "Verily, Nārāyaṇa alone existed" is established as referring to the manifestation of Śiva at the time of the initial creation, prior to the birth of Brahmā, Īśa, and the others, while Nārāyaṇa alone remained. Therefore, his status as the root-source of the entire universe [is not contradicted].

There is no contradiction, because Brahmā and the others will be established as created by Nārāyaṇa; therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), Paramaśiva is obtained as the causal agent in their production. If the word *āsīt* (was) signifies "origination," then the restriction *ekaḥ* (one alone) serves to exclude everything else that possesses origination. Consequently, [the text] lacks the capacity to establish the existence of Paramaśiva. Even if some capacity were somehow present, [it would be like the statement] "This indeed is the first sacrifice," which [refers only to] the Jyotiṣṭoma.

She is the fulfiller of all sacrifices... having worshipped her... from the vision of that which is beyond [the three], the mention of the "three forms" (*trimūrti*)—which possesses contraction—is not intended to establish the true existence of the form of Paramaśiva, who is the root of all; for it would contradict many Śrutis [that teach otherwise]. Moreover, if there were such a contraction [of the number of liberated souls], then even according to the opponent's view, in order to preserve the support for the eternally free sages (*nityasūri*), one must admit that the [scriptural] intent is merely to exclude those who are other than the eternally liberated. Therefore, in various places...

Although usage [of the term] referring to *kāla* (time), *saṃsarga* (conjunction), and so forth is frequently observed in both the world and the Veda, nevertheless, here too—in this concluding section—due to compliance with a more powerful single *śruti* (Vedic passage), the procedure of Nārāyaṇa is not obtained; rather, because of the intent (*tātparya*) of the worship of Śiva, that usage refers specifically to the manifestation from Paramaśiva. For this very reason, in place of the expression "he was" (*āsīt*), the phrase "he appeared as the dispeller of darkness" (*prādurāsīttamonudaḥ*) is used, signifying the manifestation from Paramaśiva, the presiding deity of *tamas*.

It has been stated [that this is not the case]. Nor should it be suspected that the phrase "the non-arising of darkness" (*tamo'nudaya*)—ending with a future passive participle—is merely a qualifier of the one who is about to manifest, serving as an illustration of this direction. For, having established the state of the world as being in the form of darkness at the beginning of creation by means of the verse "This was then enveloped in darkness," the subsequent statement "Then the Blessed Self-existent One... describes a form that manifests; it is impossible for such a form to have been the presiding controller of the previously established darkness. Therefore, it is a qualifier of the one who manifests.

Furthermore, this would result in a lack of logical connection with the verse immediately following that addressed to Sāvitrī. For that [verse], being characterized by attributes such as being beyond the senses and being graspable, aims to exclude any distinction between the Supreme Lord and the "Self-born" (Svayambhū) under discussion. The phrase "one should say 'twenty-six'"—due to the restrictive force of the particle *eva* which negates the injunctive power [of the preceding part]—does not enjoin his state of being self-originated; rather, the portion "he manifested himself" (*svayamudbabhau*) functions as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the attribute of self-origination already referred to in the previous verse by the term "Self-born."

Furthermore, if the term "dispeller of darkness" (*tamo'nuda*)—which refers to the presiding lord over the darkness known as *māyā*, the primordial nature of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—were a qualifying attribute of Svayambhū, there would be no possibility of the contingency that he is distinct from the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), nor would there be any relevance to establishing his non-difference from Him. In this alternative view, however, by stating the manifestation of Svayambhū from the Lord who is the presiding lord of darkness, the contingency of his being distinct from Him arises; for it is logically untenable for the individual soul (*jīva*) to be Svayambhū.

To ward off the suspicion that there might be a plurality of Īśvaras due to the absence of a single Lord for that [Tamas] as well, and because its absence must be stated, the following verse— which intends to show that the Supreme Lord Himself, as the presiding deity of Tamas, becomes manifest at the beginning of creation in a different form consisting of the Nārāyaṇa-mūrti produced by a specific limiting adjunct (upādhi)— fits perfectly. Therefore, in the phrase "tamo'nudaḥ," the word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) denotes the source from which [Tamas] is separated, and the one who causes the manifestation is indeed the Supreme Lord.

Regarding the passage beginning with "praśaṃsitāram" (the one who praises), because it accords with the determination of the Supreme Brahman heard in the concluding portions of the scripture, it is established that Paramaśiva alone is the subject; thus, the conclusion also attains this same single meaning. Nor should it be argued that when the manifestation of the Self-born (Svayambhū) is mentioned, there is no need for a manifestor due to contradiction. For "self-born-ness" (svayambhutva) consists in not manifesting by one's own will without another [cause], and this is not contradicted even when a manifestor exists. Otherwise, [it would be impossible] compared to the sun and other such [manifestors].

Having manifested [as such]... because of the attainment of self-existence (*svayambhūtvāpatti*) and because of the identity of meaning (*ekārthya*), even when that [word *damana*] is mentioned, the word *damo nudaḥ* ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*) refers exclusively to Śiva.

Thus, through both logic (*nyāya*) and scriptural support (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that the *Mahopaniṣad*, which aims to establish that Nārāyaṇa—who has attained the state of Mahādeva—is the agent of the creation of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) headed by the elements (*bhūta*) and the sense organs (*indriya*). This is understood in the *Nārāyaṇīya* and other passages.

Even so, this same conclusion applies to what is seen [in other texts]. Nevertheless, how can there be the establishment of non-contradiction with all [scriptural evidence]? For in the mantra "yo brahmāṇam," in the mantra "yo devānām," and in the mantra "devānām īśvaraḥ," it is established that prior to the emergence of the gods, Brahmā was produced from Paramaśiva.

Furthermore, in the Śruti passage "atha viṣṇum" following these, and in the *Aṣṭamūrti-brāhmaṇa*, it is stated by that very same [text] that Viṣṇu and Rudra are his [Brahmā’s] creators. Also, [it is said]: "The golden egg... [emerged from] the ocean of Rudra."

From *vīrya* (potency), Brahmā first came into being there; Viṣṇu was born as Jātavedas, and so on, according to the Śruti. In the form of the deity named Rudra, a physical manifestation (*mūrti*) is produced from the *vīrya* cast into the *rasa* (fluid) by the one who identifies with the supreme form (*paramūrti*). That *vīrya* became an egg, possessing the luster of a thousand rays.

Viṣṇu entered that [egg] directly by the power of my Śakti; furthermore, by my command, he obtained the name Nārāyaṇa. Having raised the objection that—given the statements in the Vāsiṣṭha, Laiṅga, and other scriptures regarding the creation of Rudra by Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa, and given the system of the Mahopaniṣad and other texts which establish that the entire universe other than those two was created by Nārāyaṇa—it would be impossible to determine that Brahmā and Rudra were the creators [of Viṣṇu], he says: ||50||
In one aeon Brahmā arises from you, and in another Hari, and yet in another Hara; O Lord, you produce the first [of these], while the other two are produced subsequently.

Because of this, neither superiority nor even absolute isolation (kaivalya) belongs to anyone—so say those skilled in extracting the essential principles from the multitude of restrictive rules. On this point, the venerable Vāyu says:
Having gratified that father, the Supreme Lord, through austerity,
Rudra was created by Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa in a previous kalpa.
In another kalpa, Brahmā— who consists of Rudra, Viṣṇu, and the world—
likewise created the Lord Viṣṇu;
and again, Brahmā created Brahmā, and Bhava created Nārāyaṇa.
In this manner, throughout kalpa after kalpa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara [arise].
The great seers have described various accounts of the end of kalpas concerning those who are born as enemies to one another, each seeking victory over the other.

"Their power is explained as arising from their mutual interaction. Thus, the fault in asserting a state of inequality among them has also been shown by that very [author]: "Those who are intent on the obsession 'this one is superior' and 'that one is not' certainly become *yātudhānas* and *piśācas*; of this there is no doubt. So it is said.

And thus, just as when it is heard that "whatever he takes from the *juhū* is for the *prayājas*, and whatever he takes from the *upabhṛt* is for the *anuyājas*," there is a scriptural statement regarding the *ājya* in both the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt* being for the *prayājas* without distinction; yet, by setting aside that [general] statement, [the rule] "he pours together [the butter] at the *barhis*-offering" and "he pours together the *upabhṛt* [butter] for the *juhū*"—due to the specific context of the pouring together of the *upabhṛt* butter—is restricted to the scope of the specific preceding and succeeding *prayājas*. In the same way, in various scriptural passages, [the relationship] between the Ordainer, Viṣṇu, and this [sacrificer]...

The scriptural mention of [Viṣṇu’s] creative agency is established by the force of the supporting explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) cited above; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. By this, the reading of certain Śruti and Purāṇa texts has been addressed.

Any attempt to establish Viṣṇu as the supreme [deity] based on statements regarding his being the cause of Brahmā and Rudra is refuted, because there likewise exist statements concerning Brahmā and Rudra being the causes of their own respective qualities and forms. As for the claim that those [statements] refer to him [Viṣṇu] through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *sattva*...

That too is incorrect. For it is stated in numerous Purāṇas that "Then Brahmā, having arisen from that [state], beheld the world as empty. Furthermore, the *Sūtagītā* states: "He whose being (*sattva*) has entered into Māyā... he is Rudra and no other"; and the *Vasiṣṭharāmāyaṇa* states: "The gods, such as Hara and others, are *sattva*. His brothers said to him: "Rudra is served by *sāttvika* people; [he grants] liberation... and "One should worship... Since *sattva-yoga* is thus established even for Brahmā and Rudra, [the claim of Rudra's] being *tāmasa* is refuted by this.

Even the disparaging talk of fools is silenced. For me, who desires to bring about the destruction of this world for those beings who are constantly afflicted by the foul-faced cycle of existence and who long to find rest through the experience of self-bliss shining forth upon the departure of even a slight distraction; it is like a physician who, knowing the root cause of a disease, employs violence toward the patient in order to pacify the affliction caused by the seizing [of the illness]—for such a one, there is not the slightest [sin].

In this matter, skill (*naipuṇya*) alone is the operative factor, according to the principle stated in the *Śiva Purāṇa*. This is because [the Lord] is characterized as an ocean of unsurpassed compassion; because it is impossible for Him to be subject to the *guṇas* at the beginning of creation (*brahmadau*) and so forth;

because sleep, laziness, and the like—which are effects of *tamas*—are not established in Him; and because it is impossible to even suspect His subjection to them on the mere basis of *tamas* being present there. As for what is said in the *Vārāha*, *Gāruḍa*, and other Purāṇas regarding the forms of the *guṇas*...

The establishment of Viṣṇu’s superiority by demonstrating his causality with respect to Brahmā and Śiva, as well as his specific qualities such as being *sāttvika* and so forth, should not be considered a significant point of contention; for otherwise, in the *Kālikā-khaṇḍa* and other texts, the great sages headed by Anila and others would not have determined Rudra’s superiority therein. As it is said: "When you were under the influence of sleep in the ocean, you were seized by a mere fraction of a portion of *tāmasa* [quality]."

"Furthermore, how did you become *sāttvika*? and so forth; for such statements from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* and other texts would result in the determination of Rudra’s superiority as well. Therefore, [the opponent argues that] everything is merely intended as praise; enough of this attempt to characterize what is not a proper object of characterization. The essential point is that, consequently, even the three [deities] are indeed equal in terms of their fruit. Now, in the context of establishing the equality of the three, he presents the position favoring Rudra’s superiority along with its supporting arguments: ||51||

Some say that Hara is superior even to Druhiṇa (Brahmā) and Madhujit (Viṣṇu); in some places, the statement regarding his birth from those two refers only to a partial aspect [of his manifestation]. O Blessed One, some great sages—those who know the passages of the Śruti such as "Brahmā is higher than the High; Hari is higher than him; O Lord, Īśa is higher than him"—claim that Smarahara (Śiva) is superior to both Padmaviṣṭara (Brahmā) and Viṣṭaraśravas (Viṣṇu) in terms of name, form, conduct, attire, and so forth. Thus indeed says the venerable Parāśara: [The text continues with the citation from the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.]
From all the deities, the joyful Brahmā is remembered as supreme;
and from Brahmā, Mahāviṣṇu, the Puruṣa who protects all, [is supreme].
"Rudra, the direct cause of dissolution, is even higher than Viṣṇu"—thus it is said in the *Smṛti-gītās*.
Sūta also said:
"O best of the twice-born, you [should know] the supreme self-manifestation of Brahmā and the others."
"Even though they are equal, Rudra is the most excellent; there is no doubt in this.

Thus, Viṣṇu is remembered as the heart of Brahmā, and Śiva is remembered as the heart of Viṣṇu. Śiva is the one who joins the hearts [of the others]. Furthermore, [in the context of breath control], the *pūraka* is said to be liberation (*mukti*), the *kumbhaka* is called Viṣṇu, and the *recaka* should likewise be known as Śiva, who is beyond the perishable and the imperishable. These and other such points are to be understood from the *Kāśyapa-smaraṇa*, the *Gītāsāra*, and similar sources.

As for the descriptions found here and there of the manifestation of Brahmā or Śrīpati, he says that these too refer to His partial manifestations (*aṃśa*): "In some places... [and so on]. "The terrible [task] was spread out for me. "The Brahmins are the four-faced one.
For the sake of creation, from between the eyebrows and the nose of that Brahmā, specifically from his own place called Avimukta.
Thus say the best among the knowers of Vedānta:
Mahādeva, who is saluted by all the gods, is his partial incarnation.
"Having become Ardhanārīśvara, the treasury of compassion appeared.

Thus he stated this very same point in brief. In the *Rājadharmakaṇḍa*, the Lord Parāśara says that for the sake of creation, a son named Prabhṛti arose from the forehead of Brahmā; and in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*, Śaṅkara speaks thus to Śilāda:
By the command of that Lord who resides within the heart-lotus, a portion-born [being] emerged from the mouth of the Lord,
having burst forth from his forehead.
Thus, the portion [of Paramaśiva] is Saṃhārarudra; that is to say, he is born from him as a partial manifestation of a single part of his essence. And so it is stated in the Vāyusaṃhitā:
"The Great Lord Nīlalohita, designated by the Supreme Lord, having become the son and younger brother of Brahmā, bestows grace upon Brahmā."

The description of Rudra appearing as the son of Brahmā by the command of Paramaśiva, and the description of his appearance given in the *Āditya Purāṇa* and other texts—where he appears to fulfill a boon granted to Brahmā who had prayed, "I desire you alone as my son"—should be understood as intending the manifestation of a specific portion of him. This is because he is described in those very same texts as having been born from Paramaśiva at the beginning of a *mahākalpa* and as persisting until the end of the *mahāsaṃhāra*; whereas in the intermediate *kalpas*, such as the *Pādma* and *Vārāha*, he [reappears] again.

Furthermore, because it must necessarily be stated that the description of his manifestation during those intermediate kalpas (*pratyavāntarakalpa*) refers specifically to a particular aspect of him— due to his re-manifestation— it follows that even the manifestation of Rudra described in the *Droṇaparvan* as "then a person with three eyes on his forehead and a trident in hand was born, upholding truth, celibacy, and austerity," is the same one who, at Kailāsa, is said to be "by the side of the bull-bannered god, a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), tawny-eyed, preeminent through austerity, the Lord Nīlalohita."

By stating that Śrīkaṇṭha resides at the side [of Nārāyaṇa], even the Puranic usage is intended to signify an *aṃśāvatāra* (partial incarnation). Thus, whenever there is a description of Rudra’s inferiority to Pitāmaha (Brahmā) or Nārāyaṇa, that too is merely a display of inferiority from a worldly perspective—like that of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and other incarnations toward Daśaratha, Vasudeva, and so on—concerning specific partial manifestations designated by names such as Sthāṇu. However, regarding Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha, [the text speaks] in their primary forms (*mūlarūpa*). As for the inferiority of Rudra to [Viṣṇu], it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:

Thus was this arrangement made by Kṛṣṇa through the form of the *Sūtasaṃhitā*: "O Brahmins, Rudra, in his own form, shall perform service to Viṣṇu and Brahmā—who are himself, being his own manifestation—as their very non-modification (unchanging nature). O Brahmins, it is not merely out of compassion or a desire for the welfare of the worlds that Rudra performs service to the supreme Viṣṇu and Brahmā as his own manifestation; this is the truth that has been declared. In some places, there is a comparison [to this].

This meaning has been elaborated upon in the commentary on the eleventh verse. Thus, among the three, the view that Rudra is the most excellent (*vikatara*) is another position; this alone is accepted by all Śaivas. Even regarding those qualities and activities established in both Brahmā and Rudra, a designation of one as the other is seen everywhere based solely on the perception of a particular degree of proximity (*pratyāsakti-viśeṣa*), as in the statement: "He who knows [that] 'this is the other' and 'this is he,' etc. He who [knows] of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra...

[The opponent] has stated that [the distinction] is devoid of reality due to its non-existence. I shall establish [my position]... because of the scriptural statement regarding the recollection of [the Lord], and because they share a single purpose.

While one who is intent on establishing a distinction between the higher and lower [states] is subject to censure for exposing contradictions, there is no contradiction whatsoever even in demonstrating a gradation based on specific manifestations, as in the case of Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and the others, provided that the distinction exists in truth.

Let the investigation of other incidental qualifications rest for now. In any case, since the Blessed One, the supreme Śiva, who is accompanied by Umā, is established as the all-pervading one, he alone is to be worshipped by all; thus, while demonstrating the very purpose to be accomplished—the establishment of his status as the highest of all—he concludes [the section]. ||52||

"Let the three gods possess equal sovereignty, or rather, let Śthāṇu, who removes the fear of worldly existence, be superior among them. You alone are to be served by the entire world, for you are the gracious Supreme Śiva, the most excellent of all. Thus ends the establishment of the supremacy of the illustrious Sadāśiva over the universe in the *Śrīśivatatvaviveka*. It may be argued: "Granted that Śiva is the most excellent according to the manner stated above, nevertheless, his status as the one to be served by all is not thereby established."

Someone is served by another either because of their capacity to command or because of their ability to bestow rewards—just as a husband is served by his wife, or a king by his servant. For one whose service is not enjoined and who finds no delight in giving, even if they possess excellence, that excellence would not be a determining factor for being worthy of service. Indeed, a man superior to them would not become a servant to women simply because he is superior; nor would a greedy king be served by those seeking aid when there is another who gives more abundantly. Thus, in order to cut through the doubts of the dull-witted, which have been reinforced by the boastful talk of archers—
He establishes his state as one to be served by all. ||53||
You alone are the foremost object of service for all living beings; alas,
those base men who do not know this waste their lives in vain,
just as humans [are surpassed] by the gods, you who are accompanied by gods, asuras, and men.
O Paśupati, you have heard that these living beings are to be enjoyed like cattle.

Thus, it has been established that for all beings—including gods, asuras, humans, and others—worship of Śiva through their respective appropriate actions is mandatory. Now, he demonstrates that even among those [beings], for the gods and humans, and for the various social classes (varṇas), worship of Śiva in the form of the Liṅga is generally mandatory; and for ordinary men, worship in the form of praise, prostration, ritual service, meditation, fire-offerings (homa), and so forth, according to their own specific capacities, is likewise mandatory. ||54||
O Maheśa, the worship of Your liṅga is also eternally known through the words of the sages as the supreme duty for the four classes of gods and the four castes here on earth,
according to their respective capacities.
Even this—service to the pair of your lotus feet—has been attained.
Even among all human beings, and especially among the twice-born, it is clearly observed that the lotus feet of Śambhu are their refuge. (55)
"Indeed, for the twice-born, the Gāyatrī is the supreme object of worship;
it is well known that you are its presiding deity, O Blessed One.
Therefore, [I address] this beast among the twice-born who fails to serve your feet."
Even his entire conduct of virtuous deeds served as his clothing and ornament.
Even among the twice-born, [the author] demonstrates the necessity of the worship of Śiva for Brāhmaṇas through various means: "When [the scriptures] teach Śiva to the Brāhma�nas in the fire...
that state of being the inner controller (antaryāmitva), adorned with the young moon, [is taught] by a multitude of words recorded in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Āmnāya...

because of its abundance, the mountain-born [Śiva] declares to us that He is the deity. Having thus stated that the worship of Śiva is necessary for Brāhmaṇas in His form as the inner controller, now—
He shows that even by their very nature, those born in the Kali age [are such]. ||57||

"It is known from the Purāṇas that for those who have not yet attained [liberation], their destination is birth in a Brahmin family, especially in this current age. Therefore, having abandoned you, my mind shall resort to another; for even a learned man, though he be great, does not obtain his divine goal [if he abandons you]. Thus, by means of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of being an agent of dharma within *saṃsāra*, as established by external knowledge such as the Śrutis, there is the performance of one's respective duties, characterized by the propitiation of the Lord [Śiva] through the caste-adjunct (*varṇopādhi*), and characterized by the worship of the *liṅga*."

It has been established that for people like us, the worship of Śiva—characterized by devotion in the form of praise, salutation, and offerings according to one's capacity under the condition of being human, characterized by the state of being twice-born in the Kali age, and characterized by taking refuge under the condition of being a devotee—is mandatory. Now, he establishes this in general: even for one who seeks some minor fruit, the worship of Śiva alone must be performed for that purpose. (........... and to Gaṇeśa, and to the wise Kārtikeya.
The First Sūtra.

Because the world consists of female, male, neuter, and so forth, and because its effects are observed, there exists a creator; having withdrawn this [world], he creates it again. In the phrase "female, male, neuter, and so forth" (*strī-puṃ-napuṃsakādi*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) denotes a category (*prakāra*). This is because, according to the grammatical rule *bhuvādayo dhātavaḥ*, the word "and so forth" is explained as denoting a category even in the case of verbal roots (*dhātu*). Furthermore, in this context, "category" refers to a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*) within the manifold variety of the objects of words.

That is to say, it refers to a specific arrangement of parts (*avayava-sanniveśa-viśeṣa*). However, in the view that [the word *liṅga*] denotes the verbal proliferation (*śabda-prapañca*), its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is intended as the mode (*prakāra*). Here, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used with the elision of a gerund suffix (*lyap-lope*), just as one uses the expression "he looks from the palace" (*prāsādāt prekṣate*) in the sense of "having ascended the palace, he looked. There exists a creator of the world—the phenomenal expansion of objects (*artha-prapañca*)—which is perceived by having attained the forms of female, male, neuter, and so forth. Here, by demonstrating the diversity of the world through this qualification of the world, it is established that the creator possesses diverse knowledge (*vicitra-jñānavattva*).

In the view that the word *jagat* refers to the expansion of sound (*śabdaprapañca*), the meaning is that there exists a creator—the primordial speaker—of the world consisting of *nāda* and *bindu*, which is perceived as having the nature of female, male, and neuter. Alternatively, the ablative case is used in the sense of the instrumental; thus, the construction is: "there exists a creator of the world perceived in the forms of female, male, and neuter. Or again, *strīpuṃnapuṃsakāditvāj jagataḥ* is a single compound: "because the world originates from [the state of] being female, male, and neuter," meaning "it attains [its state] because of originating from female, male, and neuter. And because of [this] state of originating from female, male, and neuter...

The meaning is that the world is such [as it is] because of Him. Alternatively, the second reason is "because of being female, male, neuter, and so forth"; since the world is a specific configuration, the meaning is that there exists a creator. He states another reason: "because of the observation of effects. The word "effect" (kārya) here refers to the state of being an effect (kāryatva). For the state of being an effect is indeed observed in things such as sprouts; nevertheless, because the world is an effect, the meaning is that there exists a creator. Or else, first, the state of being an effect of the world is established by the reasons of its being female, male, neuter, and so forth, and its having parts (sāvayavatva).

It should be understood that it is not "the state of having a creator" (*sakartṛkatva*) that is being established, but rather [the existence of] a creator who is being established. Here, in this inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), because pervasion (*vyāpti*) is already well-known, the presentation of an example (*udāharaṇa*) is as in a proving inference (*sādhakānumāna*). And that Creator, having supported this twofold world, creates it; therefore, he is the Supporter (*dhara*), denoted by the word *Hara*, meaning the Lord (*prabhu*) whose nature is to bring forth, that is to say, the Master (*pati*). For the Master performs protection in the form of activity for that which exists in the form of potentiality (*śakti*), since the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is accepted. And its existence in the form of potentiality is as follows:

It is indeed the dissolution of the universe, for at that very moment, [the universe] dissolves into its material cause (*upādāna*). Dissolution is fivefold: one is the dissolution of the principles (*tattva*) and worlds situated within the *nivṛtti-kalā*; another is the dissolution of the principles and worlds situated within the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*; another is the dissolution of the principles and worlds situated within the *vidyā-kalā*; another is the dissolution of the principles and worlds situated within the *śānti-kalā*; and the fifth is the dissolution of the principles and worlds situated within the *śāntyatīta-kalā*, known as the Great Contraction (*mahā-saṃhāra*). Thus, Hara alone is the agent of these five types of dissolution.
The meaning is that Paraśiva alone, being the agent, is called the Lord (pati). For lordship consists in the performance of the fivefold cosmic acts (*pañcavidhakṛtya*) within the universe.

Among these, the performance of the threefold acts consisting of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal was stated in the first aphorism; however, the causality regarding the two acts consisting of concealment (*tirodhāna*) and grace (*anugraha*) toward individual souls is made explicit in the second aphorism. Therefore, because he performs the fivefold acts within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) composed of the moving and the non-moving, Hara alone is the Lord, and neither Brahmā nor Nārāyaṇa—this is the final conclusion.
Thus, the application [of the terms] should be understood in accordance with what has been stated; this concludes the first sūtra.
In the second sūtra, however, it is established that Hara performs two functions—namely, concealment and grace—with respect to the manifold of sentient and insentient beings.
By the power of her essence,
she causes [the world] to flow forth for men through their unified command.

"Other" means non-different by virtue of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Among sentient beings, [He is] non-different due to the pervasion of His own nature; among insentient things, He is perceived as non-different because He is cognized as being without distinction. For in this regard, only the *mantra* is perceived. Through the application of manifestation (*vyañjana*), there is nothing more than the *mantra*. The meaning is that Śiva likewise is perceived within the individual souls (*aṇu*) as being non-different from them. This other [Śiva], while remaining truly distinct, becomes eternal through the pervasion of the *mantra* alone. Such is the agent.

He brings about the transmigration (*saṃsṛti*) of individual souls (*aṇu*)—who are divided into the categories of *sakala*, *pralayākala*, and *vijñānakala*—characterized by the concealment of their status as enjoyers (*bhoktṛtva*).

This he effects through a cooperative cause consisting of [the body] and by means of an instrument (*karaṇa*) whose nature is the interruption of the soul's own inherent [powers], which is synonymous with ignorance (*ajñā*). The meaning is that He bestows both worldly experience (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). Thus, due to His pervasiveness, He is not other than [the soul]; yet, He is not the agent [of the soul's bondage], for He brings about the transmigration of souls through their own inherent ignorance in accordance with their karma.

The mention of "saṃsṛti" (transmigration) is an elliptical expression that includes liberation (*mukti*) as well. Thus, the meaning is that it bears fruit by bringing about both enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). For action (*karma*), which is indeed the auxiliary cause, is twofold, distinguished as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). That too is threefold, distinguished as bodily, vocal, and mental. Furthermore, action is threefold: accumulated (*sañcita*), commenced (*prārabdha*), and future (*āgāmi*). That which was earned over many previous births is the accumulated. Among those, the action that initiates the current body is the commenced. That too is threefold: commenced by desire (*icchā-prārabdha*), [commenced by ignorance, and commenced by destiny].

It is that which is undertaken by one's own desire and that which is undertaken through the desire of another. Furthermore, *prārabdha* (commenced karma) is threefold: the generative (*janaka*), the sustaining (*dhāraka*), and the experiential (*bhogya*).

During the period of experiencing *prārabdha*, future karma performed with the conceit of being its own agent—apart from Śiva, who is the true agent—is likewise of three kinds. Karma is also fivefold according to another classification: divided into the worldly (*laukika*), the Vedic (*vaidika*), the spiritual (*ādhyātmika*), the trans-mundane (*atimārgika*), and the mantric (*māntrika*). Among these, the worldly is...

That which brings about the enjoyment of the worlds situated within the *nivṛtti-kalā* is produced by *smārta* rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrifices and public works). That which brings about the enjoyment of the worlds pervaded by the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā* is the Vedic [karma], produced by sacrifices and other rites ordained by the Vedas. That which brings about the enjoyment of the worlds pervaded by the *vidyā-kalā* is the spiritual (*ādhyātmika*) [karma], produced by the meditations (*upāsana*) taught in the Vedas. [That which brings about the enjoyment of the worlds] pervaded by the *śānti-kalā*...

It should be understood that the *mārgika* [power] is produced by the practice of yoga and brings about the enjoyment of the worlds pervaded by the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*); whereas the *māntrika* [power] is produced by a specific practice of knowledge. Furthermore, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is of the nature of command (*ājñā*), is in reality one alone, yet it is designated in five ways according to its different functions as *ādiśakti*, *parāśakti*, *icchāśakti*, *jñānaśakti*, and *kriyāśakti*. Likewise, it is also designated by the distinctions of *vāmā*, *jyeṣṭhā*, and so forth. Similarly...

In Paraśiva she is called Śakti; in Vāgīśvara, Vāgīśvarī; in Sadāśiva, Manonmanī; in Īśvara, Maheśvarī; in Rudra, Raudrī; in Viṣṇu, Śrī; and in Brahmā, Sarasvatī—thus she is designated. For the category of the Lord (pati-padārtha), being in the state of dissolution (layāvasthā), the state of enjoyment (bhogāvasthā), and the state of authority (adhikārāvasthā), is one and the same, yet is designated in three ways. Through the forms of Para-nāda, Apara-bindu, Para-nāda, Apara-bindu, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, it is designated with nine divisions. The first four divisions are partless (niṣkala).

The fifth, however, is both *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts). The other four are *sakala*. Now, if it is asked how a single Sadāśiva can possess this dual nature of being both *sakala* and *niṣkala*, the answer is true; for there is no contradiction between his state of being *sakala* through his association with the *kalā* of exertion (*udyoga-kalā*) and his state of being *niṣkala* through his freedom from the impurity of limitation (*adhikāra-mala*). Furthermore, the category of the bound soul (*paśu-padartha*) is also expanded [to include these].

The construction is as follows: "No, not for us" (*neti naḥ*) means that there exists a subtle atom (*aṇu*) within the body, distinguished by its faculties (*indriya-viśiṣṭa*). This is the reason [for the existence of the self]. "No, not for us" (*neti naḥ*) is stated through the word *iti* (meaning "thus"), which arises from the intensity of the notion "no," or from the cognition of the cessation of the senses (*akṣoparati-bodha*). Furthermore, because there is no experience during deep sleep (*svāpa*), yet there is the state of being a knower (*boddhṛtva*) upon waking, the subtle atom exists within the body. By the phrase "no, not for us" (*neti naḥ*), it is explained: "no" (*naḥ*) refers to a negation (*niṣedha*) or the cognition of negation. Indeed, the word *ite* is a derivative of the root *iṇ* with the suffix *tasil* added to the fifth case ending of *indu*, signifying the cognition of that [negation]. For in a negation, there must indeed exist a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) distinct from the relation of the thing being negated. And thus: [The text continues: ...by this, it is said. "No, not for us"—from this negation, or from the knowledge of negation; the word *ite* is derived from the root *iṇ* with the suffix *tasil* following *indu* in the ablative case, expressing the cognition thereof. For in a negation, there is necessarily something else existing, namely the counter-correlative distinct from the connection of the object being negated. And so it is.

Regarding the negation of the soul as being atomic: since it must exist elsewhere [than the body] if it were not there, its existence as an atom would be established; however, due to sublation (*bādhāt*), you maintain that it is established as being the body itself. "From the intensification of 'mine-ness' (*mamatā*)," means from the intensification—that is, the heightening—of the notion of "mineness" (*madīyatā-buddhi*). From the indeclinable word *mama*, the suffix *tasil* is applied [to form *mamataḥ*]. Regarding the phrase "from the cognition of the cessation of the senses":

from the cognition, that is, the knowledge, of the cessation or departure of the senses (*akṣa*)—the eyes, ears, nose, and so forth—one realizes that the eye itself has perished, the ear, the nose, and likewise the possession of other sense organs [have perished].

Because the senses are not observed [as independent perceivers] when they have ceased their activity, and because the self, being conscious by nature, illuminates both itself and others, its cognition is easily attained. Furthermore, its existence as distinct from the body is established by its atomic dimension. As for the soul (*jīva*), it is not [merely] a particular aggregate of elements within the body; for, like the power of fire, the acceptance of this [soul] as a manifestation of those elements has already been refuted, since such a conception is untenable due to the non-observation [of the soul's qualities] during deep sleep when there is no experience. Thus it is said: "In deep sleep, there is no enjoyment."

In deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is indeed an absence of the experience of sensory pleasure or pain. For if the body were the self, then one lying on a bed of flowers while embraced by a beloved would experience that [sensory] enjoyment even then; yet, since the doctrine of the body as the self does not accept the existence of a supersensible sense-organ, there is an absence of its auxiliary conditions. It is improper to claim an absence of enjoyment [in this case], for if the atom (the self) is distinct from the body, there is certainly the experience of pleasure in the form "I shall sleep happily" during sleep. However, the experience of sensory pleasure and the like [is absent].

It does not arise precisely because of the absence of auxiliary factors such as the sense organs that transcend the senses; for in the doctrine of a self distinct from the body, the sense organ is not merely the physical globe perceived by direct observation. "Because of being the knower in cognition"—this very point already stated is established here by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Therefore, since an atom-sized living entity distinct from the body and the senses is necessary within the living body, and demonstrating that it is also distinct from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as an atom, he explains its atomic nature.
The Self, though distinct from the internal organ, is yet associated with it, like a minister with a king;
though abiding in the five states, its own powers of vision and action are obstructed by impurity.

"Ātman" refers to one whose powers of vision and action (*dṛkkriya*) are obstructed by impurity—that is, one whose powers of knowledge and action (*jñānakriyāśaktī*) have been obstructed by *āṇavamala*. It should be understood that by the term "impurity" (*mala*), both *māyika* and *kārmika* impurities are also included, because they possess the quality of veiling and coloring the limited vision. Such a self is distinct from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—characterized as mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*)—and from the principle of limited knowledge (*vidyā*). [This is expressed in such thoughts as: "my mind," "my intellect," "my ego," and "my ignorance."

Because even in those [states], an intensification of the sense of "mine-ness" (mamatā) is observed. Thus, others as well, like ministers and kings, act toward their respective duties only when accompanied by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

For in the waking state, one engages in enjoyment conjoined with both the external senses and the internal organs. In the dream state, however, having abandoned the external senses, one is conjoined with the internal organ. In deep sleep, however, having abandoned the intellect (buddhi), one is conjoined with the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) in its subtle state—which is distinct from the form of the mind—and which consists of the group beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa).

In the state of *turya* (the fourth) and the state beyond (*turyātīta*), because all the senses have ceased their activity, the analogy of the king and his ministers is stated to explain that the Self brings about the cessation of the form of sleep, like a king remaining in the innermost chamber of his harem. The essential meaning is this: even though its own powers of vision and action are obstructed by impurity (*mala*), the Self—which is distinct from the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—remains associated [with them] like a king with his ministers, and thus exists within the five states. These are the five states: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, *turya*, and the one called *turyātīta*. In this context, by the phrase "whose own vision and action are unobstructed by impurity," it is not... [text truncated].

The nature of the fivefold bond (*pāśa*), known as impurity (*mala*), power (*śakti*), action (*karman*), *māyā*, and the point (*bindu*), should be understood as having been described by way of indication. For impurity (*mala*) is like the husk of grain, the shell of a pearl, or the black crust on copper; it is not anything else. It is the obscurer of perception and action (*dṛkkriyā*), denoted by such terms as "mist," "darkness," and "ignorance. For the individual soul (*aṇu*), being by nature the Self, is omniscient like the Lord (*īśvara*). That omniscience of his is obscured by something, because it does not manifest. And that obscuring agent is indeed impurity alone. Furthermore, it is that which veils the Self, which is differentiated by various powers (*śakti*). As for *māyā*... [of that].

Because it is established as otherwise possible through causes such as time, necessity, limited capacity, knowledge, attachment, and so forth, that impurity (mala) does not cease even at the time of liberation through initiation (dīkṣā). For if one were liberated, there would be the undesirable consequence of everyone being liberated. Rather, only its powers (śaktayaḥ) are removed; or else, by means of mantra, it is rendered blunt, like the potency of poison.
Such is the nature of impurity.

The power of obstruction (*rodha-śakti*), however, is indeed the power of the Lord himself. Although it is by its very nature bestowing grace, it is metaphorically designated as the "power of obstruction" precisely because it conforms to the fetters (*pāśa*). Karma, characterized as merit and demerit, resides in the intellect (*buddhi*). When it functions within the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*)—specifically within the *bindu* and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*)—it is called "pure karma.
