On the other hand, on the impure path (*śuddhetarādhvan*), that which consists of *māyā*, *kalā*, and so forth, is a "fetter" (*pāśa*) because it brings about experience (*bhoga*) for the self when functioning within the impure *puryaṣṭaka*. *Māyā* itself is impure, insentient, and [consists of] the *kalās*; it is a fetter because it acts as a veil. For from *māyā*...

Time arises as the cause for the linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) of past, future, and present. In the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), however, time is pure and of the nature of the *bindu*. Following time, from *māyā* arises *niyati*. This is the cause of restriction (*niyamana*), because it ensures that actions yield their fruits only to the doer. After that, from *māyā* arises *kalā*; it manifests the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of the individual soul (*pāṇoḥ*). Following that is *vidyā*, which manifests the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).

Immediately after that, *rāga* (attachment), which manifests the power of desire (*icchā-śakti*), is distinct from the attributes of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*) and generates an addiction to sense objects; it is born from *kalā*. Following that, through the conjunction with the pentad beginning with *kāla* and ending with *rāga*, the [individual] attains what is called the *ātma-tattva* (the principle of the self). Then, from *māyā* by way of *kalā*, *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is born. From that, the three *guṇas*—characterized by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—which produce pleasure, pain, and delusion, are born. And because those *guṇas* are absolutely non-different from *prakṛti*, even by the metaphor of "receiving a son,"...

At the conclusion of the *Gṛhya-sūtras*: From the *guṇas* and through the process of *prakṛti*, the intellect (*buddhi*) arises, characterized by determination and known as *mahat*. It possesses eight states (*bhāvas*): among them, virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and power (*aiśvarya*) are *sāttvika*; lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*) is *rājasa*; and non-virtue (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), and lack of power (*anaiśvarya*) are *tāmasa*. Thus, the cognitive modifications (*pratyayas*), which are divided into forty-two varieties according to their powers, are also its attributes. Thereafter, through the division of the intellect into *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*, [it becomes] the *taijasa* (active) and *vaikārika* (transformative).

The egoities (ahaṃkāra) are named *bhūtādi* and so forth; therein, from the *taijasa* egoity, the five organs of cognition—named hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell—and the internal organ, the mind (*manas*), arise. From the *vaikārika* egoity, however, the five organs of action—known as speech, feet, hands, anus, and genitals—and the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) are born. From the *bhūtādi* egoity, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are born. Among those, from the subtle element of sound arises space (*ākāśa*); from the subtle element of touch arises air (*vāyu*).

From the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*) comes fire; from the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*) comes water; and from the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*) comes earth. Among these, sound is the sole quality of space (*ākāśa*); wind (*vāyu*), however, possesses sound and touch; fire possesses sound, touch, and form; water possesses sound, touch, form, and taste; and earth possesses all five qualities: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Thus, there are thirty-one principles (*tattvas*) consisting of: time, destiny, limited agency (*kalā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), attachment (*rāga*), the person (*puruṣa*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the qualities (*guṇas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*citta*), the five organs of action, the five organs of knowledge, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*), and the five gross elements (*bhūtas*).

They arise as follows: there are one hundred and eight worlds (*bhuvana*) within the principle of earth (*pṛthvī-tattva*) situated in the *nivṛtti-kalā*; fifty-six worlds within the principles from *a-gha* up to *prakṛti* situated in the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*; and twenty-seven worlds within the principles from *puruṣa* up to *kalā* situated in the *vidyā-kalā*. Thus, Māyā is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), consisting of the aforementioned worlds and principles. The Great Māyā (*mahāmāyā*) is called the Bindu (*bindu*). It is of the nature of purity, eternal, and serves as the material cause of the pure path; and it is that [Māyā].

Consisting of sound, from Mahāmāyā arise the five kalās—Śāntyatītā, Śānti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti—as well as Nāda, Bindu, Akṣara, and Mātṛkā. Among these, the Śiva-tattva first arises from Bindu; therein are four worlds. Immediately after the Śiva-tattva, the Śakti-tattva arises from Bindu;
therein are eleven worlds. Following the Śakti-tattva, the Sādākhya-tattva arises from Anubindu; therein is one world. Immediately after the Sādākhya[-tattva] is the Īśvara-tattva.

In that regard, there are eight worlds (*bhuvana*s). Immediately after the principle of Īśvara (*īśvaratattva*) is the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*). Therein are nine worlds. And this Mahāmāyā, although conducive to lower liberation (*aparamukti*), is called a "bond" (*pāśa*) because it is not conducive to supreme liberation (*paramukti*). Thus, the nature of the five bonds should be understood in brief. In this way, by means of two aphorisms, the category of the bound soul (*paśu*) has been explained together with the category of the bond (*pāśa*). Now, having raised the objection that the Lord (*pati*)—the category of the impeller of the aforementioned bound soul—is subject to transformation, he refutes it with the fifth aphorism.
They find.
The senses are won by the person, but he himself is not won by Śambhu;
if Śiva were subject to modification, O child, he would not be the beloved who leads one there.

The senses (*akṣāṇi*), presided over by the Person (*pums*), perceive and know objects such as sound and the like. Yet that Person does not preside over them independently; rather, he is impelled solely by Śambhu. [Objection: If Śambhu is the impeller of bound souls (*paśu*), then Śiva too would be subject to modification (*vikārī*). But you have not said this. For Śiva is not an impeller by means of instruments (*karaṇa*); rather, he is the beloved one who, through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) and in reality through mere proximity (*sannidhi-mātra*), acts like a magnet upon iron.
He impels [the soul] by his mere presence alone; likewise, that Śiva also leads—that is, impels—that person by his mere presence, meaning that he does not undergo any modification.

Thus, the refutation of [Śiva’s] susceptibility to modification is established by the fifth sūtra. Here, the proof of the bound soul (*paśu*) is through [Śiva’s] being the presiding controller of the senses; and by the proof of that [controller], the proof of Śiva follows. If those [senses] were not [understood as] governed by a Lord, there would be no proof of the Lord at all. Furthermore, in inference, [the subject] would be something to be known, and [the conclusion] would be... [incomplete].

If it is argued that even for Maṇu inference is stated therein regarding Īśvara, [the response is: the Nigamas and Āgamas are indeed the authority there; their validity must be asserted on the basis of being the word of a trustworthy person (*āptavākya*) because they were spoken by Him. But that is not possible if Īśvara is unestablished. For the establishment of Īśvara depends on the validity of the Nigamas and Āgamas as having been spoken by Him, and the establishment of Īśvara from the validity of those [texts] involves the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). He dispels this doubt [with the following]: "If He were invisible, His non-existence would follow; if He were visible, He would be insentient. To this, the answer is:

"The wise know the form of Śambhu to be such. Regarding the doubt: "If it were invisible"—that is, if the own-form (*svarūpa*) of Śiva or of the individual soul (*aṇu*) were invisible, being beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then there would be non-existence; or if it were visible—that is, if the own-form of Śiva or of the individual soul were known through the attainment of the means of valid cognition—then there would be insentience (*jaḍima*, *jāḍya*). To that, the answer is: "The wise know the form of Śambhu to be such," meaning they know it by avoiding both those defects, through the mental modifications (*buddhivṛtti*) derived from the Vedas and Āgamas, knowing it as the object of the manifest power of consciousness (*vyaktacicchakti*).

The meaning is that the authority of the *Nigamas* and *Āgamas* is easily established precisely because they are accepted by the great multitude (*mahājana*); thus, there is no suspicion of circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*). Indeed, the nature of Śiva is directly realized through one's own experience via meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which is assisted by reflection (*manana*) and contemplation (*nididhyāsana*), preceded by hearing the *Nigamas* and *Āgamas* and the grace of a Guru following initiation (*dīkṣā*). Since He is an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) and yet self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*), there is no suspicion of His being a mere void; this was argued in the sixth aphorism. Thus, even as the Knower of the insentient phenomenal world (*jaḍaprapañca*), Śiva—who is the object of knowledge—is [established].

[The author] strengthens the proof of the existence of the category of *paśu* (the bound soul): "In the presence of the non-conscious (*acid*), one does not know; nor do those two [consciousness and the non-conscious] know each other. He who is the knower of both the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and Śiva is the Self (*ātman*), distinct from them. Regarding the phrase "not the non-conscious" (*nācid*): he who is the knower of both the phenomenal world and Śiva is the Self; and he is distinct from them, having a nature different from those two. Because he is the knower of Śiva, whose nature is Being (*sat*), he is of the nature of Being; because he is the knower of the phenomenal world, whose nature is non-being (*asat*), he is of the nature of non-being. Thus, by virtue of being both Being and non-being, he is separate from those two.

This is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Let non-conscious matter (*acit*) itself be the knower of Śiva; why then is that [consciousness] the knower? To this he says: "Non-conscious matter does not know consciousness in its proximity," and so on. The meaning is that, just as darkness cannot exist in the presence of light, non-conscious matter—precisely because it is produced by [the power of] consciousness—cannot know consciousness. Thus, the Lord does not know non-conscious matter through conceptualization (*savikalpa-nayā*). The sense is that the quality of being an omniscient knower is irrelevant to the present context, and what is intended here is that [omniscience] which is not limited by time (*kālānavacchinna*). Now, one might further object: "Let Śiva himself be the knower of Śiva; why [seek another]?"

If it is argued that this [cognition] belongs only to the individual soul (*jñātṛtāṇu*), it is not so; for the subject under discussion is that which is to be known by the manifestation of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) through the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) produced by the Vedas (*nigama*) and Agamas. Furthermore, such knowledge does not even exist in Śiva’s own essential nature (*svarūpa*), because despite being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*), he lacks the state of being a knower of himself by means of that same power of consciousness. Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the Self alone is established as the knower of both the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and Śiva. In the presence of Consciousness and in the presence of Śiva, there is no non-consciousness at all; how then could those two know non-consciousness? They are both Consciousness itself.

The insentient (acit) and the Lord (cit) do not know one another; they do not perceive each other. According to the manner stated, the meaning should be understood through the method of positive concomitance (anvaya) as follows: that which is distinct from both the phenomenal world (prapañca) and Śiva, who are the speakers [of those two], is the Self (ātman). Thus, by means of the seventh aphorism as well, the existence of the Self is established through the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya). Having thus described the nature of the bound soul (paśu) in its isolated state and its state with attributes (sakala), he now begins to describe the nature of the bound soul in its pure state (śuddhāvasthā).
"Having remained [in this state], you do not perceive [the Self] along with the senses and the hunter"—this is the awakening.
Having abandoned those [senses], the other, the blessed one, attains that state of Śiva.

Regarding the word "having remained": it means by means of the support of the Guru in the form of the Teacher, and by Śiva acting in accordance with the descent of His power (*śaktipāta*), [one receives] the initiation through scripture which is visual, tactile, mental, or cognitive.

Having performed there the initiation of yoga—whether with seed (*sabījā*) or without seed (*nirbījā*), granting immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadā*), characterized by Śiva (*śivadharmiṇī*), characterized by the world (*lokadharmiṇī*), the initiation of the observances (*samayadīkṣā*), the special initiation (*viśeṣadīkṣā*), the purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvaśodhinī*), and the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*)—the preceptor addressed the prince, saying: "O child, you have been dwelling together with Vyā... and the [other] senses, yet you do not perceive or know You. Thus enlightened by his preceptor, the prince was awakened.

Having abandoned the senses like Kirātas, through the contemplation of identity with Him—thinking "I am Śiva, who is non-dual"—and having heard that state, which possesses a form equal to such a Śiva, the prince abandons his royal nature and attains the state of Śiva. For the state of Śiva is characterized by uncontracted knowledge and sovereignty. Therefore, the essential meaning is that one who knows Śiva attains Śiva-hood. Thus, it should be understood that the eighth aphorism has declared the pure state of the individual soul (aṇu).

The ninth sūtra states what must be done by one who has attained the state of purity: "Having seen the Lord within the self through the ray of consciousness, and having abandoned the mirage-like mental fluctuations, the wise man, having obtained the shadow of the state of Śiva, should meditate upon the five-syllabled mantra. That wise man, by means of the ray of consciousness—that is, by the vision of the power of consciousness (cicchakti)—having seen the Lord within the self and realized Him directly, crosses over the mirage of worldly existence (saṃsāra-marīcikā). He then attains the "shadow of the state of Śiva," which refers to the two feet of Śiva consisting either of mantra or of power (śakti). Upon reaching that, he should meditate on the five-syllabled mantra.
Having obtained the shade of the feet—that is, having attained the grace of Śiva—one should meditate upon the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*). One should contemplate, "I am Śiva.

Although there is indeed no identity with Śiva within oneself, nevertheless, through the contemplation "I am He," one should shatter the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*) by means of the mantras, just as the power of poison is shattered by the contemplation of oneness with Garuḍa; such a person is "wise"—this is the sense. The meditation on the meaning of the five-syllabled mantra is as follows: by the word *namaḥ*, which denotes the state of being the source (*prabhavatva*), the contemplation of identity is expressed. By the word *śiva*...

Likewise, meditation on the five-syllabled mantra "Śivo 'haṃ asmi" (I am Śiva) is to be understood. Thus, by the ninth Sūtra, [the author] declares what is to be done by one who has attained the state of purity.

By the tenth aphorism, he correctly elucidates that which is to be accomplished: "Unity with Śiva. One who has attained unity with Śiva is a perfected being (*siddha*) whose own functions are dependent upon Him; he becomes untouched by impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and so forth, and possesses self-experience. Regarding "unity with Śiva": having attained unity with Paraśiva means having known it. The suffix *-kta* is used here in the sense of the agent according to the rule beginning with "gatyartha" (Pāṇini 3.4.72), and roots meaning "to go" also carry the sense of "to know. Now, one might object: "In this context, by the word 'unity' (*aikya*), is it not a formless unity, like the reflection of the moon's disc? [The answer follows: It is indeed so.

What indeed is intended by the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva? Is it an identity through sublation (*bādha*), as in the case of "this is a thief" or "this is a post," where there is a negation of one for the sake of the other; or rather, an identity through transformation (*pariṇāma*), like gold and a bracelet; or perhaps an identity through inherence (*samavāya*), like the blueness and the lotus in "the blue lotus"; or else an identity due to the mutual commingling of attributes, like fire and its mass; or finally, an identity through inseparable conjunction (*apṛthagbhāva-saṃyoga*), like water in a pond and its moss, ghee and milk, or the ocean and the salt in the rivers and the crops?

Or else, there is non-duality through contact from time immemorial, like that of sesame seeds and their oil; or rather, non-duality through the cultivation of identity, like that between Garuḍa and his mantra-practitioner;
or perhaps non-duality by virtue of dissolution, like water on heated iron; or else non-duality through the performance of prescribed acts of union, like two lumps of clay;

or again, non-duality while remaining unmanifest, like the fire-stick and its fire; or even non-duality through suppression, like the light of a lamp and the light of the sun; or what is it but the union of a lover and his beloved?

[The opponent claims: "There is unity due to the experience of bliss, or else there is unity due to mutual affection, like that between two friends. First of all, among these fourteen positions, the first position is not possible, because it would result in falling into the doctrine of the Māyāvādins (Advaitins). Nor is this desirable, as it would entail a contradiction with the non-dualistic scriptures (*bāhyāgama*) which are engaged in refuting that very doctrine. The second [position] is not [possible], because the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva is not admitted to be sublated. The third is not [possible], because the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of both is not admitted. Nor is the fourth [possible], because the inherence (*samavāya*) of the two is not accepted in the teaching of Śiva (*śivaśāsana*).

[The first alternative is rejected] because it is not established. Nor is the fifth [alternative valid], because the mixing of the two properties is not accepted by our established doctrines (*siddhānta*). Nor is the sixth [valid], because a conjunction between two inactive [entities] is impossible; for that very reason, the seventh is also not [valid], since it would entail the possibility of disjunction at some point. Nor is the eighth [valid], because that would lead to the consequence of [the self being] non-eternal. Furthermore, that which establishes the cognition of a false unity would result in not being a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), since it would lack the nature of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). This is also true for the delusion regarding the unity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the body.

Furthermore, [the eighth alternative] would entail that [liberation] has liberation itself as its cause. Nor is the ninth [alternative] possible, because in this teaching, the merging (*ekalaya*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva is not admitted. Nor is the tenth [alternative] possible, because even if the action producing conjunction were to bring about a state of equality, it could not logically bring about identity; moreover, it is impossible to effect a conjunction between two things that are eternally unconnected. Nor is the eleventh [alternative] possible.

It cannot be the first [type of identity], because if identity were based merely on the manifestation of what was previously unmanifest, it would follow that the water in a well manifested by digging would be identical to the water in the ocean; furthermore, it would entail the loss of even the slightest light of the individual soul (*jīva*), just as the fire in the fire-drill wood (*araṇi*) loses its distinctness. Nor can it be the twelfth, because since the *jīva* and Śiva are equal, mutual sublation is impossible. Nor can it be the thirteenth, because identity is untenable between two things whose difference is manifest merely through the experience of bliss; moreover, since Śiva is the constant experience of bliss, an example contrary to that is inappropriate. Nor can it be the fourteenth, for therein...

Because Bheda (difference) is extremely clear, there is an absence of identity [between the two]. Furthermore, while Śiva is always affectionately disposed toward all things, both moving and unmoving, the individual soul (jīva) is occasionally joined with affection, friends, and enemies. Therefore, if it is asked what the proof is [for their identity], it is replied: just as one might say "the gavaya is indeed a cow," so too "this jīva is indeed Śiva"; thus, the absolute similarity between the jīva and Śiva is itself their identity. Nor should it be argued that identity must be a mere figurative identity based on similarity in every respect; for it is said: "This liberated one shines like Śiva; he is indeed Śiva, not of two kinds."

This is because what is intended to be expressed is precisely the similarity to the yoga of the pure power of consciousness (*nirmalacicchakti*) as described in the *Mataṅga* and other Āgamas. If it is argued: "Even for the liberated soul (*mukta*), there would follow the performance of the five cosmic acts (*pañcakṛtya*) through the possession of omniscience and so forth; and thus, the fallacy of asserting multiple gods (*anekaiśvaravāda*) would ensue," we reply: No. For in such passages as, "And they do not perform creation and so forth, since they are established in their own self and intent on their own welfare," the scriptures declare that they lack the agency of performing creation and the rest. Nor does it follow that the liberated souls, being devoid of the office (*adhikāra*) of Śiva, possess any superiority over those who hold the office of performing the cosmic acts.

It must be stated that [liberation] has been attained. Even though there is equality in the experience of bliss, the acts of restraint (*nigraha*) and favor (*anugraha*) belong to Śiva alone; for in that regard, there is superiority over the liberated person. This is because, even when a man who has received great wealth from a king and the king himself share an equal experience of their own great enjoyment, one observes superiority in the king alone, who possesses the power of command (*ājñā*) that the other lacks. If it is argued that, just as in the case of the king, Śiva too would be subject to suffering through the activity of performing such tasks as the restraint of others, we say no. It is merely by way of *līlā* (divine play).

Since Śiva, by his mere presence and without any exertion, effects all [the necessary] qualifications [for liberation], it is impossible for him to be subject to the suffering of a king. Now, if it is asked, "For what purpose does Śiva perform such a divine play (līlā)?

we reply: it is solely out of supreme compassion for living beings. Nor should it be argued, "How can Śiva be compassionate if he himself, through creation and so forth, defiles the already impure individual souls (paśus)? For there is no fault in adding impurity to those who are already naturally impure, just as a washerman who cleans clothes that are inherently dirty is not at fault.

Furthermore, because we do not observe any practice of defiling [the soul] with cow dung and the like; and because there is no doubt that Śiva—who, through the exhaustion of karma by means of the experience possible within the creation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) when impurity has matured, removes the impurity of bound souls (*paśu*) via initiation—is the source of supreme compassion. Nor should it be argued that such a desire could exist toward those already liberated;
for it would be irrelevant for Him, who previously emerged from being submerged in the ocean of suffering and is now submerged in the ocean of bliss, to engage in such play. Nor...
It should not be argued that it is impossible for Śiva—the signifier of the unsurpassed, eternal, pure, and supreme ocean of bliss—to engage in playful activity (*līlā*).

For His creative operations, such as the acts of creation and so forth, proceed through an beginningless succession and are thus beyond questioning. In the world, when an action is being performed by a person through a traditional lineage, if that person were to perish or be absent, and if the capacity [to continue] were still possible, then the intervention of another similar person would be feasible. However, this is not the case here.

Since the powers of destruction and proximity cannot be attributed to Śiva—who is eternally pervasive and ever-capable—therefore, the agency of creation and so forth belongs to Śiva alone, and not to the liberated soul (*mukta*). Thus, the identity between the liberated soul and Śiva consists solely in their similarity through the conjunction with the stainless power of consciousness (*cin-māyā-śakti*). In reality, however, there is an eternal, beginningless and endless inherence (*samavāya*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva. Nor is there an initial conjunction between this *jīva* and Śiva, like that between a jar and space, nor even an eternal conjunction like that between husk and grain.
Nor can there be an adventitious conjunction (*ādisamavāya*) like that between grain and salt, nor an innate conjunction (*anādisamavāya*) like that between sesame and oil.

Rather, only a beginningless and endless conjunction, such as that between Śiva and Śakti, is possible. Regarding the existence of this conjunction between these two—the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva—the scriptural statement is the authority: "Being one through pervasion, yet not different, he abides like fragrance in a flower or like oil in sesame. Thus, the meaning is that he possesses the experience of his own bliss through the knowledge of this unity.

"Dependent on Him for his own activity" means dependent on Śiva for his own activity; that is to say, he is possessed of knowledge. Being "perfected" (siddha), the Śiva-yogin, remaining untouched by impurity (mala), māyā, and so forth, becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and possesses self-experience. Some maintain that by his own power of consciousness (cicchakti), he also possesses the experience of the bliss of Paramaśiva. Others hold that one who is liberated while living experiences only the bliss of Paramaśiva. Because he is immersed in the waters of bliss, [he possesses] his own uncontracted nature consisting of vision and action (dṛkkriyā).

Others maintain that he experiences only the bliss of his own self (*svātmānanda*). The truth is that, in every respect, one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) must be possessed of the experience of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). In reality, however, for one who is liberated from the very beginning, only the experience of his own bliss is to be admitted, and not the experience of the bliss of Śiva. This is because the bliss of Śiva-nature is inherently pure.

Because it is capable of being experienced by Śiva, who is pure by nature, the bliss of the power (*śakti*) of the individual soul—which is either obstructed by impurity (*mala*) or liberated from it—is capable of being experienced only by that very soul when it is liberated from impurity. Nor should it be argued that immediately after liberation, the soul, like Śiva, possesses such purity that it experiences the bliss of Śiva;

for it is impossible for one who is immersed in the flavor of his own indivisible experience to experience another form of bliss. This is just as it is impossible for a single female body to simultaneously experience the pleasure of two different men.

Because the bliss of Śiva and Śakti cannot be experienced simultaneously by both the individual soul (jīva) and Śiva; nor should it be said that the liberated one lacks the experience of bliss altogether. For it is stated in the Kāmika and the Vidyāpāda: "Even though he is like Śiva in being fully liberated and omniscient, the supremely liberated one neither acts nor knows, like an infant.
When his consciousness is graced by the Guru’s compassionate gaze..."
Then, this primordial power of that person flows forth.
Unconditioned by space and time, free from affliction and unimpeded—
having known the Self through such characteristics, one rejoices; and by means of this [knowledge],
one may plunge undisturbed into the great ocean of innate bliss.
That is liberation, for that is indeed Nirvana; that alone is the supreme state.
O best of the twice-born, that state is sought after by all sages and yogis;
even those who attain that state do so through the yoga of Śaiva practice.
They too, having attained the supreme state which is the ultimate joy at the end of their stay,
do not perform creation and so forth, because they are established in their own self for the sake of the welfare [of all].
And likewise in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Established in the self alone, pure, one should become like Śiva in every respect.
In that very same [text]:
The omniscient, supreme, and immutable Lord, like Śiva, is established solely within his own pure self and is complete in all his limbs.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"At the end of the dissolution, having abandoned the body, one remains established in one's own self (*svātman*).
In the *Sūtasaṃhitā*, within the *Bṛhadgītopaniṣad*: [text follows].
The pure-souled one always performs the sport of delight within the Self alone;
thus, being united with the state beyond all categories (niṣṭattya), he is liberated—this is the certainty of the scripture.

"Since consciousness is of the nature of bliss, the true nature of the Self manifested upon the removal of the three impurities"—by such statements, although the individual soul (*jīva*) is of the nature of consciousness and bliss just like Śiva, there is no contradiction. Nor should it be argued that even though the soul possesses its own bliss, it does not perceive its own bliss due to being enveloped by darkness (*tamas*), but instead experiences only the bliss of Śiva through His power; for we observe that when one's own inherent taste or other qualities are not perceived—such as in the case of a gem—the taste and other qualities belonging to the object are perceived. [This is so] because of the [functioning of the] sense organs... [indriya...]

Because there is no contradiction in the apprehension of the bliss of the individual soul (*jīvānanda*), which was previously unapprehended due to its state of having the [five] senses as its final limit, once it is apprehended at the time of the removal of the stainless [veil], since that [veil] has been set aside by the stainless power (*vimala-śakti*). This is unlike the case of the coarse veils such as *mala* and so forth, where the apprehension remains defective even after their removal, because the cloth and other such coverings remain. Nor is it the case that the liberated one, like Śiva, possesses the sixfold attributes such as omniscience;

for it is said: "By the rays of consciousness empowered by the radiance of Śiva’s solar power, the practitioner, abiding in the self, perceives Śiva together with Śakti and the rest."* *Note: The term *vrati* refers to the ascetic or practitioner of yoga.*

It should not be argued that by describing [the soul] as a perceiver of Śiva accompanied by powers (*śakti*) and so forth, the experience of Śiva-bliss (*śivānanda*) also follows; for then it would follow that the bliss of the liberated (*mukta*) is also experienced. Nor is this desired, because it would follow that the bliss of a transmigrating person (*saṃsārin*) is also experienced. Nor can it be said that there is no such fixed rule, for that would result in the experience of suffering. Furthermore, it would follow that even Śiva would experience that suffering in order to establish his omniscience. However, for the omniscient yogin, there is indeed the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of bliss. That...

If it is argued that direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) does not constitute the experience of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) because the human goal consists solely in the direct realization of one’s own functioning pleasure (*svavṛtti-sukha*), we say: not so. For even the bliss of Śiva lacks the status of being one’s own functioning state; therefore, the experience of that [bliss] cannot be the human goal for a liberated person. Nor should it be said: "Just as a lover embraced by his beloved experiences that [bliss], let there be an experience of such bliss for the liberated one who is equal to Śiva, through the intense embrace brought about by the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of oneness with Him. This is because the liberated one is not [identical to] the intense [embrace of] Śiva—

Through embracing, there is the experience of Śiva’s bliss; however, that experience of one's own bliss occurs by virtue of being the cause for that embrace. It is Śiva alone who experiences Śiva-bliss. Indeed, through the firm embrace of his beloved, a lover does not experience the beloved’s bliss; rather, through that embrace, he experiences only his own bliss. For the beloved as well, it is only the experience of her own bliss, and not the experience of the lover’s bliss, because the two blisses are distinct. [Objection: But is it not like rivers that have attained oneness with the ocean?

If it is argued that for liberated souls who have attained oneness with Śiva, there is likewise a lack of awareness of their own name and form—specifically, a lack of awareness of the bliss of their own nature—that is true. In that case, let there be a loss of awareness of one's own name and form due to the fact that the river, being small in comparison to the ocean, is overwhelmed by the ocean which possesses vast majesty and immeasurable roar. However, in the case of the liberated soul and Śiva, since they possess equal greatness and their qualities are not deficient in relation to one another, there is no mutual subjugation; thus, the two distinct aspects of their own essential nature and bliss do not exist as separate entities.

How is there manifestation? Even in the world, when two persons of great majesty and equal qualities associate, the qualities of both are manifested through their renown. However, when two persons of unequal status associate, the qualities of only the superior person are seen to be manifested; the qualities of the inferior person, being overwhelmed, do not manifest. [Objection: But is it not said, by such statements as "being other yet non-other due to pervasion, existing like oil in sesame seeds," that [the individual] has attained the manifestation of Śiva?

If it is argued that the individual soul (jīva) experiences both its own non-differentiated bliss and the bliss of Śiva, then surely there would follow the undesirable consequence that it would also experience the bliss of other liberated persons who are non-different from Śiva and non-different from itself. Nor is this a desired conclusion, for it would also entail the experience of the suffering of transmigrating beings. Furthermore, even if one were to argue for the pervasion of the individual soul and Śiva—who are non-different from Śiva—on the grounds that they are like the fibers within a cotton seed or the seeds within a tamarind fruit, [this would not resolve the issue].

How can a virtuous person accept that the experience of bliss by the Mother, who is Śiva’s Śakti, is forbidden? For it has been described thus: "She alone is the supreme limit, subtle, consisting of the nectar of all directions, free from beginning and end, and virtuous; she is figuratively designated as having a form. Such descriptions have been made regarding the virtue of Śiva’s Śakti. Furthermore, if one were to describe the enjoyment of the bliss of Śiva’s Śakti by individual souls (jīvātman) or other persons, the status of Śiva’s Śakti as a devoted wife—denoted by the word *sādhvī*—would be compromised. Moreover, [one must consider] the sovereignty of Śiva’s vision, action, and bliss.

He who possesses that [power] preceded by such [characteristics] is to be understood here as the Lord (Īśvara). Giving (*dāna*) is established by scripture as being essentially knowledge and action through its own singular existence; likewise, because the liberated one possesses sovereignty like Śiva, [the power of giving] would otherwise be rendered useless, as it would follow that there would be no liberation. For in the world, one who enjoys the sovereignty of another without having enjoyed his own unimpaired sovereignty [is not truly free].

Furthermore, [otherwise] there would be the consequence of impermanence. Therefore, it is established that even if Śiva is distinct [from the soul], or even if he is non-distinct through pervasion (*vyāpti*), the cause for the liberated one’s experience of bliss is not the experience of Śiva’s bliss, but rather the experience of his own bliss. Now, an objection may be raised: "Since impurity (*mala*) and *māyā* [are present], how can the omnipresent Self (*vibhu-ātman*) remain untouched by them at the time of liberation while living (*jīva-mukti*)? If this is asked, the answer is no; because [those factors] have been rendered blunt and thus ineffective by the power of initiation (*dīkṣā*) which functions as knowledge, the power remains untouched by them. Thus, it should be understood that even by the tenth aphorism, the state of liberation while living is affirmed for the Self in its pure condition.

Now, with the eleventh aphorism, he states that although the Śiva-yogin is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and thus has no further duties to perform, he must nevertheless practice devotion to Śiva throughout his life, just as he practices devotion to the Guru and faith in the Āgamas.
The Self is the seer of the eye, and Śiva is the seer of that [Self];
therefore, one should direct the highest devotion toward Him, who is the benefactor of the Self.
Regarding the phrase "of the two eyes" (*dṛśoḥ*): the self (*ātman*) is the "seer" (*dṛk*) of the two eyes; this mention of the eyes is an illustration for all the sense organs.

Just as the self is the illuminator (*dīpaka*)—capable of making the invisible visible through the power of direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*)—so too is Śiva the "revealer" (*darśayitṛ*) of that self, manifesting the capacity for direct realization. Therefore, because he is thus the revealer, one should practice supreme devotion (*bhakti*) toward that Śiva, who is beneficial to the self. By the word "devotion," one should perform it as a continuous stream characterized by constant reflection (*manana*).

The meaning is that one should bring about a continuous stream of love (*premadhārā*). Although for a *jīvanmukta* Śiva-yogin, this stream of love arises spontaneously through his own natural devotion toward Śiva, it must nevertheless be understood that liberation is attained only by its cultivation. Thus, by means of the eleventh aphorism, it is made known that devotion to Śiva must be practiced.

Now, with the twelfth aphorism, he reveals that which is to be performed for the sake of attaining one's own self as one liberated while living (jīvanmukta): "For the sake of liberation, having approached the virtuous, one should resort to their abode, which is Śiva; thus one should know the determination of the meaning of Śaivism in the awakening of the knowledge of Śiva. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of liberation, having approached": the wise person, following the descent of grace (śaktipāta), having approached virtuous gurus, [should receive] initiation preceded by [the appropriate rites].

Having realized the ultimate truth, he should serve them by adopting their dress—the wearing of ashes and rudrākṣa beads, the cultivation of Śiva-gardens, the salutation of Śiva-devotees, the observance of the rules of conduct, and the frequenting of Śiva-temples and Śiva-sites—through the performance of garden maintenance, the sweeping of dust, the sprinkling of water, and the provision of garlands of flowers and other implements for worship.

Whether following the path of the servant, the path of the son, the path of the companion, or the path of the friend, he shall bring about the pleasure of Śiva through the ripening of the specific merit acquired by worshipping Śiva as a devotee in previous births.

One should produce delight from the very beginning. The sense is that, through the ripening of the specific merit acquired by worshipping Śiva in previous births, one should achieve the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)—consisting of knowledge, bliss, and narrative—from the very outset, even without the application of ritual action, conduct, or the components of sacrifice. It should be understood that by means of these four verses beginning with "sthitvā" and ending with "śivālayam," which describe the state of purity (*śuddhāvasthā*), the manifestation and recognition of grace (*anugraha*) has been clearly revealed. Now, [the meaning of] the second half of the twelfth aphorism:

He concludes the subject matter to be established in the *Śivajñānabodha* with the words, "one should know thus. In the *Śivajñānabodha*—that is, in that essence (*sāra*) which consists of the awakening (*bodha*) to the knowledge of Śiva (*śivajñāna*), namely the scripture of Śiva—one should understand, in the manner described above, the logical reasoning (*tarka*) that determines the definitions of the categories (*padārtha*) characterized as the Lord (*pati*), the individual soul (*paśu*), and the bonds (*pāśa*), which are the subjects expounded in the Śaiva scriptures. By virtue of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and purification, the qualified seeker established by the scripture shall attain all auspiciousness through the grace of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

The teacher Nigamajñāna, known as Sundara, has expounded this *Śivajñānabodhopanyāsa*. [Thus ends the *Śivajñānabodhopanyāsa* composed by Nigamajñānadeśika, a resident of Vyāghrapura, for the instruction of the simple-minded and for the pleasure of Saundaranātha. Salutations to the lotus feet of the venerable Guru. Salutations to the illustrious Abhrasabhāpati. May there be auspiciousness! Om.
One [form] drank the world-terrifying poison Kālakūṭa; the other drank more intensely the portion of poison for Pūtanā in the forest and the cow-pen.

One held the mountain Govardhana in his hand, uprooting the peaks of the mountains with the tips of his fingers; the other, they say, is the Lord of Viṣṇu, while the other is said to be the compassionate one who protects the universe.
Some say one is the son of Nigama (the Vedas), while they call the other the King of the Kurus (Arjuna). One is the sole protector of the women, while the other burnt the three Laṅkās.

But the other fought together with his companions; one [overcame] the enemy by the power of the nails of his lotus-feet, while the other [conquered] the foe with difficulty in battle. Among all the gods, including the Brahmins and the deities, they proclaim the supreme words of one; he who is the delight of the ears in this world, a holy ford for the Danavas and others. One was famous as the drinker of the seven oceans, while the other bound a portion of that very [ocean].

One protected the son of a sage by slaying Death with great effort; another protected the king of elephants by slaying a crocodile—who among them was superior? One is world-renowned as a man, a lover, a son, and a teacher; one is said to be the giver of the rows of fruits of those who have gone to the eternal state. One became a charioteer [of the Sun]; the other was of the nature of the sacrifice (*makha*), established in ten million fruits; and the other was the ancient destroyer in the act of universal dissolution.

"Who indeed was the charioteer [who guided] the body of Pratanu? Let the elders reflect upon this and speak the truth; we shall take refuge in him. (10) "What charioteer was there when that child, once devoured by a crocodile, did not go to the very presence of Death himself? If the Creator had fashioned a path with his own severed head, or if Viṣṇu were to descend as the agent to burn the one born from his body—then let those two, joined by His command, [act]. (11)

How is it fitting to describe you thus? You alone are the Lord of Beings (*janmāte-rathipati*); therefore, I worship you, O Auspicious One (*śiva*). Because you are the beloved of Gāyatrī, you are the father of the son of Daśaratha (Rāma) due to your status as the Lord of Chariots (*rathita*). Because you grant the desired progeny appropriate for the journey to Kailāsa, you are accompanied by your own eye along with the thousand lotuses [of Viṣṇu], and because you gave the discus to him (Viṣṇu), you are Paśupati. Furthermore, you are superior to the gods on the left (Śiva), because you are the destroyer of Kandarpa (Kāma).

Because he swallowed the poison-halberd, because he took away the necklace of black serpents, because he destroyed the triple city which was the dwelling place of the Daityas, because he conquered Dakṣa at the sacrifice and granted his own weapon to Śiva, because he defeated Indra, and because he brought about the instruction of the Teacher even within a woman’s body in the month of Mādhava— Paśupati is the most excellent of all the gods. ||2||

Because they are constantly worshipped by many people on earth with offerings of wealth, because they bestow the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*), and because they are honored by Keśava in his ten-fold form; because they bear the forms of the swan and the boar, and possess heads sought after by Brahmā and Viṣṇu; and because they are the source of prosperity (*śrī*) and are free from birth, destruction, and so forth—they are superior even to Paśupati and the other deities. (The arrangement of the enclosures: The first line consists of six parts, and the second is likewise.

The third [line] should consist of five parts; the fourth [should consist of] eight parts; the seventh should consist of three parts; the eighth should consist of six parts; the ninth should consist of six parts; and the tenth [should consist of] six parts—thus by the wise twice-born ones. Of these nine lines, all-knowing ones, the sun’s [measure] should be...; the moon’s is indeed one-sixteenth; that of Mars, however, is complete at thirty-two.

And this very [mandala] has thirty-eight squares for Jupiter, and for Saturn it is complete; Rāhu has exactly one-eighth, while Ketu, omitting six squares, follows the sequence of cleansing on all sides. This is the sequence of conjunction.
The first [syllable] should be joined with the sixth; likewise, the second with the ninth;
the third indeed with the seventh (vṛttaka); and one should place the fourth in the eighth.
The fifth is to be joined with the seventh, the sixth with the second,
the seventh with the *vṛttaka*, and the eighth should be placed in the first.

And the ninth [circle] is in the third [layer]; such is the sequence of the fetters (saṃyojana). Outside the [first] circle, there is a circle eleven finger-breadths wide, separated by an eight-petaled lotus; outside that, three concentric rings; outside that, a circle nine finger-breadths wide, in which is a sixteen-petaled lotus; and outside that, the earth-line (bhūrekhā) in the form of a square, provided with four gates.

One should fashion a circle of four finger-breadths in diameter according to one's desire by means of jewel-rings. [Thus ends the procedure for the construction of the Śrīcakra. May there be auspiciousness! In the two statements, "Hri and Lakṣmī are your two wives" and "Day and Night are your two sides," it is established that Śiva alone is the subject; Lakṣmī is Pārvatī, and Rudra’s status as her husband is thus maintained. And it is said: "The Gaṅgā fell with force upon the head of Rudra."

Overwhelmed by the transfer of that burden, she spoke to Sadāśiva: "O Bhava, being modest, do not remain here so high above me; [be near] the Supreme Person, the source of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the rest. Having bowed to Mahādeva, from that time forward, out of devotion, she merged into his matted locks with modesty (*hrī*); thus she is called *Hrī* by the wise.

In the Rudrayāmala, the supreme power of Maheśvara, known as Mahālakṣmī, who has taken root in her water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), is dark-complexioned and enchanting to all. Of her... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

In former times, millions of Lakṣmīs and Vāks were born from the multitude of [Śiva’s] powers (*jagaṇa*); millions of Haris, Brahmās, and others were produced from the splendor of Śiva. These, following their respective dissolutions, are given forth once again here and there. Therefore, it is not contradictory that the status of being the Lord of Gaṅgā and Lakṣmī is unique [to him]. Nara is Brahmā; he was created as the first living being because everything has been born [from him], and thus it is well known that the creation is his work. Rudra is primarily characterized by the quality of *rajas*; those beginning with him...

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and so forth are the inhabitants of the fourteen worlds; their collection is *nāra*. That which has this as its extended abode (*āyatam sthānam*), being the Supreme Lord who pervades all in the form of the Self—He who is the abundance of the atom (*aṇubhūmā*) devoted to the Ṛks—when the suffix *ṇa* is applied to that which has not [yet] attained it, the form *Nārāyaṇa* is produced. All the gods are indeed His portions. This is known from such scriptural authorities as "Obeisance to the Rudras," "May they be gracious unto us," and "Obeisance to the Eldest and to the Youngest."

In the chapter on the state beyond the qualities (*guṇātītavṛtti*), the Lord said: [He who is] devoted [to Me]... attains union (*sāyujya*)... among My attendants (*madgaṇa*)... Therein, the form of union is considered to be either that which is directly achieved through the means (*sādhana*)... or that which consists of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)... or the eternally established (*nityasiddha*) form. But the eternally established form is the supreme one, which is the nature of the Self for all.

Liberation is indeed the very nature of the Self; since it is eternally attained, it is designated as "attained. However, the state of delusion is established [as being removed] through the destruction of ignorance. The cessation of ignorance occurs through knowledge alone, and not otherwise. Since the destruction of ignorance is well-known, supreme liberation is nothing other than that. Liberation would be either something to be attained by the Self or not to be attained by the Self. If liberation were to be attained by the Self, then having attained it, it would be nothing other than the Self itself.

The attainment of what is to be attained by this [agent] is either a relation or indeed identity. If it is a relation, is it something to be established (*sādhya*) or eternal? If it is to be established, then let it be so; however, if it were related and eternal, [it would be problematic]. Even if it is to be established, it must be determined as either a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a negative one (*abhāva*). For positive entities that are to be established, impermanence is established. But for that which is called destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), there can never be the status of being something to be established. If, however, the property called "being to be established" exists, it could not have non-existence as its locus; it would have to have a positive entity as its substratum.

O best of the Vṛṣas, there is indeed no such thing as an eternal entity; for if it were eternal and possessed of a relation, it would be designated by that very relation. Furthermore, if liberation were already eternally established for the self seeking release, then liberation—being eternally attained—would be like [something already in hand]. O bull, liberation is now declared by you to be achieved through knowledge alone and nothing else. However, if liberation were of the nature of attaining what was previously unattained, consisting in oneness [with Brahman], that is not tenable; for the oneness of two distinct things can never be established, except through the destruction of their difference.

Or is liberation [attained] when difference remains, or rather when that difference is destroyed? Listen, O observer of vows, as to how their unity is possible: if it is argued that unity exists while difference persists, that is not tenable. For liberation, which is unattainable [otherwise], would then exist as something already attained by the one-eyed one [the individual soul]. If that liberation were already established, it would be useless even if a means were employed; for if it is considered eternally established, it cannot be something to be accomplished. If it were something to be accomplished, its impermanence has already been stated previously. Why then is its permanence not like that of cessation (*pradhvaṃsa*)?

It might be [argued that] destruction is intended as a specific [kind of entity]. Furthermore, the eternality of destruction will not exist in any way whatsoever. For that which is non-material (acidrūpa) is understood in every respect as being of the nature of non-existence; thus, its state of being a probandum is [established]. But if it were [claimed] to be of the nature of existence, then by the reason of its being an existing thing, destruction would not be established. If that were so, it would certainly not be well-founded. Even though there is an absence of the probandum-nature of prior non-existence...

Even for the destruction of an existent (*bhāva-pradhvaṃsa*), which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and is of the nature of an existent (*bhāva-rūpa*), [the cause] is eternal; however, among non-existents (*abhāva*), even though they are eternal, [this does not apply].

For those [non-existents], being unaccomplishable (*asādhya*), eternality is not the determining factor. Rather, it is [their] insentience (*acetanatva*) that is the cause. But regarding the sentient one, the eternal scripture declares his eternality. Even though he is formless, he possesses form. He is attainable through knowledge, not attainable through mere action, nor through a combination [of both]; knowledge is not...

(... and this entire form of mine (... action, however, depends upon an agent and is always distinct; here, because of the very contradiction between action and knowledge, a conjunction is never appropriate. What is the way out? That which is called "identity of form" (sārūpya), that which is called "nearness" (sāmīpya), and that which is called "residing in the same world" (sālokya)—of these, only the means of action (karmasādhana) (...)
